descs.en: A blind date. He arrived in a three-piece suit. She came straight from a crash site with dirt on her face. He tried to manage her. She laughed at him.

synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
Ren Hao fixes problems for big companies: kidnappings, scandals, the things that never make the news. He's loud, direct and used to being obeyed, and he says I love you to everyone, including the woman who runs the dumpling shop.

Xu Song-Zhu rebuilds what happened from the wreckage. Flight recorders, scorched memory boards, the last minutes of strangers. His sister sets them up at a French restaurant with candles. He orders her water and tells her to wash her face. She laughs, and tells him he's awfully bossy for a man who hasn't asked her name.

He loves her out loud from the first week. She can't say it back. And then a passenger jet goes into the sea with a hundred and eighty people on board, on his client's airline, and the woman he loves is the one who has to listen to how it ended.

Opposites · Loud hero · She can't say it · He has to learn to ask · Complete in 40 chapters, side stories to come

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
This one is loud and quick and joyful, and then, when it has to be, very quiet. Her job is listening to people's last words, and the book doesn't look away from what that costs her, or from the families who wait for them.

He tries to love her the way he protects clients, with drivers and schedules and a full fridge. She needs room, and the time to find three words she's been afraid of since she was nineteen. Watching a man like that learn to ask first, and a woman like that learn to say it, is the whole of it.

contentWarn.title: Content Warning
contentWarn.content:
21+ · For adult readers.

Loud, funny and romantic, with air accident investigation shown plainly. It includes:

• Love scenes on the page throughout

• A parent's death in an air crash, and grief years later

• Air crashes: wreckage and bodies on the water, recovery, identification, and the families who wait

• Cockpit and cabin recordings of the last moments of a flight

• A funeral, and a child who has lost a parent

• Workplace betrayal, and a relationship placed under public scrutiny

• Controlling behaviour within a loving relationship: tracking, arranging, moving in without asking, and the work of unlearning it

chapters.title: Three-Piece Suit, Flight Suit
chapters.desc: Isla sets her brother up on a blind date. Ren Hao (27) arrives in a three-piece suit with a typed agenda; Xu Song-Zhu (25, crash investigator) arrives from a light-aircraft site with fuel on her boots. He tells her to wash her face. At the taxi rank she kisses him to shut him up.
chapters.epigraph: “Did you just tell me to go and wash my face?”
chapters.content:
At three minutes past seven on Friday the thirteenth of June, 2025, Ren Hao received a message from his younger sister.

Isla (Matchmaker): She’s running late. Don’t leave.

He looked at his watch. Then at the empty chair across the table. Then at his watch again.

Ren Hao: Define late.

Isla (Matchmaker): Hao.

Ren Hao: It’s a reasonable question.

Isla (Matchmaker): She’s coming from work.

Ren Hao: You said seven.

Isla (Matchmaker): And I said she’s coming from work. Those are two different sentences.

He was twenty-seven years old. He ran a risk consultancy that occupied three floors of a tower in the business district, and he had sat across tables from men who kept armed guards in their kitchens. And his sister, who was two years younger and still owed him a laptop charger from 2019, remained the only person alive who could make him feel he was losing an argument before it had started.

He put the phone face up beside his plate, where he could see it.

The restaurant was French, expensive and quiet enough to talk in without raising your voice. There were candles on every table, in small glass cups, and white linen, and a waiter who moved as if the floor might be listening. Ren Hao had reserved the table by the window three days earlier. He had checked the menu, asked for the quieter end of the room, and passed on the one thing Isla had told him about her friend’s food: no coriander, ever, under any circumstances.

He had also prepared an agenda. It was folded in the inside pocket of his jacket, one page, typed. Not because he was excited about a blind date. He simply disliked walking into a room without knowing what it was for.

1. Introductions. Her work (air accident investigation: ask what that involves).
2. Isla: how they met.
3. Food. Wine (ask first).
4. Mutual interests, if any.
5. Second meeting: yes / no / to be confirmed.

At six minutes past, he adjusted his cufflinks. At eight minutes past, he checked the phone. At eleven minutes past, the manager came over.

“Mr. Ren. Shall we bring your guest’s water?”

“Please. Still.”

“And would you like to begin with something while you wait?”

“No. We’ll wait.”

The phone lit again.

Isla (Matchmaker): She’s definitely coming.

Ren Hao: That’s reassuring.

Isla (Matchmaker): Don’t be difficult. Practise being pleasant.

Ren Hao: I’m sitting here by myself being extremely pleasant.

Isla (Matchmaker): Practise harder.

He was beginning to suspect that his sister had arranged the evening as a punishment, which was unfair, because he had done nothing to deserve one lately. Nothing she could prove.

✦ ✦ ✦

Xu Song-Zhu had aviation fuel on her boots. There was also a streak of dried mud along her left cheekbone that she didn’t know about, a small tear at the knee of her flight suit, and a bruise coming up purple above her right wrist where a wing strut had caught it.

She had spent six hours in a soybean field forty minutes north of the city, beside a single-engine four-seater that had lost power on climb-out and been put down by its pilot, quite beautifully, between two rows of irrigation pipe. The pilot was alive. He had a broken ankle and two cracked ribs and he had cried when she told him the nose gear had done exactly what it was designed to do. She had photographed the wreck from every side, walked the ground marks from first contact to final rest, drained a sample from each fuel tank into a clean glass jar and held it up to the light, and listened for forty minutes to a farmer describe the final approach with his hands, which by the end were describing a different aircraft entirely.

By the time she was released from the scene, she had forgotten that she was meant to be having dinner with a stranger. Her phone rang as she reached the car.

“Where are you?”

“Leaving.”

“You’re supposed to be at the restaurant,” said Isla.

“I’m aware of that.”

“Song-Zhu.”

“Isla.”

A short, dangerous silence.

“Please don’t tell me you’re still at the crash site.”

“I’m not at the crash site.”

“Good.”

“I’m in the car park of the crash site.”

“That’s the same place!”

Song-Zhu laughed, and threw her bag onto the passenger seat, and looked down at herself. The flight suit was unzipped to the waist with the arms tied round it, over a black T-shirt that had been clean at five that morning. Her ponytail had given up at about noon. It was a little after seven.

“Does your brother know I’m coming from work?”

“Yes.”

“Does he know what I do?”

“Yes.”

“Then we’re all adults. He can survive a flight suit.”

“Please, for the love of God, just go to dinner.”

“I’m going.”

“And Song-Zhu?”

“Hm?”

“Don’t frighten him.”

Song-Zhu grinned at the windscreen. “No promises.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Ren Hao knew something had gone wrong with the evening when the manager crossed the room towards him for the third time with an expression of careful neutrality.

“Sir. Your guest is here.”

He looked up. The woman standing beside the manager looked. She wore a dark blue flight suit with the top half tied round her waist like a jumper, and a black T-shirt, and work boots that had been somewhere wet and agricultural. Her hair was escaping from its tie. A canvas bag hung off one shoulder. There was a dark smear on her cheek.

And she was looking straight at him. Not apologetic, not even embarrassed. Mildly curious, the way someone might look at an interesting component.

He stood. “You must be Isla’s friend.”

“I must be.” Her voice was brighter than he’d expected, and quicker. “There was an accident.”

“I gathered.”

“Good. Saves me explaining.” She looked at the chair he’d pulled out for her, then at him. “Thank you.”

She dropped the bag beside the table and sat. He waited until she had settled before he took his own seat, and saw her notice that, too.

“Nice place,” she said, looking round at the candles.

“Thank you.”

“Very French.”

“It’s a French restaurant.”

“I can tell. The water glasses are judging me.” She picked up the menu. “Do you come here a lot?”

“Occasionally. For clients.”

“Must be nice.”

The way she said it wasn’t polite. There was something a little wicked in it.

He folded his hands on the table. “I’ve ordered you still water.”

“Have you.”

“And I’ve let them know about the coriander.”

That made her look up. “Isla told you about the coriander?”

“It was the only thing she told me.”

“That’s not true. She told you I’m difficult.”

“She said you were very good at your job and very bad at arriving.”

“That’s fair.” She closed the menu. “So. What happens now? Is there a format?”

He hesitated for slightly too long, and she saw it.

“Oh, there’s a format,” she said, delighted. “What is it?”

“There isn’t a format.”

“There’s something in your jacket. You keep touching it.”

He took his hand away from his pocket. “It’s a list.”

“A list.”

“A short one. I like to know what a meeting is for.”

“This isn’t a meeting, it’s a date.” She leaned her elbows on the white tablecloth, which made the waiter twitch from across the room. “Read it to me.”

“No.”

“Then I’ll guess. One: introductions.”

He said nothing.

“Two: ask her what she does. Three: wine. Four: is there a second date, tick box.” She watched his face, and her own lit up. “I got it. I got all of it.”

“You got four out of five.”

“What’s the fifth?”

“How you met Isla.”

“November. A freight crew from overseas, both killed on a night approach. Your sister handled the families for the consulate, and I briefed them on what we knew, which was nothing yet, and afterwards she found me crying in the stairwell and gave me half a cereal bar and her number.” Song-Zhu sat back. “Done. You can cross it off.”

He looked at her. Then he took the folded page out of his pocket, unfolded it, took out his pen, and drew a neat line through item two.

She stared at him, and then she laughed out loud, a real laugh with her whole body in it, so that two people at the next table turned round.

“You actually crossed it off.”

“It’s been covered.”

“Oh, I like you,” she said. “That’s going to be a problem.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The first course was a chilled leek and potato soup, which neither of them had ordered and which the kitchen sent out with the compliments of the chef. Ren Hao tasted it, put his spoon down, and lifted one finger to the waiter.

“I’m sorry. This has gone cold.”

The waiter looked at the soup and then, for help, at Song-Zhu.

“It’s meant to be cold,” she said.

“It’s leek and potato soup.”

“It’s vichyssoise. It’s always cold. It’s cold on purpose. That’s the entire point of it.”

He looked at the bowl. The waiter looked at the ceiling.

“Take mine away anyway,” said Ren Hao, with dignity, and Song-Zhu put her face in her napkin, and when the waiter had gone she was still laughing.

“You sent back a cold soup for being cold.”

“I made an assessment based on the information available.”

“Is that what you say at work? When you’ve got it wrong?”

“I don’t often get it wrong.”

“You just did. In a French restaurant. With candles.” She pulled his bowl, before it could be collected, across to her side and ate it herself.

By the main course he had learned that she disliked people who talked too loudly in restaurants, loved convenience-store coffee with an intensity bordering on the religious, and had once slept for nine hours across four chairs in an airport in a country she refused to name. She had learned that he ran a corporate risk consultancy, that his sister worked in consular affairs and his parents taught at a university in Vancouver, and that he had an inexplicable fondness for schedules.

“Schedules are useful,” he said.

“They’re boring.”

“They prevent unnecessary complications.”

“Not every complication is unnecessary.”

He looked at her. She was cutting into her fish with great concentration. He decided not to argue.

“What do you actually do?” he said. “At a crash.”

She swallowed, and for a moment the brightness went somewhere quieter.

“Today? I walked the ground. Where it touched first, where it slid, where it stopped. Fuel samples from both tanks. Photographs of everything before anyone moves anything. Then I listened to a farmer tell me it was upside down, which it wasn’t, and a fireman tell me it was on fire, which it wasn’t either.” She shrugged. “People are very bad at describing the last ten seconds before something goes wrong. It’s not their fault. Fear rewrites things.”

“And on other days?”

“On other days there’s a recorder, and I listen to that instead.” She turned her glass on the cloth. “People think we’re there to find someone to blame. We’re not. We’re not even allowed to. We’re there to find out what happened, and why, so it doesn’t happen again. Sometimes that’s obvious in an hour. Sometimes it takes a year. Sometimes you’ve got every piece on the floor in front of you and it still won’t tell you anything.”

“Do you enjoy it?”

She thought about it properly, which he hadn’t expected.

“Enjoy is a strange word for it. Sometimes you spend three days trying to understand why a piece of machinery stopped working. And then you remember there was a person in it. Somebody’s husband. Somebody’s daughter. Somebody who was meant to be home for dinner.” She looked at her plate. “Today the somebody’s home for dinner. He’ll have a cast for six weeks. That’s a good day.”

The candle between them moved in the air from the kitchen door.

“Do you ever get used to it?” he said.

“No.” She looked up. “If I ever get used to it, I should stop doing it.”

He held her gaze for a second. Then he nodded, once. Then he looked at her left cheek.

“There’s something on your face.”

“Where?”

“Left cheek.”

She rubbed her right cheek.

“Other side.”

She rubbed her forehead.

“You’re making it worse,” he said, entirely seriously. “There’s a washroom by the bar. You might want to wash your face.”

Song-Zhu went still.

“Ren Hao.”

“Yes.”

“Did you just tell me to go and wash my face?”

“I’m suggesting that—”

“In a French restaurant.”

“There’s quite a noticeable—”

She laughed so loudly that the waiter dropped a spoon. It wasn’t a restaurant laugh. It wasn’t the kind of laugh people produce in rooms with candles to show they are having a nice time. It came straight up from somewhere under her ribs and she had to put her hand over her mouth to stop it, and couldn’t.

“Oh, you’re serious,” she managed.

“I don’t see what’s funny.”

“Nothing. Nothing’s funny. You’re very sweet.” She took a breath, and looked at him across the candle, still shaking. “You’ve ordered my water, and told the kitchen what I don’t eat, and made a list of what to ask me, and sent back the soup, and now you’re sending me to wash my face. You’re awfully bossy for a man who hasn’t asked my name.”

He opened his mouth to say that he knew her name, and realised that he had called her Isla’s friend, and nothing else, for an hour and ten minutes.

She watched him realise it. Then she leaned in, close enough that he could smell fuel and grass and something like oranges under it.

“Is this how you talk to terrorists,” she said, “or are you just nervous around girls?”

For the first time that evening, Ren Hao was caught entirely off guard. She saw it land. And then, against what was clearly his own will, his mouth moved: a small, unwilling, startled smile.

“Neither,” he said.

“Really.”

“Really. And I don’t talk to terrorists. I talk to their accountants.” He held out his hand across the table, formally. “Ren Hao.”

She looked at the hand. Then she shook it, firmly, with mud still under her thumbnail. “Xu Song-Zhu.”

“Song-Zhu.”

“That’s the one.”

He went to the washroom himself before dessert came, and came back with a wet linen napkin, and held it out to her without a word. She looked at it for a long second. Then she took it, and wiped her cheek, and he said, “Left,” and she gave him a look of pure murder and did the left.

✦ ✦ ✦

By twenty-five past nine Ren Hao had decided the evening had gone considerably better than he’d feared. By half past he had revised that.

By twenty-five to ten Xu Song-Zhu was standing on the pavement outside the restaurant, arguing with him about whether she needed a taxi.

“I can get one myself.”

“I know you can.”

“Then why are you arranging it?”

“Because it’s late.”

“It’s not late. It’s twenty to ten.”

“Your car is at the crash site.”

“I was driven back from the crash site. Somebody will drive me back to the crash site tomorrow. Crash sites are very well served.”

He held up his phone. “It’s already booked.”

“Ren Hao. I’m twenty-five.”

“I didn’t say you weren’t.”

“And I can get home by myself.”

“I never suggested otherwise.”

“Then stop looking at me as if I’m about to walk into the traffic.”

“I’m not looking at you like that.”

“You absolutely are.” She tipped her head and studied him. He wasn’t rude. He wasn’t arrogant in the usual way men with that kind of suit were arrogant. He simply seemed to have an almost medical need to make sure everything around him was working properly. A crooked picture frame probably kept him awake. She wondered, idly, what would happen if somebody hung it upside down on purpose.

“Fine,” she said.

He looked relieved. “Thank you.”

He went back to his phone to check the car’s progress. She watched him. Dark hair cut by somebody expensive. The suit fitted him perfectly, the waistcoat buttoned all the way down beneath the jacket, the cuffs exactly where cuffs were supposed to be. Even the tie looked. He looked like a man who would send a calendar invitation before asking someone to dinner.

She found that, for some reason, unbearably funny. A black car pulled into the rank. He stepped forward and opened the rear door.

“That’s yours.”

She didn’t get in. She stood in front of him and looked up at his face, which was a fair way up.

“Ren Hao.”

“Yes?”

“Do you think I’m difficult?”

He considered the question, much too seriously. “I think you’re unpredictable.”

“That’s a diplomatic answer.”

“I wasn’t trying to be diplomatic.”

“Then what were you trying to be?”

“Accurate.”

Her eyes went, for half a second, to his mouth.

He saw it. He had just enough time to register what her face was doing before she stepped in.

“One more thing,” she said.

“What?”

“You’ve been talking too much.”

And before he could ask what she meant, she took a fistful of his waistcoat and pulled him down and kissed him.

Hard. No warning, no polite little pause beforehand to see whether he minded. One moment Ren Hao was standing by an open car door with a phone in his hand, wondering whether it would be acceptable to ask her to message him when she got in. The next, Xu Song-Zhu had him by the waistcoat at a taxi rank in the business district and was kissing him as if she’d made the decision an hour ago and had only been waiting for a convenient moment to carry it out.

For a fraction of a second his free hand hovered somewhere near her waist. Then he put it there.

His other hand came up to her face, and his thumb found her cheek, carefully, on the side where the mud had been, and he kissed her back. Not politely. Her fist tightened in his waistcoat. She tasted of the chocolate from dessert and something that was just her, and when she bit his lower lip, lightly, he made a sound he hadn’t made in a public place in his adult life.

When she let go, she was smiling. He didn’t move. His tie had gone sideways. One waistcoat button had come undone and he hadn’t felt it go. For possibly the first time since he was nine years old, Ren Hao had no idea at all what to say.

“Good night, Mr. Ren,” she said.

He blinked. “That’s it?”

“What else would you like?”

His hand was still on her waist. It tightened, slightly. “An explanation would be nice.”

“Of what?”

“That.”

She glanced at his mouth again, and back up. “Think of it as a review.”

“A review.”

“Of the evening.”

“And?”

She pretended to think about it. “Not bad.”

“Not bad.”

“Room for improvement.”

“Where?”

She smiled up at him, and it was the wicked smile from the table. “Stop telling women to wash their faces.”

He laughed. It came out of him before he could stop it, short and genuinely surprised, the first unguarded sound she’d had from him all night. She liked it more than she’d meant to. In the car, the driver cleared his throat.

She stepped back, and he let go of her waist slowly.

“Good night, Ren Hao.”

“Good night.”

She got in. Then, just before the door closed, she leaned back out.

“Oh, and Hao?”

Nobody called him that except his family. He looked at her.

“Don’t make a list about me.”

The door shut. The car pulled away into the traffic, and he stood on the pavement and watched its tail lights until they were gone.

Then he looked down at himself. His tie was crooked. His waistcoat was undone by one button. His phone was still in his hand, open on the taxi app, showing her car moving away from him at forty kilometres an hour. He touched his lower lip.

Then he straightened his tie, and did up the button, and stood there a while longer anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just before midnight, Song-Zhu was sitting cross-legged on her bed with her hair wet, eating instant noodles out of the pan.

Isla (Matchmaker): ALIVE??

Song-Zhu: Unfortunately.

Isla (Matchmaker): HOW WAS IT

Song-Zhu: Your brother is strange.

Isla (Matchmaker): Oh no.

Song-Zhu: He told me to wash my face.

Isla (Matchmaker): HAHAHAHAHAHAHA

Isla (Matchmaker): I KNEW IT. I KNEW HE WOULD

Isla (Matchmaker): did he have a list

Song-Zhu: He had a list.

Isla (Matchmaker): of course he had a list. And?

Song-Zhu looked at the screen. She thought about the moment at the taxi rank when his hand had hovered and then decided. About the little crease between his eyebrows when he was trying to work something out. About the way he had said Song-Zhu, once.

Song-Zhu: He’s quite handsome.

Isla (Matchmaker): I KNOW

Song-Zhu: Very annoying, though.

Isla (Matchmaker): ALSO KNOW

Song-Zhu: I kissed him.

Three dots appeared. Disappeared. Appeared again.

Isla (Matchmaker): YOU WHAT

Isla (Matchmaker): WHERE

Song-Zhu: Taxi rank.

Isla (Matchmaker): I’m going to be sick. I’m so happy. Inspector Song is looking at me like I’ve been shot

Song-Zhu: Tell the inspector good night.

She dropped the phone on the duvet, and finished her noodles, and found that she was smiling at the wall.

✦ ✦ ✦

A little after midnight, across the city, Ren Hao sat at his desk with his jacket over the back of the chair and his waistcoat on the bed and his tie somewhere in the bathroom, and wrote an email.

He had her address. Isla had sent it in March, along with a photograph of the two of them at a dumpling place and the message you would like her, she would hate you, try anyway. He read his draft three times before he sent it.

To: Xu Song-Zhu
Subject: Dinner, Friday 13 June: minutes
Present: Ren Hao, Xu Song-Zhu.
1. Introductions. Completed, eventually. Apologies for the delay on my side.
2. Item two covered by Ms. Xu without prompting.
3. Soup. Ms. Xu correct. Noted for the record.
4. Washroom. Withdrawn, with apologies.
5. Review (taxi rank). Received. Room for improvement accepted.
6. Any other business: I would like another opportunity.
Ren Hao

He looked at it a long time after it had gone. It was, he thought, possibly the most ridiculous thing he had ever written. He didn’t regret it in the slightest.

He had come to a blind date with a typed agenda, a three-piece suit and a clear idea of how the evening was going to go. He had left with a crooked tie, an undone button, a soup he had been wrong about, and the distinct suspicion that he was going to see this woman again. He was right.

He just didn’t know yet how thoroughly she was about to rearrange his life.

chapters.title: Follow-Up
chapters.desc: She answers his midnight minutes with a voice note from a field. A twin turboprop on its back, two people on board; she pulls the recorder from the tail. He turns up at the hangar fence with lunch for twelve.
chapters.epigraph: “She’s not my friend. She’s a menace.”
chapters.content:
At seventeen minutes past eight on Saturday morning, a voice note arrived on Ren Hao’s phone from a number he didn’t have.

He was in his office on the top of his three floors, alone except for the cleaners, halfway through an exposure report on a shipping client with a habit of sailing through places it shouldn’t. He knew who it was before he opened it. Nobody else he knew would answer a midnight email with a voice note. Forty-three seconds. He pressed play.

A low mechanical roar filled the office, and then a clank, and somebody a long way off shouting about a trolley, and then her.

“Good morning, Mr. Ren.”

The roar dipped. An engine somewhere, being run up.

“Before you start: yes, I’ve eaten breakfast. Yes, I’ve washed my face. Both sides. I took your very important advice about personal hygiene extremely seriously.” A pause, in which he could hear her smiling. “I have a question, though. Is it rude to answer an email with a voice note? Because you sent me minutes, Hao. With numbered items. And I thought this would be more fun than replying properly.”

He looked at the email in his sent folder. 12.14 a.m. Subject: Dinner, Friday 13 June: minutes. He had thought, at the time, that it was charming. In daylight it looked like something a lawyer would send. He pressed play again.

“Anyway. I’m at an airfield up north. We’ve got a twin down in a field beside the perimeter.” Her voice changed. It didn’t drop or go dramatic. It simply went quieter, as though she had stepped into a smaller room. “Two on board. Neither of them made it. I’m waiting for the photographer to finish before anyone touches anything. There’s something I want to check in the tail.”

The engine noise again. A metallic clang.

“Sorry. I should go.” A breath. “Item six. Any other business. Next time I’m choosing the restaurant. I’ll tell you when I’ve got an evening.” And then, with the smile back: “Try not to schedule me, Hao. Bye.”

The recording ended. He sat still, and then played it a third time. Not for the accident. He had heard enough to understand that her work wasn’t something she talked about lightly, and he wasn’t going to treat two deaths in a field as an anecdote. It was the last part.

Try not to schedule me.

He saved the number. He typed her name, and then, after a moment’s thought, added something in brackets, and looked at it, and left it. Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots)

His phone rang. Joyce, his assistant, who didn’t believe in weekends for anybody else.

“Good morning, Mr. Ren. The board call’s been moved from ten to eleven, and finance would like to know if you’re coming to lunch.”

“Cancel lunch.”

A short pause. “Cancel your lunch, or cancel the lunch?”

“Mine. Send them my apologies.”

“Shall I book you somewhere else?”

He looked at the phone in his other hand. “No. I’ll sort out lunch myself.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At a quarter to nine, Xu Song-Zhu was standing in a field of wet grass two hundred metres from the end of a runway, looking at what was left of a twin-engine turboprop.

It had come in low on a charter from the coast, a businessman and his pilot, and it had touched the top of a line of trees short of the threshold and cartwheeled. The left wing had folded back along the fuselage at an angle that made the whole thing look. The nose had gone into the soft ground up to the windscreen. Police tape ran round it on stakes. The fire crew had gone. The two bodies had been taken away at dawn, after she’d seen them, after the photographer had seen them, after everything had been written down in the order it had been found.

She pulled her gloves tighter.

“Photographs complete?”

“All done,” said Dexter. He was two years senior to her and had a clipboard for every occasion. “Overview, ground marks, both wings, the engines, the cabin.”

“Positions?”

“Marked and measured.”

“Anything moved before we got here?”

“The fire crew cut the right cabin door to reach the passenger. Everything else is as found.”

“Write that down on its own line, with the time they gave you. I don’t want anyone in six months thinking the door came off on impact.”

He wrote it down. “Tail’s clear. The panel’s intact.”

“Then let’s go.”

They walked round to the back of the aircraft along the plank path the police had put down, so nobody would tread on anything that mattered. The tail had come through better than the rest. On a type this size the cockpit voice recorder sat in the tail cone, behind a small access panel, a bright orange box the size of a shoebox with FLIGHT RECORDER DO NOT OPEN stencilled on its side in two languages, because the one thing that was never actually black about a black box was the box.

Song-Zhu crouched by the panel and didn’t touch it.

Photographs first. The panel closed. Then the panel open, the recorder in its tray, the connectors still attached. The identification plate, close enough to read the serial. Then measurements. Then, and only then, her hands.

The recorder wasn’t magic. People always talked about it. It couldn’t tell you what anyone had intended. It couldn’t tell you what had broken. It certainly couldn’t tell you what the two men inside had been thinking in the last thirty seconds, while the trees came up. What it could give you was sound: voices, switches, alarms, the engines, the wind on the airframe, the noise a propeller makes when it starts to go wrong. And sound, put alongside the wreck and the maintenance logs and the radar and the weather and the farmer with his hands, could sometimes tell you a great deal.

She released the connectors one at a time, slowly, while Dexter photographed each one. Then she lifted the unit out, heavier than it looked, and held it in both hands for a second the way she always did, not superstitiously, she would have said, but because there were two people’s last minutes in it and it seemed rude to just put it in a bag.

“Seal.”

He held out the evidence bag. She put the recorder in and sealed it and signed across the seal, and he signed under her, and wrote the time.

“Chain of custody,” she said. “It stays with me until the lab has it in their hands. Nobody plugs anything into it. Nobody opens it to have a look. If a journalist asks, we’ve recovered the aircraft’s recorders and they’ll be examined in due course.”

“Recorders, plural?”

“It hasn’t got a data recorder. It’s not required to have one. But they don’t need to know that today.”

Dexter grinned. “Long day?”

“Looks like it.” She stood up, and her knees cracked. “And if you’re about to ask about my date, I’ll put you in the bag with the recorder.”

“I wasn’t going to ask.”

“Who told you?”

“Your friend Isla rang the duty phone at ten past seven last night to ask if you’d left the site yet.”

“She’s not my friend. She’s a menace.” Song-Zhu peeled off one glove and looked at her phone. There was a new email. Ren Hao. She opened it standing in the wet grass.

Good morning, Song-Zhu.
Thank you for your message. I’m sorry about the two people on board. I hope the work goes safely.
Understood on dinner. I’ll leave the arrangements to you, as requested.
One question: do you prefer Song-Zhu, or Zhu?

She looked at it. Then she smiled at the screen in a way that made Dexter look at her and then carefully look away. She typed with one thumb.

Song-Zhu: Song-Zhu. Zhu sounds like you’re calling me in for a disciplinary.

And then, a second later:

Song-Zhu: Don’t worry. I’m very hard to discipline.

She put the phone in her chest pocket and the glove back on, and went back to work.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just before twelve, Ren Hao was standing outside a chain-link fence at the edge of a small airfield with lunch for twelve.

He hadn’t set out to bring lunch for twelve. That was an important distinction, and he intended to make it to anyone who asked.

At a quarter past nine he had rung a restaurant he trusted and ordered a few meals. At nine thirty-two she had replied to his email. At nine forty-six he had sent her a message asking whether she had had lunch. At nine forty-seven she had sent him a photograph of an empty paper coffee cup on the bonnet of a car.

Ren Hao: Is that meant to be an answer?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): 👍

He had looked at the thumbs-up for some time. At nine fifty-one he had made a decision. He had rung the restaurant again and asked how many people normally worked at an air accident site on a Saturday, and the restaurant had said they had no idea, and he had said, then make it twelve.

At eleven fifty-two that decision had him standing by a delivery van in a pale blue shirt with the sleeves rolled to the elbow, and dark trousers, and a watch that had cost more than the van.

The driver was looking at him. “You sure this is the place, sir?”

“Yes.”

“All twelve?”

“Yes.”

“You work here?”

“No.”

The driver looked at the food, and at him, and at the fence. “Right.”

Beyond the fence was a flying club: a squat hangar with its doors half open, a windsock, a row of small aircraft tied down on the grass, and, past them, at the far end of the runway, a white tent and blue tape in a field. Two police cars. A truck with a crane. In front of the hangar, at a long table, a handful of people in dark overalls were bent over laptops and paper.

He saw her straight away. Dark blue flight suit again, zipped to the collar this time, hair pulled up off her neck, a clipboard against her hip. She was talking to a man at the end of the table. Even from the fence he recognised the way she moved: quickly.

He found that he was smiling. He rang her.

On the other side of the fence, Song-Zhu glanced down at her chest pocket, frowned, and answered.

“Hello?”

“Good afternoon.”

She looked at her watch. “It’s eleven fifty-three.”

“Good nearly afternoon.”

“Hm.” He could hear the table, the laptops, a radio. “Are you busy?” she said.

“Are you?”

She looked at the clipboard, and at the two colleagues waiting for her, and at the sealed bag on the table in front of her that had two men’s voices in it. “Not at all. I’m on holiday.”

He laughed, and she smiled at the sound before she could help it.

“That’s unfortunate,” he said. “I’m outside.”

“Outside where?”

“The fence. By the gate with the sign about dogs.”

She turned round slowly. Across fifty metres of tarmac and grass, on the other side of the chain-link, there was a man in a pale blue shirt standing beside a van with a great many paper bags.

“Ren Hao.”

“Yes.”

“What are you doing?”

“I brought lunch.”

“How much lunch?”

A pause. “Twelve.”

She shut her eyes. “Why twelve?”

“I didn’t know how many of you there would be.”

“So you bought lunch for twelve people. Without asking me.”

“It seemed simpler.”

She laughed. Not politely. Dexter, at the table, looked up from his photographs to see what had happened.

“You’re unbelievable,” she said into the phone.

“Is that a yes?”

“That is a very expensive way of finding out whether I’m hungry.”

“Are you?”

She looked at the empty cup on the table by her elbow, and at the time on her phone, and at the bag with the recorder in it, and thought about the fact that she had last eaten something at five that morning in a petrol station.

“Yes,” she said.

“Good. Come out.”

She ended the call. Dexter was watching her.

“Who was that?”

She looked at the fence. “A problem.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She came through the gate in the fence and stopped three metres away from him and looked at the bags, and at him, and at the bags again.

“Hello,” he said.

She pointed at the bags. “Is that really twelve?”

“Yes.”

“You came all the way up here.”

“Yes.”

“On a Saturday. In that shirt. To bring me lunch.”

“To bring lunch to whoever’s working with you.” He held one bag out separately. “And this one’s yours.”

She looked inside. A box of rice and chicken and greens. A separate box of cut fruit. A bottle of water. And tucked between them, flat and neat, a small packet of wet wipes.

She lifted the packet out with two fingers and held it up between them.

“What’s this?”

“Wet wipes.”

“I know what wet wipes are, Hao.”

“Good.”

“Are you implying something?”

His eyes went, briefly and with enormous restraint, to her cheek.

Her hand flew up. “Is there something on my face?”

“Not at the moment.”

She gasped. “You’re still thinking about last night.”

“I remember it very clearly.”

She shook the packet at him, and she was laughing, and trying not to, and failing. He looked so composed standing there in front of a chain-link fence, by a van, with lunch for twelve, entirely unaware of how ridiculous he looked. Polished shoes. Of course. Her own boots had grass and mud to the ankle. Of course. Sleeves rolled with exactly the same number of turns on each arm. Not a crease anywhere.

“You look like you’re on your way to a board meeting,” she said.

“I came from the office.”

“And you thought an air accident site was a nice place for a picnic?”

“I’ve eaten in stranger places.”

“Name one.”

“An airport.”

“That’s not strange.”

“A hospital corridor.”

“Still not strange.”

“A building site in the rain, under a tarpaulin, with a client whose foreman had just been kidnapped.”

She stopped. “All right. That one’s better.”

He looked pleased with himself.

“Don’t look so pleased,” she said.

He laughed. And then, more seriously, because he had also been looking past her, at the tent in the field and the blue tape and the crane: “I’m sorry about this morning. The two of them.”

She looked at him. He wasn’t saying it to be polite. He’d heard her voice note and understood what was in it, and he was saying so, once, plainly, and then he would leave it alone.

“Thank you,” she said.

“Do you know how much this cost?” she said, after a moment, looking at the bags, because it was easier.

“Yes.”

“Are you always this reckless with money?”

“Only when I’m trying to make a good impression.”

She opened her mouth and found she didn’t have an answer. Then she grinned. “That’s dangerous.”

“Why?”

“Because I might start expecting it.”

His face did something gentle. “That wouldn’t be a problem.”

It wasn’t that it was a romantic thing to say. It was that there was no hesitation in it at all. He said things as if he meant them and saw no reason to dress them up. No performance. No attempt to make it sound like more than it was. Just a plain statement, set down between them like a box of rice. She looked away first.

“Come on,” she said. “Inside. Before you bankrupt yourself feeding the entire aviation industry.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The hangar was louder than he’d expected. Someone was running a compressor at the far end. A radio on a shelf was playing a song from ten years ago. The flying club’s own aircraft had been pushed to one side to make room for the investigators’ tables, and a small, offended-looking man in a club jacket was making tea for everyone in a corner.

Song-Zhu put her bag on the table. “Everyone. Apparently we’re having lunch.”

Heads came up.

“This is Ren Hao,” she said, pointing. “He’s an overenthusiastic delivery service.”

Ren Hao inclined his head. “Good afternoon.”

Dexter looked from him to her, and from her to him, and smiled slowly.

“Don’t,” said Song-Zhu.

“I haven’t said a word.”

“Your face has.”

There were nine of them in the end, including the man making tea, which left three boxes over, which Ren Hao gave to the two police officers at the tape and the crane driver, without making anything of it. He was introduced to Dexter, who did the photographs and documentation and was about to be insufferable about all this. To Mabel Wong, the investigator-in-charge, a small grey-haired woman with reading glasses on a cord, who shook his hand and looked at him for exactly three seconds longer than was comfortable. To two engineers from the authority, and two technicians, and the flying club’s chief instructor, who had known the dead pilot for twenty years and wasn’t eating much.

They thanked him. He thanked them back. He didn’t make a speech about the food or the money, or ask any questions about the aircraft. He helped put the boxes out along the table, and then stood at the end of it with his own lunch and listened. Song-Zhu watched him over her rice.

There was something unexpectedly nice about seeing him out of the restaurant. He was still impeccable. Still polite. Still the sort of man who seemed to have been born knowing where to stand when somebody took a photograph. But he wasn’t treating the hangar. He didn’t flinch at the compressor. He didn’t ask why everything was so dirty. When the chief instructor started, haltingly, to talk about the dead pilot, about how he’d learned to fly here at seventeen and once landed a glider in a car park, Ren Hao put his box down and gave him his whole attention, and didn’t say anything at all until the man had finished.

He listened. When anyone spoke to him, they had all of him.

“Your boyfriend’s generous,” Dexter murmured beside her.

Song-Zhu choked on her water. “He’s not my boyfriend.”

Dexter raised his eyebrows. “Yet.”

She gave him a look that should have killed him where he stood. He grinned, and across the table Ren Hao looked up at exactly the wrong moment, while she was still glaring, and their eyes met.

She looked down at her rice. Dexter laughed under his breath.

“Eat your lunch,” she told him.

“Yes, ma’am.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Ren Hao was halfway through his own lunch when he noticed that she hadn’t touched hers.

She was standing at the far end of the table with a technician, going through a run of photographs on a laptop, pointing at something. The box was open in front of her. The chopsticks were still lying on top of it, side by side, unused.

He looked at his watch. Then at her. Then at the box.

He waited one minute. Then another. Then he went round the table.

“Song-Zhu.”

“Hm?”

“Your lunch.”

She looked down at it. “Oh.”

“You’re not eating.”

“I will.”

“When?”

She blinked at him, and then smiled, slow. “You’re doing it again.”

“Doing what?”

“Managing me.”

He paused. “I was reminding you.”

“I know.” She picked up the chopsticks and ate a piece of chicken, pointedly, looking at him. “See? Eating.”

“Good.”

“You’re very easy to please.”

“Not particularly.”

“No?”

He looked at her steadily. “Not where you’re concerned.”

Her chopsticks stopped halfway to her mouth. Dexter, two places down, became and deeply interested in a photograph of a wingtip. Mabel Wong turned a page in a manual she had certainly already read.

Song-Zhu looked at Ren Hao. He was perfectly calm. Not even slightly embarrassed. She put the piece of chicken in her mouth, chewed it, swallowed it, and then pointed the chopsticks at his chest.

“You’re dangerous,” she said.

“So I’ve been told.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty-five past one he was preparing to leave, and had already stayed much longer than he’d meant to.

He had learned in that hour and a half that her working days had no shape at all, that investigators spent a great deal of their lives waiting for other people to finish things, and that Song-Zhu drank coffee when she was tired and forgot to drink water even when the bottle was in her hand. He had learned that she was more serious at work than she had been at dinner. Not cold. Focused. There was a difference. She didn’t rush. She asked precise questions. When a technician got a number wrong in the log, she corrected it so lightly and so quickly that the man hardly noticed he’d been corrected.

She was good at her job. He liked watching her do it. He liked it more than was probably sensible.

“You’re going?” she said, at the hangar door.

“I should.”

“Already?”

“It’s nearly half past one.”

“That’s practically still morning.”

“Would you like me to stay?”

She thought about it, honestly, and he liked that, too. Then she looked out at the field, at the tent and the tape.

“I’ve got to go back to work.”

“I know.”

“There’s a lot still to do.”

“I understand.”

She looked at him for a second. Then she stepped closer.

“Thank you for lunch.”

“You’re welcome.”

“And for bringing enough for everybody. Even the man with the tea.”

“Of course.”

“You’re not going to ask me when I’m free next?”

“You said you wanted to choose.”

“I do.”

“Then I’ll wait.”

She narrowed her eyes. “Can you actually wait?”

“Yes.”

“How long for?”

“That,” he said, “is a difficult question.”

She laughed. He took a card out of his shirt pocket and held it out.

She looked at it. “What’s this?”

“My number.”

“You already have my number. I’ve got yours. I sent you a voice note.”

“That’s my mobile. This is the office.”

She stared at him, and then at the card, and then burst out laughing. “Ren Hao. Do you have a different phone number for every department of your life?”

“Not every department.”

“That’s worse!”

But she took it, and turned it between her fingers. Thick white card, his name in plain black letters and under it Managing Director, and nothing else. She slipped it into the chest pocket of her flight suit, behind her phone. Then she reached up and straightened his collar.

It was already straight. He knew that. She knew that. But her fingers stayed at the edge of it a moment longer than they needed to, against his neck, and he stood still and let them.

“There,” she said.

“Thank you.”

She stepped back. “Try not to miss me too much.”

He didn’t even have to think about it. “I already do.”

Her smile faltered. Only for a second. But he saw it, and he liked having seen it, more than he would have been able to explain.

She shook her head. “Go.”

“Goodbye, Song-Zhu.”

“Bye, Hao.”

He walked back towards the gate. She stood in the hangar door and watched him go: polished shoes on wet grass, the shirt still somehow immaculate, posture still annoyingly perfect. A man who had just spent his Saturday feeding nine strangers at an air accident site because a woman had sent him a voice note.

Oh, she thought. This is going to be interesting.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just after two Ren Hao was back in his car. Mr. Yau, who had driven for the firm for six years and noticed everything and said almost nothing, glanced at him in the mirror as they pulled out onto the airfield road.

“Was lunch all right, sir?”

“Yes.”

“Good.” A pause, while they waited at a junction. “Was the food satisfactory?”

Ren Hao looked out at the field going past, the white tent getting smaller. He thought about the noise of the hangar, and the smell of fuel and wet grass, and the way she had laughed at the wet wipes, and the way her fingers had stayed at his collar.

“Very,” he said.

His phone buzzed.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): The team says thank you. The tea man says you can come back.

Ren Hao: You’re welcome. Did you finish yours?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Yes, Dad.

He laughed, alone in the back of the car, and Mr. Yau’s eyes flicked to the mirror and away again.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Dexter says you should come again.

Ren Hao: Does Dexter.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): He likes free lunch. I told him you’re not a canteen.

Ren Hao: Thank you for clarifying.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): But you can come again.

He read that one twice.

Ren Hao: I’d like that.

Ren Hao: When?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Hao.

Ren Hao: Sorry.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Let me survive this investigation first.

Ren Hao: Take your time.

A minute later she sent a photograph with no caption. An evidence bag with an orange box inside it, sealed, signed twice across the seal, a label in her handwriting. Lying on a steel table in a hangar, under a strip light.

He looked at it a long time. He understood that she hadn’t sent it to show off. She’d sent it the way you’d tell someone this is where I am, and this is what I carry, and I wanted you to know.

Ren Hao: Be careful.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Always.

He put the phone down on the seat beside him. Outside, the fields gave way to the ring road and the ring road to the city. His afternoon was waiting for him: three reports, two calls, and a meeting that had already been moved twice. And he was sitting in the back of his own car thinking about a woman in a flight suit who had told him not to schedule her.

For once, he didn’t mind having something in his life he couldn’t plan.

And at a flying club hangar on the edge of an airfield, Xu Song-Zhu was doing exactly what she’d said she would. Surviving the investigation. Logging a recorder. Walking the ground marks a second time. Though every so often, between one photograph and the next, she caught herself smiling at her phone. Which was becoming inconvenient.

chapters.title: What She Listens To
chapters.desc: Noodles behind the cargo terminal. He asks what she does; she tells him she listens to the last thirty minutes of strangers. A pilot’s words she won’t repeat. In the car park she kisses him against his car.
chapters.epigraph: “All the time. Sometimes I ask the recording questions.”
chapters.content:
Ren Hao had started to recognise the sound of his phone when it was her.

It was an embarrassing development, and he was aware of it. He had a perfectly functional phone, on which he received messages from colleagues, clients, partners, his sister, and a great many people who wanted to tell him things that could have been an email. He didn’t check it without a reason. And yet now, whenever the screen lit, some small, involuntary part of him hoped it was a photograph of something badly lit, with a one-word caption.

It was Thursday evening, the nineteenth of June. He was in the back of the car outside a client’s building, having just left a meeting that had run forty minutes longer than it should have, and Joyce had sent him three reminders, and Mr. Yau was waiting to be told where to go. The screen lit.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Dinner.

It was a photograph of a plastic tray containing something that might once have been rice, something that might once have been vegetables, and something brown.

Ren Hao: What is that?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Food.

Ren Hao: I can see that.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Then why ask?

Ren Hao: Did you cook it?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I bought it. From a machine. The machine cooked it. Badly.

Ren Hao: Can you cook?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I can cook.

Ren Hao: What can you cook?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Eggs.

He laughed. In the mirror, Mr. Yau’s eyes moved to him and away.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Also instant noodles. Every time they taste different.

Ren Hao: How?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Depends how much water I put in. It’s a skill.

Ren Hao: Have you eaten it?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I’m eating it right now. Look at me eating. You?

Ren Hao: Not yet.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Why?

Ren Hao: Work.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Work isn’t food.

Ren Hao: Neither is your photograph.

She sent him an emoji of a middle finger. He smiled down at it in the back of his own car like a teenager, and then the next one came.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Are you free tonight?

His face changed.

Ren Hao: I can be.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): That’s a suspicious answer. You sound like a man who has to rearrange a government to have dinner.

Ren Hao: I’m not that important.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Good. Then come and get me. I’m choosing.

She sent an address. And a moment later:

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Don’t wear a suit.

He looked down at his charcoal trousers, his white shirt, the tie.

Ren Hao: Why?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Because I’ll look at you and feel underdressed and then I’ll have to be rude to you about it.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Wear something normal. You own something normal?

He put the phone in his pocket.

“Home first, please,” he told Mr. Yau. “And then somewhere else.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The address turned out to be a gate in a long grey fence on the far side of the airport, in the part of it that the public never saw: the operational compound, where the aviation authority kept its engineers, its stores and, in a low brick building with no sign on it at all, its accident investigators. There was a barrier, and a security hut, and a guard who looked at Ren Hao’s car and then at his own clipboard and then back at the car with the expression of a man deciding whether to be impressed.

Song-Zhu had told him to wait outside the barrier. So he waited, standing beside the car in a navy polo shirt and black trousers. Normal, by her definition. He had even left his watch at home, which had felt, on the way out of the door, like going out without his trousers.

He suspected he was taking the instruction more seriously than she had meant him to.

At fourteen minutes to eight she came through the side gate. Grey T-shirt under a dark jacket, hair tied loosely at the back, her staff lanyard round her neck and a takeaway coffee in one hand, though it was evening. When she saw him she stopped. She looked him slowly up and down, from the polo shirt to the shoes and back, and then she smiled.

“Well.”

“What?”

“You look normal.”

“Is that a compliment?”

“From me? It’s practically a proposal.”

She came up to him. Close to, he could see she was tired. Not crash-site tired; something underneath that, that sat behind her eyes.

“Have you eaten?” he said.

She stared at him, and then laughed. “Oh my God.”

“What?”

“Is that the first thing you’re going to say to me? Every time?”

“Would you rather something else?”

“Yes.”

“Such as?”

She stopped right in front of him and looked up. “Hello, Song-Zhu. You look beautiful tonight.”

He looked at her, gravely. Then, without the slightest change of expression, he said, “Hello, Song-Zhu. You look beautiful tonight.”

She burst out laughing. “You’re hopeless.”

“You asked.”

“I know I asked.” She took a sip of her coffee, which was the sort of thing he would normally have said something about at this hour, and he didn’t. She glanced at the car. “Did you drive yourself?”

“No.”

“Of course you didn’t.” She looked at Mr. Yau, who was looking at the barrier. “Hello, Mr. Ren’s driver.”

“Good evening, miss,” said Mr. Yau, to the barrier.

Ren Hao opened the passenger door for her. “Where are we going? You said you were choosing.”

“There’s a noodle place behind the cargo terminal. The pilots go there. The soup’s very hot and the tables are very sticky and you’ll hate it.”

“I won’t hate it.”

“Then I’ll be very disappointed,” said Song-Zhu, and got in.

✦ ✦ ✦

The noodle place had six tables and a television showing a football match nobody was watching, and the soup came in bowls the size of hubcaps, and the man at the counter knew her name and didn’t know his and wasn’t interested in finding out. Ren Hao ate everything. He didn’t comment on the tables. She watched him not commenting on the tables with enormous enjoyment.

It was quieter than their first dinner. Not because they had run out of things to say. Because she had a great many stories, and most of them started halfway through and required him to ask three questions before he understood what she was talking about. He didn’t mind. He liked listening to her. He liked how she used her hands, and how her eyebrows went up when something was funny before she’d said why, and how she sometimes stopped in the middle of one story because she’d remembered another one that was better.

She was in the middle of telling him about a colleague who had locked himself out of a secure room with his own lunch inside when she noticed him looking.

“You’ve gone quiet.”

“I’m listening.”

“With that face?”

“Which face?”

“Your serious face.”

“This is my face.”

“That’s unfortunate for you,” she said, and he laughed, and she went back to her noodles looking pleased.

After a while he said, “Can I ask you something?”

“Depends.”

“On?”

“Whether I want to answer it.”

“That’s fair.” He put his chopsticks down. “What do you actually do? I know what your job’s called. I’d like to know what it is.”

She looked at him across the steam. Then she put her own chopsticks down too.

“All right. You know about black boxes.”

“The flight recorders.”

“Two of them, on most aircraft. Neither of them’s black. They’re orange, so you can find them in a field or at the bottom of the sea.” She held up one finger. “The flight data recorder. That’s numbers. Height, speed, heading, what the engines were doing, what the controls were doing. On a modern airliner it’s thousands of things, many times a second.” A second finger. “And the cockpit voice recorder.”

She paused.

“That’s the one people want to know about.”

“Why?”

“Because it’s people. Four channels. One microphone in each pilot’s headset, one for whoever’s in the jump seat, and one in the ceiling that picks up the whole cockpit. Everything they say to each other. Everything they say on the radio. Every switch, every warning, every noise the aeroplane makes.” She turned her glass slowly on the sticky table. “The old ones kept the last thirty minutes, on a loop, and recorded over the rest. Newer ones keep two hours. The newest ones keep twenty-five. But the part I live in, nearly always, is the last thirty minutes.”

He had gone still.

“We download it in the lab,” she said. “Then somebody has to listen. There’s a room for it. Soundproofed. No windows. You sit in front of a screen with the waveform on it, four lines, and the timeline from the data recorder underneath, and you put on a pair of very good headphones and you play it. Again and again. A second at a time sometimes. You match the voices to the numbers. You work out who said what, and when, and what was happening to the aircraft when they said it. Then a group of us sits down and makes a transcript, and argues about every word.”

“And it’s you who listens.”

“Among other people. It’s mostly me who listens first.” She smiled a little. “It’s good, being alone in there. I talk to myself.”

“Do you?”

“All the time. Sometimes I ask the recording questions.”

“Does it answer?”

“Never. Very rude.” She looked pleased that he’d almost smiled. Then she looked at him properly. “Do you want to know what the hard part is?”

“Tell me.”

“People think it’s hearing somebody die.” She said it without any drama at all, which made it heavier. “Sometimes it is. But that isn’t usually the bit that stays with you. It’s the ordinary things. One pilot asking the other one if he’s checked something. Somebody saying the weather’s better than forecast. Somebody laughing. A radio call. Somebody saying they’ll be home tomorrow and they’ll bring something back.” She looked down at her hands. “Everything sounds completely normal. Right up until it doesn’t.”

The football went on silently on the television above them.

“You spend hours,” she said, “listening to people who have no idea that they’re about to become an investigation.”

He didn’t say anything. Then: “You’re listening to the last thirty minutes of strangers’ lives.”

Her fingers stopped on the glass. He had understood. Not all of it. But enough.

“Sometimes less,” she said. “Sometimes more.”

He didn’t ask the next question. He reached over instead and filled her glass from the metal jug, and she watched him do it, and then looked away towards the window.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Can I tell you something?” she said, while the man at the counter was taking their bowls.

“Of course.”

She seemed to decide how much of it, and then she began. “There was a pilot. Not the one this week. Someone from a long time ago. Another country, a freighter, a night flight. They’d been having trouble for nearly forty minutes and they didn’t know what it was. At first it’s all procedure. Checklists, readings, calls. They’re doing everything right. And then it gets worse.”

He waited.

“And there’s a point where one of them stops talking about the aircraft.” She swallowed. “He says something about his family. Something very ordinary. He asks the other one to tell his wife something.”

The restaurant went on around them: the clatter in the kitchen, the television, the door.

“I remember thinking he sounded tired,” she said. “And then he said something else.”

He waited. She didn’t go on. For a moment he thought she’d changed her mind about telling him at all.

Then she shook her head. “I’m not going to tell you what he said.”

“All right.”

“I can’t.”

“You don’t have to.”

“It’s not mine.” She looked at the table. “It belongs to his wife. If it’s in the report, it’s because it had to be. Otherwise it stays in the room.” She gave a small laugh with no humour in it. “That’s the strange part. I can’t tell you what I had for lunch on Monday. But I could tell you exactly how his voice went on that word. I could draw it for you. I know where it sits on the waveform.”

Ren Hao’s jaw had tightened.

“Does it stay with you?”

“Sometimes.”

“What do you do with it?”

“Work, mostly.”

He didn’t look convinced, and she saw.

“Don’t do that face.”

“Which face?”

“The one that says you want to fix it.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

“You’re thinking about it.”

“Perhaps.” He leaned back. “Some recordings must be worse than others.”

“Some are hard because you can hear the fear. And some are hard because you can’t.” She folded the paper napkin into a small square. “Sometimes they’re completely calm. You hear them doing their jobs, talking to each other, flying the aeroplane. And then the recording just ends. That’s all. Thirty minutes of somebody’s life, and then nothing.”

He looked at her across the table, and for once didn’t have anything ready to say.

He was used to difficult conversations. His whole business was people in situations they couldn’t control. He had sat across from men who’d lost companies overnight, from families who’d had a phone call in the night with a ransom figure in it, from clients trying hard not to look as frightened as they were. He understood distress. He understood fear.

But this was something else. She sat in a room with no windows and listened to the moment people stopped having a future. And then she went home, and ate noodles out of the pan, and sent him photographs of terrible dinners and made jokes about eggs.

“How long have you been doing it?” he said.

“Three years. Nearly. I came in straight from university.”

“Does anyone ever ask how you are?”

She blinked. It was such a simple question, and she found she didn’t have an answer ready for it.

“Sometimes. At work. Mabel does.”

He nodded. And then, gently: “And outside work?”

She looked at him. He wasn’t smiling now. He wanted to know.

“Not really,” she said.

Something moved in his face. Not pity. She’d have hated pity, and he seemed to know that. It was more as though he had just found a whole room in her life that he hadn’t known was there, and was standing in its doorway.

She reached across the table and stole the last piece of pickled radish from his saucer.

“Don’t look so sad.”

“I’m not sad.”

“Your eyebrows are.”

He laughed. She smiled.

“I’m all right,” she said. “Honestly.”

He looked at her a moment longer. “All right.”

“That’s it?”

“What else?”

“I don’t know. You usually have an opinion.”

He thought about it. “I don’t think you need me to tell you how to feel about your work.”

Her face softened. “Good.”

“But if you ever want to talk about it, I’ll listen.” And then, as if it were nothing: “Even if it’s three in the morning.”

She smiled. “That’s a dangerous promise.”

“I know.”

“I might actually ring.”

“I hope you do.”

She stared at him for a second across the empty bowls. Then she laughed under her breath. “You’re really something, Hao.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was nearly eleven when they came out. He’d sent Mr. Yau home at nine and said he would drive her himself, in the car the firm kept for exactly that sort of evening, which she found extremely funny. The car park behind the cargo terminal was nearly empty. A few vehicles sat under the yellow lights, their windows reflecting the sodium glare, and somewhere beyond the fence a freighter was running its engines up for the night.

She walked ahead of him, swinging her bag by its strap.

“You’re quiet,” she said.

“Am I?”

“You’ve stopped telling me what to do.”

“I don’t think I do that.”

“You told me to wash my face.”

“That was a reasonable suggestion.”

“You brought lunch for twelve people.”

“They were working.”

“You’ve asked me if I’ve eaten about forty-seven times.”

“I have not.”

“Forty-six.” She stopped by his car and turned round, and the brightness went out of her face. “Did I make you uncomfortable? Talking about it?”

“No. Why would you think that?”

“Because I don’t usually tell people. About the room.”

“Why not?”

“Because people don’t know what to do with it. Some go quiet. Some get curious in a way I don’t like, as if I’ve got something juicy in my bag. And some start telling me how brave I am.” She wrinkled her nose. “I hate that.”

“Why?”

“Because I’m not brave every day. Some days I’m just tired. And I don’t want people to think I’m sad all the time. I’m not. I like my job. I like understanding things. I like that once in a while somebody changes a procedure somewhere because of what I heard, and nobody ever has to hear it again.” She looked down at her trainers. “But I don’t want to spend my whole life being the girl who listens to people die.”

He stepped closer. “You’re not,” he said.

She looked up.

He took her hand. “You’re Song-Zhu.”

“That’s a very simple answer.”

“I know.”

“Not especially impressive.”

“I’m not trying to impress you.” His thumb moved over her knuckles. “You’re the woman who argues with me about water and sends me photographs of food from a machine, and thinks twelve people can be fed out of one bad decision. And you’re very good at your job.”

Her smile went. “How do you know?”

“Because I listened to you talk about it.” He looked down at her. “You care about getting it right. Even when getting it right is the worst part. I don’t need to understand all of it to respect it.”

Something tightened in her chest that she hadn’t expected.

She looked at him for a long moment in the yellow light. Then she stepped forward into him, without warning, and he caught her almost before he knew he’d moved. His arms went round her. She put her face against his chest. Neither of them said anything.

He held her carefully. Not too tightly, not as if he were trying to keep her there. Just enough to let her rest. She closed her eyes. His shirt smelled of soap and of something woody, and his hand moved slowly up and down her back, and under her ear she could hear his heart. Steady. Unhurried. It was absurdly comforting, for a sound.

“You’re very warm,” she said into his shirt.

“Thank you.”

She laughed against him. “That wasn’t a compliment.”

“I’ll take it anyway.”

She stayed a little longer. Then she lifted her head. He looked down at her with an expression she hadn’t seen on him yet: not the amused one he wore when she was being difficult, not the patient one when she wouldn’t answer. Something quieter underneath both.

He touched her cheek. “All right?”

She nodded. And then, before he could say anything else, she took a handful of the front of his polo shirt and kissed him.

It wasn’t like the first time. There was no taxi waiting, no joke on the end of it. She hadn’t done it to see what would happen. She had spent an evening telling someone about the room with no windows, which she never did, and he had listened without trying to make it smaller, or make it brave, or make it go away. He hadn’t told her to be strong. He hadn’t offered to solve it. He’d just held on.

So she kissed him, because she wanted to. His hand came to her waist, and the other went into her hair at the back of her head, and for about three seconds he kissed her back with enormous restraint.

Then she pulled him closer, and the restraint went.

He made a low sound against her mouth and turned them both, without seeming to decide to, until her back was against the cold side of his car, and he had one hand flat on the roof beside her head and the other spread on her lower back, and he was kissing her slowly and thoroughly and not at all like a man in a polo shirt being normal. She held on to his shirt with both fists. The freighter beyond the fence went up to full power and the noise came across the car park like weather, and she laughed into his mouth, and he lifted his head.

“Song-Zhu.”

“Hm.”

“You’re going to crease my shirt.”

She stared at him. “Are you serious?”

“Entirely.”

She pulled him back down by the collar. “Then stop talking.”

He laughed into the kiss, and this time there was nothing careful in it. She chased his mouth when he drew back an inch, and he liked that so much he did it again on purpose to make her do it again. She liked the way his composure went every time she did something he hadn’t expected. She liked that she could do that to him in a car park.

When he finally lifted his head, she was smiling.

He brushed a strand of hair off her face, and his thumb stopped on her cheekbone.

“You’re beautiful,” he said. Quietly. No joke on it. No conditions.

She blinked. Then her mouth curved. “You’re getting better at this.”

“At what?”

“Being my date.”

“Good to know.” He didn’t move his hand. “You’re making it very hard to say good night.”

“Good.”

“You’re trouble.”

“You knew that.”

“I did,” he said, and kissed her once more, and then made himself open the passenger door.

✦ ✦ ✦

He drove her home. She sat with one leg folded under her and looked out of the window, and for once didn’t talk. The radio was on low. At a red light he glanced at her.

“Tired?”

“A bit.”

“Shall I turn it off?”

“No. It’s nice.”

A few minutes later she said, “Can I ask you something?”

“Of course.”

“Why did you say yes to the blind date?”

He considered it. “Isla asked.”

“That’s all?”

“She said she knew someone I’d like.”

“And you believed her?”

“She’s usually right about people. It’s very irritating.”

“That’s unfortunate,” said Song-Zhu.

“Why?”

“Because now she’ll be unbearable.”

“She already is.”

She groaned. “Don’t tell her anything.”

“I haven’t.”

She was quiet for a few more streets. Then, looking straight ahead, with a small smile: “Did you like me? When you first saw me?”

“Would you like the honest answer?”

“Obviously.”

“I thought you looked as if you’d had a very hard day.”

She turned and stared at him, and then laughed. “That’s not what I asked!”

“I know.” He watched the road. Then, after a moment: “Yes.”

She went quiet.

“I liked you,” he said.

“With the mud?”

“With the mud.”

“And the boots?”

“Yes.”

“And when I laughed at you?”

“That,” he said, “was probably when I was sure.”

She looked at him a long time in the passing streetlight.

“Oh,” she said, low, and smiled out of the window all the way home.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just before midnight he walked her to her door. Third floor, a corridor with a flickering light, a pot plant someone had given up on. She stood with her keys in her hand. He stood a step away. Neither of them seemed in any hurry.

“Good night,” he said.

“That’s it?”

“What would you like?”

She took one step towards him. “You’re the one who’s good at arranging things.”

“I thought you didn’t want to be scheduled.”

“I don’t.”

“Then?”

She tipped her head. “Improvise.”

He laughed, low, and put his hand on her waist and kissed her, and she smiled against his mouth, and he kept his hand there afterwards.

“Better,” she said.

She unlocked the door. Then she turned back. “Hao?”

“Yes?”

“Thank you for listening.”

His face went soft. “Any time.”

She leaned out of the doorway and kissed him again, quickly, a little playfully, and said good night, and went in. He waited in the corridor until he heard the lock turn.

✦ ✦ ✦

A little after midnight her phone buzzed on the pillow.

Hao (Three-Piece): Home.

Song-Zhu: Good.

Song-Zhu: I liked tonight.

Hao (Three-Piece): So did I.

Song-Zhu: Even though I talked about work all night?

Hao (Three-Piece): Most of all because you did.

A pause.

Song-Zhu: You’re not scared of me?

Hao (Three-Piece): Should I be?

Song-Zhu: I listen to dead people for a living.

Hao (Three-Piece): I run a company for people having the worst day of their lives.

Song-Zhu: That’s not the same.

Hao (Three-Piece): No. It isn’t. But I don’t think either of us needs to be frightened of the other.

She looked at that a long time and didn’t answer straight away.

Song-Zhu: You’re quite good at this, Hao.

Hao (Three-Piece): At what?

Song-Zhu: Making people feel all right.

Hao (Three-Piece): I don’t do it for everybody.

Song-Zhu: Oh?

Hao (Three-Piece): No.

Song-Zhu: Why me, then?

He thought about it, sitting in the dark in the firm’s car outside her building, with the engine off. About a woman who’d arrived at a French restaurant in boots that smelled of fuel. Who had kissed him at a taxi rank to shut him up. Who sent voice notes from hangars and ate dinner out of a machine, and could talk about death with a composure that frightened him, and then laugh at a badly cooked egg.

Hao (Three-Piece): Because I like you.

A few seconds.

Song-Zhu: I like you too.

Song-Zhu: Don’t let it go to your head.

Hao (Three-Piece): I’ll do my best.

Song-Zhu: Good night, handsome.

Hao (Three-Piece): Good night, beautiful.

✦ ✦ ✦

There were recordings Xu Song-Zhu would remember for the rest of her life. A warning tone. A voice going quieter. The last transmission before a frequency went silent and stayed silent. She would remember them because remembering them was part of the job.

But that night, lying in the dark with her phone beside her on the pillow, she found herself remembering other things instead. The warmth of him through a polo shirt. His voice in the car park. The way he’d asked whether anyone outside work ever asked her how she was.

She rolled onto her side and smiled at the wall, and then reached for the phone again.

Song-Zhu: Hao?

He replied at once.

Hao (Three-Piece): Yes?

Song-Zhu: Next time I’m choosing again.

Hao (Three-Piece): I know.

Song-Zhu: And I want dessert.

Hao (Three-Piece): Of course.

Song-Zhu: And you have to kiss me before I go in.

A pause.

Hao (Three-Piece): I don’t think that will be a problem.

She grinned at the ceiling.

Song-Zhu: Good boy.

Across the city, Ren Hao put the phone down on the seat beside him and sat smiling at the steering wheel of a parked car. He had spent his whole working life learning to see risks coming. To prepare for them, plan for them, stand in the way of them before they arrived. He was good at it. He was, frankly, excellent at it.

And he was beginning to understand that Xu Song-Zhu wasn’t something he wanted to prepare for.

He wanted to be there for her. All of it. The parts he couldn’t plan most of all.

chapters.title: His Firm
chapters.desc: She visits his firm: three floors, a receptionist’s birthday, a kidnap negotiation live on a screen. After hours, explicit, against the glass on the thirty-second floor.
chapters.epigraph: “Tonight you’re just Hao.”
chapters.content:
At sixteen minutes past nine on Friday the fourth of July, Xu Song-Zhu discovered that Ren Hao was a great deal more frightening at work.

Not that she’d expected otherwise. She had seen restaurant managers address him in a particular tone. She had seen crowds in doorways part for him without quite noticing they were doing it. She had seen him look at his watch when someone took too long to answer a question, which was a habit she intended to cure.

But a man in a restaurant was one thing, and a man in his own territory was another. And Ren Hao’s territory, it turned out, was three entire floors of a glass tower in the business district, with its own lifts.

She stood in the lobby with her head tipped back.

She had a lieu day after a week of nights on the twin from the airfield, and she had said, on the phone on Tuesday, you’ve seen where I work, now I want to see yours, and he had said Friday, so fast that she suspected he had been waiting for her to ask. She had imagined an office. A nice one, possibly. She hadn’t imagined an atrium.

Hao (Three-Piece): You’re here?

Song-Zhu: I think so. There’s a very tall building in front of me. Might be yours.

Hao (Three-Piece): I’ll come down.

Song-Zhu: Don’t. I’m already inside. Your receptionist is looking at me.

Her phone rang.

“Don’t move,” he said.

She laughed. “Are you sending security?”

“No. I’m coming down myself.”

“I’m not a fugitive, Hao.”

“I know.”

“Then why do you sound like you’re running an extraction?”

“Wait there,” he said, and she could hear him smiling, and he rang off.

The receptionist was a woman of about sixty with silver hair in a neat bun and a cardigan in a shade of coral that took real courage, and a name plate on the desk that said Ruby. She smiled politely. “Good morning. May I help you?”

“I’m here for Ren Hao.”

Ruby’s expression changed by about a millimetre. Song-Zhu saw it. “Mr. Ren? Do you have an appointment?”

Song-Zhu thought about that. “Sort of.”

“May I take your name?”

“Xu Song-Zhu.”

Ruby typed. Her eyes moved over the screen and widened, slightly. Then she looked up again with something new in her face that Song-Zhu couldn’t quite read: delight, possibly, held down hard by professionalism. “Miss Xu. Please do take a seat.”

Song-Zhu sat. She was wearing a fitted white blouse, dark trousers and low heels. Her hair was loose. She had put on make-up, which she did roughly four times a year, and she was quite pleased with it.

“Song-Zhu.”

She turned. He was coming across the lobby from the lifts in a charcoal three-piece suit, a white shirt, a dark tie, his jacket done up, every hair in place, looking every inch like the man who owned the building. Or at least like a man who could make everyone in it nervous by asking what time it was.

His face changed when he saw her. The seriousness went somewhere and the smile came instead.

“Hello.”

“Hello.”

And before she had finished standing up, he had pulled her into a hug, a proper one, both arms, his chin for a second against her hair. In the middle of his own lobby.

“Missed you,” he said into her hair.

She smiled into his shoulder. “We saw each other on Monday.”

“Four days.”

“You’re counting?”

“Yes.”

She pulled back to look at him. “You’re very cuddly for someone who looks like he fires people before breakfast.”

He didn’t answer that, because he had turned to the desk. “Ruby. Happy birthday.”

“Oh, Mr. Ren, you didn’t have to—”

But he had already gone round the end of the desk and hugged her too, the sixty-year-old receptionist, firmly, briefly, lifting her an inch off the floor so that her reading glasses swung on their chain, and set her down again. “There’s a cake in the fourth-floor kitchen and nobody’s allowed to touch it until you’ve had the first slice. Joyce has orders.”

“Thank you, Mr. Ren,” said Ruby, pink to the hairline, straightening her cardigan.

Song-Zhu stared at him.

A man carrying a stack of folders came past. “Mr. Ren.”

Ren Hao turned, and Song-Zhu watched his whole face reorganise itself into something cool and level. “Morning, Raymond.”

“Morning. The revised exposure assessment’s in your inbox.”

“I’ll have it back to you before eleven.”

“Thank you, sir.” Raymond’s eyes flicked to Song-Zhu. “Good morning, miss.”

“Hi,” said Song-Zhu.

Raymond walked on, quite fast.

She leaned in. “He’s frightened of you.”

“He isn’t.”
