“His shoulders were up round his ears. You’ve just hugged Ruby off the floor and he’s frightened of you.”

“Ruby’s been here longer than I have.” He took her hand. “Come on.”

She looked down at their hands. “You hold hands with people at work?”

“No.”

“Interesting.”

“You aren’t people,” he said, and then heard it.

She stopped in the middle of the lobby. “That’s a terrible sentence.”

“I meant—”

“I know exactly what you meant.” She squeezed his fingers. “Lead on, boss.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The first of his floors was the client floor: advisory and corporate risk, meeting rooms in glass, open-plan desks, a printer somewhere at the back making a noise like a goose in pain. People were working. Phones were ringing. Everyone who passed Ren Hao said good morning to him, and every one of them, as they said it, stood up a little straighter.

“Do you do something to them?” she murmured.

“No.”

“You’re sure?”

“Quite.”

“You should smile at them more.”

“I smile.”

“At me.”

“That’s still smiling.”

On the floor above, Joyce met them at the lift. She was in her early thirties, with a tablet under one arm and a phone at her ear, and at her feet, sitting perfectly upright on a small tartan cushion beside the desk, was a white dog about the size of a loaf of bread.

Joyce ended her call. “Mr. Ren. Your eleven o’clock’s confirmed. The overseas team need you to approve the revised security budget, and Raymond needs a signature.”

“Thank you, Joyce.”

And then Ren Hao looked down. The dog had stood up. Its tail was going so fast its whole back end was moving. Song-Zhu watched his face change entirely.

“Oh, hello,” he said, in a voice she had never heard him use.

He crouched down in the three-piece suit. The dog came straight to him, sniffed his fingers, and put both front paws on his knee, and he laughed.

“Hello, sweetheart. Hello. Have you been good? Have you? Have you been the best girl on the floor?”

“She’s been waiting for you,” said Joyce, with no expression whatever.

“Has she?” He rubbed the dog’s ears with both hands. And then, in a voice considerably softer than anything he’d used on his staff: “I love you. Yes, I do. I love you.”

Song-Zhu froze. She looked at Joyce. Joyce looked at her. Then both of them looked down at the managing director, who was still crouched on the carpet in a suit worth more than Song-Zhu’s car, entirely unbothered.

“I love you,” he told the dog again, scratching under her chin. “You’re the only one in this whole building who never gives me any problems.”

The dog licked his wrist.

“Exactly,” said Ren Hao.

Song-Zhu folded her arms slowly. So that was how it worked. The staff got brief instructions. The clients got carefully chosen words. The receptionist got a hug and a cake. And a small white dog on a tartan cushion got declarations of love.

He stood up, and only then seemed to remember she was there.

“What?”

“Nothing at all, darling.”

He narrowed his eyes. “Why are you smiling?”

“I’m not.”

Joyce looked hard at her tablet.

“This is Joyce’s dog,” he said, with as much dignity as a man could manage while brushing white hair off his trouser leg. “Momo.”

Song-Zhu crouched. “Hello, Momo.” The dog came to her at once and leaned her whole weight against Song-Zhu’s shin, and Song-Zhu rubbed her ears and looked up at him. “Does she know you love her?”

“Yes.”

“Good. Wouldn’t want her to get the wrong idea.”

He laughed. Joyce, finally, gave up and smiled.

✦ ✦ ✦

The top floor was quieter. Smaller offices, a room full of screens he called operations, and a pair of secure meeting rooms with no windows and a keypad on each door. One of them had its door propped open, and inside, a whole wall was a screen. Song-Zhu stopped in the doorway.

A map, with three pins on it in a country she recognised from the shape of the coast. A list of names, half of them initials. A timeline down one side, every entry with a time beside it to the minute. And in one corner, an open call window with no picture, just a waveform moving.

A man with a headset was speaking. “Ask her to repeat the question exactly as it was put. Word for word. Don’t paraphrase.”

A woman’s voice on the speaker, a long way away, answered in a language Song-Zhu didn’t speak, and someone at the table translated under their breath.

“Kidnap for ransom,” said Ren Hao, beside her. “A client’s regional manager. Taken on Tuesday between two sites. We’re advising the family and his company. We’re not police, and we don’t talk to the people who have him. The family’s chosen someone to do that, his brother-in-law. We sit behind him.”

Song-Zhu watched the timeline. Entries every few hours. Call 3, 14.52. Demand restated. Communicator held position. Call 4, 21.10. Proof-of-life request sent.

“What’s proof of life?”

“Questions only he can answer. The name of his first dog. What he ate on his wedding day. If they can’t get the answer, they probably haven’t got him, or he isn’t well enough to give it.” He nodded at the screen. “The answers came back last night. Right first time. He’s alive.”

She looked at the timeline. She recognised the shape of it immediately. Not the subject; the way it was built. Every contact logged. Every time to the minute. Every change written down the moment it happened, before anyone had a chance to remember it differently.

“You have someone there?” she said.

“Local partners. Not ours, but we’ve used them since our first year.”

“And the family?”

“A separate team sits with them. They don’t need to watch this.”

One of the analysts turned round. “Mr. Ren. Something’s come in.”

He was across the room in three steps. “What is it?”

“Another message to the family’s phone. Different number. Local team’s checking it now.”

“Nothing goes to the family until it’s verified. Keep the liaison informed. Log the number, and the time it came in, and preserve the message exactly as received. If it’s a second group trying to cash in, I want to know before they do.”

“Understood.”

Song-Zhu watched him. There was nothing of the man who’d hugged Ruby in his voice now, or the man on the carpet with the dog. His questions were short and exact. He listened all the way to the end of what anyone said. When he gave an instruction it was so clear that nobody had to ask him what he meant. He wasn’t loud. He didn’t need to be.

When he came back she said, “You’re good at that.”

“At what?”

“Being in charge of something terrible.”

He looked at her for a second. “Thank you.”

“Don’t look so pleased.”

“I’m accepting a compliment.”

“Of course you are.”

The analyst again. “Mr. Ren, the family liaison’s asking if you can join the next call.”

“Five minutes.” He turned to her. “Would you wait in my office? There’s coffee.”

“Go. I’m fine.”

He touched her arm. “And don’t wander into any rooms with keypads on the doors.”

She looked deeply offended. “Do I look like someone who wanders into restricted areas?”

He looked at her for a long, frank moment. “Yes.”

She laughed. “Go!”

✦ ✦ ✦

His office was at the far end of the top floor, and it was big without being decorated: a large desk facing the window, a meeting table, a low leather sofa, shelves of reports and a few books with broken spines that he had clearly actually read. And the window. The whole of the outer wall was glass, floor to ceiling, and the city stood below it in the morning haze, roads that looked like drawings, the harbour flat and grey at the edge of everything.

She went and stood against it. Then she turned round and looked at the room.

“Three floors,” she said, to nobody. “Ridiculous.”

On the desk there was one photograph, in a plain frame: Ren Hao at about eighteen, with his arm round a much smaller girl in a school blazer, both squinting in sunlight, a lot of trees behind them. She picked it up.

“You’re snooping,” he said from the doorway.

He’d loosened his tie. He had a folder in his hand. He looked, for a second, tired, and then he saw her by his desk and didn’t.

“Everything all right?” she said.

“For now.”

She held up the photograph. “Isla?”

“The day I left for university.”

“She’s cute.”

“She’ll be pleased you said so.”

“You’re very fond of her.”

“She’s my sister.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“It’s the only one you’re getting,” he said, and came and took the photograph out of her hands and put it back exactly where it had been, at exactly the same angle, and she watched him do it and bit the inside of her cheek.

“Are you always this serious at work?” she said.

“Usually.”

“Even when people make jokes?”

“Depends on the joke.”

“You’re going to hate me here. I make a lot of jokes, and I don’t respect authority.”

He stepped closer. “That’s unfortunate.”

She tilted her head. “Are you going to discipline me?”

His eyes went slowly over her face. “Not in front of my staff.”

She laughed out loud, and he laughed too, and then he put his arms round her by the window and held on, and said into her hair, “Missed you,” again, as if he’d been saving it.

“You’re getting repetitive.”

“Is that a problem?”

She put her face against his shoulder. “Not yet.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By twenty to seven that evening, Song-Zhu had learned three things.

One: his office had an excellent view at every hour of the day, and the best one was at dusk, when the lights came on in the tower opposite floor by floor like somebody filling in a form.

Two: he was a great deal more patient with her than he was with his staff, although he had been patient with his staff, too, all afternoon, in a way they clearly didn’t believe and were waiting to be punished for.

Three: Joyce’s dog liked her better than it liked him.

This last had become a matter of personal pride. She had spent twenty minutes on the floor by Joyce’s desk while he took a call, and when he came to find her, Momo followed her all the way to the lift and sat down in front of the doors and refused to be called back.

“She’s attached to you,” said Joyce.

“Good taste,” said Song-Zhu.

Ren Hao looked down at the dog. “Traitor,” he said, with great tenderness.

The regional manager had been released at ten past four, alive, thinner, at a petrol station on a road with a number for a name, and the brother-in-law had rung the operations room afterwards and cried down the phone for three minutes and nobody in the room had said a word. Ren Hao had gone round the room afterwards and shaken every person’s hand, and then gone to his office and shut the door for a quarter of an hour, and when he came out he had sent everyone home.

Now it was nearly seven. The top floor had emptied. The lights over the empty desks had gone to their evening setting, and beyond the glass the city was turning blue.

He was standing at his desk going through a document. She was sitting on the edge of his meeting table, swinging one foot.

“Are you nearly done?”

“Nearly.”

“How nearly?”

“Ten minutes.”

“You said that twenty minutes ago.”

“I was interrupted.”

“By who?”

He gave her a look over the top of the page. She smiled innocently. He put the document down.

“All right.”

She sat up. “Really?”

“Really.”

He came round the desk. She looked at him, and then past him at the dark glass, and back. A slow smile.

“Your office is very nice.”

“Thank you.”

“Very private.”

“Is it?”

“Nearly.” She slid off the table. “Do you ever bring anyone in here?”

“Clients.”

“Apart from clients.”

“Staff.”

She stopped in front of him. “Ren Hao.”

“Song-Zhu.”

“You’re being difficult on purpose.”

“Am I?” he said, perfectly straight-faced, and she took hold of the front of his waistcoat in one fist the way she had at the taxi rank.

He looked down at her hand. “Careful.”

“Why?”

“You’ll undo it.”

She looked at the buttons. Six of them, small, horn, done up all the way. She looked back up at him.

“Maybe I want to.”

His face changed. Not by much. Just enough.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first kiss was hers. She pulled him down by the waistcoat before he could say anything sensible, and he made a sound into her mouth and his hand came to her waist, and he kissed her back slowly.

She disagreed. She tugged at the waistcoat with both hands. Something gave with a small sharp tick and went skittering across the floor.

He lifted his head. “That was a button.”

“Then you’d better take it off before I find the rest of them,” she said, and he laughed against her mouth, low and helpless, and she felt it all down her body.

“Impatient,” he said.

“Very.”

“I’d noticed.”

He caught her wrists, gently, when she reached for the jacket. “Let me.”

She raised an eyebrow. “Very commanding, Mr. Ren.”

“Would you rather do it yourself?”

She pretended to think about it. “No.”

He let her go and stepped back half a pace and took his jacket off and laid it over the back of the sofa. Then he started on the waistcoat, one button at a time, five of them, watching her face the whole time, and she watched his hands and forgot to be funny. The tie. The cufflinks, which he put on the desk, side by side. And then he came back to her in his shirtsleeves with his collar open, and the city behind him gone dark blue and full of lights, and she realised she was holding her breath.

“You’re staring,” he said.

“I’m appreciating.”

“Are you?”

“Enormously.”

He put both hands on her face and kissed her again, and this time it wasn’t slow at all.

He walked her backwards while he did it, three steps, four, until her shoulders met the window. The glass was cold through her blouse, and she gasped at it, and he stopped at once.

“Too cold?”

“No. Don’t you dare stop.”

He didn’t. He undid her blouse with the whole city behind her, one button and then the next, slowly enough that it was obviously on purpose, and when it was open he put his mouth to her throat, and then her collarbone, and she put her palms flat on the glass on either side of her because she had to hold on to something.

“Can anyone see?” she said, not much caring.

“Thirty-second floor. Tinted glass. They’d need a helicopter.”

“You’ve checked.”

“I check everything,” said Ren Hao, against her skin, and then, lower, in a voice she had never heard from him in any restaurant: “Do you want to know what I’m going to do first?”

Her breath went. “Tell me.”

So he told her. Quietly, plainly, the way he’d given instructions in the room with the screen: exactly, and in order, and with nothing left out. What he was going to take off her, and in which order. Where he was going to put his mouth. How long he intended to stay there. What he was going to do when she started to shake, and what he was going to do after that. It wasn’t a performance. It was a man who said what he meant, saying it to her, a foot from her face, with his hands on her waist, and every word of it went through her like current.

And then he did all of it. In that order.

He unzipped her trousers and drew them down her legs and she stepped out of them and her shoes at once, and he knelt in front of her on his own office carpet and kissed the inside of her knee, and then higher, and higher, until she was saying his name at the ceiling with her head back against the glass. He didn’t hurry. He had said he wouldn’t. He kept to the order he’d given her as if it were a contract, and when she tried to pull him up too soon he held her hips against the window and said, “Not yet. I told you what comes next,” and she laughed, and swore at him, and then couldn’t do either. She came with her hands spread flat on the cold glass and the whole lit city at her back and his name in her mouth, and he held her up through it, and afterwards he stayed where he was a moment longer with his forehead against her stomach, breathing as hard as she was.

Then he stood up. She pulled at his shirt with fingers that weren’t working properly, and the buttons were too small, and she gave up and dragged it up over his head, and he let her. His belt. The rest. She put her hand on him and his eyes closed.

“Now,” she said. “Now, Hao.”

He turned her round, gently, so she was facing the city, her palms on the window, and he stood behind her and kissed the back of her neck, and his hand came round and spread low on her stomach to hold her against him. And he took her slowly. So slowly she thought she would lose her mind. Telling her, all the way, what he was going to do and then doing it, every word a half-second ahead of his body, so that she knew exactly what was coming and still couldn’t bear it when it came. The glass fogged under her hands and cleared and fogged again. Somewhere in the tower opposite a cleaner was hoovering an empty floor, small and far away and lit, and Song-Zhu watched her through the haze of her own breath and didn’t care about anything at all.

“Tell me if it’s too much,” he said against her ear.

“It’s not enough.”

He laughed, a breath against her neck, and gave her more, and then more, and when she said his name in a voice that broke in the middle he stopped talking altogether. He came with his face pressed into her shoulder and one hand flat on the glass over hers, their fingers laced, and the sound he made was so unlike anything she had heard from him in a restaurant or a lobby or a room full of screens that she kept it, and took it home, and thought about it for a week.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards they lay on the sofa, which was too short for him, with his jacket over both of them like a blanket.

The city was all lights now. He had drawn the blinds halfway at some point, so that the bottom half of the window showed the two of them reflected, a tangle on dark leather, and the top half showed the towers and the sky.

“Your staff,” she said, into his chest, “would be devastated.”

“Why?”

“They think you’re terrifying.”

“Perhaps I am.”

She lifted her head and looked at him. “Not with me.”

He looked back at her a long time. “No,” he said. “Not with you.”

There was something in the way he said it that made her smile go away, and something softer come instead. She touched his face. Then she kissed him, and he kissed her back with his hand moving slowly up and down her spine, and when he lifted his head he looked at her.

“Song-Zhu.”

“Mm.”

“Was that all right? The glass.”

“It was so far beyond all right that I’d like it in writing.”

He laughed. “Tell me if I ever do something you don’t want.”

“I will.”

“Even in the middle.”

“Even in the middle,” she said. “I’ll tell you. I’ll probably shout it.”

He nodded, as if a term had been agreed.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty-five to nine she was sitting on his sofa in her blouse, buttoned wrong, with her hair completely destroyed and her lipstick nowhere at all, watching Ren Hao stand in front of the mirror by his door and try to rescue his shirt. She started laughing.

He looked at her in the mirror. “What?”

“Your appearance.”

He looked down at himself. The shirt was creased from collar to hem. His hair was doing something it had clearly never been allowed to do before. One side of his collar was folded inwards.

“You’re very pleased with yourself,” he said.

“Extremely.”

He came over and bent and kissed her. She ran a finger along his collar and turned it the right way out.

“You’ll have to fix your tie.”

“I’m not putting it back on.”

“And your hair.”

“Song-Zhu.”

“And there’s a button somewhere under your desk. Off a waistcoat that was made in a shop with no sign.”

He looked at her. “I’ll find it tomorrow.”

“I’ll find it now,” she said, and got down on her hands and knees on his carpet and found it in under a minute, under the radiator, and held it up to him between finger and thumb like a recovered component. “Here. Logged. Chain of custody.”

He took it from her and looked at it, and at her, kneeling on his floor in a blouse buttoned wrong with his button in her hand, and put it in his trouser pocket carefully, the way she’d held the recorder in the field.

“Dinner,” she said, getting up. “I want dinner. And dessert. And I want to go somewhere you don’t have to be Mr. Ren.”

“Where would you like?”

She thought about it. “Somewhere with noodles.”

“Again?”

“Always.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In the lift on the way down she leaned against the wall with her hand in his.

“Can I ask you something?”

“Of course.”

“Do you actually love your job?”

He thought about it. “Most of the time.”

“Even the terrible parts?”

“Sometimes because of them.” He looked at the numbers going down. “People only ring us when something’s already gone wrong. We can’t always stop it. But we can help them understand what happens next. Some things are just bad. Some people make choices that hurt other people. Sometimes the most we can do is make the damage smaller.”

She was looking at his face. “You sound like me.”

“Perhaps.”

“Do you get tired of it? Fixing things?”

“Sometimes.”

She was quiet for a floor or two. Then: “Well. Don’t try to fix me.”

“I know.”

The doors opened on the lobby, empty now, Ruby’s desk dark with a slice of birthday cake on a plate under a napkin on the corner of it, clearly left for somebody. He let her go out first. And then, as they crossed the atrium, he said, “But I do reserve the right to buy you lunch.”

She laughed so much the security guard looked up. “That’s not fixing me.”

“No.”

“And no more wet wipes.”

“We’ll see,” said Ren Hao.

✦ ✦ ✦

At a quarter to ten, at a noodle shop with plastic stools by the ferry pier, his phone buzzed.

Joyce (and Momo): Mr. Ren, Momo is sitting outside your office again.

He looked at the message, and then across the table at Song-Zhu, who was eating his noodles because she’d finished her own.

Ren Hao: Tell her I’ll see her on Monday.

Joyce (and Momo): She’s not waiting for you. She’s waiting for Miss Xu.

He turned the screen round and showed her. Song-Zhu gasped with delight.

“She’s waiting for me.”

“She’s waiting for food.”

“Don’t be jealous.”

“I’m not jealous of a dog.”

“She loves me,” said Song-Zhu, with deep satisfaction.

“She loves everybody.”

“She does not. She hates Raymond.”

He laughed, and she leaned across the table and kissed his cheek with noodle broth on her mouth, and went back to his bowl.

“Do you know what I found out today?” she said.

“What?”

“You’re not half as frightening as everyone thinks.”

“Is that so.”

“Mm.”

“That’s a shame.” He reached across the table and caught her hand. “I quite like being frightening.”

“You can be frightening on Monday,” she said, and squeezed his fingers. “Tonight you’re just Hao.”

He looked at her a moment. Then he lifted her hand and put his mouth to her knuckles.

And for the rest of the evening, that was exactly who he was.

chapters.title: Hooked
chapters.desc: He can’t stop. His driver follows her taxi for nine nights. She notices the plate, does the biscuit test, and laughs, which is worse. He fires Mr. Yau; she makes him rehire him with a raise.
chapters.epigraph: “Well. You do. But I like you anyway.”
chapters.content:
By the middle of July, Ren Hao had a problem.

It wasn’t a complicated problem. He understood its cause, its symptoms, and roughly what a solution would look like. He simply had no intention of applying one.

The problem was Xu Song-Zhu. More exactly, the problem was that she could vanish for fourteen hours, send him a voice note containing thirty seconds of engine noise and one cheerful sentence at the end, and improve his entire day. He had become humiliatingly easy to please.

At eighteen minutes to seven on Monday morning, a photograph arrived: a paper cup of coffee balanced on the wing of an aircraft, with the sun coming up behind it.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Breakfast.

Ren Hao: That’s coffee.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Very observant. Are you a detective?

Ren Hao: Have you eaten?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I’m drinking coffee.

Ren Hao: That isn’t eating.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): You sound like my mother.

Ren Hao: Your mother sounds sensible.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Don’t. It’s too early.

Across the breakfast table at his flat, Joyce, who had come round with the week’s papers because he had a seven o’clock call, was reading his diary aloud.

“Your half past eight’s moved to nine.”

“All right.”

“The revised report’s ready for you.”

“Good.”

She waited. He was still looking at his phone.

“Is there anything else?” he said.

“No, Mr. Ren.”

“Thank you.”

The phone buzzed again.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): There’s a cat here.

A photograph. A small, extremely ginger cat sitting beside a red toolbox with the expression of someone who has been sent the wrong file.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): He’s supervising. His name is Chairman.

Ren Hao: Is he being paid properly?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): He gets fish.

Ren Hao: Fair compensation.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): And unlike some people, he doesn’t ask me if I’ve eaten every twenty minutes.

Ren Hao put his coffee down.

Ren Hao: Have you?

The dots appeared. Disappeared. Appeared.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I hate you.

He smiled at the screen for so long that Joyce gathered up the papers and left him to it. He suspected that wasn’t entirely true.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first hangar had been an accident. The second had been an excuse. By the third, even Mr. Yau had stopped asking why they were going there.

Ren Hao told himself he was visiting a client. The client in question was a maintenance contractor whose risk assessment his firm had finished in June, and which wasn’t expecting a visit from the managing director on a Tuesday afternoon, or ever. Neither was Song-Zhu.

She was standing by the engine of a cargo aircraft on a stand, with a clipboard under her arm, listening to a technician explain something about a bearing. Hair tied back. A dark blue work shirt, practical trousers, boots. A thumbprint of grease on her cheekbone.

He stood in the hangar door for several seconds without moving.

He had been in the middle of an argument with a senior partner when he’d decided to leave the office. He had been thinking about her since lunch. He had promised himself ten minutes.

Then she looked up, and saw him, and smiled, and the argument with the senior partner stopped existing.

“Ren Hao?”

He lifted a hand. “Hello.”

She looked at the technician, and back. “What are you doing here?”

“Working.”

She looked round the hangar. “Here?”

“Nearby.”

“How nearby?”

He considered it. “Near enough.”

She laughed. The technician looked between the two of them with interest. “Your boyfriend?”

Song-Zhu’s eyebrows went up. Ren Hao said nothing whatsoever. She looked at him. He looked back at her.

“He’s a visitor,” she told the technician.

“Right,” said the technician. “Visitor.”

When the man had gone she came across to him with the clipboard against her chest. “You know, if you keep turning up at my work, people will start thinking you’ve got a hobby.”

“I have.”

“What is it?”

He looked down at her. “You.”

“That’s not a hobby, that’s a symptom.”

“You’re very difficult to fit into a diary.”

“Good,” she said, and reached up and wiped a smear of grease off his sleeve that she had put there herself, a second earlier, with her thumb. “Now you’re dirty. Now you belong here. Coffee? The machine makes something that’s legally coffee.”

He went with her. And when she reached back for his hand without looking, he took it without thinking about it at all.

The visit after that wasn’t an accident either. It was a briefing: his firm had been asked to sit in on a safety and security review for a ground-handling contractor at the airport, and the meeting room happened to be in the same building as the investigators’ office. He finished at quarter past four. At seventeen minutes past he messaged her.

Ren Hao: Are you still in the building?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Unfortunately.

Ren Hao: Where?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Why?

Ren Hao: I’d like to see you.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): That’s very direct.

Ren Hao: It was a direct question.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Second floor. Don’t interrupt.

He found her at a desk with two colleagues, one hand holding a pen and the other propping her cheek, frowning at a long document full of times. He stood behind her chair. She knew he was there before she saw him.

“Don’t.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“You’re standing there. Loudly.”

“Would you rather I sat?”

She looked up, finally, and her mouth went sideways. He pulled a chair over and sat beside her.

For twenty minutes he watched her work. He didn’t understand most of what was on her screen. But he liked the way she frowned at it, and the way she tapped the end of her pen on her thumb, and the way she murmured a sentence to herself under her breath before she typed it, as if checking that it sounded true. She was quick. She was meticulous. When one of her colleagues disagreed with her about a timing, she listened all the way to the end before she answered, and then she was right.

She didn’t need to be the loudest person in a room. She only needed to be correct.

When she closed the document she turned her chair round to face him. “You’re still here?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“I told you why.”

She looked at him, and shook her head, smiling. “You’ll get bored.”

“I doubt it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By the end of the week, Joyce had learned not to ask why he was leaving the office early. Mr. Yau had learned the same thing. The only person who hadn’t learned anything was Ren Hao, who remained convinced that he was being discreet. He wasn’t being discreet.

Mr. Yau had driven for the firm for six years. He was dependable, quiet, and good at knowing what Ren Hao wanted before Ren Hao had finished deciding to want it. He also noticed things, and wrote them down in a small black notebook he kept in the glovebox, a habit from an earlier job he didn’t talk about.

On Monday he noticed that Mr. Ren had asked for the long way back from a client, past the airport’s operational compound.

On Tuesday he noticed that Mr. Ren had cancelled a dinner seven minutes after receiving a voice note.

On Wednesday he noticed that Mr. Ren had asked him to wait outside a hangar for forty-five minutes.

On Thursday, at ten past eleven at night, Mr. Ren rang him at home and asked him to follow a taxi.

Not a company car, not a client’s car. A taxi.

Mr. Yau, who was in his slippers, put down his tea.

“Sir?”

“She’s leaving the compound now. Her phone’s nearly out of charge. I’d like to know she gets home.”

There was a pause long enough to have a whole opinion in it.

“Understood, sir.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Ren Hao had his reasons, and they were good ones, and he went over them all on Thursday night in his flat while he waited for a message.

Her hours had no shape. She sometimes left a site long after midnight, too tired to notice how late it had got. She had mentioned, as a joke, a taxi breaking down on the expressway at one in the morning and the driver suggesting she walk. She had mentioned, as another joke, a driver who’d taken a route she didn’t recognise and talked the whole way about his ex-wife. He knew the numbers on what happened to women alone in cars at night in every city his firm worked in, because it was his job to know them.

He had imagined a dozen small things going wrong. And then, without quite deciding to, he had arranged for one of them not to.

He didn’t consider it surveillance. He considered it a precaution.

That distinction, he was going to discover, existed entirely inside his own head. At ten to midnight his phone buzzed.

Mr. Yau (Wheels): Miss Xu has arrived home safely, sir.

Ren Hao: Thank you.

Then, a minute later, as if from a different man:

Ren Hao: Home?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Alive. Battery 2%. Night x

He looked at the x for some time.

He told himself he would stop after two or three nights. Then there was another late shift, and another. By the second Wednesday it had become part of the end of his day: dinner, the last emails, a message from Mr. Yau, and then a message to her. He was learning to read her moods from her punctuation. A full stop meant she was tired. An exclamation mark meant she was amused. Three question marks meant he’d said something stupid. No punctuation at all meant she was eating.

He had got good at reading her. He hadn’t yet got good at understanding her.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was in a meeting when the last one came: six people in the boardroom on the thirty-second floor, a slide deck about a response strategy for a client with a factory fire, a director halfway through a sentence.

Mr. Yau (Wheels): Miss Xu has arrived home safely, sir.

Ren Hao: Thank you.

“Mr. Ren?”

He looked up. “Go on.”

“We were on the second option.”

“Go on,” he said again, and put the phone away, and the meeting went on.

A little before midnight, at home, he had just taken off his watch when she rang.

“Hello,” he said.

“Hello, Mr. Ren.”

Her voice was suspiciously cheerful. He smiled anyway. “Hello, Miss Xu.”

“Are you busy?”

“No.”

“Good.”

He sat down on the edge of his bed and undid his collar. “Is something wrong?”

“Nothing’s wrong.”

He waited.

A tiny laugh came down the line. “You’re very trusting.”

“Should I be worried?”

“Probably.” And then, lightly, as if she were asking him to pass the salt: “Do you know a Mr. Yau?”

Ren Hao went entirely still. One second. Two.

“Yes,” he said.

“Your driver?”

He shut his eyes. “Yes.”

“Lovely man,” said Song-Zhu.

He said nothing at all. And she laughed. Not angrily, not even especially offended. She sounded genuinely, profoundly delighted. Which was much worse.

“Song-Zhu.”

“Yes?”

“Where are you?”

“At home. Where else would I be? Mr. Yau’s just told you.”

He put his free hand over his face.

“He’s very professional,” she said. “He hasn’t said a word to me all week. That’s the funny part. He just keeps being there.”

“Being there.”

“Well. Following.” He could hear her settling into a chair, getting comfortable for this. “I noticed on Tuesday. A grey saloon, no company badge, two cars back on the expressway. I thought it was a coincidence. Then Wednesday, same car. Thursday, same car. So I wrote the plate down in my notebook, because I’m a professional, and today I tested my theory.”

His stomach turned over. “How?”

“I changed my route. I asked the taxi to go round by the old fish market, which nobody goes round by, ever. And there he was.” She was laughing again. “Then I went into a convenience store and bought a packet of biscuits and came out of the other door onto the other street. And he was waiting on the corner across the road. He’d worked it out. He’s good, Hao. Where did you find him?”

“Did he approach you?”

“No. I approached him. I knocked on his window and asked him if he’d like a biscuit.”

Ren Hao made a sound he hadn’t made since he was fourteen.

“He said no thank you, miss,” said Song-Zhu. “Very polite. And then I asked for his card, and he gave it to me, because I think he’d decided it wasn’t worth lying, and I said I’d sort it out with his boss. And now I’m sorting it out with his boss.”

“Did he frighten you?”

“No.”

“You’re sure?”

“Hao.”

He stopped. She was still smiling. He could hear it. But there was something under it now.

“Why?” she said.

He didn’t have an answer ready, which wasn’t a thing that happened to him.

He could have said that he worried. That her hours were impossible. That he knew, professionally, what the world was like for a woman in a taxi on her own at one in the morning. All of it was true. None of it answered what she’d asked.

“I wanted to know you got home safely,” he said.

She was quiet.

“You could have asked me.”

“I do ask.”

“Yes. And I tell you.”

“I know.”

“Then why the driver?”

He rubbed his thumb along his eyebrow. “I thought it would be better to make sure.”

She let out a small laugh. It wasn’t amused, this time.

“Ren Hao.”

“Yes.”

“I’m not a confidential package.”

He looked at the floor. “I know.”

“Do you?”

He didn’t answer straight away.

She sighed. And then, to his astonishment, she laughed again. “Oh my God. You actually put a tail on me.”

He winced. “Please don’t call it that.”

“What should I call it?”

“An arrangement.”

“An arrangement.” She was laughing so hard now he could hear her trying to breathe. “You had me followed home for nine nights and you want to call it an arrangement.”

He lay back on the bed and looked at the ceiling. He had negotiated with hostile boards and talked a frightened man down from a ledge on the seventeenth floor of a hotel and spent whole nights co-ordinating people who were trying hard not to panic. He had never in his life been as completely defeated as he was by one woman laughing at him down the phone.

“I’ll stop it,” he said.

“Good.”

“I’ll tell him tomorrow.”

“No, don’t.”

He frowned at the ceiling. “Don’t?”

“Not tomorrow. Tomorrow’s Saturday. The poor man’s followed my taxi for nine nights in his own time. Let him have a lie-in.”

“You’re defending him?”

“Of course I’m defending him. He didn’t ask to be your romantic security detail.”

“Song-Zhu.”

“Yes, darling?”

“You’re enjoying this.”

“Enormously.”

He laughed despite himself, and she heard him, and her voice came down out of the laughter into something quieter.

“Listen. I know you worry. And I like that you care. I really do. But you have to let me decide what I need. If I want someone to pick me up, I’ll ask. If I need help, I’ll tell you. I’m not going to get into the wrong car to prove a point. I’m twenty-five and I take apart aeroplanes.”

“I understand.”

“Do you?” she said.

He thought about it before he answered, which she noticed. “Yes.”

A pause. “Good. And tell Mr. Yau I said thank you.”

“You’re thanking him?”

“He got me home, didn’t he?”

“Song-Zhu.”

“Good night, handsome,” she said, and rang off.

He lay there a long time with the phone on his chest. Then he rang his driver.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday morning Mr. Yau was in Ren Hao’s office at eight o’clock exactly, in a pressed jacket, with his notebook in his inside pocket.

“Sit down, please.”

Mr. Yau sat.

Ren Hao folded his hands on the desk. “I owe you an apology.”

Mr. Yau looked genuinely surprised. “Sir?”

“I asked you to follow Miss Xu’s taxi. It was outside your job and it was wrong of me. The responsibility is entirely mine.”

“I was following an instruction, sir.”

“I know. That’s why it’s mine.” He paused. “She knows.”

“Ah,” said Mr. Yau. “Yes. She does.”

“She wasn’t pleased.”

“Understandable, sir.”

“I won’t ask you to do anything like it again.”

“Very good, sir.”

There was a silence. Then Ren Hao opened a drawer and took out a single sheet of paper, and said, “I think it’s best if you leave the firm.”

For the first time that morning, Mr. Yau looked alarmed.

“Not because of your work,” said Ren Hao. “Your work’s been flawless for six years. Because I put you in a position you should never have been put in, and I don’t want you carrying the weight of my private decisions round in your glovebox. You’ll have a full year’s salary and the best reference I’ve ever written.”

Mr. Yau looked at the paper, and at him.

“Sir. With respect. I don’t think that’s necessary.”

“You’re not being dismissed for doing what you were told.”

“Then what for?”

“So that you’re never in a position where you feel you have to do something like it again.”

Mr. Yau considered that. Then, carefully: “I understand your concern for Miss Xu, sir.”

Ren Hao looked out of the window. “That’s not relevant.”

“No, sir,” said Mr. Yau, and stood up. “Thank you for the opportunity, Mr. Ren.”

Ren Hao picked up his pen to sign, and his phone rang.

Song-Zhu.

“Good morning,” he said.

“Good morning. Have you sacked Mr. Yau?”

He shut his eyes. “How do you know that?”

“Because I rang him. To ask how he was.”

He opened his eyes again. “You rang him.”

“I had his card, didn’t I? I said I’d sort it out. He said you’d asked him in for a conversation, and he sounded like a man walking to the gallows.” A pause. “Have you?”

“Not yet.”

“Yet.”

“I was going to.”

“Why?”

“Because I put him in an impossible position.”

She was quiet for a second. Then: “Hao. You’re being ridiculous again.”

He laughed once, with no humour in it. “I know.”

“Did he do anything wrong?”

“No.”

“Was he rude to me?”

“No.”

“Did he frighten me?”

“No.”

“Then why are you punishing him?”

“I’m not punishing him.”

“You’re sacking him. For your mistake.” Her voice was clear now. “You made a stupid decision. You’re allowed to apologise for it without making somebody else lose his job. That’s not taking responsibility, that’s moving it onto him and calling it generous.”

He looked at the door. Mr. Yau was standing just outside it in the corridor, straight, studying a fire-safety notice.

“I understand,” he said.

“Do you, though?”

“I’m starting to.”

“Good. Keep him.”

“Song-Zhu—”

“And give him a pay rise.”

“Absolutely not.”

“Why not?”

“Because you don’t negotiate my payroll.”

“I’d be very good at it.”

“You would not.”

“I’d be excellent at it.” She was smiling again. “You’ve already decided, haven’t you.”

He looked at the sheet of paper on his desk. “Have a good day, Song-Zhu.”

“You too, darling,” she said, and rang off.

He tore the sheet in half, and then in half again, and put it in the bin.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Come back in, please, Mr. Yau.”

Mr. Yau came back in and sat down again.

“I’ve reconsidered,” said Ren Hao. “Your job is unchanged. Your duties are unchanged. The additional arrangement ends here, permanently. And your salary goes up from next month.”

Mr. Yau looked at him. “May I ask why, sir?”

“Because you did your job well, and then you did something that wasn’t your job well too, because I asked you to, and handled it better than I did. You shouldn’t pay for my bad judgement. I should.” He picked up his pen. “And if Miss Xu rings you again, you may answer.”

“Of course, sir.” Mr. Yau stood. At the door he stopped, and after a moment, with great care, he said, “She’s a very nice young woman, sir. She bought me biscuits. I’ve still got them in the car.”

Ren Hao stared at him. Then he laughed out loud.

“Get out, Mr. Yau.”

Mr. Yau, smiling slightly, got out.

✦ ✦ ✦

She rang that evening. He was still at his desk.

“Did you keep him?”

“Yes.”

“With a rise?”

“Yes.”

“Excellent.” She sounded deeply satisfied. “And did you apologise? Properly? Not one of your board apologies.”

“Properly.”

“Good.”

He leaned back. “Are you going to review all my management decisions now?”

“Only the ones involving my taxi.” She paused. “Actually, I’ve got a question. A real one.”

“Go on.”

“Why didn’t you just tell me you were worried?”

He went quiet. Outside his window the evening traffic moved in long slow ropes of light.

On his desk, beside the photograph of him and Isla, there was a new one. Joyce had found it on the firm’s social account, from a client dinner the week before, and printed it and put it there without a word: Song-Zhu at a restaurant table laughing at something out of the frame, and him beside her, not laughing, looking at her. He hadn’t known anyone had taken it.

“I don’t know,” he said at last. “I suppose I thought that if I could make sure you were safe, I wouldn’t have to bother you with it.”

“You don’t bother me when you worry, Hao.” A pause. “Well. You do. But I like you anyway.”

“How generous.”

“Very.” And then: “I’d rather you told me than arranged me. Do you understand the difference?”

He thought about it, properly. “I think I’m starting to.”

“Good. And if you want someone to pick me up—”

“I’ll ask you.”

“You’ll ask me.”

“And you’ll say no.”

“Probably,” said Song-Zhu. “But sometimes I’ll say yes. And then it’ll be because I wanted it.” She was quiet a second. “You know you’re allowed to miss me without organising a transport operation?”

“Am I?” he said.

“Yes,” she said, and kissed him to prove it.

“That’s a relief.”

“Poor Mr. Yau. Reporting my arrival every night like a weather forecast.”

“He was very efficient.”

“Don’t encourage him.” And then, quieter, as if she’d only just decided to say it: “I miss you too.”

He stopped moving. It was such a plain sentence. She’d said it the way she’d have told him the weather. As if she had no idea what it did to him.

“When can I see you?” he said.

“Tomorrow. There’s a noodle place by the ferry pier. I want noodles.”

“You always want noodles.”

“And you’re not allowed to send a car.”

“I’ll take a taxi.”

“Good.”

“Will you be there?”

“Maybe.”

“Maybe?”

“You’ll have to come and find out.” He could hear her smiling. “Without anyone following me.”

He looked at the clock, and at the report he hadn’t finished, and closed it.

“You’re stopping work?” she said, hearing it.

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because I miss you.”

A silence, and then a small, pleased laugh. “There. Was that so hard?”

“Extremely.”

“Good night, Hao.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He got there just after seven on Sunday. She was already at a table by the window in a pale blue shirt with the sleeves rolled up, and when she saw him she smiled, and he bent and kissed her cheek before he sat down.

“Did you come on your own?”

“Yes.”

“Nobody behind a lamp post?”

“Nobody.”

“Excellent.” She pushed a menu at him. “I’ve ordered. You can choose dessert. I’m very generous.”

And then, from the bag by her feet, she took out a small paper bag and put it on the table between them. He opened it. Inside was a packet of biscuits, the same brand, the same flavour, from the same convenience store.

“For your driver,” she said sweetly. “He gave his to the security guard at your building. I checked.”

Ren Hao looked at the biscuits. And then he laughed so loudly that the man at the next table dropped his chopsticks.

“You’re unbelievable.”

“I know.”

He put the biscuits carefully to one side and reached across the table and took her hand, and she let him.

For a long time they sat like that, talking about her week, his meetings, a coffee machine at the hangar that had finally died with dignity, a client of his who had tried to negotiate a deadline with the confidence of a man who’d never read his own contract. She laughed. He listened. She stole his pickles.

And somewhere between the noodles and the dessert, Ren Hao understood something.

He had spent nine nights making sure he knew where she was. And the thing he actually wanted was much simpler than that, and much harder.

He wanted her to tell him. Not because she had to. Because she wanted to. He squeezed her hand.

She looked at their hands, and then up at him. “You’re doing that face.”

“Which one?”

“The one where you’ve just decided something.”

“I have.”

“Should I be worried?”

“No.”

“What is it?”

He lifted her hand and kissed her knuckles. “I’m going to keep missing you. Out loud.”

She stared at him. “That’s your big decision?”

“Yes.”

“Very impressive.”

“I thought so.”

She shook her head, and leaned across the table, and kissed him: quick and warm and on purpose. When she sat back he was smiling.

“Better than following my taxi?” she said.

“Much.”

“Good,” said Song-Zhu, and went back to her noodles.

He watched her a while. He was, he realised, entirely and rather helplessly hooked.

And the worst part was that she knew it. She knew it, and she was having a wonderful time.

chapters.title: The Schedule
chapters.desc: He makes her a colour-coded week. She burns it in the sink. The fight ends against the sink and then on her sofa, explicit, laughing, over the laundry he doesn’t mention.
chapters.epigraph: “Because I don’t want you to run my life.”
chapters.content:
Ren Hao had made a mistake. It was a beautiful mistake. A meticulous, colour-coded, professionally formatted mistake, printed on heavy cream paper, three pages long, in a navy folder with a clear plastic cover.

He had spent three evenings on it. He had taken into account her working hours, as far as anyone could know them; her briefings; her site visits, which came without warning; her journey to the compound; her eating habits, which frankly required intervention; and the fact that she sometimes forgot to sleep when a case got interesting. He had even left blank spaces. He thought the blank spaces were generous.

At twenty-three minutes past ten on Saturday the ninth of August, he arrived at her flat with the folder under one arm and a bag of groceries in the other. At twenty-four minutes past, she opened the door.

She was barefoot, with her hair clipped up in a way that had clearly happened by accident, in an enormous T-shirt with a faded cartoon rabbit on the front. She looked at the folder. Then at him.

“What’s that?”

“Good morning.”

“What’s in the folder, Hao?”

“Something I made.”

She narrowed her eyes. “Is it legal?”

He laughed. “Yes.”

“Is it expensive?”

“Not especially.”

“Is it about me?”

He smiled. “Yes.”

She looked at him for another long second, as if deciding whether to let a known hazard into the building. Then she stood aside.

“Come in. I already regret this.”

He kissed her cheek on the way past. “You’re welcome.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Her flat was small. A living room with a sofa that had seen things, a kitchen open to it along one wall, one bedroom, and a narrow balcony looking at the back of the next building, where someone kept a great many orchids. There were books in stacks by the sofa, not on shelves. A jacket over a dining chair. Three mugs on the coffee table in three stages of abandonment. A laundry basket in the hall, overflowing, and beside it, on the floor, a heap of clean clothes that hadn’t yet made it into anything, and one sock that had escaped altogether and was lying on its own in the doorway like a casualty.

Ren Hao noticed all of it. He said nothing at all.

She took the groceries into the kitchen. “Coffee?”

“Please.”

“Make it yourself.”

He looked at her.

“You’re in my house,” she said. “I’m the host. Hosts delegate.”

“Understood.”

While he worked out which of her cupboards held mugs and which held, apparently, only lids, she sat on the arm of the sofa and opened the folder. And stopped.

XU SONG-ZHU · WEEKLY ROUTINE (DRAFT)

Underneath it was a week. Monday in pale blue. Tuesday in green. Wednesday in a soft yellow. Blocks for meals, for work, for travel, for rest, for exercise, and one, every day, in a careful lilac, labelled personal time.

She stared at it. She turned the page. Another table. She turned it again. And at the bottom of the third page, in a small, beautifully aligned box with a hairline border, a note:

Flexible adjustments may be made in line with operational requirements.

She slowly lowered the folder.

“Hao?”

He came out of the kitchen with two mugs. “Yes?”

“What is this?”

He put her coffee on the table in front of her. “Your schedule.”

She looked at him. At the folder. Back at him.

“My what?”

“A weekly schedule. A draft.”

“Why?”

“Because your hours are irregular,” he said, reasonably, “and you forget to eat.”

She stared at him. He went on, entirely unaware that he was standing on something that was about to go off.

“I’ve built in room to change it. Your work can’t be predicted, I know that, so it’s flexible.”

She pointed at a block. “What’s this?”

“Tuesday.”

“I know what Tuesday is, Hao.”

“Then—”

“Why is there a lunch box on Tuesday?”

“Because you should eat lunch on Tuesday.”

“And why is there a rest box?”

“Because you should rest.”

She looked up slowly. “Am I a person,” she said, “or a department?”

He laughed. “You’re a person.”

“Then why have I got opening hours?”

He came and sat beside her on the sofa. “I thought it might help.”

She turned another page. “Why is Thursday pink?”

“That’s your lighter day. Usually.”

“Why is Saturday orange?”

“Because you usually work Saturdays.”

“And what’s this?” She put her finger on a long empty box at the end of Saturday.

He leaned over. “That’s for us.”

She went quiet. “For us,” she repeated.

“I thought we could keep Saturday evenings.”

She looked at the box. Then she shut the folder, gently, and put it on her knees.

“Ren Hao.”

“Yes?”

“Can you hear yourself?”

He looked genuinely puzzled. “Why?”

She stood up. “No reason.”

He watched her walk into the kitchen with the folder. “Song-Zhu?”

She opened a drawer, and took out the long-nosed lighter she used for the hob, which hadn’t sparked on its own since spring.

He frowned. “What are you doing?”

She took the first page out of the plastic sleeve. Then the second. Then the third.

“Song-Zhu.”

She ran the tap, a little, so the sink was wet.

He stood up. “Wait.”

She held the corner of Monday over the sink, and clicked the lighter.

A small blue flame caught the cream paper and turned orange and began, neatly, to climb.

Ren Hao stared. For one long second neither of them moved. Then she dropped all three pages into the wet sink together, and they flared, and curled, and Tuesday went brown and Wednesday went black and the lilac boxes marked personal time went up in a little rush of light, and she turned the tap on full, and it was all over in a hiss and a smell of smoke and wet ash.

She looked at him across the kitchen.

“Flexible adjustments,” she said.

He shut his eyes. “Oh my God.”

She started to laugh.

✦ ✦ ✦

He wasn’t angry. That was the first thing she noticed.

He stood in her kitchen looking at the soggy black remains of three evenings’ work, and his face was hard to read. Not offended, not quite amused. Mainly bewildered, like a man who had pressed a button and watched the lift go sideways.

She dried her hands on a tea towel. “Don’t look like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like I’ve drowned your firstborn.”

“You’ve burned three evenings.”

“You made me a timetable.”

“I made you a schedule.”

“That’s worse.”

He looked at her. “I was trying to help.”

“I know.”

“Then why did you set it on fire?”

She leaned back against the counter.

“Because I don’t want you to run my life.”

His face changed. Only a little. “I wasn’t trying to run your life.”

“Hao.”

“I wasn’t.”

She looked at him, and saw that he meant it, and that he was trying, really trying, to explain himself. And she knew he cared. That was the whole trouble. He cared so much that he sometimes forgot there was a difference between looking after someone and organising them.

She made her voice softer. “I know you worry about me.”

“I do.”

“I know you want me to eat and sleep and not spend sixteen hours in a room listening to other people’s worst moments.”

“That seems a reasonable thing to want.”

“It is. But I don’t want to be one more project on your desk.”

He looked at her, and then at the sink, where the ash had settled into a dark wet mess around the plughole.

“You’re not a project.”

“Then don’t give me opening hours.”

He let out a breath. “All right.”

She studied him. “All right?”

“Yes.”

“You’re not going to argue?”

“I don’t think I can win an argument with someone who sets fire to the evidence.”

She burst out laughing. He tried hard to keep his face straight and lost. She held out her hand, and he took it, and she pulled him across the kitchen and put her arms round his waist, and he held her and rested his chin on her head. For a moment it was quiet.

Then he said, into her hair, “I did leave you a blank evening.”

She lifted her head. “What?”

“Saturday. It was blank. Completely.”

She stared at him, and then started to laugh again. “Oh, you’re unbelievable.”

“I thought you’d appreciate the flexibility.”

She shoved his chest. He caught her hand. And that was when the argument became something else.

✦ ✦ ✦

It happened because she was still laughing, and he was still holding her hand, and he was looking at her with that patient, slightly helpless expression that always made her want to kiss him until he forgot whatever sensible thing he’d been about to say.

She took a step closer. He looked down at her, and something in his face went still.

“You’re planning something,” he said.

“Maybe.”

She took hold of the front of his shirt with her wet hand.

“Should I be worried?”

“Very.”

She kissed him. He answered at once, his free hand coming to her waist, and she leaned back against the edge of the sink and pulled him with her. It was warm and familiar and still had a little of the fight left in it. She could feel it in the way he held her: a fraction harder than usual, a half-second’s pause before he kissed her again.

She drew back an inch. “Still cross?”

“No.”

“Sure?”

“Yes.”

“Because I can burn the folder too.”

He laughed against her mouth, and kissed her again, and this time he was smiling. Her hands went up his chest to his shoulders, leaving damp prints on his shirt, and when she touched his face her fingers were still wet from the tap and smelled faintly of smoke.

He looked at her hand on his cheek. “You’re wet.”

“Your fault.”

“How is it my fault?”

“Your schedule caused a domestic incident.”

He kissed her palm. She kissed the corner of his mouth, and then his jaw, and then his mouth again, and his hand went flat against the small of her back and pulled her off the sink and against him.

“Are we still arguing?” he said.

“I haven’t decided.”

“Take your time.”

She bit his lower lip, and he made a low sound, and stopped asking questions.

✦ ✦ ✦

A few minutes later he discovered that there was a considerable difference between visiting her flat and trying to cross it with his eyes shut.

He’d been trying to get them both towards the sofa without either of them letting go when his foot caught the laundry basket and he nearly went down. He looked at the basket. He looked at the heap of clean clothes beside it on the floor, which came up to his shin. He looked at her.

She was watching him with great interest, waiting to see what he’d say. He said nothing at all.

“Careful,” said Song-Zhu.

“Thank you.”

Then, without any warning whatsoever, he picked her up.

She shrieked, and laughed, and grabbed his shoulders with both hands. “Hao!”

“Yes?”

“Put me down!”

“Why?”

“Because you’re carrying me!”

“I’d noticed.”

She was laughing too hard to argue. He settled her higher against his chest, her legs round his waist, and looked at the heap between them and the sofa, and stepped over it, the whole of it, the shirts and the towels and the escaped sock, without looking down and without a single word, like a man crossing a stream he’d crossed every day of his life.

“You’re very good at obstacles,” she said into his neck.

“I have excellent spatial awareness.”

“Congratulations.”

“Thank you.”

He put her down on the sofa, which complained, and stood over her, breathing a little harder than he would have admitted. His hair had come out of place. His shirt had her wet handprints on it. She reached up and pushed a piece of hair off his forehead.

“You’re handsome,” she said. “Even when you’re carrying me over the laundry.”

“Most of all then,” said Ren Hao, and kissed her.

✦ ✦ ✦

The sofa wasn’t built for two people to forget the rest of the world on. It was too narrow. One of the cushions kept sliding. She complained about it twice. He ignored the cushion both times, and then took it and threw it across the room without looking where it went.

She was laughing when she pulled his shirt up over his head. She was still laughing when he got her T-shirt off, the rabbit and all, and put his mouth on her breast, and then she wasn’t.

Her hands went into his hair. He kissed his way down her stomach and she lifted her hips so he could drag her shorts down, and he did, and knelt on her floor between her knees and pulled her to the edge of the cushions by her thighs, not gently, and she gasped and said his name in a way that had a laugh at the back of it and then no laugh at all. He was rough with her because she wanted him to be, and she told him so, and he listened. She held onto the back of the sofa with one hand and his hair with the other and came with her heel digging into his shoulder and her head thrown back against a cushion that was halfway to the floor.

Then she sat up, flushed, her hair everywhere, and pushed him back by the shoulders until he was the one sitting on the sofa, and climbed into his lap.

“My turn,” she said.

He looked up at her. “Is that on the schedule?”

“The schedule’s in the sink.”

“So it is,” he said, and she undid his belt and his trousers and he lifted his hips to let her pull them down, and she took him in her hand and watched his face change, and then she sank down onto him, slowly, all the way, until he swore under his breath in a language she didn’t know he spoke.

She rode him on her terrible sofa in the middle of a Saturday morning with the sun coming in through the balcony door and the orchids next door going pink in it. She set the pace. She set it slow until he begged her with his hands on her hips, and then fast until he couldn’t speak at all, and he let her. She laughed when the sofa knocked against the wall, and he laughed too, breathless, and then they both stopped laughing because neither of them could spare the air. He held her by the waist and looked up at her. When she came the second time she leaned down and put her forehead against his and said his name into his mouth, and he followed her a moment later with his arms locked round her back and his face in her neck.

For a long time they didn’t move.

“Your neighbours,” he said eventually, into her shoulder.

“My neighbours are eighty-three and seventy-nine and they’ve both been deaf since 2019.”

“Are you sure?”

“I’m a professional investigator,” said Song-Zhu, and he laughed until she nearly slid off him.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty to six, Song-Zhu was lying on the sofa with her head on Ren Hao’s chest and his arm round her and a blanket she didn’t remember fetching over both of them. His shirt was somewhere. Her hair was a disaster. The afternoon sun had moved slowly across the floor and was now lying on the laundry heap, which he still hadn’t mentioned.

She was tracing a line on his palm with one finger.

“You’ve gone quiet,” she said.

He looked down at her. “Don’t start.”

She laughed, because it was her line, and he’d stolen it on purpose.

After a while she said, “Are you still upset about the schedule?”

“No.”

“Really?”

He held up one hand, like a man taking an oath. “On my agenda.”

“You’re not going to make another one?”

He thought about it. “No.”

“Promise?”

“I promise.”

“Because if I find another folder—”

“I’ll burn it myself.”

“Good boy,” she said, and he shook his head at the ceiling, and ran his fingers through her hair.

They lay there a while in a silence that was comfortable and only a little sticky. Then he said, “Can I ask you something?”

“Mm.”

“Would you tell me when you know you’re going to be working late?”

She lifted her head. He went on before she could answer.

“Not so I can arrange anything. Not so anyone can pick you up. Just because I like knowing when I’ll hear from you. So I’m not sitting there waiting for a message and inventing reasons why it hasn’t come.”

She looked at him. “Yes,” she said. “I can do that.”

“All right.”

“I’ll forget, sometimes.”

“I know.”

“And sometimes I won’t know until the last minute myself.”

“That’s all right. Tell me then.”

She touched his cheek. “You’re getting better at this.”

“Slowly.”

“Very slowly.”

He turned his head and kissed the inside of her wrist. “And I’d like to know when you’re free.”

“Why?”

“So I can ask to see you.”

She looked at him a long time. Then she reached up and kissed him, properly.

“That,” she said, “is much better than a lilac box.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At quarter past six he finally got up. He found his watch under the coffee table and his shirt behind the sofa, and his tie was apparently in the bedroom, though he couldn’t remember either of them going in there. His jacket was hanging off a dining chair on top of hers.

He stood and looked round the room. Then he looked at her, still on the sofa under the blanket, watching him with a smile.

“What?” he said.

“Nothing. You’re very easy to tease.”

And then he saw the laundry heap again, in the evening light, in all its glory.

He looked at it. He looked at her. She raised one eyebrow and waited. He turned his back on it.

She burst out laughing. “Good decision!”

He picked up his jacket, and came back, and bent to kiss her. “Have you eaten?”

She stared at him.

He stopped. “Sorry.”

“No, you can ask,” she said, laughing. “You’re allowed one a day.”

“Have you?”

“Not since breakfast.”

“Would you like to go out?”

She thought about it, and shook her head. “Can we order something?”

“Of course.”

“Something messy.”

“All right.”

“Something you couldn’t possibly put in a colour-coded food plan.”

“I’ll do my best.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Just after seven they were eating takeaway on her sofa out of the cartons: noodles, and a spicy aubergine that went everywhere, and dumplings with chives and prawn. Song-Zhu had one leg tucked under her. Ren Hao was trying hard to keep the aubergine off his trousers.

She watched him struggle a while, and then handed him a napkin.

“Thank you.”

“You’re welcome.” A pause. “You know what?”

“What?”

“I liked the blank Saturday.”

He looked at her. “Did you?”

“Yes.” She ate a dumpling. “Next time, don’t give it a colour.”

“Understood.”

“And don’t call it personal time. It sounds like a dentist.”

“All right.”

“Just ask me.”

He nodded. “I will.”

She leaned over and kissed his cheek. He put his carton down.

“Can I make one suggestion?”

She narrowed her eyes. “Depends.”

“Dinner. Once a week. Any night. You choose the night, every week, when you know your week.”

She thought about it. “That’s not a schedule.”

“No.”

“That’s a date.”

“Exactly.”

She nodded slowly. “Approved.”

“Thank you.”

She leaned back against him, and after a while said, “By the way, I’ve kept the ash.”

He looked down at her. “Why?”

“I thought you might want it back.”

He stared at her. Then he laughed. “Keep it.”

“Sentimental?”

“Evidence.”

“Of what?”

He put his mouth to her hair. “That I should never make you a timetable again.”

She laughed into his shoulder. “Good.”

He held her a little closer. And for once, Ren Hao let a whole evening happen without organising one minute of it.

chapters.title: His Sister Likes Her Too Much
chapters.desc: Isla and Song-Zhu, two glasses of wine and every secret of his childhood. The ten minutes at nine. A kiss in the corridor; Isla shouts.
chapters.epigraph: “You’re different with her.”
chapters.content:
Ren Hao made one mistake when he invited Song-Zhu to dinner with his sister. He assumed Isla would behave.

In hindsight it wasn’t a reasonable assumption. His younger sister had always had a gift for getting information out of people. She was charming when she wanted to be and disarmingly sweet when she didn’t, and entirely incapable of leaving a subject alone once it interested her. It was why the consulate sent her to sit with families on the worst night of their lives. It was also why he had never once in twenty-five years won an argument with her at a dinner table.

And Song-Zhu interested her enormously. She had known Song-Zhu for nine months, since a cold night in November and half a cereal bar in a stairwell. She had never yet known her as the woman her brother was in love with. At twenty-four minutes to six the messages began.

Isla (Matchmaker): What does she drink?

Ren Hao: Wine, I think.

Isla (Matchmaker): Red or white?

Ren Hao: You know her. Ask her.

Isla (Matchmaker): I’m asking you. As a test.

Ren Hao: Then I don’t know.

Isla (Matchmaker): Terrible boyfriend.

He looked at that for some time.

Ren Hao: I’m not her boyfriend.

Isla (Matchmaker): That’s not what I asked.

He put the phone down. It buzzed again.

Isla (Matchmaker): Does she like flowers?

Ren Hao: Isla.

Isla (Matchmaker): What

Ren Hao: Please don’t interrogate her.

Isla (Matchmaker): I’m welcoming her into the family

Ren Hao: She’s coming for dinner.

Isla (Matchmaker): Exactly. A family dinner.

He could hear her smiling through the screen.

Ren Hao: Behave.

Isla (Matchmaker): love you too

Ren Hao: I regret introducing the two of you.

Isla (Matchmaker): I introduced YOU. Know your place

✦ ✦ ✦

Song-Zhu arrived just after six. He opened the door before she could ring.

She was in a plain black dress and a light cardigan, with small gold earrings, her hair loose on her shoulders, and a bottle of wine held against her chest like a shield. He looked at her. Then he smiled.

“Hello.”

“Hello.”

He bent and kissed her, rather longer than a greeting at a front door strictly required. When he let her go she held up the bottle.

“Peace offering.”

“For whom?”

“Your sister. I hear she’s dangerous.”

“Who told you that?”

“You did. You texted me behave this morning. Three times.”

“That’s because I know you.”

She kicked off her shoes in the hall, onto the rack, where his own shoes stood in a straight line, and she looked at the straight line and then at him and visibly decided not to say anything about it.

“I’m extremely well behaved,” she said.

He looked at her.

“Most of the time.”

“Song-Zhu!” Isla came out of the kitchen in a cream blouse with her hair tied back and a wooden spoon in her hand, and threw both arms round her, spoon and all. “Finally. Finally. In his flat. With his shoes all lined up. Look at you.”

Song-Zhu laughed into her shoulder. “Hello, Isla.”

Isla held her at arm’s length and looked at her as if she’d brought her up herself. Then she turned to her brother.

“Why didn’t you tell me she looked like this when she’s not covered in fuel?”

“Because that would be a strange thing to tell my sister.”

“Not at all strange.”

“You’ve met her. You’ve had lunch with her eleven times. You introduced us.”

“In a stairwell,” said Isla, “and at a dumpling shop, and once in a hospital car park. Never in earrings.” She took Song-Zhu by the hand. “Come in. I’ve been waiting all afternoon. I’ve got things to tell you.”

Ren Hao watched the two of them go down the hall. He looked at the bottle of wine in his hands. Then at the empty doorway.

He had a feeling he was about to become irrelevant in his own flat.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dinner was meant to be simple. He’d ordered from a place Isla liked, and laid it all out properly on the table in dishes, with serving spoons, because he wasn’t a man who could put a takeaway carton on a table with a guest at it. Song-Zhu looked at the serving spoons and then at him and bit her lip.

For the first twenty minutes it went exactly as planned. Isla asked about work. Not the questions people usually asked; the right ones. How long it took to get a recorder downloaded when the box had been in seawater. Whether the families got told before the press. Whether it ever got easier.

“Some of it does,” said Song-Zhu. “You learn how to do the work. You learn what to expect.”

“And the rest?”

“You learn how to carry it.”

Isla nodded. She didn’t ask for more. She of all people knew where those conversations went. She asked instead what Song-Zhu did when she wasn’t working.

“Sleep.”

“That’s it?”

“Sometimes I eat.”

“You’re my kind of person,” said Isla.

From across the table, Ren Hao said, “She also likes making trouble.”

Song-Zhu turned. “Excuse me?”

“Nothing.”

“Does she?” said Isla, delighted.

“Regularly.”

“He’s exaggerating,” said Song-Zhu.

“He isn’t,” said Isla.

Ren Hao looked at his sister. “Whose side are you on?”

“Hers. Obviously. I’ve been on her side since November. You’ve only been on it since June.” Isla poured another glass of wine, and that was where it began to go wrong for him.

✦ ✦ ✦

It started with school.

“Was he always like this?” said Song-Zhu.

Isla’s eyes lit up like a runway. Ren Hao put down his fork. “Don’t.”

Isla ignored him completely. “Like what?”

Song-Zhu gestured at him with her glass. “Very organised. Very serious. Looks like he was born in a tie.”

“Oh,” said Isla, “you have no idea.”

“Isla.”

“What?”

“Eat.”

“I am eating. Look. Food.” She turned back. “He used to pack his school bag every single night. Books in order of the timetable. Pencils sharpened to the same length. Homework in the front pocket. If I borrowed anything, he knew.”

“That is not true.”

“It is entirely true.”

“I didn’t mind you borrowing things.”

“You minded when I didn’t put them back.”

“That’s different.”

Song-Zhu leaned in. “What happened if you didn’t put them back?”

“He’d come and stand in my bedroom doorway and ask where his ruler was.”

“At eleven o’clock at night?”

“Sometimes.”

Song-Zhu turned and looked at him. He gave her a warning look across the serving spoons. She gave him a beautiful smile.

“That’s adorable.”

“It isn’t.”

“He made lists for our parents,” said Isla.

Song-Zhu’s mouth fell open. “No.”

“Yes. Things he thought needed mending in the house. With priorities.”

“Please stop,” said Ren Hao.

“He once made a list,” said Isla, “of everything I was doing wrong.”

Song-Zhu started laughing. “What?”

“I was eight. He was ten. Apparently I wasn’t using my time efficiently. So he made me a timetable.”

Song-Zhu stopped laughing. Slowly, with enormous ceremony, she turned her head and looked at him. He looked at her.

She looked at him for a long, long moment, and then she put both hands flat on the table and laughed until there were tears in her eyes, and Isla, who had no idea why it was this funny, laughed too, simply because Song-Zhu was.

“Oh my God,” said Song-Zhu. “Oh my God.”

He put his hand over his face. “Can we please move on.”

“No. Wait.” She held up one finger. “You made your eight-year-old sister a timetable.”

“It was a completely different situation.”

“How?”

“She kept forgetting her homework.”

“He was so annoying,” said Isla, fondly.

“You asked me to help.”

“I was eight.”

“And I helped.”

“Was it colour-coded?” said Song-Zhu, sweetly.

He looked at her for so long that Isla stopped laughing and looked between the two of them, and narrowed her eyes, and filed it away.

“It might have been,” he said.

Song-Zhu put her face in her napkin. He looked at the pair of them. Two women. Two glasses of wine. One shared target. He had been outnumbered in his own home for less than an hour.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Tell her about the cake,” said Isla.

“No.”

“What cake?” said Song-Zhu.

“There’s no cake.”

“When he was thirteen,” said Isla, “he tried to bake a birthday cake for our mother. He followed the recipe exactly. He weighed everything on the kitchen scales. He wrote the oven temperature on a sticky note and put it on the oven.”

“You’re leaving out the part where you distracted me.”

“I was helping.”

“You were eating the chocolate.”

Isla waved her fork. “Anyway, it came out completely flat.”

“It was meant to be a dense cake.”

“It was a biscuit,” said Isla.

“It was not a biscuit.”

“It was a biscuit with ambitions.”

Song-Zhu bent forward over the table, helpless. He sat back in his chair. He had never been so comprehensively betrayed by a blood relative.

“Have you got more?” said Song-Zhu, wiping her eyes.

“Oh, so many.”

“Please.”

“No,” said Ren Hao.

“Please.”

He looked at her. “You too?”

“I’m getting to know you.”

“You’re getting to know my childhood.”

“Same thing,” said Song-Zhu, and he shook his head and didn’t argue, because he could see that for her it was.

Isla turned her glass slowly by the stem. “And there’s the time he cried.”

Everything about Ren Hao went still. Song-Zhu looked at him.

“Cried?”

“Don’t,” he said.

“The first maths competition he lost,” said Isla, more gently. “He was thirteen. He’d prepared for months. He thought if he worked hard enough, he couldn’t lose. And he came second, by half a mark, and he went into his room and wouldn’t come out.”

Song-Zhu’s face had changed.

“What did you do?” she said.

“I sat outside his door.” Isla smiled down at her plate. “I didn’t know what to say. I was eleven. So I just sat there on the floor, with my back against it, until he came out. It took about three hours. I read a whole book.”

Song-Zhu looked at Ren Hao. He was trying to look. There was a small tightness round his mouth.

“That’s lovely,” she said.

“He was annoying,” said Isla. “But he was mine.”

He reached for his glass. “You’re making me sound pathetic.”

“You were thirteen.”

“Still.”

Under the table, Song-Zhu found his hand. He looked up. She wasn’t teasing him now. She just held on. He turned his hand over and squeezed her fingers once, hard, and didn’t let go straight away. And then Isla ruined it.

“He also had a truly terrible haircut.”

“Show me,” said Song-Zhu instantly.

“No,” said Ren Hao.

“Show me.”

“Absolutely not.”

Isla was already reaching for her phone.

✦ ✦ ✦

A little after eight he went into the kitchen to refill the water jug. When he came back, the two of them were on the sofa with their heads together over Isla’s phone, and Song-Zhu had one hand over her mouth.

On the screen was a boy of about fifteen with hair that was much too long, a school shirt tucked into trousers belted somewhere round his ribs, holding up a certificate with the grave expression of a man receiving a state honour.

“What,” said Ren Hao from the doorway, “is that.”

Song-Zhu looked up at him with shining eyes. “Oh, Hao.”

“Give me the phone.”

“No,” said Isla, holding it out of reach.

“Isla.”

“Your hair,” said Song-Zhu.

“That was a long time ago.”

“It was beautiful,” said Isla.

“It was a crime.”

“You look so serious,” said Song-Zhu.

“I was receiving an award.”

“For what?”

“Academic performance.”

“He came first,” said Isla. “In the whole school. It was the year after the maths thing. He never came second again in his life.”

Song-Zhu looked up at him. “Of course you did.”

“What does that mean?”

“It means you were born holding a spreadsheet.”

Isla laughed so much she slid sideways off the sofa cushion. Ren Hao took the phone out of her hand while she was helpless, and sat down on Song-Zhu’s other side.

“Enough.”

Song-Zhu leaned against his arm. “Can I have the photograph?”

“No.”

“Please?”

“No.”

“Just the one.”

He looked down at her. She smiled up at him. He sighed.

“Fine.”

“I’ll send it to you,” said Isla, from the floor.

“Don’t.”

“Already done.”

Song-Zhu kissed his cheek. “Thank you.”

He looked at her. “You’ve been here two hours.”

“And?”

“And you’re already conspiring with my sister.”

“She’s very informative,” said Song-Zhu.

✦ ✦ ✦

By a quarter to nine the dinner table had fallen into chaos. Isla had taken her cardigan off. Song-Zhu had moved from the sofa to the floor and was sitting cross-legged against Isla’s knees. The wine was nearly gone. Ren Hao was in the kitchen doorway with two plates, having attempted for the fifth time to clear the table and been prevented for the fifth time by a new story.

School. University. His first job. The afternoon he’d locked himself out of the house in Vancouver at fourteen and climbed in through the cat flap as far as his shoulders. The weekend he’d spent trying to mend a broken radio rather than admit to their father that he’d broken it.

At one point Song-Zhu laughed so much she put her head down on Isla’s knee. He stood and watched them.

He had never seen his sister like this with anyone he had been seeing. Not quite. Isla was sociable by nature and professionally kind, but she was careful about who she let in. She didn’t tell people about the cat flap. She didn’t open the door to the small private country that had only ever had two people in it, him and her, a long way from their parents’ house, in a city neither of them had been born in.

And here she was, opening it. Laughing. Looking at Song-Zhu as if she had known her for years.

It made something warm settle in his chest. And something else, slightly alarming, settle beside it: a strong suspicion that the two of them together were going to be impossible to manage.

“Do you know what I like about him?” said Isla.

He stopped in the kitchen doorway with the plates.

“What?” said Song-Zhu.

“He always turns up.”

He didn’t move.

“Always,” said Isla. “Even when he’s busy. Even when he’s exhausted. If I ring him, he answers. When I was small and I had an exam he used to wait outside my classroom and pretend he was just walking past. With a snack. Every time.”

“You were always late,” he said.

“I was eight.”

“You were late at eight and you’re late now.”
