Isla ignored him. “He’d sit there with his own books, waiting. As if it were nothing.”

Song-Zhu looked up at him in the doorway. He shrugged, holding the plates. “You were my sister.”

“Exactly,” said Isla.

There was a little silence. Then Isla said, as if it followed: “Wei Long’s like that. Differently. But like that.”

Song-Zhu sat up. “The inspector.”

“The inspector.” Isla’s whole face went soft in a way her brother hadn’t quite got used to yet. “Did I ever tell you about the ten minutes?”

“No. What ten minutes?”

“At nine o’clock in the morning,” said Isla, “on the days I’ve got business at the station, I go up to his floor and sit on the corner of his desk. And he stops. Whatever he’s doing. He puts the pen down and he looks at me. For ten minutes. He asks me if I’ve eaten, or if I’ve slept. Sometimes we hardly say anything. The whole squad room just waits.” She smiled at her glass. “Then I get off the desk, and he picks up his pen, and that’s that.”

Song-Zhu watched her. “And you like that?”

“I love it.”

“Why?”

Isla thought about it. “Because he doesn’t want anything from me in those ten minutes. He isn’t fixing anything. He’s not managing me. He just stops, and he’s there. And now, whenever I walk in, the whole floor goes quiet before I’ve got to his desk.”

Song-Zhu’s face had gone soft.

“I want one,” she said.

Isla turned. “What?”

“One of those.” Song-Zhu looked up at the kitchen doorway. “Ten minutes.”

Ren Hao looked at her over the plates. “You want to come and sit on my desk at nine?”

“No. You’d make a spreadsheet of it. You’d book it.” She pointed at him. “I want you to stop. When I ring you at nine. Whatever you’re doing, whoever you’re with. Ten minutes, and you stop.”

“You work completely unpredictable hours.”

“So whenever I ring at nine.”

He looked at her, sitting on his floor with his sister’s knee behind her shoulder, asking him for the one thing he had never once in his working life given anybody.

“All right,” he said.

She looked up at him properly. “Really?”

“Really.”

Isla looked from one to the other, and then gave her brother a long, slow, unmistakable look.

“What?” he said.

“Nothing.”

“Don’t.”

She smiled into her wine. “You’re both very sweet.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By ten past ten Isla was still talking. Ren Hao had given up all pretence of clearing anything and was sitting on the floor with them, his back against the sofa, Song-Zhu’s shoulder against his. Isla was describing the time Wei Long had brought her breakfast to the consulate after a night shift, and had looked so offended when she left half the toast that she’d eaten it later, cold, at her desk, so as not to hurt his feelings.

“You left half?” said Ren Hao.

“I wasn’t hungry.”

“Then why did you ring me at eleven that night complaining you were starving?”

“Because I was hungry later.”

Song-Zhu laughed against his arm.

“The pair of you,” he said, shaking his head.

“Don’t you dare,” said Isla, pointing at him. “You rang me at midnight once to ask if I’d locked my front door.”

Song-Zhu turned her head slowly. He shut his eyes.

“Why?” said Song-Zhu.

“She was living on her own.”

“I was twenty-two,” said Isla.

“Exactly.”

“I’d been living on my own for two years.”

“I know.”

“Then why?”

He opened his eyes and looked at her. “Because once, you hadn’t.”

Isla opened her mouth. Shut it. Turned to Song-Zhu. “You see?”

Song-Zhu was laughing too much to answer. “You’re exactly the same,” she managed. “Both of you. The same person in two sizes.”

“That’s unfortunate,” said Ren Hao.

“Not really,” said Song-Zhu, and leaned on him.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just after ten Song-Zhu finally stood up. “I should go.”

Isla looked up at once. “Already?”

“I’ve got a briefing at eight.”

“Stay a bit.”

“I’d love to. I can’t.” She went and found her shoes, which had been moved, in her absence, onto the rack, into line.

“I’ll walk you out,” said Isla.

“I’ll take her,” said Ren Hao, already holding her bag.

Isla gave him a look. “Of course you will.”

Song-Zhu put on her shoes and turned and hugged Isla, who held on to her.

“Thank you for coming,” said Isla.

“Thank you for telling me about the ruler.”

Isla pulled back. And then, without any teasing in it at all: “I’m really glad it’s you.”

Song-Zhu’s face softened. “Me too.”

Isla glanced at her brother. “Good. Because I’m keeping her. Whatever you do.”

“Do I get a say in this?”

“No,” said both of them.

✦ ✦ ✦

The corridor outside the living room was dim and quiet. He walked her towards the front door. She put her hand in his.

“Good evening?” he said.

“Very.”

“She likes you.”

“I’d noticed.”

“Too much.”

Song-Zhu laughed. “She’s lovely.”

“She is.”

At the door she stopped and turned round.

“Thank you.”

“For what?”

“For letting me meet her. Like this. As this.”

He looked at her. There was something unusually gentle in her face. He tucked a strand of hair behind her ear.

“I wanted you to.”

“She told me things you’d never have told me.”

“Unfortunately.”

“Very unfortunately.” She stepped closer. “Your childhood was adorable.”

“It was perfectly normal.”

“You made your sister a timetable.”

“Once.”

“You’re still making timetables.”

“You’re never going to let that go.”

“Never,” she said, and pulled him down by his shirt and kissed him.

He caught her round the waist. It began, and then she smiled against his mouth and he kissed her again, harder, his hand going into the hair at the back of her head, and she held the front of his shirt in both fists and pulled him closer, and for a few seconds the corridor went away. There was only her mouth and her hands and the warmth of him, and his breath when he—

“OH!”

They broke apart. Ren Hao shut his eyes.

From the end of the corridor, Isla’s voice rang out, loud enough to be heard in the flat downstairs. “YOU TWO!”

Song-Zhu burst out laughing.

“Isla!”

“THE DOOR IS RIGHT THERE!”

Song-Zhu put both hands over her mouth. Isla appeared at the end of the corridor holding a tea towel, looked at them, looked at her brother, looked at Song-Zhu’s hand still twisted in his shirt.

“Sorry,” she said, not sounding sorry in the least. “I thought you’d left.”

“We were leaving,” said Ren Hao.

“Clearly.”

Song-Zhu was laughing too much to speak.

Isla pointed the tea towel at her brother like a weapon. “Behave.”

He stared at her. “She’s my girlfriend.”

The words came out by themselves. No preparation. Not the faintest hesitation. He hadn’t known they were coming until they were already in the corridor. Silence. Song-Zhu turned and looked up at him. He looked down at her.

For one second neither of them said anything at all.

Then Isla’s eyes went wide. “Oh?”

He turned his head. “Don’t.”

“Oh, that’s interesting.”

Song-Zhu’s cheeks had gone pink. She was looking at the floor, and smiling at it.

Isla made a small, delighted noise, like a kettle. “Well! That’s wonderful!”

He rubbed his forehead. “Please go back to the kitchen.”

“I’m going. I’m going.” She turned, and then turned back. “Good night, girlfriend!”

“Good night!” said Song-Zhu.

He looked at her. “You’re encouraging her.”

“She’s lovely.”

“She’s a menace.”

Song-Zhu reached up and kissed him again, quickly, in the doorway. “Good night, Hao.”

“Good night.”

She opened the door, and then turned. “Tell Isla I’ll text her.”

“I will.”

“And tell her I want the haircut in better resolution.”

“Absolutely not,” said Ren Hao, and she laughed all the way down the corridor to the lift, and he stood in his doorway and waited until the doors had closed on her.

✦ ✦ ✦

When he came back into the living room, Isla was on the sofa drinking a glass of water.

“Well?” she said.

He picked up two empty wine glasses. “Well what?”

“Your girlfriend.”

He glanced at her. “Yes?”

She didn’t smile. “You really like her.”

He didn’t answer straight away. Then he said, “Yes.”

His sister watched him. There was no teasing in her face at all now. Only affection, and something older.

“She’s good for you,” she said.

He looked down at the glasses in his hands. “I know.”

“You’re different with her.”

“How?”

“Less like you’re about to chair a meeting.” She tipped her head. “Happier.”

He looked at the door. Then back at his sister. “She makes things easy.”

“Does she?”

He thought about it. Song-Zhu wasn’t easy. She was unpredictable and stubborn and occasionally capable of setting fire to three pages of careful planning in her kitchen sink. But being with her was easy in a way he hadn’t expected. He didn’t have to perform. He didn’t have to impress her. He could just be the man who made his sister a timetable at ten, and she would laugh at him for it and hold his hand under the table.

“Yes,” he said. “She does.”

Isla got up and hugged him, and he held on to her longer than usual.

“Thank you,” he said.

“What for?”

“Tonight.”

“You’re welcome.” She stepped back. “Next time, I’m inviting her without you.”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because she’ll spend the whole evening laughing at me.”

“Exactly,” said Isla, and went to get her coat.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just after eleven his phone lit.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Home.

Ren Hao: Good.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Your sister is lovely.

Ren Hao: She likes you.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Too much, apparently. She’s sent me the haircut.

He shut his eyes.

Ren Hao: I’m disowning her.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): And a photo of the cake.

Ren Hao: I’m changing my number.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Don’t. I like this one.

He laughed.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Can I ask you something?

Ren Hao: Anything.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Are we actually boyfriend and girlfriend now? Or did you just say it to get rid of her?

He looked at the screen. He remembered the corridor. How the words had come out of him before he’d thought them. She’s my girlfriend. He hadn’t planned it. It had simply been true, and his mouth had known before he did.

Ren Hao: Would you like to be?

A few seconds.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I thought I already was.

He smiled at the screen.

Ren Hao: Then yes.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Good.

Ren Hao: Good?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Very good. Good night, boyfriend.

He sat on the edge of his bed and smiled at his phone like an idiot.

Ren Hao: Good night, girlfriend.

A minute later the phone rang. Isla.

“What?”

“Did she get home?”

“Yes.”

“Good.” A pause. “Did you tell her?”

He looked at the ceiling. “Tell her what?”

“That you love her.”

He didn’t say anything.

Isla laughed. “Oh, you haven’t.”

“Good night, Isla.”

“Ren Hao—”

He rang off. Then he looked at Song-Zhu’s last message again.

He hadn’t said it yet. Not because he didn’t feel it; he had felt it for weeks, at a hangar fence and in a car park and on a terrible sofa. He hadn’t said it because he was beginning to understand that some things should be said when they were ready to be said. And he wanted her to hear it in a moment that belonged only to the two of them.

Not shouted down a corridor, not interrupted by his sister with a tea towel.

Though, knowing Isla, he suspected that might be impossible. The phone buzzed once more.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): One more thing.

Ren Hao: Yes?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Ten minutes at nine. I’m going to ring you on Monday. Be ready.

Ren Hao: I’ll be ready.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): No schedule.

Ren Hao: No schedule.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Just you.

He looked at that a long time.

Ren Hao: Just me.

And for the first time that night, he didn’t think about what came next. He simply looked forward to Monday, and to nine o’clock, and to stopping.

chapters.title: A Typhoon at the Airport
chapters.desc: A typhoon closes the airport. He brings a camp bed, a suit carrier and soup. A go-around in the storm. Explicit: the camp bed collapses.
chapters.epigraph: “You brought a bed to an airport. In a typhoon.”
chapters.content:
At seventeen minutes past four on Tuesday the second of September, Ren Hao received a photograph of a unhappy sky.

It was nearly all grey, with a bruise of darker cloud piled up over the airport perimeter, and in one corner the wing of an aircraft, wet, under rain coming in sideways.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Getting ugly.

He was in a meeting. Across the table his head of operations was explaining a restructure of the crisis-response team in a voice that suggested the restructure would take some time. Ren Hao looked at the photograph under the table.

Ren Hao: Are you still at the airport?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Duty investigator for the storm. I’m here till it’s gone.

Ren Hao: Have they stopped flights?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Not yet. Soon.

Ren Hao: Are you going home?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Hao.

He knew that one.

Ren Hao: What?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I’m working.

He put the phone on the table, screen down against his knee.

“Go on,” he said.

His head of operations went on. Ren Hao managed to listen for about thirty seconds.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Departures stopped. They’re reviewing arrivals.

He looked at the message. At the clock on the wall. Back at the message.

Ren Hao: Let me know when they close.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): You’re doing the thing.

Ren Hao: Which thing?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): The thing where you pretend not to worry while secretly preparing to take over the weather.

Ren Hao: I don’t have that authority.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Good. Stay humble.

He spent the next forty minutes conducting an entire meeting about crisis response while thinking about nothing but the weather.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just after six, the airport suspended all flights.

The typhoon had come further west than forecast, and faster. The wind was climbing past the limits for landing on either runway, the rain was taking the visibility down with it, and the warning across the city had gone to its second-highest level. Somewhere in the operations centre people were moving aircraft to alternates, finding stands for the ones already on the ground, and telling thousands of passengers that nobody knew anything yet.

A voice note arrived. Behind her, voices, footsteps, a phone ringing, the hum of a building full of computers.

“Well, handsome. Looks like I’m sleeping here.”

He listened to it twice and rang her. She answered on the fourth ring.

“Hello.”

“Where are you?”

“Investigators’ office. The one by the cargo apron.”

“Are you safe?”

“I’m in a concrete building built to survive things hitting it. Yes.”

“Have they given you somewhere to sleep?”

A pause. “There’s a sofa.”

He shut his eyes. “Song-Zhu.”

“What?”

“Is it a comfortable sofa?”

“It’s a sofa.”

“That’s not an answer.”

“It’s a sofa with ambitions,” she said, and laughed at his silence. “I’ll live, Hao.”

“I know.” And then, because he couldn’t not: “Have you eaten?”

She sighed theatrically. “And there it is.”

“Have you?”

“No.”

“I’ll bring you something.”

“It’s a typhoon.”

“So I’ve been told.”

“The airport’s shut.”

“I’ve also been informed.”

“The roads will be awful.”

“I’ll manage.”

She was quiet. Then he heard her smile. “You’re coming.”

“Yes.”

“All right.” Another pause. “Bring soup.”

“What kind?”

“Hot.”

“That’s not a kind.”

“The kind that tastes like you’d like me to survive the night.”

“Understood.”

“And Hao. Don’t bring a whole office.”

“I wasn’t planning to.”

“One person. One boyfriend. One soup.”

He smiled at the window, where the rain had started hitting the glass of the thirty-second floor in handfuls. “One boyfriend?”

“Don’t get excited.”

“Already done,” said Ren Hao.

✦ ✦ ✦

By half past seven he had packed for a small expedition.

A thermal container of soup from the place with the good broth by his office. A box of rice. Bottled water. A bag of fruit, cut. A phone charger and a portable battery, fully charged. Two changes of clothes, his and hers, the hers being a cotton shirt and soft trousers he’d bought on the way, in her size, which he knew because he had looked at the label on her cardigan in his hall on the night of the dinner with Isla. A towel. Socks. All of it in a suit carrier.

The suit carrier was the item that made Mr. Yau look at him in the basement car park.

“Are you staying the night, sir?”

“No.”

Mr. Yau looked at the suit carrier.

“She may need something dry,” said Ren Hao.

Mr. Yau nodded. He had learned not to ask too many questions this summer.

Then Ren Hao went back into the storeroom by the lifts and came out with a folding camp bed, the kind that came in a canvas bag with a handle, which the firm kept for operations nights and which nobody had ever, to anybody’s knowledge, unfolded. Mr. Yau looked at the camp bed.

“Sir.”

“What?”

“Do they allow beds?”

Ren Hao stopped. It was a fair question. “I’ll ask.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The airport was chaos by the time they got there. Rain hammered the roof of the car. The expressway moved in jerks, headlights smearing across it. Staff in yellow jackets were waving traffic away from everywhere it wanted to go. Mr. Yau got them round the back to the cargo side by a route Ren Hao didn’t know existed, through a gate where a guard came to the window with water running off his hood and looked at the camp bed on the back seat a long time.

“Visiting the investigators,” said Ren Hao.

The guard rang through. Then he waved them on with the air of a man who’d seen stranger things in a typhoon but couldn’t immediately think of one.

Song-Zhu came down to the door of the low brick building. Hair pinned up anyhow, a loose grey shirt under a dark jacket, black trousers, trainers, a pen behind one ear. She looked tired. And when she saw him standing in the rain with his arms full, her face changed, not much, but enough.

“Hello.”

He kissed her cheek. “Hello.”

Then she saw the bags. Her eyes went from the soup to the suit carrier, and from the suit carrier to the long canvas bag with the handle.

“Hao.”

“Yes.”

“What’s that?”

“A camp bed.”

“I can see it’s a camp bed.”

“I thought you might want it.”

She looked at him for several seconds in the doorway with the wind trying to get in round her. Then she began to laugh.

“You brought a bed.”

“It’s portable.”

“You brought a bed to an airport. In a typhoon.”

“To the investigators’ office, technically.”

She leaned on the door frame, helpless. He took her bag off her shoulder for her. “Don’t laugh. It’s practical.”

“You’re unbelievable.”

“Thank you.”

“It wasn’t a compliment.”

“I’ll take it anyway.” He held up the suit carrier. “And clothes.”

“For who?”

“You.”

Her laughter went quiet. “You brought me clothes.”

“Your office has a sofa. Not a wardrobe.”

She shook her head, and then she stepped forward into the rain-noise and put both arms round his waist, and held on.

He stood still and let her. The rain beat on the glass canopy over the door. She put her cheek against his wet shirt.

“Thank you,” she said.

“You’re welcome.”

She let go. “Come on. Before security decides you’re opening a hotel.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The investigators’ office hadn’t been designed for anyone to sleep in. It had been designed for work: desks crowded with files, monitors on arms, a wall of photographs and charts from cases that were still open, a meeting table, a kettle with a sign on it that said DESCALE ME, I BEG YOU. The lights were too bright. The air-conditioning was too cold. There were four other people in it, at desks, with headsets round their necks, who looked up when Ren Hao came in carrying a camp bed and then, as one, looked back down again.

“Duty team,” said Song-Zhu. “Ignore them. They’re very good at it.”

She took him through to a little room off the end of the corridor, a box with a desk, a filing cabinet, a window onto the dark cargo apron and a sofa that looked as if it had been bought specifically to discourage anyone from sleeping on it.

“This is mine for the night. Duty investigator’s rest room. The door locks. There’s a radio,” she pointed at a handset on the desk, crackling, “and a screen, so if anything happens I see it when they do.”

On the screen, the airport’s approach radar turned slowly, a handful of small labelled blips crawling round the edges of the storm like insects round a lamp.

He looked at the sofa. She watched him look at it.

“Don’t.”

“I haven’t said a word.”

“Your face has said four.”

“That’s where you were going to sleep?”

“Yes.”

He put down the bags and unzipped the canvas and began to unfold the camp bed. It had a great many joints. She watched him struggle with the second leg and read the instruction tag sewn to the canvas.

“Do you want help?”

“No.”

He pulled. The frame made a worrying metallic noise.

“Hao.”

“I’ve got it.”

“You’re fighting a bed.”

“I’m assembling it.”

“You’re losing.”

He looked up. She was smiling. He pulled again. The leg clicked into place. He stood up, slightly out of breath. “There.”

She came over and pressed one hand flat on the canvas. It dipped. She pressed harder. The whole thing wobbled from end to end like a nervous animal.

She looked at him. He looked at the bed.

“Well,” she said.

“It’s fine.”

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

She sat down on it. The camp bed gave a sharp metallic crack. They both stared at it.

She stood up again, slowly. “Let’s not push it.”

“Probably wise.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The soup was still hot.

She ate it at the desk, out of a proper ceramic bowl he’d brought because he couldn’t bring himself to give anyone soup in a carton, while he leaned on the filing cabinet and watched the radar turn. She’d changed into the dry clothes he’d brought: the soft cotton shirt, the loose trousers. And then she found the socks at the bottom of the suit carrier, a new pair, still on their cardboard, and held them up.

“Did you buy me socks?”

“I bought socks.”

“Why?”

“Because yours are wet. And you’re here all night.”

She looked at them and then at him. “You’re getting good at this.”

“At what?”

“Being useful without being asked.”

“I’ve always been useful.”

She pointed the spoon at him. “Don’t spoil it.”

He laughed. She ate. For a while the room was quiet except for the rain on the window and the radio murmuring on the desk, the tower talking to the last few aircraft holding out over the sea.

He watched her. She was tired enough that she’d stopped being bright for him. Her shoulders had gone forward a little. Every so often she pinched the bridge of her nose, and went back to the soup.

He wanted to ask whether someone else could do this. He wanted to suggest she lie down. More than anything he wanted to tell her to sleep.

Instead he pulled the second chair up beside her.

“How bad is it?”

“Bad enough. Nothing’s happened. That’s the good part.” She nodded at the screen. “We’ve had diversions all evening. Two holding. One coming in now that’s been holding for forty minutes, a freighter, to see if there’s a gap. If there isn’t, he’ll go somewhere else.”

“And if something happens?”

“Then I’m the first one who has to know. That’s what duty means. If anything goes wrong on that runway tonight, I start the clock. Who to ring, what to keep, what to stop anyone touching.” She put the spoon down. “Mostly it means sitting here all night while nothing goes wrong, and being very glad.”

He looked at her soup.

“Finish eating.”

She smiled. “That’s a reasonable request.”

He looked so pleased with himself that she didn’t have the heart to say anything else.

✦ ✦ ✦

Before she went back to the duty room to check in, she said, “Give me your phone.”

He gave it to her. She did something to it, and something to hers, and gave it back. On his screen was a map of the airport with a small blue dot in the middle of the cargo side.

“Location,” she said. “Just for tonight. The compound’s three kilometres across and nothing’s signposted. If you go out to the car and get lost I’m not sending a search party in this.”

“And you can see me?”

“I can see you. You can see me. It’s a typhoon. It’s practical.” She pointed at him. “Tonight.”

“Tonight,” he agreed.

✦ ✦ ✦

A little before ten, the room changed. Not the way it looked. The lights stayed too bright. The rain kept coming against the window. A cold coffee sat abandoned on the desk. But something went through the building, and she felt it before anyone said anything.

On the radio the tower’s voice went flatter and quicker. On the screen, a single blip that had been crawling in from the sea on the line of the runway was suddenly much closer to the edge of everything. Song-Zhu stood up.

He stepped back out of her way without being asked.

“What is it?” he said, low.

“The freighter. He’s on finals.” She was watching the screen, and listening to the radio, and her hand had gone out flat onto the desk. “The wind’s changing over the threshold.”

The radio crackled. A pilot’s voice, calm, much too calm.

Wind shear, going around.

The blip, which had been coming down, stopped coming down.

On the screen, beside it, a small data block changed. Height. Ground speed. The numbers flicking. Coming down still, for a second, a second more, even with the engines at full power, the air going out from underneath him. Song-Zhu stopped breathing.

Ren Hao saw it. Her hands were braced on the edge of the desk. Her lips had parted. Her eyes didn’t move from the screen at all. She didn’t blink. The tower said something and the pilot said something back, and she didn’t move. Then the number went up.

Slowly. Then less slowly. The blip lifted off the line of the runway and went out over the sea again, climbing.

Climbing, runway heading. Request diversion.

Song-Zhu breathed out.

The whole room seemed to breathe out with her. Down the corridor someone said, quite loudly, “Okay,” and somebody else laughed, too high.

She picked up the radio handset from its cradle and pressed the button and spoke into it, and her voice was absolutely steady.

“Duty investigator. I want the tower recording from the start of his approach preserved. Radar data, same window. The wind readings from both ends of the runway at one-second intervals. And somebody ring his company now, before he lands at the alternate, and ask them to pull the voice recorder breaker as soon as he’s at the gate, so the last two hours don’t get recorded over while they sit there with the power on. Ask them to confirm in writing.”

Someone acknowledged. She put the handset down. She stayed in front of the screen. Ren Hao stayed behind her. He didn’t ask if she was all right. Not yet.

He watched the radar turn in her eyes. The aircraft was still in the air. The storm was still out there. And she was already working out what had happened, and what could be known about it, and what had to be kept so that one day someone could.

He had seen her work before. He had never seen her like this. There was nothing chaotic in her now. Nothing funny. No mischief at all. Just attention: a complete, disciplined concentration so total that the rest of the room seemed to fall away from her like water off a wing.

After a few minutes she stepped back. Her shoulders came down. She rubbed her forehead with the heel of her hand. He picked up the bowl.

“Soup?”

She turned. For a second she looked at him. Then she smiled.

“Yes.”

He gave it to her. She held it in both hands without eating any of it, just for the warmth, and he put his hand on her back between her shoulder blades for a moment and took it away again.

“Thank you,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

By about eleven it was over, as far as anything was over. The freighter had landed at an alternate two hundred kilometres up the coast, on a dry runway, without a scratch. Its company had pulled the recorder breaker at the gate and sent a scanned form to prove it. The tower tapes were being copied. The wind data was being exported. Tomorrow someone would sit down and decide whether it was a serious incident or just a pilot doing his job very well in a typhoon, and Song-Zhu thought it was probably the second.

There would be no conclusions tonight. There was no reason to rush any.

When she came back into the little room he had moved the camp bed against the wall under the window and put the towel folded on it, and her bag at the end of it, and the battery plugged in beside it.

She looked at it. “You’re serious about this.”

“Yes.”

She pressed the canvas. It wobbled. He looked at it. She looked at him.

“Maybe I’ll take the sofa,” she said.

“No.”

“Maybe you take the sofa.”

“I’ll be fine.”

She raised an eyebrow. “You’re staying?”

He looked at her. “Did you think I’d leave you here?”

“I thought you might have to go home.”

“I can work from here in the morning.”

“You can?”

“I brought my laptop.”

“Of course you did,” she said. “In the suit carrier. Next to my socks.”

He took her hand and drew her towards him and kissed her cheek, and her temple, and she looked up at him.

“You look tired,” she said.

“So do you.”

“I’ve been working.”

“So have I.”

“Have you?”

“I assembled a bed.”

She laughed into his chest. “Heroic.”

He held her a little tighter, and then he kissed her properly, slow and warm, and she put her arms up round his neck and let him.

When they stopped she rested her forehead on his.

“Stay with me,” she said.

“I’m here.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Just after midnight the building had gone as quiet as a building in a typhoon could go. The duty team down the corridor were taking it in turns to watch the screens and put their heads on their arms. The radar turned. The rain had changed direction and was hitting the other side of the building now, a long low roar like the sea.

She’d locked the door. He’d changed into the clean shirt from the suit carrier. She was sitting on the edge of the camp bed watching him with an expression he recognised.

“What?” he said.

“Nothing.”

“That’s never true.”

She held out her hand. He took it. She pulled, and he sat beside her, and the camp bed creaked like a ship. They both looked down at it.

She pressed her lips together. “Don’t laugh.”

“I’m not laughing.”

“You are. Inside.”

She leaned over and kissed him. He kissed her back with one hand at her waist, and it went deep almost at once. Her fingers went into his hair. He kissed her jaw, the side of her neck under her ear where she liked it, back to her mouth.

It was different, being together here. Not his flat with its lined-up shoes, or hers with its laundry. A small room at the edge of an airport, with the radio murmuring on the desk and a storm coming in off the sea and four exhausted colleagues thirty metres away down a corridor. Surrounded by her work. By the knowledge that out there in the dark the weather was still going.

And she wanted him, in the middle of it. And he wanted to be the thing she came back to.

She drew back an inch. “You’re still wearing trousers.”

He looked down. “Yes.”

“That’s very formal of you.”

“I came from work.”

“You’re at my work now.”

“Is that an instruction?”

“It’s a strong suggestion,” she said, and he laughed against her mouth and did as he was told.

She pulled her borrowed cotton shirt off over her head and dropped it on the floor. He looked at her in the light from the radar screen, blue and moving, and put his mouth on her collarbone, and then lower, slowly, until she arched against him and her breath went ragged. She pushed him down onto his back on the canvas and the frame complained and she ignored it. She took his clean shirt off him, button by button this time, deliberately, looking at him the whole time, and kissed her way down his chest, and when she got to his belt she looked up at him and he’d stopped breathing the way she had at the screen.

She took him into her mouth, and he said her name to the ceiling of the duty investigator’s rest room in a voice that had absolutely nothing professional left in it, and put one hand over his own mouth, because of the corridor. She laughed round him and he nearly died. She was slow and wicked and thorough and she stopped every time he got close, on purpose, and looked up at him, and waited, until he took his hand off his mouth and said please out loud.

Then she climbed up him and took him inside her, and they both went still.

“Look at me,” she said.

He looked at her. She started to move. He put his hands on her hips and held on, and she rode him slowly on a camp bed in a typhoon with the rain roaring on the far wall and the radar sweeping blue light across her skin every four seconds, and he watched her face in that light. He sat up, so he could hold her properly, so he could put his mouth on her throat. She wound her arms round his neck. The rhythm went from slow to something else. He was saying her name into her shoulder and she was saying his into his hair, because of the corridor, and it was getting harder to be quiet, and harder, and she was right there, she was so close, she was—

At half past midnight, the camp bed collapsed. There was no warning worth mentioning. One moment he was holding her with one arm round her back and the other braced on the canvas. The next, a metal leg folded neatly underneath them like a knee. The frame lurched. The canvas tipped.

He made a startled sound. She grabbed his shoulders. And the two of them went down together, sideways, in a tangle of aluminium and canvas and limbs, onto the carpet tiles.

It wasn’t loud. But it was spectacularly undignified. A clatter of metal. A soft thump. Then silence.

For two seconds neither of them moved. He was half on the floor and half inside the wreckage of the frame. She was on top of him, staring down into his face from three centimetres away with her hair hanging round both of them. Then she started to laugh.

It wasn’t a quiet laugh. She buried her face in his neck to muffle it and it shook her whole body, and his, and she couldn’t get a breath.

“Are you hurt?” he said into her hair.

She shook her head, still laughing.

“Song-Zhu.”

“I’m fine. I’m fine. Are you?”

He looked sideways at the camp bed. One leg had folded entirely in on itself. Another stuck out into the room at an angle that shouldn’t have been possible. He shut his eyes.

“I brought a defective bed.”

She lifted her head. “You brought a defective bed to my work.”

“It was meant to be practical.”

She was crying with laughter now. Down the corridor somebody called, “Everything all right, Song-Zhu?” and she called back, “Filing cabinet,” in a voice so steady and so completely professional that he had to put his face in her shoulder.

She looked down at him. His hair was ruined. His clean shirt was somewhere under the frame. There was a small crease between his eyebrows, as there always was when he couldn’t understand how a thing had gone wrong. She smoothed it out with her thumb.

“Are you all right?”

“Yes.”

“Good,” she said. “Because I’m not finished.”

And she kissed him, there on the floor, and moved against him, and he was still inside her, and they both remembered that at the same moment. He laughed against her mouth, low and helpless, and then stopped laughing, and rolled them both over off the wreckage onto the carpet with his hand behind her head so it didn’t hit the floor, and finished what they’d started. Slowly at first, laughing, his forehead on hers, both of them shaking with it, and then not slowly, and not laughing, the rain roaring on the far wall and the floor hard under her back and her heels locked behind his thighs. She came with her mouth open against his shoulder, biting down so as not to make a sound, and he followed her with his face in her hair and a sound he couldn’t stop, and a long way off down the corridor somebody turned up the radio.

✦ ✦ ✦

A little after one they were still on the floor. He’d pulled the towel and the blanket off the wreckage and spread them on the carpet tiles. The camp bed lay against the wall like something that had been shot.

She lay on her side with her head on his chest. His arm was round her. One desk lamp was on. The radar went on turning on the screen. Outside, the storm went on.

“You’ll have to buy a new bed,” she said.

“I know.”

“Not that one.”

“No.”

“A sturdy one.”

“I’ll research it.”

She lifted her head. “Don’t.”

He laughed. “All right.”

She put her cheek back down on him. After a while she said, “Thank you for coming.”

He put his mouth against her hair. “Of course.”

“You didn’t have to.”

“I know.”

“I like that you came.”

His arm tightened. “Good.”

She traced a line along his ribs. “Today was strange.”

“Because of the storm?”

“Because everything stopped, and we couldn’t.” She was quiet. “The whole city stopped. Nobody could fly. Thousands of people sleeping on terminal floors. And we couldn’t stop, because the one time we stop is the one time something happens.” She swallowed. “When he went round, I knew it was the right thing. He did it perfectly. You could hear it in his voice. But when you’re watching the numbers you still feel every one of them. You’re waiting for the one that doesn’t go up.”

He didn’t say anything. He held on.

“I hate that,” she said. “The second when you don’t know what comes next.”

“I can imagine.”

“Do you get it? At work?”

He thought about it. “Often.”

“What do you do?”

“Decide with what I’ve got. Accept what I haven’t got. Keep going.”

She smiled against him. “That’s very you.”

“It works.”

“Sometimes.”

“Sometimes,” he agreed.

“Do you think we’re alike?” she said, after a while.

“In some ways.”

“Which?”

“You take your work seriously. So do I. You hate being told what to do. So do I.” He paused. “And we both care about people a great deal more than we’d ever admit.”

She laughed. Then she turned her face and kissed his chest. “That’s a nice thing to say.”

“It’s true.”

She settled again, and a few minutes later, nearly asleep, said, “Hao?”

“Mm.”

“Next time, just bring soup.”

“Understood.”

“And a blanket.”

“All right.”

“No furniture.”

“Noted.”

She lifted her head one last time and looked at him. “And no lists.”

He kissed her temple. “No lists.”

“Good boyfriend,” she said, and tucked herself back against him, and was asleep before he’d answered.

✦ ✦ ✦

A little before seven, she woke to the sound of the door being unlocked from outside with the duty key.

The blanket had slipped to her waist. He was still asleep beside her on the floor with one arm folded under his head. His shirt was wrinkled, his hair was a disaster, and without its usual composure his face looked about nineteen.

She smiled. Then she sat up carefully, and pulled the blanket up, and looked at the camp bed lying against the wall with its legs in the air. She began to laugh without making a sound.

He opened one eye. “What?”

She pointed. He followed her finger, and shut his eye again.

“Don’t.”

“Good morning,” she whispered.

He looked at his watch. “Is it?”

“Apparently.”

The door opened. Dexter came in with a mug of coffee, on his way to the radio charger in the filing cabinet, and stopped dead at the sight of the two of them on the floor under a blanket, and then at the camp bed, and then at the two of them again. There was a short silence.

“Good morning,” said Song-Zhu, pleasantly, from the floor.

Dexter looked at Ren Hao. Then at the camp bed. Then at Ren Hao again.

“Morning,” he said.

And he walked to the filing cabinet, took out the charger, and walked out again, and shut the door, without asking a single question.

Ren Hao watched the door close. “Very professional.”

“He’ll tell everyone by eight,” said Song-Zhu.

“Will he?”

“Everyone. Mabel will put it in the duty log. Oh-six-forty-two. Camp bed: total loss.”

He put his arm over his eyes. She leaned down and kissed his cheek.

“Your bed’s made an impression.”

“I will never bring furniture here again.”

“Good,” she said, and held out her hand to pull him up off the floor. “Come on. We’ve both got work.”

He took her hand. And as they got to their feet he looked once more at the camp bed with its legs in the air.

He had brought soup, and dry clothes, and a blanket, and somewhere for her to sleep. The weather had seen to the rest.

That, he supposed, was the trouble with planning for a typhoon. It never kept to the schedule.

chapters.title: The Loudest Man She Knows
chapters.desc: He says I love you in a restaurant, at volume. Half the room applauds. She can’t say it back. She kisses him instead.
chapters.epigraph: “I didn’t say it to get an answer.”
chapters.content:
Ren Hao had never been any good at keeping things to himself.

He said what he meant. He asked for what he wanted. He told people when they had done well and when they’d disappointed him and when he thought they were about to make a terrible mistake, in that order, often in the same meeting. He said good morning to the security guards by name. He told his assistant’s dog he loved her. He rang his sister to remind her to take an umbrella when she was already standing under one.

And he had recently acquired a girlfriend, a fact he appeared to find tremendously enjoyable.

Song-Zhu had been finding this out for a fortnight. He rang her at lunch. He sent her photographs of things that reminded him of her, including an aggressively ugly ceramic duck in a shop window on Harbour Road with the single caption you. He kissed her hello wherever they were, as if there were no conceivable reason to wait. And he used the word girlfriend with a frequency that suggested he was making up for lost time: to Joyce, to Mr. Yau, to a waiter, once to a man from a utility company who had rung about his meter.

She was still getting used to it. Not to him. To being loved that openly, in daylight, in front of people.

That Saturday she was going to find out exactly how openly.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You’re staring,” he said.

Song-Zhu looked up from the menu. They were in a restaurant in the business district, soft lighting and dark wood and the kind of distance between tables that made private conversation possible, which was why he’d chosen it, because she’d mentioned once that she wanted to try their fish. He’d booked a table for two. She had arrived twelve minutes late. He had kissed her hello and said absolutely nothing about it.

Progress.

“I’m reading,” she said.

“You’ve been reading the same page for four minutes.”

“Maybe it’s a very interesting page.”

“What does it say?”

She looked down. “That the fish here costs about the same as my car.”

“Useful.”

“Very.”

The waiter came. She chose a steamed fish with ginger and a dish of greens; he chose beef, and asked for an extra plate so they could share, and she watched him ask for it and found she liked it more than she’d expected to.

“How was your week?” she said.

“Busy.”

“That’s always your answer.”

“It’s always true.”

“Anything interesting?”

He told her about a difficult client meeting, a new analyst who had completely misunderstood a reporting line, and an argument between two of his department heads that had somehow, by a process nobody could explain, become his fault. She listened, and asked questions in the right places. Then she told him about a briefing, an administrative delay on the freighter from the typhoon, which had been signed off as a textbook go-around in under a week, and a colleague who had accidentally sent a photograph of his lunch to the all-staff group.

“What was it?”

“A boiled egg. A very sad one. Alone on a plate.”

“That’s unfortunate.”

“He captioned it the usual suspect.”

He laughed, properly, the laugh that made his eyes go narrow and his shoulders come down. She liked making him do that. He had a face that could make a whole room reconsider its choices, but when he laughed like that he looked younger. Less like a managing director. More like the boy Isla had described, who made lists for his parents and baked a cake that came out as a biscuit.

She rested her chin on her hand and looked at him.

“Now you’re staring,” he said.

“Maybe you’re very interesting.”

He smiled.

She rolled her eyes. “Don’t steal my lines.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The food came. They shared the beef, argued about which part of the fish was the best part, and agreed that the greens were much better than either of them had expected.

At one point he reached across the table and wiped a spot of sauce from the corner of her mouth with his thumb.

She looked at him. “I could have done that.”

“I know.”

“Then why did you?”

“Because I wanted to.”

She stared at him for a second. Then she smiled. “You’re very affectionate.”

“Is that bad?”

“No.”

“Good.” He took her hand across the table and his thumb moved over her knuckles, and she looked down at their hands lying there on the white cloth between the plates.

There were people all round them. He never seemed to care much about that. He didn’t make a show of it. He just didn’t see any reason to hide it.

She was still learning what to do with that. Not because she didn’t want it. Because sometimes being cared for so openly made her feel.

He saw her face change. “What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

He waited.

She looked up. “You’ve got your knowing face on.”

“I know several things.”

“Such as?”

“You don’t like the greens as much as you said.”

She laughed. “That’s not true.”

“You’ve moved them all to my side of the plate.”

“Because you’re bigger. You need more greens.”

“That’s your reasoning?”

“It’s scientific.”

He shook his head, smiling. Then the smile went somewhere quieter.

“I like having dinner with you.”

“I like having dinner with you too.”

“Even when I steal your greens?”

“Because you steal my greens.”

He squeezed her hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dessert came at fourteen minutes past nine. She’d chosen something with chocolate and cream. He had ordered a small fruit tart because he’d said he didn’t want anything too sweet, and was now eating half of hers.

She watched him take another spoonful. “Didn’t you say you didn’t want dessert?”

“I changed my mind.”

“How convenient.”

“Yours looked better.”

“It still looks better.” She pushed the plate towards him. “Just eat it.”

He did. Then he put his spoon down. She was scrolling through the photographs on her phone to show him a vending machine at the cargo terminal that sold, as far as anyone could tell, only boiled eggs and umbrellas. He wasn’t looking at the phone. He was looking at her.

At the way her hair had fallen forward over one shoulder. At the small crease between her eyebrows as she tried to make the photograph bigger. At the way she was already laughing before she’d got to the end of explaining why it was funny.

He had known for some time that he was in trouble.

He had liked her from the first evening, when she’d come into a French restaurant late with fuel on her boots and asked if he was nervous around girls. He’d liked her more at the taxi rank. And then she’d brought chaos into a life he had arranged carefully, and he had somehow started looking forward to every single interruption.

He liked her first thing in the morning. He liked her when she was so tired she was cross. He liked her talking about her work and he liked her complaining about the food. He liked her terrible flat. He liked her terrible jokes. He liked that she could make him feel entirely ridiculous and entirely himself in the same five minutes.

And a while now he had been thinking something he hadn’t said. It was getting difficult to keep it in.

“Song-Zhu.”

She looked up from the phone. “Mm?”

He smiled at her.

“I love you.”

She blinked.

He went on, apparently quite unaware that the restaurant around them had gone a little quieter. “I really love you.”

At the next table a couple looked round. Song-Zhu went entirely still.

He was still holding her hand. His face was open and warm and completely unguarded, the way it never was at work, the way she had only ever seen it in the dark.

And then, because he was Ren Hao, he said it again.

“I love you.”

Louder. Much louder. The voice he used to stop a boardroom.

A waiter carrying a tray of glasses stopped in the middle of the floor. Someone at the next table smiled. A woman by the window put her glass down slowly.

Song-Zhu stared at him. “Hao.”

“What?”

“Your voice.”

He looked puzzled for one second. Then he realised. “Oh.”

He looked round. Several people were smiling at them. A man in a grey suit lifted his glass in their direction. A woman near the door started to clap. Someone else joined her. And then, as if somebody had given a signal, half the restaurant was applauding: the waiter with the tray, the couple at the next table, an elderly man in the corner who clearly had no idea what was going on and was clapping anyway out of solidarity.

Song-Zhu wanted the floor to open and swallow her.

Ren Hao looked round at all of them, and laughed, and lifted one hand in a small, awkward acknowledgement, like a man who’d been thanked for holding a door.

“Thank you,” he said.

“Don’t encourage them,” she hissed.

He turned back to her, and his smile was enormous.

“Sorry,” he said.

He didn’t look sorry. Not in the slightest.

✦ ✦ ✦

She had imagined him saying it. Of course she had.

She’d wondered when it might happen. Whether it would be some quiet evening at his flat, or in the middle of an argument, or in some ordinary moment, over the washing-up, with no warning. She had imagined saying it back. She had even practised it once, on her own in her flat, with her toothbrush in her mouth, and it had sounded perfectly simple. Three words. Easy.

And now he was sitting there in front of her, looking at her. And she couldn’t say it.

The words were there. Somewhere. Caught behind something tight in her throat.

She loved him. She knew that much. She loved the way he listened. The way he remembered small things. The way he could be serious without being cold, and look after her without making her feel weak. She loved his ridiculous concern about her meals. She loved that he had carried a broken camp bed into an airport in a typhoon because he wanted her to be comfortable. She loved that he had never once made her feel strange about the parts of her life that were hard to explain.

But saying it out loud was a different thing.

It felt like opening a door and finding that there was no way to shut it again.

She had spent years learning how to let things go. How to accept that people disappeared. How to keep going when something ended with no warning at all. Her whole working life had taught her that ordinary things changed in an instant. And here was a man who loved her.

She wanted to meet him there. She wanted to give him the same certainty back. She couldn’t make her mouth move.

His smile went softer. “Hey.”

She looked at him.

He leaned forward a little. “Are you all right?”

She nodded. He waited. She looked down at their hands.

“I’m sorry,” she said.

His face changed. “What for?”

“I—”

She swallowed. He didn’t hurry her. Around them the restaurant was slowly going back to its own noise: a glass, a laugh, the waiter moving on. But the space between the two of them was quiet.

“I can’t say it,” she whispered.

He looked at her. Then his thumb moved, gently, over the back of her hand.

“That’s all right.”

She looked up fast. “It isn’t that I don’t—”

“I know.”

He said it straight away. No hesitation. No disappointment in it anywhere.

She searched his face. “You do?”

He nodded. “I know.”

She looked away. He lifted their joined hands and kissed her knuckles.

“You don’t have to say anything because I did,” he said. “I didn’t say it to get an answer.”

Her eyes stung, and stupidly.

“I said it,” he said, quieter now, “because I love you. That’s all it was for.”

And somehow that made it worse. Not because he’d hurt her. Because he hadn’t. Because he had given her room to be frightened without making her feel guilty for it. She looked at him. Then she stood up.

He looked up at her, startled. “Song-Zhu?”

She came round the table. He got to his feet as she reached him, and before he could ask her anything at all she took hold of the front of his shirt in both hands and kissed him.

It wasn’t careful. It wasn’t polite. She kissed him as if she were trying to put everything she couldn’t say into the small space between their mouths. Her hands went up to his shoulders. His arms came round her. For one second he seemed completely taken by surprise. Then he kissed her back.

The restaurant was still watching. Somebody made a delighted noise. Song-Zhu didn’t care at all.

When she finally pulled away she rested her forehead against his. His eyes were bright. She was still holding his shirt. He smiled.

“All right,” he said.

She looked at him. “All right?”

“I’ll take that.” He nodded, slowly, as if accepting the terms of something. “That’s a yes. I’m taking it as a yes.”

She laughed, and her eyes were wet. He brushed his thumb under one of them.

“Don’t cry.”

“I’m not crying.”

“You’re a terrible liar.”

She laughed again, and he put his mouth briefly to her hair, and then said, with a quiet certainty that made her chest ache: “I understand.”

She nodded. She didn’t know whether he did. But she wanted him to.

✦ ✦ ✦

They left ten minutes later. He paid while she waited by the door, still warm from the kiss, and when they stepped out onto the pavement he reached for her hand, and she gave it to him.

The night air was cool. The traffic on the main road went past steadily, and the city seemed entirely unconcerned that her boyfriend had just declared his love to a room full of strangers and been given a round of applause for it.

She looked sideways at him. “You’re ridiculous.”

“I’ve been told.”

“You said it so loudly.”

“I didn’t realise.”

“Half the restaurant clapped.”

“That was kind of them.”

She laughed. He looked at her.

“Are you embarrassed?”

“Mortified.”

“Sorry.”

She stopped walking. He stopped too. She looked at him for a moment under the streetlight.

“Don’t be sorry.”

He smiled faintly. “All right.”

She put her arms round his waist. He held her.

“I just wasn’t expecting it,” she said into his coat.

“I know.”

“Or the applause.”

“That surprised me too.”

She leaned back to look at him. “You’re not upset? That I didn’t say it?”

His face went soft. “Song-Zhu.”

She waited.

“I don’t need you to say anything before you’re ready to. I’d much rather hear it when you mean it and want to say it. Not because you’re worried I’ll be disappointed if you don’t.” He paused. “I’m not disappointed. I’m in love with you on a pavement. It’s a very good evening.”

Her throat went tight again. She put her cheek against his chest. He put his chin on her hair.

“And for the record,” he said, “I liked the kiss.”

She laughed into his coat. “Good.”

“Very much.”

“You’re unbearable.”

“Apparently.”

She lifted her face, and he kissed her again, and this time it was quieter. No applause. No audience. Just the two of them under a streetlight on a Saturday night, and a taxi going past slowly with its window down, and the driver whistling.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the car he drove with one hand on the wheel and the other lying on the console near hers. She sat beside him watching the city go past. After a while she reached over and took his hand and laced her fingers through his.

He glanced at her. She was looking out of the window.

“Can I tell you something?” she said.

“Of course.”

“I don’t think I’ve ever been loved like this.”

His fingers tightened a little.

“Not like it’s something you have to hide,” she said. “Or something you have to earn by being useful. You just say it.”

He was quiet. “I don’t see a reason not to.”

“I know you don’t.” She smiled faintly at the window. “That’s the frightening part.”

At a red light he lifted her hand to his mouth.

“I don’t want you to ever have to wonder whether I love you,” he said.

She turned to look at him. “I don’t.”

“Good.”

She looked at him a long time. Then she leaned over and kissed his cheek.

“That was nice,” he said.

“Don’t get greedy.”

“I already am.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At her building he walked her to the door. She turned under the awning to face him.

“Thank you for dinner.”

“You’re welcome.”

“And for the public announcement.”

He laughed. “I’ll try to keep the next one private.”

“Please do.”

He put his hand on her cheek. “Good night.”

She caught his wrist. “Wait.”

He waited. She stood close.

“I love being with you,” she said. It came out carefully.

His face went soft. “I love being with you too.”

“And I love the way you love me.”

He smiled.

She ran her thumb over the inside of his wrist. “I just need a bit of time.”

“Take it,” said Ren Hao. “Take as long as you like. I’m not going anywhere.”

She kissed him once more and stepped back. “Good night, boyfriend.”

“Good night, girlfriend.”

She went in. He stood on the pavement until he saw her reach the lift.

✦ ✦ ✦

A little before midnight his phone lit on the passenger seat.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Home yet?

Ren Hao: Nearly.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Drive carefully.

Ren Hao: I will.

A few seconds passed.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Hao?

Ren Hao: Yes?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I didn’t say it because I’m scared.

He pulled in at the side of the road and looked at the message.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Not of you.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Of how much it matters.

He read it twice.

Ren Hao: I understand.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Do you?

Ren Hao: I think so. And you don’t have to explain anything else tonight.

There was a pause.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): You really are very loud.

Ren Hao: I know.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Most of all when you love someone.

He looked at that a long time.

Ren Hao: Most of all then.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Good night.

Ren Hao: Good night. I love you.

He put the phone down on the seat. Then he picked it up again.

Ren Hao: Sorry. Once more for luck. I love you.

The reply came almost at once.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): HAHAHAHA

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Keep saying it.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Good night, Hao.

He sat in the car at the side of the road and laughed to himself.

He wasn’t going to stop saying it. Not because he needed to hear it back, not because he expected her to catch up by any particular date. But because he had spent far too much of his life believing that affection was something to be measured, and managed, and kept in its proper place.

She had asked him to keep saying it. So he would. Loudly, if necessary.

And one day, perhaps, she would say it back.

Until then he would wait. He was good at waiting, when something mattered.

chapters.title: Not Yet
chapters.desc: Why she can’t: her father, a cargo pilot, and fifty seconds of his recorder at nineteen. He sits with her all night on the kitchen floor.
chapters.epigraph: “I wanted to say it back. When you said it. I wanted to so much.”
chapters.content:
At twelve minutes past eight on Sunday evening, Ren Hao’s phone lit on the dining table beside a dinner he hadn’t touched.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Are you busy?

He was going through a document on his laptop.

Ren Hao: Not especially. What’s wrong?

The dots appeared. Went. Came back.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Can I come round?

Ren Hao: Of course.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I don’t want to go out.

Ren Hao: We don’t have to.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I don’t want to eat either.

He looked at that one a while.

Ren Hao: All right.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Can you just be there?

He shut the laptop.

Ren Hao: Yes. I’ll be here.

✦ ✦ ✦

She arrived a little before nine. He heard the lift, and then her footsteps in the corridor, slower than usual, and opened the door before she knocked.

She was standing there with her hands pushed into the pockets of her jacket.

She looked tired. Not the ordinary tiredness after a long shift, which he had come to know by now. Something else. Something held much too tightly behind her eyes.

He didn’t ask what had happened. He stood aside.

“Come in.”

She walked past him. He shut the door and watched her put her bag down by the sofa. She didn’t take off her jacket. She didn’t say anything about the shoes lined up in the hall. She didn’t ask what he’d been working on, or look at his untouched plate and tell him off for it. She just stood in the middle of his living room.

He went to her slowly.

“Hey.”

She looked at him. “Hi.”

He touched her cheek. “Would you like a hug?”

Her mouth trembled. She nodded. He drew her in. At first she stood still against him, her arms at her sides. Then her hands came round his waist and she pressed her face into his chest.

He held her without saying anything. He could feel her breathing change. Not crying, not yet. Just trying hard not to.

After a while he put his mouth against her hair. “Would you like to sit down?”

She nodded into his shirt. He took her to the sofa. She sat at one end, and then moved along when he sat down beside her, until she was against him, and he put his arm round her. For several minutes neither of them spoke.

Then she said, low, “I think I owe you an explanation.”

He looked down at her. “What for?”

“Last night.”

He knew at once. The restaurant. The applause. The three words she hadn’t been able to say back.

His hand moved slowly up and down her arm. “You don’t owe me anything.”

“I want to tell you.”

“All right.”

She looked at her hands. Then at the window, where the city was dark and full of other people’s lights.

“I’ve never told anyone this,” she said.

He didn’t move at all.

“My father was a pilot.”

She said it simply, the way she’d have given someone an aircraft’s registration.

“A cargo pilot. He flew freighters. Mostly nights. Sometimes he’d be gone for three days, sometimes a week.” Her fingers had found a loose thread on her sleeve and were working at it. “When I was small I thought it was the best job in the world. He’d come home with stories about places I’d never heard of. He brought me things from airports. Tiny souvenirs. Postcards. Terrible little toys.” A faint smile. “He once brought me a snow globe from somewhere with a name I couldn’t say. I dropped it two days later on the kitchen tiles.”

He smiled gently. “What did he say?”

“That he’d get me another one.”

She swallowed.

“He didn’t.”

He waited.

“He died when I was nineteen.”

The room went quiet. His arm stayed round her shoulders, but his hand stopped moving.

She took a breath. “There was an accident. His aircraft went down on a cargo flight. At night.”

She didn’t say where. She didn’t give him a date. She didn’t describe the aircraft, or the weather, or who had been waiting for it at the other end. She didn’t have to. He understood that she was walking slowly up to something she had spent six years walking round.

“I’m sorry,” he said.

She nodded. “Thank you.”

He didn’t ask what happened. She looked at him as if she’d noticed that.

“I was already doing engineering by then. Aerospace. Second year. Not because I wanted to do this. I liked aircraft. I liked how they worked. He used to explain things to me when I was little. The flaps. Why the wings bend.” The smile went. “After the accident I started reading everything I could find. I wanted to know what had happened. I wanted to know what the investigators knew, and what they were looking at, and what the recorders could tell them. I read every final report from every freighter accident in the last twenty years. In the university library. At night.”

He listened.

“I was nineteen,” she said. “I thought if I understood enough, I’d understand why he wasn’t coming home.”

Her voice caught. She stopped. He squeezed her shoulder, gently. She shut her eyes.

“And then,” she said, “I heard him.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It hadn’t been meant to happen.

That was the first thing she told him, and she told it. Cockpit recordings were protected. Every investigator was taught that on their first day, and she had been taught it since: the voice recorder belonged to the investigation, and nobody else, not the airline, not the police, not the press, not the families, ever heard it. The words that mattered went into the report as a transcript, as few as possible, and the rest stayed in the room for ever.

But there had been a family briefing in the spring, five months after the accident, in a meeting room at the investigators’ offices in the country where he’d come down. Her mother had sat through two hours of slides. And at the end her mother had asked the investigator-in-charge, an older man with tired eyes, whether her husband had been afraid. Just that. Was he afraid.

And the investigator-in-charge had looked at her a long time, and then at Song-Zhu, nineteen, beside her, with a notebook full of questions, and had said that he couldn’t answer that. And then he had asked them both to wait. And he had gone out, and come back forty minutes later with a laptop and a form, which they had both signed, promising never to repeat or record or describe what they heard. And he had played them fifty seconds.

“He told us afterwards it was the only time in thirty-one years he’d ever done it,” she said. “He said he’d probably lose his job if anyone found out. He didn’t. He retired two years later. He sent me a card when I qualified.” She looked down. “I’ve never told anyone because it was his secret too. Not just mine.”

Ren Hao had gone still beside her.

“What did you hear?”

“Him.” Her voice had gone small. “His voice. The other pilot. The radio. The ordinary sounds in a cockpit. I knew his voice better than anyone’s in the world. I could pick it out across a crowded airport. I knew when he was tired. I knew when he was pretending not to be annoyed.” A little broken laugh came out of her. “I could tell when he was drinking coffee.”

His thumb moved on her shoulder.

“And then I heard it on that laptop,” she said, and her eyes had filled. “Not on the phone. Not telling me he’d be home on Friday. Not asking if I’d done my homework. Just him. Doing his job.”

She pressed her lips together.

“He sounded completely normal,” she said. “That’s what I couldn’t stand. He was talking to the other pilot. Ordinary calls. He was doing everything he was meant to do. He sounded exactly like my dad. The same voice that used to tell me to put a coat on when it was cold.”

A tear ran down her cheek.

“And I kept waiting.”

He took her hand. “For what?”

She shook her head. “I don’t know. For him to say something that would explain it. For him to sound frightened, so I’d understand. For him to say my name.” She wiped her cheek with the heel of her hand. “But he didn’t. He was just there, and then it stopped. The investigator stopped it. It was fifty seconds and it wasn’t even the end. I don’t know what came after. I’ve never known. That’s what I’ve got.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Ren Hao had negotiated with people who were terrified. He had sat across from executives who had lost everything, and listened to families who had had the worst phone call of their lives, and watched men twice his age try and fail to speak when they understood that no amount of money was going to change what had happened.

He knew how to sit through a silence. He knew how to let someone finish.

But there was something about watching her try to say this that made him feel entirely helpless.

She spent her days listening to other people’s last recordings. She knew how to handle them. She knew how to document them, preserve them, analyse them, separate what could be known from what couldn’t. And once, she had been a nineteen-year-old with a notebook, sitting beside her mother, listening to her father’s voice in a room where he would never hear hers again.

“Was your mother all right?” he said. “Afterwards?”

“No.” She looked at their hands. “We didn’t talk about it. Not on the plane home. Not ever. She’d lost him too. I didn’t want to make her hear it again through me.” Her voice dropped. “And I didn’t want anyone to think I was strange. For wanting to hear it.”

“Why would anyone think that?”

“Because I’d asked. In my notebook, the first question on the list. Can we hear the recorder. My mother asked if he was afraid. But I’d asked first, at the start of the meeting, and they’d said no, and I was angry.” She swallowed. “Because I wanted to hear my father’s voice even though I knew what I’d be listening to. Because part of me thought that if I could hear him, I could have him for a bit longer.”

His face went soft. “Song-Zhu.”

She shook her head. “I know how it sounds.”

“No.”

“I know it isn’t rational.”

“You’re not required to be rational about losing your father.” He held her eyes. “You were nineteen. You wanted to hear someone you loved. There’s nothing strange about that. Not one thing.”

Her face crumpled. He drew her in against him, and this time she cried.

It wasn’t dramatic. She didn’t sob, or struggle to breathe. The tears just came, and kept coming, and didn’t stop: six years of carefully held-down grief, finally given somewhere to go.

He held her. He didn’t tell her to stop. He didn’t tell her it would be all right, because he didn’t know that. He didn’t tell her that her father would have been proud of her, because he hadn’t known her father and he wasn’t going to turn her pain into a sentence that made him feel better. He just held on.

When at last she pulled back she wiped her face with both hands and gave him a small embarrassed smile.

“Sorry.”

He frowned. “What for?”

“Your shirt.”

He looked down. There was a wet patch on his shoulder the size of a hand. He looked back at her.

“Song-Zhu. It’s a shirt.”

“It’s an expensive shirt.”

“I have others.”

She laughed, weakly.

“Many others,” he said, and she laughed again, with less pain in it. He pushed her hair back from her face.

“Water?”

She nodded. He brought her a glass and sat back down, and she drank a little and put it on the table.

“I don’t know why I couldn’t tell you last night,” she said.

“You don’t have to know.”

“I wanted to say it back. When you said it. I wanted to so much.” She rubbed her eyes. “But I thought about my father. About the laptop. About how for years I believed that if I loved someone enough, I could somehow keep them. And I couldn’t. I couldn’t save him. I couldn’t even understand what happened. I just had to accept that one day he was there and the next day he wasn’t, and some tired man in an office in another country knew more about the end of my father’s life than I did.”

He took her hand. She held on.

“And when you said you loved me I was happy. I was so happy, Hao. And I was also more frightened than I’ve been since I was nineteen.” Her voice shook. “Because I know what it feels like. I know what it does to you. And I don’t want to spend every day waiting for the phone to ring at four in the morning.”

“You don’t have to.”

“I know that. In my head.” A small helpless laugh. “My head’s very good at knowing things.”

“And the rest of you?”

“The rest of me is stupid.”

He lifted her hand and kissed it. “No. The rest of you is grieving.”

She looked at him.

“Those aren’t the same thing,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

A little before midnight they moved to the kitchen. She’d said she wanted more water, and then she’d said she wanted to sit somewhere else, and he followed her without asking why.

She lowered herself to the kitchen floor with her back against the cupboard under the counter. He looked at her for a second. Then he sat down beside her.

“You’re sitting on the floor,” she said.

“Yes.”

“Your trousers.”

“They wash.”

“You really don’t mind?”

He looked round at the tiles. “Should I be sitting somewhere else?”

“No.”

He stretched his legs out. “Then I’m perfectly comfortable.”

She leaned her head back against the cupboard door. For a while they listened to the flat: the fridge humming, a car somewhere below, the clock on the wall moving on by a minute and then another.

“Can I tell you something else?” she said.

“Of course.”

“I’ve never told anyone about the laptop. Not anyone. Not my friends. Not my colleagues. Not Mabel. Not Isla.”

He turned to look at her.

“Mabel knows my father died,” she said. “It’s on my file. Everybody knows that, it’s why half of them think I took the job. But nobody knows I heard him. You’re the only person in the world except my mother and a retired man in another country.”

He took that in. She had told him about her work, about the people she listened to, about what stayed with her. But never this. Never the reason she understood, better than anyone in that building, what it meant to listen to a voice that wasn’t ever going to speak again.

He didn’t ask why she’d chosen him. He didn’t want her to feel she owed him a reason for the trust.

“Thank you for telling me,” he said. “I know that wasn’t easy.”

She nodded. “Don’t tell anyone.”

“I won’t.”

“Not Isla.”

“I won’t.”

“Not even if she asks. She’ll ask.”

The corner of his mouth moved. “She asks a great many questions.”

“Exactly.”

He squeezed her hand. “It stays with me.”

She looked at him, and then put her head on his shoulder.

✦ ✦ ✦

A little after twelve he made tea. He’d asked if she wanted some and she’d said no, and he made it anyway and left it on the counter within reach of her hand in case she changed her mind.

When he came back down to the floor she was looking at a photograph on her phone.

“Your father?”

She nodded, and turned the screen towards him. A man in a pilot’s shirt with the sleeves rolled up, standing in front of the nose of a big grey freighter on a sunny apron, one hand up to shade his eyes. Smiling at whoever held the camera. He looked ordinary. Warm. A little amused, as if he knew something funny he hadn’t told anyone yet. Her smile was exactly his.

Ren Hao looked at it a long time. “He’s handsome.”

She laughed. “He knew.”

“Did he?”

“Very much.”

“That sounds familiar.”

She looked at him sideways. “Don’t flatter yourself.”

He laughed. She zoomed in on the photograph with two fingers until it was just her father’s face.

“He used to send me pictures like this. From work. A picture of the sky out of the cockpit window, and something stupid underneath. The clouds are behaving today. Bumpy over the sea, tell your mother I’m fine.”

“He sounds funny.”

“He was.”

She looked at the screen a long time. Then she said, “I miss him.”

He put his arm round her. “I know.”

“No. I mean.” She swallowed. “I miss him in ordinary ways. I miss asking him stupid questions. I miss him telling me my shoes were ugly. I miss him ringing me from some airport at three in the morning his time to ask if I’d eaten.” She looked at him, and her eyes were wet again. “I miss someone who knew me before I was this.”

He turned towards her.

“Everyone I meet now knows me as Song-Zhu,” she said. “The investigator. The one who listens to recordings. The one who can tell you what happened. But he knew me when I was just his daughter.”

He put his mouth to her temple. “You’re still his daughter,” he said.

She shut her eyes. “Even now?”

“Most of all now. You don’t stop being somebody’s daughter because they’re not here any more.” He brushed a tear off her cheek with his thumb. “And you don’t have to stop missing him just because you’ve learned how to live without him.”

She leaned into him. For a long time neither of them said anything at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

A little before two, she said, “Do you think I’m going to be hard to love?”

He looked at her. “Why would you think that?”

“Because I don’t know how to do this properly. Be with someone. Let someone get this close. Have someone who expects me to come home.” She waved a hand vaguely at the two of them. “Have someone who tells me he loves me in a restaurant, at volume.”

He laughed, low. She smiled. Then it went.

“I can’t promise you nothing will happen,” she said.

He took her hand. “I don’t need you to.”

“People say things like for ever.”

“I know.”

“But nobody knows. Nobody.”

He nodded. “You’re right.”

She looked surprised that he hadn’t argued.

“I can’t promise nothing will happen,” he said. “I can’t promise you life will always be kind. I run a firm whose whole business is that it isn’t.” His thumb moved over her knuckles. “But I can promise I won’t make you carry anything on your own while I’m here.”

She stared at him. “And if I get scared?” she said.

“Tell me.”

“What if I can’t?”

“Then sit next to me.”

“What if I don’t know what to say?”

“Then don’t say anything.” He smiled a little. “I seem to have got quite good at sitting on floors.”

She laughed through her tears. He kissed her hair.

“There’s no exam, Song-Zhu. You don’t have to pass anything.”

She looked at him. “You’re very annoying when you’re sensible.”

“I’ll try to be less sensible.”

“Please don’t.”

She put her head back on his shoulder.

✦ ✦ ✦

A little before three, the tea on the counter was stone cold.

A little after three, she fell asleep against him.

He didn’t move. His back was starting to hurt. One leg had gone to sleep. The tiles were cold through his trousers. He could have carried her to the bedroom. He could have fetched a blanket. But she’d fallen asleep with her hand wrapped round his, holding on, and he didn’t want to wake her for anything. So he stayed. He watched the clock.

A little before four, she shifted, and her fingers tightened round his. He looked down. She was still asleep. He pushed a strand of hair off her face.

There was something unbearable in it, he thought. That she had spent so much of her life listening to other people’s losses and kept her own so completely private. He thought about her at nineteen, sitting at a table in a meeting room in another country, listening to fifty seconds on a laptop, waiting for a voice to say something that would make the world make sense again.

He wished he’d been there. Not to change anything, not to explain the accident. Just to sit next to her afterwards, on the plane home, and give her somewhere to put her head, and tell her she didn’t have to be composed. But he hadn’t known her then.

All he could do was be here now. And he would be.

✦ ✦ ✦

A little after five she woke. For a moment she didn’t know where she was. Then she felt his arm round her, and lifted her head.

He looked down at her. “Morning.”

She blinked. “Morning.”

“Did you sleep?”

She nodded. “Did you?”

“A little.”

She looked round at the kitchen floor. At the clock. Back at him. “You’ve been here all night?”

“Yes.”

“On the floor?”

“Yes.”

“Why didn’t you move me?”

“You looked comfortable.”

She stared at him. “Your back must be killing you.”

“Not especially.”

She put her hand on his shoulder. He winced.

She narrowed her eyes. “Ren Hao.”

He laughed. “All right. A bit.”

She looked at him for a long moment in the grey light. Then she leaned forward and kissed his cheek. “Thank you.”

He held her face. “You’re welcome.”

She rested her forehead against his. And then, in a whisper, she said, “I want to say something.”

He went still. She looked into his eyes, close. He could see her trying. He could see the words come right up to the edge of her and stop, the way a car stops at the edge of a cliff.

“I can’t,” she said. “Not yet. I’m sorry. I’m so sorry. I’m not ready to say it.”

“Then don’t.”

“But I’m not going anywhere.” Her voice was shaking. “I want you to know that. I don’t know how to say the other thing yet. But I came here last night instead of sitting on my own kitchen floor, and I’ve never done that, not once, not with anyone. That’s what I’ve got. That’s what I can say.”

He didn’t answer straight away. Not because he didn’t know what to say. Because he wanted to let her have it, the whole of what she’d just given him, without trampling on it.

“That’s enough,” he said. “That’s more than enough.”

She gave a shaky laugh. “You’re not going to make a speech?”

“I wasn’t going to.”

“You’re thinking about one.”

“Maybe.”

“Don’t.”

“All right.”

She kissed him. And this time, when she pulled back, she didn’t look frightened. Just tired. And a little lighter.

“Not yet,” she said, against his mouth.

“Not yet,” he agreed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just after six he helped her up off the floor. She stretched, and her knees cracked, and she made a face.

“Kitchen floors,” he said. “Not ideal.”

“You chose to sit on it.”

“I did.”
