“Nobody made you.”

“No.”

She looked at him. “Thank you for staying.”

He brushed her cheek with his thumb. “Always.”

She raised an eyebrow. He heard it, and corrected himself.

“Whenever you want me there.”

“Better,” she said.

She picked up her phone off the counter. There was a message from Mabel, asking whether she was coming in for the morning review. She wrote back that she’d be in after lunch. Then she put it down.

“Do you want to go home and rest?” he said.

She thought about it. Then she looked at him. “Can I stay here for a bit?”

“Of course.”

She took his hand, and they went down the hall together. At the bedroom door she stopped.

“Hao?”

“Yes?”

“About my father.”

“You don’t ever have to talk about him again if you don’t want to.”

“I know.” She looked at him. “But I think I’ll want to tell you more. One day. There’s one more thing I’ve got of his. Not tonight.”

He nodded. “Whenever you’re ready.”

She smiled faintly. “Not today.”

“Not today.”

She slipped her hand into his, and he followed her in.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later that morning, while she slept, he sat on the end of the bed in yesterday’s clothes and looked at her.

Her phone was charging on the bedside table. Her jacket was over his chair. One of her socks had somehow ended up by the door.

He loved her. He had said it in a restaurant, in a car, by message, and he would say it again on the pavement outside her building, and to Joyce, and to Mr. Yau, and probably to the man about the meter. But now he understood something he hadn’t understood before.

For her, those words weren’t only an invitation to be happy. They were an invitation to risk losing something again.

He couldn’t take that fear away. He couldn’t rewrite what had happened to her father. He couldn’t give a nineteen-year-old in a meeting room another fifty seconds.

But he could love the woman who’d grown up afterwards. The woman who laughed much too loudly, forgot to eat, worked through typhoons, and sometimes sat on kitchen floors because there were things she couldn’t say anywhere else.

He bent and put his mouth lightly to her hair. She stirred. And then, without opening her eyes, she reached across the sheet for his hand. He took it. And stayed.

chapters.title: His Client, Her Crash
chapters.desc: A client of his owns the group behind the airline in her next investigation. Both of them declare it. He offers to drop the client; she tells him not to.
chapters.epigraph: “You know that even the appearance of influence can sink a report.”
chapters.content:
On the night of Thursday the second of October, at eighteen minutes to eleven, a seventy-seat turboprop landing in heavy rain at the city airport touched down long, aquaplaned, and left the end of the runway at sixty knots into the soft ground beyond it. The nose gear folded. The aircraft broke behind the wing. The first officer and one passenger in the second row were killed. Nineteen people were taken to hospital. The aircraft would never fly again.

Song-Zhu wasn’t on duty that night. She heard about it the way everyone did, from a news alert on her phone at a quarter past eleven, in bed, and sat up, and didn’t sleep.

On Monday morning she was put on the team.

✦ ✦ ✦

She told him that evening, at his flat, over two cartons of noodles she’d brought with her.

She had meant to tell him over dinner in an ordinary way. Complain a little about the paperwork. Ask him whether a particular sentence in the terms of reference was as badly written as she thought it was. Tell him, without telling him anything that mattered, that she’d be busy for a few months and he’d hear less from her.

“I’ve been put on the turboprop,” she said, and named the operator, which had been on every front page for four days.

Ren Hao put his chopsticks down. It was a small thing. A fraction of a second. But she was trained to notice things that stopped.

“What?”

He didn’t answer straight away. Then he said, “The airline belongs to a holding group. The man who owns the group has been a client of mine for five years.”

For a moment neither of them said anything at all. Then Song-Zhu leaned slowly back in her chair.

“Well,” she said.

“Well?”

“That’s inconvenient.”

He gave a short laugh, though his face stayed serious. “Very.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She put her carton down. “How close?”

“Corporate risk and crisis work. A range of things over the years. Business continuity. Executive protection. Two internal investigations. Reputation.”

“For the airline itself?”

“Not on this accident. Nothing on this accident.”

“Before?”

“Yes. Through the holding company, and some of their senior people. There’ve been projects that touched the airline.”

She nodded slowly. “Then we’ve got a problem.”

“Yes.”

He said it without any hesitation at all. She studied his face.

“You’re not going to tell me it’s fine?”

“No.”

“Good.”

“Because it isn’t automatically fine.” He pushed his carton aside. “Even if neither of us has done anything wrong. It matters what it looks like. If anyone asks, in a year, at an inquiry, whether the investigator on this accident was living with the man who advises the owner, the answer can’t be yes, but nobody thought to mention it.”

She smiled faintly. “Look at us. Two adults behaving responsibly.”

“Don’t sound so surprised.”

“I’m enjoying it. It’s so rare.”

“Have you declared it?”

“I only got the assignment at ten this morning. I hadn’t known there was anything to declare until about forty seconds ago.” She looked at him. “I’ll go to Mabel first thing.”

“Do.”

“And you?”

“Compliance at eight. I’ll declare the relationship, the scope of the work, the people. And I’ll ask to be taken off anything that could touch this.”

“Good.”

He looked at her steadily across the table. “Song-Zhu. I need you to hear something.”

She raised an eyebrow. “Go on.”

“My client cannot get anywhere near your investigation through me. I won’t ask you for anything. Not a detail, not a direction, not a feeling. I won’t discuss anything I happen to know about it with anyone connected to him.”

“I know.”

“I mean it.”

“So do I.” She leaned forward. “You’re not getting the file.”

The corner of his mouth moved. “I wasn’t going to ask.”

“You’re not getting the witness list.”

“Understood.”

“You’re not getting anything off the recorders.”

“Song-Zhu.”

“And if your client asks you what the investigators are doing, you don’t answer. Not I can’t say. Nothing. You change the subject to his golf.”

“I know how confidentiality works.”

“I know you do. I’m saying it out loud so it’s been said. So that if anyone ever asks me, I can say we said it on the sixth of October, at your dining table, over noodles.”

He looked at her. Then he nodded. “Fair.”

She picked her chopsticks back up, and stopped halfway. “Will he try to contact you?”

“Probably. If he’s heard about us. He’ll want advice on the response. He may want more than that.”

“Then you’ll have to be careful.”

“I will.” He looked at her. “So will you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning, before eight, Song-Zhu went into Mabel Wong’s office and shut the door and declared a potential conflict of interest.

She said that her partner had an existing professional relationship with the owner of the airline’s parent group, and that his firm had in the past done work that touched the airline itself. She didn’t give unnecessary details about his business. She didn’t make the connection sound smaller than it was. And she didn’t suggest for one moment that she was immune to it because she trusted him.

Mabel listened, with her reading glasses on their cord, and asked six questions, and wrote down the answers in a hand so small it was nearly illegible. Then she asked for it in writing, signed and dated.

“It’ll go to the review,” she said. “Until they’ve looked at it, I’ll note it on the file, and I’ll keep you away from anything that would be hard to explain. If they think it’s too close, you’ll come off.”

“I understand.”

“You’d mind.”

“I’d mind,” said Song-Zhu. “I’d do it.”

Mabel looked at her over the glasses. “You know that even the appearance of influence can sink a report.”

“Yes.”

“Good.” Mabel took her glasses off. “Is he worth it?”

Song-Zhu looked at her, startled. Mabel had never in three years asked her a single personal question.

“Yes,” she said.

“Then write it properly,” said Mabel, and put her glasses back on.

At her desk Song-Zhu sent one message.

Song-Zhu: Declared.

Hao (Three-Piece): Good.

Song-Zhu: Written version by tonight. Review after that.

Hao (Three-Piece): Same here. Compliance has it. Potential conflict, not an automatic withdrawal for either of us. They’ll look at the actual work.

Song-Zhu: Sensible.

Hao (Three-Piece): Disappointing, isn’t it.

Song-Zhu: I was hoping for a courtroom scene.

Hao (Three-Piece): We can arrange one after work.

Song-Zhu: Bring snacks.

✦ ✦ ✦

His meeting with compliance lasted forty-three minutes.

He declared the relationship in full. He listed every project that had touched the airline or its parent in five years, every executive he’d dealt with, the nature of each piece of work and what the firm was still contracted to do. He said plainly that his partner was a member of the investigation team. And he asked to be taken off anything to do with the airline’s response to the accident, or anything that could possibly overlap with the investigation.

His head of compliance, a precise woman of fifty who had once made him sit an online ethics course on the same afternoon as a hostage release, asked whether he meant to go on running the client at all.

He considered it. “I don’t know yet.”

“Would you step away from the whole account, if it came to it?”

“Yes.”

“Even if the client objected?”

“Yes.”

She made a note. “Then I’ll look at what safeguards we can put in and talk to the partners. Until I come back to you, you don’t touch anything connected with the accident or the airline’s handling of it.”

“Agreed.”

“And you receive nothing from your partner about the investigation.”

“I won’t.”

“And she receives nothing from us.”

“Understood.”

When he got back to his office, Joyce had left a note on his keyboard. The owner had rung. Twice. He wanted to speak to Mr. Ren personally.

Ren Hao looked at the note for several seconds. Then he rang back.

✦ ✦ ✦

The client wasn’t pleased.

“I hear you’ve got a connection to the investigation.”

Ren Hao sat down behind his desk. “I have a personal relationship with one of the investigators.”

A pause. “Your girlfriend.”

“Yes.”

“And you didn’t think to tell me.”

“She was assigned yesterday. I declared it as soon as I knew there was an overlap. This morning.”

The client breathed out heavily down the line. “Can she tell you what they’re looking at?”

“No.”

“Come on, Ren. I’m not asking for the file. Just a sense of where they’re going. Whether it’s the crew. Whether it’s us.”

“I can’t give you that.”

“You could ask her what the team thinks.”

“No.”

The voice hardened. “You’re being difficult.”

“I’m being clear.”

Another pause. “This is serious. Two people are dead. The airline needs to understand what these people are likely to conclude.”

“The airline needs to co-operate fully with the investigation and preserve every record it has,” said Ren Hao. “It must not try to anticipate the investigators’ conclusions or influence them through anybody. Including me. Above all not through me.” He heard himself say it and let it stand. “My firm has declared the relationship. I’m taking no part in any work on this accident. Compliance is reviewing the rest of the account.”

“You’re dropping us?”

“I’m considering whether I can go on running the account without an unacceptable conflict.”

“Five years, Ren.”

“I know.”

“And you’ll walk away because your girlfriend has a case?”

Ren Hao’s face didn’t change at all. “I’m going to make sure nobody can reasonably say that your company, or that investigation, got any special treatment because of me. That protects you too. You’ll see that in about a year.”

The client said nothing. Then the line went dead.

Ren Hao put the phone down on the desk. He looked at it a while. Then he pulled his laptop towards him and began, line by line, to write it all down: the time of the call, who had said what, in what words. Nobody had asked him to. It was simply what she would have done.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came to his office a little after seven with two cartons of noodles in a paper bag. She’d changed out of work clothes into a black top and jeans, hair tied back.

He was standing at the window. He turned round.

“Hello.”

She held up the bag. “Dinner.”

“You’re saving my life.”

“Don’t exaggerate. It’s noodles.”

He kissed her. She kissed him back and then stood back. “How was your day?”

“Complicated.”

“Mine too.”

He took the bag. “Has your review said anything?”

“Not yet. They’re thinking about safeguards. I might come off. Depending.”

“That makes sense.”

She looked at him. “And your client?”

He told her about the call. Not the words, which were his client’s; the shape of it. When he’d finished she was quiet a long time.

“You shouldn’t have to drop him,” she said. “Because of me.”

He looked at her. “I’m not deciding it because of you.”

“You’re thinking about it because of the investigation.”

“Yes.”

“And because I’m on it.”

“Yes.”

She put the bag on his desk. “Then don’t.”

“Song-Zhu—”

“Listen to me.” She came closer. “You built this relationship with him over five years. Before you ever met me. If you can keep working with him without going anywhere near the accident or the investigation or anything to do with it, then you should be allowed to. That’s your work. It’s yours.”

“And if the overlap’s too wide?”

“Then your compliance woman decides that. Not me. Not you, either, standing at a window feeling noble about it.”

He studied her face.

“I don’t want you to make a decision that hurts your business because you think it’s what you have to do for me,” she said. “I’d never be able to stop seeing it.”

“I don’t think I have to do anything for you.”

“You’re standing there thinking about dropping your biggest client.”

“Because the conflict might be serious.”

“And if it is, you step back. But not because I’m your girlfriend. Because it’s right. Those aren’t the same reason, and I need you to know which one you’re using.”

He was quiet.

She reached for his hand. “I don’t want to be the reason you lose something you’ve built. I don’t want to be the reason for anything you didn’t choose for yourself.”

His fingers closed round hers. “You’re not.”

“Then don’t make me into it.”

He looked at her a long time. There was something familiar about the way she was saying it. Not the words. What was underneath them. She didn’t want to be managed. She didn’t want him reorganising his working life round her without asking what she actually wanted. She wanted him to trust her judgement about her own life, and his. He breathed out.

“All right.”

She raised an eyebrow. “All right?”

“I won’t decide anything on my own tonight. I’ll let compliance look at it and decide whether the safeguards are enough. If they’re not, I’ll step back from what needs stepping back from, or from the whole account. If they are, I’ll keep him, and keep every inch of this accident away from me.”

“That’s reasonable.”

“You’ve thought about this.”

“I had a whole day to think about it.”

“Did you?”

She smiled. “Some of us work, Hao.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They ate at his desk, because he still hadn’t finished reading the preliminary note compliance had sent him. She sat in the chair opposite with one leg folded under her and ate straight out of the carton. He had put his on a plate. She looked at the plate, and at him.

“You’re still doing that. Making a takeaway look like a state dinner.”

“I like plates.”

“I know you do.” She took a piece of beef off his. He looked at her. “You’ve got loads.”

“That’s not the point.”

She took another. He let her.

After a while she said, “Does he know it’s me? By name?”

“He knows you’re on the team. He knows your name.”

“Then he knows he can’t come near me.”

“He shouldn’t.”

“If he does, I’ll report it.” She looked at him across the desk. “And I won’t tell you I’ve reported it.”

“I know.”

“Good.” She smiled a little. “That’s going to be the strangest part of this. Not telling you things.”

He reached across and took her free hand. “Are you worried?”

“About the case?”

“About this. Him. Us.”

She thought about it properly. “A bit.” She looked at their hands. “But I don’t think we should pretend we haven’t got working lives just because we’ve got each other. That’s how people end up in reports.”

“Agreed.”

“You’re allowed clients I don’t like.”

“That’s a relief.”

“You’re allowed to disagree with me.”

“That happens fairly often.”

She kicked him under the desk. He laughed.

“And you’re allowed to tell me when I’m being unreasonable,” he said.

“I already do.”

“Very effectively.”

He lifted her hand and kissed it. “Thank you.”

“For what?”

“For not asking me to make this easier by pretending it isn’t there.”

She shrugged. “We’re adults.”

He looked at her. “Sometimes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Just after ten his phone rang. Compliance. She stayed where she was by the window, looking out at the city, and didn’t listen to anything she didn’t need to hear.

When he put the phone down, she turned round.

“Initial view’s done,” he said. “There’s a conflict. They don’t think the whole relationship has to end.”

“What safeguards?”

“I’m walled off from anything to do with the accident, the airline’s response, or any inquiry that comes out of it. Another partner takes all of that. I won’t see the files or be in any of the discussions. The rest of the account gets looked at again every quarter. If keeping it separate stops being realistic, I step away completely.”

She thought about it. “That sounds right.”

“It is.”

She came and leaned against the edge of his desk. “How do you feel?”

“Relieved.” A pause. “And annoyed.”

“At the client?”

“Partly.”

“At me?”

“No.”

“At all of it?”

“Yes.”

She nodded. “That’s allowed.”

He reached for her hand. “And you?”

“Still waiting for mine.”

He squeezed her fingers. “Whatever they decide, I won’t ask you to change anything for me. And I won’t expect you to tell me anything.”

“Good.”

“You’re very demanding.”

“You’re very trainable,” said Song-Zhu, and leaned down and kissed him.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, at the lift, she turned round.

“Do you regret it?”

“Regret what?”

“Having a client who owns an airline.”

He laughed. “That’s a very specific question.”

“I’m serious.”

He considered it. “No. I regret the overlap. I regret that it means we both have to be careful. But I don’t regret building something with someone before I knew you existed.” He touched her cheek. “And I don’t regret you.”

“Even when I’m difficult?”

“Most of all then.”

She kissed him, and he put his hand at the back of her neck and held her there a moment.

“Don’t drop him for me,” she said against his mouth.

“I won’t.”

“Don’t let him push you either.”

“I won’t.”

“And don’t let this be something we fight about.”

He smiled. “I’ll do my best.”

“That’s all I’m asking,” she said, and stepped into the lift.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Tuesday of the following week, her review came back. The disclosure was accepted with safeguards. She stayed on the team. Her access to the material followed the same rules as everyone else’s. The conflict went on the file, and any approach, any contact, any attempt by anyone to reach her through anyone, would be logged and reported.

His firm kept its wall. The client stayed with the firm. Another partner took every call about the accident.

Neither of them got anything from the other. Neither of them asked.

On Friday evening she sent him a photograph of a page of her notebook. At the top, underlined, in her small fast hand:

Things I’m not telling my boyfriend
1. The investigation.
2. The witnesses.
3. The recorders.
4. What I want for dinner.

He laughed alone in his office.

Ren Hao: I see you’ve adopted a robust information policy.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Very strict.

Ren Hao: What do you want for dinner?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Soup. And no business.

Ren Hao: Agreed.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): And you have to tell me one thing that happened at work today that has nothing to do with aeroplanes. Anything. The printer. Raymond.

Ren Hao: Raymond wore a bow tie to a board meeting.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I need photographs.

There was a pause. Then:

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I’m glad you’re keeping him.

Ren Hao: I’m glad you told me to.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Don’t make me responsible for your business decisions.

Ren Hao: I wouldn’t dare.

He looked at the screen, and then sent one more.

Ren Hao: I love you.

The reply took a minute.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Keep saying it.

He read it twice, and smiled, and put the phone down.

There were things they could share and things they couldn’t. And for the first time, Ren Hao understood that keeping the line between the two wasn’t a distance between them. It was part of how they stayed close.

chapters.title: Chaos in Three Parts
chapters.desc: A week of her life as he sees it: a training hangar, a funeral, karaoke. Friday, nowhere at all: explicit, all day in bed.
chapters.epigraph: “On Tuesday I learned that your work smells terrible.”
chapters.content:
By Monday evening, Ren Hao had come to a conclusion. He didn’t understand how Song-Zhu fitted an entire week into one day.

He had known she was busy. He had known her hours had no shape, that her phone went off at impossible times, and that her idea of a free afternoon was occasionally an hour eating noodles beside a hangar. But knowing a thing and living inside it were different.

On Monday the twentieth of October she rang at thirteen minutes past seven to ask if he wanted dinner. At nineteen minutes past she rang back to say she was still at work. Just after eight she sent a photograph of a sandwich from a vending machine. Just after eight she informed him that the sandwich was a personal insult. A little before nine she asked if he could come over. And a little after nine, when he got there, she had forgotten she’d asked.

He found her on the floor of her living room in a ring of paper, wearing one sock, holding half a packet of crackers.

“Oh,” she said, looking up. “Hello.”

“Hello.”

She looked at the clock. “You’re early.”

“It’s nine.”

“Exactly.” He looked at the papers. “Are you working?”

“No.” He waited. She looked at the papers too. “Not officially.”

He laughed, and she held out her hand, and he stepped over a stack of books and let her pull him down onto the floor beside her.

“Did you eat?” she said.

“Yes.”

“What?”

“Dinner.”

“What dinner?”

He looked at her. She smiled. “Sorry. Your habit. It’s catching.”

He kissed her cheek. “You’re allowed to ask.”

She leaned on his shoulder. “Good. Because I’m starving.”

He looked at the crackers. “Those aren’t dinner.”

“They’re emotionally supportive,” she said, and he laughed, and ordered food, and that was how the week began.

He had thought he’d be spending a few evenings with his girlfriend. He was about to discover that dating Xu Song-Zhu was less like being invited into someone’s routine and more like being handed a pass to a production with no script, no fixed cast and a suspicious amount of instant noodles.

✦ ✦ ✦

Tuesday 21 October: the hangar

He had expected a hangar to be impressive. It was. What he hadn’t expected was the smell: metal and hydraulic oil and dust and fuel and something underneath all of them he couldn’t name.

It was the authority’s training hangar, on the far side of the airfield from everything that mattered, and once a year the investigators gave it over to a day for fire crews and new recruits and anybody else who might one day be first to a wreck. Inside, under a high roof, sat the fuselage of an old regional jet the authority had bought for a dollar from a scrapyard years ago and had been taking apart on purpose ever since. Song-Zhu was teaching the morning session. She had put Ren Hao’s name on the visitors’ list herself, under partner, and given him a laminated pass on a lanyard that said VISITOR in red letters, and he was wearing it with more pride than anything he had ever worn to a board meeting.

She had told him to wear shoes he could walk in. He had. She’d told him not to wear anything he loved. He had obeyed that too: dark trousers, a plain shirt, a jacket he didn’t much mind.

She looked him up and down when he arrived. “Good.”

“Thank you.”

“You look nearly employable.”

“Nearly?”

“Don’t get excited.” She pushed her safety glasses up into her hair. “Stay behind the yellow line. Don’t touch anything. If anyone in a hi-vis tells you to move, move.”

“Do you think I’m incapable of following instructions?”

“I’ve seen you with a camp bed,” said Song-Zhu.

He stood behind the line for three hours and watched her teach twenty-two firefighters and nine new investigators how to approach a wreck. Where to put their feet. What not to move. Why the position of a single switch in the cockpit might matter more than anything else on the site, and why the most important thing to do with a flight recorder you’ve just found was absolutely nothing at all until someone with a camera arrived. Her voice changed when she taught. It didn’t go colder. It went exact. She didn’t try to sound clever. She was trying to make sure that one day, on a hillside at four in the morning, somebody in this room got it right.

He found he was watching her a great deal more than the aircraft.

At one point she turned and caught him at it. “What?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re staring.”

“I’m observing.”

“That’s my job.”

“I’m borrowing it.”

She laughed, and pointed at the floor beside his shoes. “Stay.”

He put up both hands. “Yes, ma’am.”

In the break, Dexter came and stood beside him at the line with a cup of tea. “She doesn’t usually bring people here.”

Ren Hao looked at her, across the hangar, kneeling by an open access panel with three firefighters crouched round her. “Doesn’t she?”

“Never. She’s protective of the work.” Dexter looked at him sideways. “How are you finding it?”

“There’s much more patience in it than people think.”

Dexter nodded slowly, as if that were the right answer to an exam question he hadn’t known he’d set.

From across the hangar Song-Zhu shouted, “Dexter! Stop interviewing my boyfriend!”

Ren Hao turned. She was smiling at him over the panel. He liked the word in her mouth. Not because it was new any more. Because she said it.

✦ ✦ ✦

They ate lunch outside on a low concrete wall in the thin October sun, rice in boxes from the canteen and coffee he’d brought from the city. She sat with one foot on the ground and the other swinging.

“So?” she said.

“So?”

“Your review. Of the hangar.”

“Very professional. Very dusty. Your colleagues are nice.” He took a sip of coffee. “And you look extremely attractive when you’re telling firefighters off.”

She nearly dropped her chopsticks. “Hao.”

“What?”

“Don’t say things like that when I’m eating. I’ll choke and you’ll have to do first aid in front of twenty-two firefighters.”

“They’d have it covered.”

She laughed. Then, more quietly: “Did you actually like it?”

“Yes.”

“Most people think it’s boring.”

“I don’t.”

“Why not?”

He thought about it. “Because I got to see something that matters to you. I’ve heard you talk about it. I think I understand it a bit better now. Why you never say I think. Why you always say we found.”

She looked at him. Then she leaned her shoulder against his.

“I like having you here,” she said.

“I like being here.”

She was quiet for a bit. Then she said, “Tomorrow’s going to be different.”

He waited.

“A funeral. The first officer from the turboprop. His family asked if any of the team would come. Mabel and I said yes.”

His face went still. He understood immediately; she could see him understanding it.

“Should I not come,” he said. It wasn’t quite a question.

“No.” She said it gently. “Not inside. It’s his family’s. And you’re—” She stopped. “You know what you are, to that airline.”

“Yes.”

“I’d like you to drive me, though. If you don’t mind waiting.”

“I don’t mind waiting,” said Ren Hao.

She put her hand in his and held it until the end of the break.

✦ ✦ ✦

Wednesday 22 October: the funeral

She hardly spoke in the car. He drove. She sat beside him in a plain black dress and a dark coat, her hair tied back neatly, almost no make-up at all. She had told him whose funeral it was, and nothing else, and he didn’t ask. When they got there he parked well down the road from the entrance, out of sight of it, and turned the engine off.

She looked at the building. Then at her hands.

“Thank you for doing this,” she said.

“Go. I’ll be here.”

She leaned across and kissed his cheek, and got out.

He watched her walk up the road. At the door she stopped to speak to a woman in black who took both of her hands and held them, and Song-Zhu bent her head and listened.

Ren Hao looked away. He didn’t want to watch her. He knew she wasn’t. He also knew there were times when even the strongest person on earth needed somewhere to put something down.

He waited. She came back almost an hour later. Her eyes were red. She got into the passenger seat and didn’t put her seat belt on, and he didn’t start the car.

“His daughter’s seven,” she said.

He didn’t say anything.

“She kept asking when her dad was coming home. And her mother kept telling her he couldn’t.” Song-Zhu looked straight ahead through the windscreen. “She had a yellow dress on. And a toy aeroplane. A big plastic one, too big for her hand. She wouldn’t put it down.”

He reached across the console. She took his hand.

“I didn’t know what to say to her,” she said.

“You didn’t have to say anything.”

“I know. I wanted to.” She turned her face to the window. “Sometimes I hate that I know what comes next. I know the questions families ask. I know how long they’ll have to wait. I know what we can tell them and what we can’t. I know there are things we’ll never be able to answer. And I know that even when we do answer them, it won’t bring anybody back.”

He held on to her hand.

“I don’t want to become someone who thinks that’s normal,” she said.

“You won’t.”

She made a sound that wasn’t a laugh. “How do you know?”

“Because you’re sitting here frightened that you might.” He waited until she looked at him. “You’re allowed to get used to doing your job. Nobody’s asking you to get used to people dying.”

Her eyes filled again. He put his hand on her cheek, and she leaned across the console into him, awkwardly, the handbrake in the way, and he held her as well as a man could across the front of a car.

“I don’t want to go home yet,” she said into his coat.

“Then we’ll stay here.”

They sat in the parked car for twenty-three minutes. He knew because he looked at the clock once. She had shut her eyes. Her hand stayed in his.

When she lifted her head at last she said, “Sorry.”

He frowned. “Again?”

“Old habit.”

“Let’s retire it.”

She laughed, faintly. He wiped her cheek with his thumb. “Would you like to eat something?”

“Not really.”

She changed out of the black dress and into soft trousers and one of his old shirts, which she had stolen in August and never returned, and sat on her sofa with her feet under her. He made tea. She held it without drinking it.

“I don’t want to talk about today any more,” she said.

“All right.”

“Can we talk about something stupid?”

“Certainly.”

“Tell me something embarrassing about yourself.”

He considered it. “I once fell asleep in a lecture at university.”

“That’s not embarrassing.”

“I was in the front row.”

“Still not embarrassing.”

“The professor asked me a question.”

“And?”

“I answered it. Apparently correctly. In my sleep.”

She stared at him, and then she burst out laughing, properly, for the first time all day.

“That isn’t embarrassing, that’s showing off.”

“I was mortified.”

“Tell me another one.”

He did. He told her stories from his life that he had never once thought were interesting, all afternoon, and she laughed at some and asked questions about others, and when she finally fell asleep against him with the cold tea on the table her hand was still lying over his.

✦ ✦ ✦

Thursday 23 October: karaoke

The idea was hers. Naturally.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Free tonight?

Ren Hao: Yes.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Karaoke.

Ren Hao: All right.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): You didn’t even ask why.

Ren Hao: Do I need to?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): No. Bring your singing voice.

Ren Hao: I have one.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): We’ll see.

She opened her door just after seven in a dark green top and jeans with her hair loose, and he stood on the landing and looked at her, and said, “You’re beautiful,” before he’d said hello.

She rolled her eyes. “You’re very predictable.”

“Good evening.”

“Good evening,” she said, and kissed him, and picked up her bag. “Come on. I want to hear you sing.”

“Why?”

“Because I want to,” said Song-Zhu, which in her language meant a great deal more, and he heard it, and went.

The room was small: a big screen, two microphones, a long sofa against the wall, and a table she’d already covered with drinks and snacks. She had booked two hours. He strongly suspected she intended to use every minute of them.

She picked up the song list. “What’s your favourite song?”

“I don’t know.”

She stared at him. “You don’t know?”

“I listen to music. I don’t have a favourite.”

She looked at him. “Then I’m choosing.”

The first song was one he knew. The second was one he didn’t. The third was a duet. He looked at the screen, and then at her.

“No.”

She held out a microphone. “Yes.”

“I don’t know this song.”

“That’s the point.”

She started singing. She didn’t care much about hitting the notes. She sang with enormous enthusiasm, missed lines, laughed halfway through verses because she’d misread the words, and danced in her seat. He joined in where he could. And then, at the bridge, she turned her microphone towards him, and he sang the line on his own. She stopped.

He stopped too. “What?”

She was looking at him with her mouth open. “You can sing.”

“I told you.”

“I thought you were lying.”

“I sang in a choir until I was fourteen.”

“You were in a choir?”

“In Vancouver. Isla will have photographs.”

“Isla is going to send me every one of them,” said Song-Zhu, with deep satisfaction. “Sing the next bit.”

He did. She watched him with an expression that made him lose his place.

“You’re distracting me,” he said.

“Good.”

By the second hour she’d become ambitious. An old love song. Then another one. Then a ballad with a chorus so high he refused point-blank to attempt it. She sang it anyway, at full volume, standing on the sofa, and he applauded, and she bowed, and then she put the microphone down and sat beside him and leaned into his side.

“You’re not bad,” she said.

“Thank you.”

“Not good.”

He put his arm round her. She put her head on his shoulder. The next song began, a slow one, and neither of them reached for a microphone. The words scrolled up the screen. She looked up at him. He looked down. And halfway through the first verse, she kissed him.

He laughed against her mouth. The music went on. She kissed him again, and he put his microphone down on the table and turned to her properly, his hand at her waist, and she pressed closer, and somewhere on the recording a man’s voice rose dramatically into the chorus, and she broke away just long enough to laugh.

“You’re missing your part.”

He looked at the screen. “I’ve lost my place.”

“Terrible,” she said, and kissed him again, and her microphone rolled off the sofa onto the floor, and neither of them picked it up until the song had finished and another had started and finished too.

When they left she was still laughing. He carried her bag. She held his hand all the way to the car.

“You’re a good singer,” she said.

“Thank you.”

“Much better than I expected.”

“That’s a very low bar.”

“I’m pleasantly surprised.” She looked at him sideways. “You’re handsome. You’re a good kisser. You’re very patient. And I like you.”

He stopped walking on the pavement, and turned her round, and kissed her.

“That last one,” he said, “is my favourite.”

“Good,” said Song-Zhu.

✦ ✦ ✦

Friday 24 October: nowhere at all

A little after eight on Friday morning his phone woke him.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Don’t make plans today.

Ren Hao: I haven’t got any.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Good.

Ren Hao: What’s happening?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Nothing. Absolutely nothing. Here. Come over.

Ren Hao: What time?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Now.

Ren Hao: I’ll be there in twenty minutes.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Fifteen.

Ren Hao: That’s not enough time.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): You’re a managing director. Manage.

He was there a little before nine with a bag of breakfast. She opened the door in an enormous T-shirt and soft shorts with her hair in a loose knot, and looked at the bag, and stepped aside.

He put breakfast on the counter. She came up behind him and put both arms round his waist and kissed the side of his neck, and then his cheek when he turned, and then his mouth.

“Is this the plan?” he said against it.

“This is the plan.”

“Sounds excellent,” said Ren Hao, and she took his hand and led him to the bedroom, and breakfast stayed on the counter for three hours.

They didn’t hurry. That was the first thing he noticed. There was nowhere to be. No reservation, no meeting, no phone that had to be answered. She had put hers on silent and face up on the windowsill, deliberately, where they could both see it doing nothing. He had left his laptop in the bag by the door. The curtains were half open and the morning light lay across the bed in a long pale stripe.

She kissed him slowly, and stopped now and then to look at him, and smile, and start again.

“What?” he said.

“I like looking at you.”

“Good answer.”

There was something wonderfully unhurried about all of it. They talked between kisses. They laughed. She told him his hair looked ridiculous in the morning and he told her that was her fault, and she said she accepted no responsibility for his appearance, and he said that was a shame because he was now officially her problem, and she kissed him to stop him talking, and after a while the talking stopped on its own.

He undressed her as if he’d been given all day for it, which he had. She lay back in the stripe of sun and let him, and watched him look at her, and liked it. He put his mouth on her throat, her collarbone, the soft inside of her elbow, the curve under her breast, her hip, the back of her knee, taking his time over every one of them as if they were all equally important, until she was laughing and impatient and then neither, just breathing. When he finally pushed into her she wrapped her legs round him and held him there, still, deep, and they stayed like that a long time doing almost nothing at all, kissing, moving barely, in no hurry, until the not-hurrying became unbearable and she said his name in a voice that meant now, and he gave her what she wanted.

Afterwards she lay on his chest in the sun and he played with her hair, and neither of them said anything a long time.

At some point he reached for the clock on the bedside table. She caught his wrist.

“No.”

“I was checking the time.”

“Why?”

“Curiosity.”

“Don’t be curious,” said Song-Zhu, and put his hand back on her waist where it had been.

They remembered breakfast a little before twelve. It was cold. She sat cross-legged on the bed eating cold toast while he opened the boxes.

“Your breakfast has failed.”

“It’s technically still food.”

“Cold food.” She made a face at a mouthful, and he laughed and reached for his phone to order something else, and she held out her hand.

“Come back.”

“You’re not eating?”

“Later.”

He put the boxes on the floor and came back.

✦ ✦ ✦

A little after one his phone rang. Joyce.

“Mr. Ren, I’m sorry to disturb you. The shipping client wants to know if you’ll look at the revised document before the end of the day.”

He looked down at Song-Zhu, who was drawing small idle patterns on his forearm with one finger.

“Send it to me. I’ll look at it later.”

“Shall I set up a call?”

“No. I’ll ring you if I need to.”

He put the phone down on the bedside table, screen up, out of reach. She looked up at him.

“Work?”

“Yes.”

“Do you have to go?”

“No.”

She smiled. Then, more seriously: “You’re allowed to work, you know. I don’t want to keep you from things.”

He pushed her hair back off her cheek. “You’re not keeping me from anything. I chose to be here.”

Her face softened. She kissed him. And the afternoon began.

Just after three she decided she wanted him to make her tea. At twelve minutes past she decided she didn’t want tea. At nineteen minutes past she wanted tea again. He stood in her kitchen in his boxers looking at the kettle.

“Are you sure?”

“Yes,” she called from the bedroom.

“Milk?”

“No.”

“Sugar?”

“Maybe.”

He turned round. “Song-Zhu.”

She appeared in the doorway wrapped in a sheet, smiling. “What?”

“Do you want tea or not?”

She crossed the kitchen and put her arms round his waist. “I want you.”

“Is that difficult?” she said, looking up.

“Extremely,” said Ren Hao, and put the kettle down.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was evening when she decided she wanted him to beg.

She didn’t tell him that. She’d been teasing him for the best part of an hour. A kiss, and then a retreat. A smile, and then a change of subject. Her hand flat on his stomach, and then gone, just as he reached for her. He’d been patient. He was beginning to regret quite how patient.

She lay beside him on her side, propped on one elbow, watching his face with enormous interest.

“You’re enjoying this,” he said.

“Very much.”

“Are you going to keep doing it?”

“Doing what?”

He gave her a look. She laughed. He leaned towards her. She leaned away.

“Song-Zhu.”

“Mm?”

“Come back here.”

She shook her head. “Ask nicely.”

He smiled. “Please.”

She considered him. Then she leaned in and kissed him, deep and slow, and let him believe for one long moment that she’d finished, her hand sliding down his stomach and lower and closing round him, and he groaned into her mouth—

And then she let go, and pulled away, and lay back on her pillow with her hands folded on her chest like a woman at rest. He stared at her. She laughed out loud.

“You look frustrated.”

“I wonder why.”

She touched his cheek with one finger. “You’re very handsome when you’re frustrated.”

“That’s not helping.”

“I know.”

He caught her hand and kissed her palm. Then he looked at her, and there was no joke left in his face at all.

“Please,” he said.

Her smile went softer. “Please what?”

He held her eyes. “Please stop making me wait. I can’t. I want you so badly I can’t think. Please, Song-Zhu.”

She looked at him a long time. For once he wasn’t making a joke of it, or managing it, or being reasonable. He was asking. Plainly, out loud, with nothing held back. And she found she loved hearing him ask more than she had loved almost anything.

She rolled over onto him, slowly, and leaned down until her mouth was against his.

“All right,” she said.

She took him inside her in one long slow movement and he made a sound she’d never heard before, low and broken and grateful, and his hands came up to her hips and held on. She rode him slowly at first, watching him, and then not slowly, and he said her name over and over, and please again, and yes, and she gave him every single thing he asked for, until he couldn’t ask for anything any more, and came with his head pressed back into her pillow and his whole body arched up into hers, and she followed him a moment later with her forehead on his chest and his heart going under it like something trying to get out.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later the flat was quiet. The city lights had come on beyond the curtains. She lay with her head on his chest and one leg over his under the blanket, and he ran his fingers through her hair, and she was nearly asleep.

“Hao?”

“Mm.”

“Did you have a good week?”

“An interesting one.”

She laughed. “That’s not an answer.”

“On Tuesday I learned that your work smells terrible.” She lifted her head in outrage. “On Wednesday I learned that sometimes the most useful thing I can do is wait in a car. On Thursday I learned that you sing very loudly and have no respect at all for the key a song was written in.”

“I sing beautifully.”

“Of course.”

“And Friday?”

He looked down at her. “Friday was perfect.”

She put her cheek back down. “How was mine, do you want to know?”

“Tell me.”

“On Tuesday I got to show you something that matters to me. On Wednesday I didn’t have to be on my own afterwards. On Thursday I got to be ridiculous.” She lifted her head. “And on Friday I had you all to myself. That’s my favourite part.”

He kissed her, and drew her closer.

“You’ve seen a lot of my life this week,” she said after a while. “The nice parts and the hard parts.”

“Yes.”

“And you’re still here.”

“Of course I’m still here.”

“I think I like that,” she said, low, as if it were a confession.

A little before midnight his phone buzzed on the bedside table. He reached for it. She caught his wrist without opening her eyes.

“Tomorrow. Whatever it is.”

“All right.” He put the phone down. “Good night.”

“Good night.”

He looked at her hair spread on his chest, and said it, because he always would.

“I love you.”

She was quiet for so long he thought she’d already fallen asleep. Then, without opening her eyes, so softly he almost didn’t hear it, she said, “Keep saying it.”

He smiled into the dark. “I will.”

A pause. And then, sleepily: “Not too loud.”

He laughed under his breath. “I’ll try.”

She was asleep in a minute. He stayed awake a little longer, listening to her flat. Four days, he thought. A hangar. A funeral. A karaoke booth. And then a day with no destination at all. He had seen her competence and her grief and her laughter, and the particular kind of mischief she kept only for him. He had learned that loving Song-Zhu didn’t mean knowing what she’d do next.

It meant being willing to go with her. And, now and then, being prepared to give up on breakfast.

chapters.title: He Gives Up Managing
chapters.desc: He gives up managing for a week and it nearly kills him. At 3 a.m. her phone rings; he checks her location once, and tells her at breakfast. She forgives him in the doorway.
chapters.epigraph: “You can worry. Just don’t make it a project.”
chapters.content:
Ren Hao lasted six days.

Six days without asking Mr. Yau to keep an eye on anything. Six days without reminding her to eat, sleep, drink water or take a break. Six days without checking whether her plans had changed, whether she’d got somewhere safely, or whether the weather might affect her journey home. He didn’t make a timetable. He didn’t suggest a shared calendar. He didn’t even ask what time she thought she’d finish.

He was, by every measurable standard, behaving like a perfectly normal man in a relationship. He hated it.

It had been his idea, which made it worse. On the Sunday night, the ninth of November, lying in her bed, he had said into the dark, “I’m going to try something this week,” and she had said “Oh no,” and he had said, “No arranging. Nothing. For a week. To see if I can,” and she had been quiet for a moment and then turned over and kissed him hard, which he had taken as encouragement.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday he woke at twenty to seven and reached for his phone.

Nothing from her. He looked at the screen. He put it down. He picked it up again. Still nothing. The last message was from the night before.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Going to sleep. Don’t miss me too much.

Ren Hao: I’ll try.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Good boy. Night.

He smiled at it. And then noticed that she hadn’t said whether she’d got home first. She’d been at the compound till ten.

His thumb hovered. Did you get in all right? He deleted it. He put the phone face up on the bedside table and looked at the ceiling.

At twelve minutes past seven he picked it up again. He was becoming ridiculous.

At half past eight Joyce came into his office with a document. “The revised proposal, Mr. Ren.”

“Thank you.” He looked at the first page. “Is Wednesday with the regional team confirmed?”

“Three o’clock.”

“Good.”

Joyce stayed where she was. He looked up. “Anything else?”

She hesitated. “Are you all right?”

He blinked. “Yes.”

“You’ve looked at your phone twelve times since I came in.”

He looked at the phone. Then at her. “Have I?”

“Yes, Mr. Ren.”

“Is that a problem?”

“No, Mr. Ren.” She gave him a small polite smile, and then, because she had worked for him for four years and Momo was waiting for her outside the door: “Are you waiting for someone?”

He went back to the document. “Apparently.”

Joyce nodded, as if this explained everything, and left. A little before twelve:

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Alive.

Ren Hao: Good.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): That’s all? Good?

Ren Hao: Would you like a more enthusiastic response?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Yes.

Ren Hao: I’m overjoyed to hear you’re alive.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Much better. Busy day. Don’t wait up tonight.

He looked at that.

Ren Hao: All right.

He didn’t ask what she was doing. He didn’t ask when she’d finish. He didn’t offer a car. He put the phone down. And then spent the next forty minutes wondering whether she’d eaten.

✦ ✦ ✦

Tuesday was worse. At quarter past nine at night she sent a photograph of a convenience-store rice ball.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Dinner.

Ren Hao: That’s dinner?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Don’t judge me.

Ren Hao: I wasn’t going to.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): You were.

Ren Hao: I was considering it.

She sent another photograph: a paper cup of coffee.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Also dinner.

Ren Hao: That isn’t food.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): It’s brown.

Ren Hao: So is the table.

She sent a row of laughing faces. Then:

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Miss you.

His face softened.

Ren Hao: Miss you too.

He nearly asked what time she’d be home. Instead he wrote:

Ren Hao: I hope the rest of the evening goes smoothly.

She sent back a single heart. He put the phone down. He was beginning to suspect the entire exercise had been designed specifically to reveal the weaknesses in his character.

✦ ✦ ✦

Wednesday brought rain. Heavy rain. He could see it walking across the harbour from the thirty-second floor. At half past six a photograph came through: a wet road, a grey sky, the edge of a hangar roof with water pouring off it.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Weather is disgusting.

Ren Hao: Agreed.

Then he looked at the photograph again. She was outside. In that.

He typed: Have you got an umbrella? Deleted it. Typed: Are you still at the hangar? Deleted that too. Stood up. Walked to the window. Sat down again.

A little before seven he finally wrote:

Ren Hao: Let me know if you need anything.

The answer came almost at once.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I know.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): You’re doing really well, Hao.

He stared at the screen. He hadn’t realised she knew how hard it was.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday, at exactly nine o’clock in the morning, his phone rang.

He was in the middle of a meeting with three partners and a man from an insurer, who was explaining a clause. Ren Hao looked at the screen. Song-Zhu. Nine o’clock. He stood up.

“Excuse me,” he said to the room. “Ten minutes.”

He walked out into the corridor and answered, and leaned against the wall by the window.

“Hello.”

“You picked up,” she said, sounding astonished.

“You rang at nine.”

“I know. I wanted to see if you’d actually do it. Are you in a meeting?”

“Yes.”

“With who?”

“Three partners and an insurer.”

“And you walked out?”

“I said ten minutes.”

There was a short silence on the line, and when she spoke again her voice had changed. “Hao.”

“Yes.”

“I haven’t got anything to tell you. I just wanted the ten minutes.”

“Then have them.”

So she had them. She told him about the rain, and about Dexter falling asleep in the canteen with a spoon in his hand, and about a pigeon that had got into the records room and been there for a week, it turned out, eating a filing system. He laughed. She laughed. At the end of the ten minutes exactly, she said, “Go back to your insurer,” and rang off, and he stood in the corridor longer with the phone against his chest, and then went back in.

The insurer was looking at him with deep suspicion. Raymond, who had heard the whole thing through the glass, was looking at the ceiling.

“Where were we,” said Ren Hao.

✦ ✦ ✦

Thursday evening she rang again. He picked up before it had finished ringing once.

“Hi.”

“Hi.”

She sounded amused. “Are you busy?”

“No.”

“Really?” She sounded delighted.

“Truly. Not in a meeting, not saving anyone.”

“Not in a meeting? Not saving a company?”

“Not currently.”

She laughed. “Good.” He leaned back in his chair. “How are you?” he said.

“Fine. Tired.”

“Have you eaten?”

There was a pause. He closed his eyes.

She burst out laughing. “Four days, Hao. You lasted four days.”

“I asked a question.”

“You asked the question.”

He put his hand over his eyes. “All right. I apologise.”

She laughed again, and then her voice went soft. “Thank you for trying.”

“How do you know I’m trying?”

“Because you haven’t once asked me where I am. And because you walked out of a meeting with an insurer this morning.” A pause. “I don’t want you to stop caring, you know. That’s not what this is. I like that you ask if I’ve eaten. I like that you worry when I’m out late. I just don’t want you to feel you have to keep me safe every minute of the day. And I don’t want you to think that if you stop checking, something terrible will happen.”

He didn’t answer straight away.

“I know you can’t always help it,” she said.

“I can help it.”

“Maybe.”

He laughed. “You’re very encouraging.”

“I’m honest.” Another pause. “I miss you. Can I see you tomorrow?”

“Yes.”

“Don’t make plans.”

“I won’t.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Friday was hard. Not because anything happened. Because nothing did.

She didn’t message him after the morning. He knew she was working. He knew she forgot her phone existed when a case got difficult. He knew all of it.

A little after three he looked at his phone. Nothing. Just after four. Nothing. A little before six he opened their conversation and closed it again. At twenty past six:

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Free?

Ren Hao: Yes.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Come over.

Ren Hao: On my way.

He left the office without his laptop. Joyce watched him go past her desk with nothing in his hands at all and said, “Good night, Mr. Ren. Have a nice weekend,” in a voice that suggested she was going to tell Momo about this.

“I intend to,” he said.

Song-Zhu opened her door in a loose grey T-shirt and shorts with her hair damp from the shower. She looked at him, and then at the empty space beside him.

“No bag?”

“No.”

“No laptop?”

“No.”

“No folders?”

“No.”

“Look at you,” she said, and he stepped in and put his hands on her waist.

“Don’t sound so surprised.”

She kissed him, and then pulled back. “How was your week?”

“Terrible.”

She laughed. “Really?”

“Awful. I’ve been trying very hard not to interfere with your life, and I’ve discovered I have an extremely irritating personality.”

She laughed into his chest. “I could have told you that.”

“I needed to find out for myself.”

✦ ✦ ✦

For the first part of the evening, they did nothing at all. She lay on the sofa with her legs across his lap and they watched a film neither of them cared about. She commented on the plot. He agreed with her. At one point she looked up.

“Are you bored?”

“No.”

“You’re quiet.”

“I’m watching.”

“You’re not. You’re thinking.”

“Am I not allowed?”

“Not tonight.” She put her hand on his jaw. “That bit. Where you clench it. You’re pretending not to worry.”

He breathed out, and made himself lean back. “Better?”

“Much better.” She settled against him. “You’ve got very good at noticing.”

“I’ve always been good at noticing.”

“I know. That’s the trouble with you.”

A little after eleven she fell asleep on his shoulder. He reached for the blanket and put it over her. Her phone was on the coffee table. He looked at it, and looked away. A few minutes later he looked again. He wondered whether she’d had work messages. Whether someone might ring. Whether she might have to go somewhere.

He knew none of it mattered. He knew he was supposed to be practising something else.

He looked at her sleeping face, and shut his eyes, and told himself: he wouldn’t check. He wouldn’t ask. He would trust her.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just after three in the morning, her phone rang on the coffee table.

He was awake at once. She wasn’t. He looked at the screen. Duty Officer. He picked it up and put it into her hand, and touched her shoulder.

“Song-Zhu. Work.”

She was sitting up and answering before her eyes were fully open. “Xu.” She listened. He watched her come all the way awake in about four seconds, the sleep going out of her face. “Which runway? Anyone hurt? Has the operator pulled the recorder breaker? Then ring them again and tell them to do it now, before anyone powers anything up. I’ll be there in forty minutes.”

She ended the call and was already on her feet.

“I’ve got to go. A freighter scraped its tail landing. Nobody’s hurt. But it’s mine.”

He stood too. “All right.”

She pulled on trousers, a jumper, her lanyard. “Sorry.”

“Don’t be.”

She stopped at the door with her bag and looked at him in the dark. “I’ll ring you when I can.”

“All right.”

She went. He heard the lift, and then nothing.

He stood in her living room. The flat was quiet. He looked at the clock. Nineteen minutes past three. Then at the door.

He knew she was perfectly capable of getting to an airport. He knew she’d driven to a hundred call-outs before she’d met him. He knew she’d ring when she could. He also knew he wasn’t going to sleep. He lasted until eighteen minutes to four. Then he opened the map on his phone.

They had turned on location sharing on the night of the typhoon, in September, in a small room at the end of a corridor, for tonight, because the compound was three kilometres across and nothing was signposted. Neither of them had turned it off. He had never once looked at it since.

His thumb hovered over her name. He told himself he only wanted to see she was moving. That he wasn’t going to ring. That he wasn’t going to do anything. He opened it.

A small blue dot, on the airport perimeter road, moving towards the cargo gate.

He watched it for perhaps five seconds. Then he closed the map.

He sat down on the arm of her sofa in the dark. He felt better. And immediately, he hated himself for it. Because the relief hadn’t come from trusting her. It had come from knowing where she was.

He put the phone face up on the table, where he could see it and not touch it, and didn’t open the map again. But it was too late. He’d done it.

✦ ✦ ✦

A little after eight, she came back with two paper cups of coffee.

He was in her kitchen making eggs. He looked up. “You’re back.”

“Obviously.” She held out a cup. He took it. “How long have you been up?”

“Since you left.”

She frowned. “You should have gone back to sleep.”

“I couldn’t.”

She came and kissed his cheek. “Poor thing.”

He put the coffee down.

“Song-Zhu. I need to tell you something.”

Her face changed, slightly. “All right.”

He made himself say it in order, the way he’d have wanted a report. “After you left, at about quarter to four, I looked at your location. On the map from the typhoon. I saw you on the perimeter road. I closed it. I didn’t ring you. I didn’t ring anyone. I didn’t do anything else. I looked once, and I closed it.”

She didn’t move. “Why?” she said.

He could have given her the easy answer. That it was three in the morning. That the call had been sudden. That he was worried. All of it was true. None of it was the whole truth.

“Because I was anxious,” he said. “And I wanted to know where you were. I knew you were fine to go. I knew you’d ring when you could. I wanted to see it for myself anyway.” He looked at her steadily. “I told you I wouldn’t keep track of you. And then I did. I’m sorry.”

She put her coffee down on the counter.

“Did you think something had happened to me?”

“No.”

“Would you have looked if you hadn’t promised not to?”

He thought about it honestly. “I don’t know.”

She nodded slowly. “That’s an honest answer.”

“I don’t want to make excuses.”

“I know.” She folded her arms. “Did you look more than once?”

“No.”

“Did you keep watching?”

“No. Five seconds. Then I closed it.”

She looked at him a long time. “Why are you telling me?”

He answered at once. “Because you should know. Because I don’t want you to find out in six months and wonder what else I’ve done without telling you.”

Something in her face eased.

“Thank you for telling me,” she said.

He nodded.

She picked her coffee back up and drank some of it and looked at him over the top of the cup. “You’re not going to ask if I’m angry?”

“Are you?”

She thought about it. “I’m not happy you looked. I’m glad you told me.” She put the cup down. “Hao, I know you worry. I know last night was hard. I know you heard a phone at three in the morning and couldn’t go back to sleep. But I don’t want you to turn my location into the way you deal with being frightened.” His face tightened. She went on. “If something happens, I’ll tell you what I can. If I need help, I’ll ask. And if I don’t ring straight away, it doesn’t mean something terrible’s happened. It means I’m under an aeroplane.”

“You’re right.”

“I need you to trust me.”

“I do.”

She raised one eyebrow. He corrected himself. “I’m learning to.”

“Better,” she said, and almost smiled.

✦ ✦ ✦

They ate the eggs standing up at the counter. Neither of them mentioned the map for several minutes. Then she said, “Do you want me to turn it off?”

He put his fork down. “I’d like to take myself off it. If you’re happy keeping yours for anything practical. I don’t want the option there every time I’m anxious.”

She looked at him, considering. “You don’t have to do it because you feel guilty.”

“I’m not doing it because I feel guilty. I’m doing it because I know myself.”

She nodded. “All right.”

He took out his phone and removed himself from her location and turned the screen so she could see the confirmation. She glanced at it.

“Thank you.”

“I am sorry,” he said.

She reached across the counter and touched his hand. “I know. You look miserable.”

“I feel miserable.”

“Don’t.” She squeezed his fingers. “I don’t need you to be perfect, Hao. I need you to be honest with me. Most of all when you’ve got it wrong.”

“All right.”

She looked at his plate. “Also, you made too many eggs.”

“I made enough for two.”

“There’s enough for four.”

“I was hungry.”

“You’re a terrible liar,” said Song-Zhu, and the tension in the kitchen let go, not because the mistake had gone anywhere, but because he’d told her the truth and she’d decided to stay in the room with it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, when she was getting ready to go back to the compound for the morning review, he stood by her door.

He didn’t ask where she was going. He didn’t ask when she’d be back. He didn’t offer to drive. He handed her the jacket she’d left on the sofa.

She took it. “Thank you.”

“You’re very quiet,” she said, putting it on.

“I’m trying not to ask six questions.”

She laughed. “You can ask one.”

He thought about it. “Can I see you tonight?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

“Don’t book anything.”

“I won’t.”

“Don’t arrange anything.”

“I won’t.”

“Don’t send me a reminder.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

She gave him a look. He laughed. “I genuinely wasn’t going to.”

She opened the door. Then she turned back in the doorway, with her bag on her shoulder and the jacket half on, and looked at him.

“Hao.”

“Yes?”

“I forgive you,” she said. “For the map. All of it. I’m not keeping it.”

He stood still. She came back the one step from the doorway, and took his face in both her hands, and kissed him. Not. As if she were stamping something. And when she let go she stayed close.

“Don’t do it again.”

“I won’t.”

“If you’re frightened, tell me. You don’t have to pretend you’re fine.”

“I know.”

“And you don’t have to turn into someone who never worries about me either.” Her thumb moved on his cheek. “You can worry. Just don’t make it a project.”

He laughed. “I’ll try.”

She narrowed her eyes. “Don’t make a plan.”

He laughed properly then. “All right.”

“I love it when you laugh like that,” she said, and then looked at him, startled, as if she’d heard what else was nearly in the sentence, and he saw it too, and neither of them said it.

“I love you,” he said instead, because one of them could.

She stood in her doorway with her hand still on his face.

“Keep saying it,” said Song-Zhu.

“I will.”

She smiled, and went. He stood in the doorway until the lift doors had shut behind her.

He didn’t look at the time. He didn’t open the map. He didn’t ring anyone to ask whether she’d arrived. He simply closed her door, and washed up the extra eggs, and trusted that if she wanted him, she knew exactly where he was.

chapters.title: Her Recorder
chapters.desc: Her father’s pocket recorder, and the four minutes of air traffic she copied onto it at twenty and never played. She plays it with him in the room. Afterwards, explicit and very quiet: she leads.
chapters.epigraph: “I want to be close to someone who’s alive.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Ren Hao noticed was that she’d tidied her flat.

Not thoroughly, not even particularly well. There were still books stacked on the floor by the sofa, a cardigan over a dining chair, and a mug on the windowsill he suspected had been there since Tuesday. But the kitchen counter was clear. The coffee table was empty. And the small heap of things that usually lived beside her television had been moved somewhere else.

He stood in the doorway on Saturday the thirteenth of December, holding a paper bag of dinner.

“Should I be worried?”

Song-Zhu looked up from the sofa. “About what?”

“Your flat.”

“What about it?”

“It’s unusually organised.”

“Are you saying I live in a mess?”

“I’m saying I recognise your natural habitat, and this isn’t it.”

She laughed. “Come in, handsome.”

He came in and kissed her. She took the bag and looked inside. “You brought noodles.”

“You said noodles.”

“And dumplings.”

“And dumplings.”

She looked up at him. “You’re a good man.”

“I’ve been told.”

“By who?”

“Mainly myself.”

She laughed, and put the food on the counter, and he watched her. She was different tonight. Not unhappy, not far away. Just quieter. Her hair was tied low at the back of her neck. She was wearing an old oversized white shirt with the sleeves pushed up, and soft trousers. No television on. No music. Her phone was on the arm of the sofa, dark.

She had been waiting for him.

“Everything all right?” he said.

“Yes.”

He waited. She smiled faintly. “Don’t do that.”

“Do what?”

“Look at me like you’re trying to find the fault.”

“I’m looking at my girlfriend.”

“You’re looking at her like she’s a suspicious document.”

He laughed. “All right. I’ll look at you differently.” He put his hands on her waist and kissed her cheek. “Better?”

“Much.”

She leaned into him, and for a moment they just stood like that in her kitchen. Then she said, low, against his shirt:

“I want to show you something.”

“All right.”

“Something I’ve never shown anyone. My mother knows I have it. She doesn’t know what I put on it.”

His face changed. He didn’t ask what it was. He nodded.

“Okay.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t bring it out straight away. First they ate.

She sat across from him at her small dining table and stole dumplings from his bowl and he let her. He asked about her week. She told him about a colleague who had saved an entire folder of evidence photographs under the name final_final_revised_ACTUAL, and said she intended to resign on principle, and he laughed. She was almost herself. Almost.

When they’d finished she washed up. He dried without being asked.

Then she went into her bedroom. He stayed in the kitchen. He heard a drawer open, and then another, and then a pause that went on a long time.

When she came back, she was holding a small black zip case, old, the corners worn smooth, one corner scuffed pale.

She held it against her stomach with both hands.

“Come and sit,” she said.

He sat beside her on the sofa. She didn’t open the case. Her thumb went back and forth over the worn corner.

“It’s my father’s,” she said.

He remembered the photograph on the kitchen floor. A man in a pilot’s shirt in front of a freighter, one hand up against the sun, smiling at whoever held the camera. He remembered her telling him, at three in the morning, about fifty seconds on a laptop in another country. He remembered there’s one more thing I’ve got of his. Not tonight. He’d never asked her about it again.

Now she was offering. She unzipped the case. Inside, in a little bed of grey foam, lay a pocket voice recorder: silver, the size of a cigarette lighter, with a small speaker grille and a scratch across its face, the kind of thing people had used in offices before phones did everything.

“He used it for his logbook,” she said. “Notes after a flight. Times, fuel, things he wanted to remember to write up properly. And when he was away for more than three nights, he used to make little recordings for me, and post the card home in an envelope. The clouds are behaving. Bumpy over the sea, tell your mother I’m fine. Did you finish your homework, I’m checking when I’m back.” She swallowed. “This was on his desk at home when it happened. My mother gave it to me after the funeral. I’ve never played anything he recorded on it. Not once. I can’t.”

He didn’t say anything. He waited.

“When the final report came out,” she said, “a year after, the investigators sent the families a copy of the air traffic control recording. Not the cockpit. The cockpit’s never released, I told you. But what the controllers hear, what goes out on the radio, that’s different. Anyone at that airport with a scanner could have heard it that night. They sent it to us, if we wanted it, on a disc, with a letter saying we didn’t have to listen.” She looked down at the little silver thing in the foam. “I was twenty. I copied the last four minutes onto his recorder. Onto a new card, so I wouldn’t lose his. Because I wanted his voice to be in something that was his, not on a disc from an office.”

“And you’ve listened to it.”

“No.” She shook her head. “I made it, and I zipped the case, and I put it in the drawer. I’ve never pressed play. Six years.”

He understood. Not a recording she’d never heard; she had heard fifty seconds from inside the cockpit and would never forget a breath of it. This was a recording she had made with her own hands and never once let herself hear.

“Do you want to?” he said.

She nodded. Then shook her head. Then gave a small embarrassed laugh. “I don’t know.”

He moved a little closer. “You don’t have to.”

“I know.”

“We can put it back.”

“I know.” She looked at him. “But I think I want to. Tonight. With you here. I think that’s why I tidied the flat.”

He nodded once. “Then I’ll stay.”

Her eyes moved over his face. “Don’t say anything while it’s playing.”

“All right.”

“And don’t try to make me feel better afterwards.”

“I won’t.”

She swallowed. “Just stay.”

He held out his hand, palm up, on the sofa between them. “I’m here.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She lifted the recorder out of the foam. Her fingers were steady. She switched it on, and the little screen lit pale green, and showed one file, and a time. 04:00.

She sat with it in her lap a long time without pressing anything.

Then she looked at him. “Can I hold your hand?”

He turned his hand over. She put hers into it. It was cold. He closed his round it. She pressed play.

✦ ✦ ✦

A hiss. The particular hollow crackle of a radio frequency at night. And then a controller’s voice, a stranger’s, calm and quick, giving someone a heading and a height. And then her father.

Ren Hao had heard her talk about him. He had seen him in a photograph, squinting in the sun. He had heard her describe the sound of his voice from memory on a kitchen floor at three in the morning.

This was different. It was a living voice. A man reading back an instruction in the ordinary rhythm of an ordinary working night. Calm. Professional. A little dry. Tired, in a way you could only have heard if you had spent years remembering him. Song-Zhu stared at the little green screen.

The controller again. Her father again. A callsign, numbers, a frequency. The plain language of the air at night, the same language Ren Hao had heard on a radio in a small room in a typhoon, said by a man whose daughter was now sitting on a sofa holding his hand.

Ren Hao kept his eyes on her. He watched her shoulders tighten, a little at a time. He watched her thumb press into his knuckle. He watched her lean, slightly, towards the little speaker, without knowing she was doing it. The voices got quicker.

Her father said something about a problem with an engine, in exactly the same tone he’d have used to say the clouds were behaving. The controller asked him to confirm. He confirmed. He asked for a turn back. The controller gave it to him. There was nothing in his voice at all but work. Song-Zhu stopped breathing properly.

Ren Hao felt her hand tighten until it hurt. He didn’t move. He didn’t speak.

The last four minutes of a man’s working life went by in her small tidy living room. Not like a story, not like a film. No music, no narrator, nobody explaining anything to the people listening. Only two voices, and the hiss between them.

At one point her father’s voice came clear, a single short transmission, and her eyes filled, and she leaned forward a little further, as if she could get closer to him, as if there were something on it she might have missed when she was twenty and had copied it without listening. Then the controller called his callsign. There was no answer. The controller called it again. Patient. Level.

Nothing. The hiss. Again. A little quicker. Nothing. Again.

And then the controller’s voice changed, for the first time in four minutes, slightly, and he said something to somebody else in the room with him, away from the microphone, and called the callsign one more time, and the recording ended. The little green screen went back to 00:00.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t move. The room was absolutely silent. Somewhere below, on the street, a car went past with music playing and was gone.

Her face had gone still. Her eyes were full, but she wasn’t crying yet. She looked at the recorder in her lap. At the black case on the table. Back at the recorder.

“I thought he’d sound different,” she said. Her voice was hardly there. “He sounds exactly the same. He sounds like Dad.”

Ren Hao’s throat closed.

“I know that’s stupid,” she said.

He said nothing; he had promised. But he held on.

“He was working. He was talking about an engine like it was the weather. He sounded like he was going to finish his shift and come home.” She swallowed. “And then the man kept calling him. And he didn’t answer. The man kept calling him, Hao, and he didn’t answer.”

One tear ran down, and then another.

“I’d forgotten how he sounded when he was tired,” she said. “I remembered his laugh. I remembered him ringing me in my first year at university. I remembered him telling me not to stay up. But I’d forgotten that voice. The working one.”

He let go of her hand at last, only so that he could put his arm round her and draw her in. She came. Her forehead went against his shoulder. Her hands took two fistfuls of his shirt.

For a while she cried without making much sound at all.

He didn’t tell her it was all right. He didn’t tell her she was strong. He didn’t tell her that her father would have wanted her to be happy. He held her, one hand at the back of her head and the other flat between her shoulder blades, and let her.

“I thought I’d be ready,” she said at last, into his shirt.

He put his mouth against her hair. Now, he thought, he could speak. “Nobody’s ready to hear someone they miss.”

“I wanted him to say my name. I knew he wouldn’t. He was flying an aeroplane. But I wanted it.”

“I know.”

“I kept waiting.”

“I know.”

“And the man kept calling him.”

He held her tighter, and didn’t say anything else a long time, because there wasn’t anything that wouldn’t have been smaller than what she’d just heard.

When at last he did speak, it was only: “You wanted to hear your father.”

She nodded into him.

“That’s all it was,” he said. “That’s enough.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They stayed on the sofa a long time. Eventually she lifted her face. Her eyes were red. She looked embarrassed.

“Sorry.”

He frowned. “For what?”

“For crying all over your shirt again.”

He looked down at the wet patch, and back at her. “This shirt’s seen worse.”

A weak laugh. “Like what?”

“You once tipped an entire bowl of soup down it.”

“That was an accident.”

“You said it was an experiment.”

“It was a very successful experiment,” she said, and nearly smiled, and he wiped under one of her eyes with his thumb.

“Thank you,” she said.

“For what?”

“For not saying anything.”

“You asked me not to.”

“I know.” She looked at him. “You listened.”

He nodded. She leaned up and kissed him, small and unsteady, and then rested her forehead on his.

“I don’t want to hear it again tonight.”

“We won’t.”

He switched the recorder off and laid it back in its grey foam, and held the case out to her, and waited for her to tell him where it went. She took it. She stood up and carried it into the bedroom and he heard the drawer, and when she came back her hands were empty.

She didn’t turn the television on. She didn’t put music on. She came and stood in front of him where he sat.

“Hao.”

He looked up. “Yes?”

She held out her hands. He took them and stood.

For a moment she looked at him. Then she seemed to give up on explaining. She reached for the top button of his shirt.

He looked at her fingers, and then at her face.

“Song-Zhu.”

She stopped. “Mm?”

“Are you sure?”

“I want you.” Her voice was quiet and clear.

He searched her face. Not for permission; for whether she was choosing this, or running from the room she’d just been in. She understood what he was looking for. She put one hand on his cheek.

“I’m here,” she said. “I’m not hiding. I want to be close to someone who’s alive.”

He covered her hand with his. “All right.”

She undid the first button. Then the second. Slowly. There was nothing playful in it tonight. No joke about the price of his shirt, no remark about board meetings. She simply undressed him, one button at a time, and he stood still and let her, and when she got to the last one she pushed the shirt off his shoulders and it fell over the arm of the sofa.

She put her palm flat on his chest, over his heart, and left it there, feeling it go. As if she were making sure.

He looked at her. She kissed him. He kissed her back but didn’t take over. Tonight she was leading. He followed.

She took his hand and walked him to the bedroom, and at the doorway she stopped, and for one second her eyes filled again. He lifted his hand to her face. She leaned her cheek into his palm. Then she turned her head and kissed it, and drew him in.

✦ ✦ ✦

Only the lamp by the bed was on.

She stood in front of him and undid his belt, unhurried, all her attention on her hands and on him. He touched her cheek.
