She took his hand and put it on the first button of her own shirt, and he understood, and undid it, and the next, and the next, and the old white shirt slid off her shoulders onto the floor. They undressed each other slowly and without a single word. No declarations. No questions about tomorrow. No attempt to make it mean anything it didn’t have to mean.

She lay down and drew him down with her, and pulled the blanket over both of them, and kissed his shoulder.

Then she reached for him, and he met her halfway.

It was quiet. Deliberate. A language neither of them needed to translate. She moved at her own pace, slow, so slow, guiding his hand where she wanted it and holding it there, and he stayed attentive to every small change in her face and her breath, every pause, every time she drew him closer. When he was inside her she held his face in both her hands and looked at him, and didn’t look away, and he didn’t either. They moved together almost without moving. The lamp. The sheets. Her breath on his mouth.

Once, a tear slid from the corner of her eye down into her hair.

He stopped, at once. She shook her head against the pillow. Not sadness, exactly. Something more complicated than that, and older. She held on to him and moved again, and he understood that she wanted him to keep going, and kissed the wet place by her eye, and kept going, slowly.

There was no need to fill the silence. No need for her to tell him what she felt. He understood that tonight she wanted to be held, and to touch and be touched, and to have the plain, warm, breathing proof of another living person against every part of her. So he stayed close. So close there was no space between them anywhere. And when she came it was without a sound, her fingers digging into his back and her mouth open against his throat and her whole body trembling under him a long time, and he followed her with his face in her hair and her name on his breath, and didn’t let go of her afterwards at all.

When at last she lay with her head on his chest, he wrapped both arms round her and held her until her breathing slowed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Much later, she spoke.

“Hao?”

“Mm.”

“Do you think you’d know his voice now? If you heard it again?”

He thought about it carefully. “I think I’d know it because you would. I know what he sounds like now. Not because I knew him. Because you’ve let me hear him.”

Her eyes went soft. “He was funny.”

“I believe you.”

“He was terrible at cooking.”

“That explains something.”

“What?”

“Your relationship with the kitchen.”

She laughed faintly. Then went quiet again. “He sang when he made breakfast.”

“Badly?”

“Terribly.”

“Then I’d have liked him,” said Ren Hao.

“He’d have liked you,” she said. “He’d have told you your shoes were too shiny. And then he’d have liked you.”

He didn’t answer. He put his mouth to her hair.

She settled against him. After a long time she said, “I don’t think I’ll play it again for a long time.”

“You don’t have to.”

“But I’m glad I did.”

He found her hand under the blanket. “So am I.”

She looked towards the bedroom door, beyond which a small silver thing lay in a drawer in grey foam. For six years she had kept those four minutes. Tonight she’d listened. They hadn’t given her an explanation. They hadn’t changed anything. They hadn’t brought her father home.

But she had heard him again. Not as a photograph, not as a memory she had to keep polishing so it wouldn’t fade. As a voice. Her father’s working voice, reading back a heading at night, alive.

And she hadn’t been on her own when it ended.

✦ ✦ ✦

At sixteen minutes past two, he woke briefly. She was asleep with one hand on his chest. Her face was relaxed, but there was still a faint dried trace of tears under one eye. He reached for the tissues on the bedside table and carefully wiped it away.

She stirred. “Hao?”

“I’m here.”

She didn’t open her eyes. “Don’t go.”

Something in his chest turned over. He bent and put his mouth to her temple. “I’m not going anywhere.”

She moved closer. He held her. Outside, the city went on without them. Inside, the room stayed quiet. And for once neither of them tried to make the silence go away.

chapters.title: Christmas With Two Professors
chapters.desc: Vancouver. Two professors, delighted. Her flight suit makes his mother cry. Her first snow, a hedge, and a kiss at minus twelve.
chapters.epigraph: “Nobody told me it squeaks.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Song-Zhu noticed about Vancouver was that the air hurt her face.

The second was that Ren Hao found this extremely entertaining.

“Stop smiling.”

“I’m not.”

“You are. I can see it from inside my scarf.”

They were standing on the kerb outside the arrivals hall at a quarter past four on Christmas Eve, with the light already going blue, and the cold coming off the car park like something with an opinion.

“I’ve never seen you so offended by weather,” he said.

“I’m not offended. I’m being attacked.” She pulled the scarf up over her nose. “Why is it like this?”

“Because it’s winter.”

“That’s not an explanation. That’s a word.”

“It’s a season.”

“Hao. I have flown for thirteen hours to meet your parents. I did not agree to have my face fall off.”

He took her gloved hand and pressed his mouth to the knuckles through the wool. “Your face is still there.”

“Give it time.”

She had spent the flight alternately asleep on his shoulder and interrogating him. Were his parents strict. Had they liked his previous girlfriends. Had he been a difficult teenager. Had he ever failed an examination. That last one had offended him.

“Of course I’ve failed things.”

“What?”

“A statistics paper in my second year at university.”

“You?”

“I disagreed with the marking scheme.”

“You failed statistics because you argued with it.”

“I failed it once,” he’d said, with great dignity, “and passed it the following summer with the highest mark in the year, and wrote to the examiner to tell him.”

She had laughed so loudly that the man across the aisle had taken his headphones off to see what he was missing.

Now she looked up at him from inside the scarf. “Are they really excited?”

“My mother has rung me four times since we landed. We landed forty minutes ago.”

“To ask about me?”

“To ask whether we’ve eaten.”

Song-Zhu’s eyes went soft over the wool. “And your father?”

“Pretending not to be excited. He sent me a list of restaurants he thinks you should try, and asked whether you prefer museums or galleries, and then he sent a second email saying the first one was only a suggestion.”

“That’s adorable.”

“It’s very him.”

“What if they don’t like me?”

He stopped, with the case handle in his fist, and turned fully round to her on the kerb.

“Song-Zhu.”

“What?”

“My mother has been asking me about your flight suit since September. My father has read the summary of every report your authority published in the last five years, so he’d have something to ask you at dinner. They are going to adore you. I’m worried they’ll adopt you and send me back.”

She looked at him, over the scarf.

“That’s a very confident statement.”

“I know my parents.”

“Do you know me?”

“Unfortunately,” said Ren Hao, and she hit him in the arm with her glove, and then put the gloved hand into his coat pocket with his and kept it there.

✦ ✦ ✦

They had a hire car, because his father had wanted to come to the airport and his mother had wanted to come to the airport and Ren Hao had said, at length, on the telephone, that nobody should drive to the airport on Christmas Eve in the snow, and won.

She hadn’t known there would be snow. She saw it first on the motorway, the verges grey-white under the lights, and then on the trees, every branch picked out.

“Hao. Is that snow?”

He glanced across. “Yes.”

“Real snow.”

“Real snow.”

She put her gloved hand flat on the window. “I’ve never seen it.”

He took his eyes off the road for one second to look at her. “Never?”

“Never. My father brought me a snow globe once, from an airport. I dropped it on the kitchen tiles two days later. That’s the closest I’ve been.”

He drove a while without saying anything. “Then you’ll see enough to make up for it,” he said.

She didn’t answer. She was watching the flakes come at the windscreen in the headlights, out of the dark, endlessly. He had seen her at a crash site with fuel on her boots. In a karaoke booth with a microphone. On a kitchen floor at three in the morning. At a funeral in the rain from a car across the road. He had seen her furious and laughing and crying and entirely unbothered by the fact that she could make a room of hardened men listen when she wanted to.

He had never seen her look like this. As if somebody had opened a door onto a room she’d had no idea was there.

✦ ✦ ✦

The house was at the end of a street of wooden houses with their porch lights on. It had a wreath on the door, lights wound up the stair rail inside, and so many books that they had come out of the shelves and were living on the stairs.

His mother had the door open before they were out of the car.

She was small and quick, with silver at her temples and a voice that had spent thirty years in lecture halls and had never once needed raising. Behind her was a tall man in glasses and a wool cardigan, holding a cup of tea he had clearly forgotten about.

“Ren Hao!”

She hugged her son on the porch, hard, and held on. Then she stepped back and looked at Song-Zhu.

For one second Song-Zhu saw something in her face, and understood it: not recognition, because they had never met, but the look of someone matching a person to a great many things she’d been told.

“Xu Song-Zhu,” his mother said warmly.

Song-Zhu dipped her head. “Good evening, Professor Ren. Thank you for having me.”

“Oh, no. None of that.” And she pulled Song-Zhu into a hug that was immediate and warm and smelled of oranges and cloves, without any of the awkwardness Song-Zhu had spent an hour on the plane preparing for. “You’re even prettier than in the photographs.”

Song-Zhu went still inside the hug. “Photographs?”

On the step below, Ren Hao closed his eyes.

His father made a small sound into his tea that might have been a laugh.

“Don’t look at me like that,” said his mother over Song-Zhu’s shoulder. “You sent them.”

“I sent one.”

“Several.”

“Mum.”

“One from a restaurant. One from your office, with the harbour behind her. One from a karaoke bar, which was blurred, but we could tell she was winning. One from...”

“Mum.”

Song-Zhu turned round slowly, still in his mother’s arms. A smile was spreading across her face that he knew he would be paying for until the new year.

“How many?” she said.

His father answered, gently, from the doorway. “Enough for us to know you make him very happy.” He held out his free hand. “Welcome to Vancouver, Song-Zhu. Come in before you freeze. Isla rang this morning. She sends her love, and says to tell you she’s staying with her inspector this year and you’re to report back on everything.”

“She told me to watch you both at dinner,” said Song-Zhu, shaking his hand. “And take notes.”

“Good. Isla always wanted a research assistant,” said his father, and stood aside to let her in.

✦ ✦ ✦

Inside it was warm all the way through. A tree took up one corner of the living room, hung with paper things that children had made a long time ago. Something was roasting. There was a fire.

His mother took her coat and then took her hands, and frowned at them.

“You’re frozen. Have you eaten?”

“On the plane.”

“That doesn’t count.”

Ren Hao, behind her with both cases, said, “I told you.”

His mother gave him a look. “Don’t stand there. Take her case up. She’s in the blue room.”

“Am I being dismissed?” he said.

“Yes.”

Song-Zhu turned to him and smiled sweetly. “Go on, then.”

He gave her a long look, and went up the stairs with the cases, stepping over the books.

His father brought her tea in a mug that said I’d rather be reading. “Now. You’ll want to call us something.”

“Professor Ren?”

“There are two of us,” said his father. “It’s a practical difficulty.”

“Then I’ll say Professor and you can both answer.”

He considered this with real pleasure. “That’s very efficient.”

“I’m an investigator. I work with what I’ve got.”

“Come and sit. My wife has been preparing for you since November.”

From the kitchen: “I can hear you!”

“Good!” called her husband, and sat down opposite Song-Zhu by the fire as if a weight had come off him.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dinner wasn’t an interrogation, which she had expected. It was worse. It was interest.

His father taught literature and translated poetry out of three languages in the evenings. His mother taught political science and had once, Ren Hao said, reduced a visiting minister to silence with a single follow-up question. They both had the habit of asking something and then actually waiting.

“When you investigate an accident,” his mother said, putting down her fork, “do you begin with the most likely explanation?”

Song-Zhu thought about it. “We begin with what we can establish. The most likely explanation is a trap, if you start treating it as a conclusion. Everybody’s already decided what happened before we’ve opened the hangar.”

“And you have to un-decide them.”

“I have to decide nothing for as long as I can.”

His mother nodded slowly. “That’s what I tell my graduate students about elections, and they never believe me.”

“Do you find it hard?” said his father. “When people want an answer?”

“Sometimes.” She looked down at her plate. “Families want to know why someone didn’t come home. The airline wants to know if it’s their fault. The newspapers want it by Thursday. Everyone wants the not-knowing to stop.” She turned her glass a little on the cloth. “But the report has to be honest. Even if the honest answer for a year is that we don’t know yet.”

“That sounds rather like scholarship,” said his father.

“With considerably more wreckage,” said Song-Zhu, and his mother laughed out loud.

Ren Hao, beside her, said almost nothing for the whole meal, which his mother noticed, and looked at her husband about, and didn’t mention. He was watching his parents listen to her. She wasn’t performing. She wasn’t trying to impress anyone. She was simply being herself, at his parents’ table, with his mother’s good napkin on her knee, and they were leaning towards her.

Something in his chest that had been braced since September let go.

✦ ✦ ✦

The flight suit had been his mother’s idea. She’d asked in September, on the telephone, whether Song-Zhu would bring it. I’ve never seen one. Not a real one. Only on the news. Song-Zhu had laughed, and said it smelled of hangar, and packed it anyway, washed and folded at the bottom of the case.

So on Christmas morning, before anyone else was down, she put it on.

It was the working one, not a dress one: dark blue, the authority’s patch on the shoulder, her name over the breast pocket, a scorch near one cuff from an engine she’d got too close to, and a mend on the knee in thread that didn’t quite match. She looked at herself in the long mirror on the back of the blue room door and felt ridiculous, and went down anyway.

His mother was in the kitchen in her dressing gown with the kettle. She turned round. And stopped.

“Oh,” she said.

“You asked,” said Song-Zhu. “Last September. I hope it’s not too strange. It’s only the...”

“May I?”

Song-Zhu held out her arm. His mother put the kettle down and touched the sleeve, the stitching on the patch, the name. Her fingers found the scorch at the cuff, and the mend on the knee, and stayed on the mend.

“You go to the sites.”

“Yes.”

“In this.”

“Usually. It depends what’s there.”

“And you climb into them. The aeroplanes. Afterwards.”

“Someone has to,” said Song-Zhu.

“You’re very young.”

“I hear that a lot.”

“Does it frighten you?”

Song-Zhu thought about lying, and didn’t. “Sometimes.”

“Good,” his mother said.

Song-Zhu blinked. “Good?”

“I’d worry about you if you said it didn’t.” She looked at the name over the pocket. Then at Song-Zhu’s face. Her eyes had filled all at once, all the way. “He told us about your father. Only that he was a pilot, and that he died, a long time ago. Nothing else. He said the rest was yours.” She took Song-Zhu’s hand. “I’ve been thinking since September how proud he’d be. Standing in his kitchen, in his daughter’s... I’m sorry. I’m sorry, it’s Christmas, I don’t...”

She was crying properly now, laughing at herself, wiping her face with the back of her wrist.

Song-Zhu didn’t move. Nobody said that to her. People said I’m sorry for your loss, and it must have been hard, and is that why you do it? Nobody had stood in front of her in a kitchen on Christmas morning and said the one thing she had never let herself think in so many words.

“Thank you,” she managed.

His mother squeezed her hand hard. “And I’m so glad my son found you. Even if he does send too many photographs.”

“Mum.”

They both turned. Ren Hao was standing in the kitchen doorway in a jumper with his hair still wet, looking from his mother’s face to Song-Zhu’s.

“Don’t interrupt,” said his mother.

“I’m not interrupting. I live here at Christmas.” He came across the kitchen and put his hand flat on Song-Zhu’s back, low, and looked into her face. Her eyes were wet. His went gentle. “All right?”

“Your mother likes my flight suit.”

“I love her flight suit,” said his mother, and blew her nose on a piece of kitchen roll.

Ren Hao looked at his mother, and then at Song-Zhu, and then he smiled, slowly, the way he hardly ever did in public.

“Of course you do,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Christmas Day went slowly, the way it should. Breakfast with too much of everything. Presents under the tree. Her mother rang from her aunt’s in the afternoon, where she went every year, and spoke to Song-Zhu for twenty minutes, and then asked to speak to Ren Hao, and Song-Zhu watched him go pink in his parents’ living room as he answered questions in his best and most careful Chinese.

His mother gave her gloves, lined, the warmest she’d ever owned. His father gave her a book: a slim old collection of poems about flight, in translation, with his own pencil notes in the margins. “I’ve marked the ones that are honest,” he said. “Most poets have never been in an aeroplane. You’ll be able to tell.”

Ren Hao gave her a small box. Inside, on a fine chain, was a silver snowflake no bigger than her thumbnail.

She looked at it a long time. Then up at him.

“Hao.”

“For the globe,” he said, so that only she heard it. “The one on the tiles.”

She couldn’t say anything. She turned round and held her hair up off her neck, and he fastened it, and his fingers lingered on the nape of her neck afterwards, warm, a second longer than they needed to. When she turned back she had her hand over the pendant.

Across the room his mother leaned towards her husband.

“They’re very sweet.”

“Yes.”

“Don’t you think?”

“I said yes.”

“You’re not saying enough.”

He turned a page of his book. “Would you like an essay?”

“At least a paragraph,” said his wife, and he laughed, and didn’t write it, and reached across the sofa and took her hand instead.

✦ ✦ ✦

The snow began again at about three, with the light going.

Song-Zhu saw it first, from the window. “Hao.”

He looked up from the chair by the fire.

“It’s snowing. Again.”

“It does that here.”

“Can we go out?”

“You’re wearing socks.”

“I own shoes.”

“It’s minus twelve.”

“Your mother told me. She said it’s the coldest Christmas in eleven years. She said it like a compliment.” She was already pulling on her coat. “Come on. Before it stops.”

His mother appeared in the kitchen door. “Where are you going?”

“Outside,” said Song-Zhu. “To see the snow.”

His mother looked at her, at the new gloves already on her hands, and smiled the whole way across her face. “Take the thick scarves. The red ones, by the door.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The cold hit her like a wall.

She stepped off the back step onto the garden path and stopped dead. The garden she’d seen the night before, dark lawn and black hedges, had gone. In its place there was a white, silent, rounded country she’d never been in: the lawn smoothed over, the hedges bulked up into soft walls, every branch of the old tree at the end loaded and drooping, the fence posts wearing caps. The flakes came down out of a grey-violet sky without any sound at all.

It was the quietest place she had ever stood. Quieter than a recorder room. She could hear her own breath.

She crouched and pressed her glove into the snow and watched it sink, and looked at the print it left.

“It squeaks,” she said, astonished.

“When it’s this cold.”

“Nobody told me it squeaks.”

She scooped up a handful. It fell apart. She tried again and packed it hard and held up a lopsided lump.

“Look.”

“Very impressive.”

“It’s my first.”

“I can tell.”

She threw it at him. It burst on his chest and left a white star on his black coat. He looked down at it. Then at her.

“Sorry,” she said.

“No, you’re not.”

“Not particularly.”

He bent, quite slowly, and gathered up a handful of snow.

She backed away. “Hao.”

He packed it between his gloves without hurrying, looking at her the way he looked at people across a negotiating table.

“Hao. Don’t.”

He smiled.

She pointed a gloved finger at him. “I am a guest in your parents’ house.”

He threw it. It got her on the shoulder and a cold spray of it went down the inside of her collar, and she shrieked, and for one second there was absolute silence in the white garden. Then she went for him.

She slipped on the path at once, and he caught her round the waist before she went down, and the two of them staggered together into the drift beside the hedge, and he turned as they fell so that he hit the snow first, on his back, and she landed on top of him.

The breath went out of both of them. Snow everywhere: in his hair, on her lashes, down both their necks.

She lay on his chest and laughed until she couldn’t breathe.

“You’re supposed to be a gentleman,” she said.

“I’m off duty.”

“You’re never off duty.”

“I’m lying in a hedge,” said Ren Hao. “This is as off duty as I get.”

She stopped laughing. She looked down at him. His cheeks were red with cold, his eyelashes had snow on them, and there was a flake melting slowly on his lower lip, and he was looking up at her through the falling snow with an expression she’d only ever seen on him in the dark.

“Hold still,” she said.

She pulled her right glove off with her teeth, and let it drop into the snow, and touched his face with her bare hand. He hissed at the cold of her fingers. She laid her palm along his jaw anyway and felt him warm under it. Then she kissed him.

His mouth was cold. That was the first thing. Cold on the outside, and then, when his lips parted under hers, so warm inside that she made a small helpless sound against him. Their breath went up between them in one white cloud. He brought his arms round her and held her down against him on top of the snow, one hand spread wide on her back through the coat and the other coming up under the edge of the red scarf to the back of her neck, his gloved fingers on her skin, at the place where he’d fastened the chain.

She kissed him slowly, then not slowly. She opened his mouth with hers and licked into it, tasting cold and cinnamon from his mother’s biscuits and him. He made a sound low in his chest that she felt more than heard, and his hand on her back slid down and pressed her hips into his, through two coats and all of it, and held her there.

Snow was falling on the back of her neck. She didn’t care. She kissed the flake off his lip. She kissed the corner of his mouth, and his cold cheekbone, and his eyelid with snow on it, and came back to his mouth and kissed him again, deep, with her bare hand going numb on his jaw and her whole body warm.

When she lifted her head at last they were both out of breath. His lips were red. So, she knew, were hers.

“Minus twelve,” she said.

He looked up at her, dazed. “What?”

“The coldest Christmas in eleven years. And I came outside in it to kiss you in a hedge.”

“That’s very romantic.”

“I’m a very romantic person.”

“I’ve noticed,” he said, and his voice had gone rough. He pulled her bare hand off his jaw, and looked at her red fingers, and put them inside his coat, against his shirt, against his heart, and held them there with his own hand over the top through the wool. “You’ll lose a finger.”

“Worth it.”

“Not to me.”

She lay on him in the snow, with her hand warming against his chest, and the flakes coming down on both of them, and looked at him.

“I didn’t know it would be this quiet,” she said.

“It’s the snow. It swallows the sound.”

“Everything I do is listening,” she said. “And this is the first place I’ve been where there’s nothing to hear.”

He didn’t say anything to that. He just held her hand against his heart where she could feel it going, and turned his head, and kissed her wrist, at the cuff of her coat, where the pulse was.

From the house, faintly, came a sharp tapping on glass. They both looked. His mother was at the kitchen window, holding up two mugs and pointing at them meaningfully. Beside her, his father had lifted his book in front of his face.

Song-Zhu dropped her forehead onto Ren Hao’s chest and laughed until she shook.

✦ ✦ ✦

They came in twenty minutes later, soaked to the knees, with snow in their hair and the red scarves stiff with frost.

“Goodness,” said his mother. “Look at your faces.”

“We had a snowball fight,” said Song-Zhu.

“Did you?”

“He attacked me.”

Ren Hao, peeling off his coat, said, “She threw the first one.”

“He threw the second one down my neck.”

His mother looked at her son. “Ren Hao, you are twenty-seven years old.”

“Twenty-seven and three-quarters,” he said.

“That doesn’t help.”

From the armchair by the fire, his father lowered his book. “Who won?”

Song-Zhu put her hand up.

“That’s not what happened,” said Ren Hao.

“Do you have evidence?”

He opened his mouth. He shut it.

“Then the matter is settled,” said his father, and went back to his book, and turned a page with deep satisfaction.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night the house went quiet early, the way old houses did when everyone in them had eaten too much. His parents’ door closed at half past ten. The heating ticked in the walls.

At eleven the door of the blue room opened without a sound, and Ren Hao stood in it in a T-shirt and old flannel trousers, barefoot.

“My mother,” he said, low, “is directly underneath us.”

Song-Zhu sat up in bed. She was wearing his jumper. “Then don’t step on the board by the wardrobe. It creaks.”

“How do you know which board creaks?”

“I’ve been listening to this house for two days. It’s my job.”

He stepped over the board by the wardrobe, and closed the door, and she held the duvet up, and he got in.

He didn’t do anything a while except lie against her back with his arm round her, in the narrow bed, under the slope of the ceiling, with the snow light coming blue through the curtains. Then he put his mouth to the back of her neck, below her hair, on the fine silver chain, and left it there, and she shut her eyes.

“Hao.”

“Mm.”

“Your mother’s directly underneath us.”

“I know.”

She turned over in his arms. “So we’ll have to be very quiet.”

He looked at her in the blue dark, and something in his face went still and dark and focused, and she felt it all the way down.

“You,” he said against her mouth, “have never been quiet in your life.”

“I’m a professional listener. I can be quiet.”

“Prove it.”

She kissed him. He kissed her back slowly, deep and unhurried, his hand coming up under the jumper and spreading warm on her bare back, and she made a sound, small, and he stopped at once and put his thumb against her lower lip.

“That,” he whispered, “was not quiet.”

“That was barely anything.”

“My mother marks essays for a living. She’ll have heard the full stop.”

She bit his thumb, gently. He breathed in through his nose. And a long time after that they lay in his parents’ blue room and kissed without a sound, slow and wet and endless, her hands in his hair, his hand flat and still on the small of her back under the wool, holding her against him, both of them shaking with the effort of not making a noise, until she was flushed all over and he was breathing.

Then the board by the wardrobe creaked on its own, the way old houses did, and both of them froze, and then she pushed her face into his chest and laughed without any sound at all until the bed shook.

He held her through it. He kissed her hair.

“Next year,” he said, “I’m booking a hotel.”

“Next year?” she said into his T-shirt.

“If you’ll come.”

She lifted her head and looked at him. “Ask me next year,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the evening of the twenty-sixth his father asked her into the study.

It was the smallest room in the house and had the most books in it: shelves to the ceiling, papers in drifts on the desk, a reading lamp by an old armchair. His mother came too, and sat on the arm of the sofa with her tea.

“He has an impressive library,” said Song-Zhu, looking along a shelf.

“He has an impressive library of books he says he’s read,” said his mother.

“I have read them.”

“Not all of them.”

“Most.”

“Some,” said his wife, and Song-Zhu laughed, and sat in the armchair when she was told to.

For a while they talked about the book of poems, and which ones were honest. She’d read six of them in bed that morning. She told him the one about a night landing was right and the one about the pilot thinking about his lover on final approach was wrong, because on final approach you thought about nothing except final approach.

“I knew it,” said his father with deep satisfaction, and wrote something in the margin.

Then he asked her about her father. Not what had happened. He asked whether her father was why she’d chosen aviation.

She considered it properly, because he deserved that. “Partly. He used to bring me things from airports. And he taught me to ask questions. He didn’t always like the answers I came up with.”

“That sounds like a father,” said his mother.

“He wanted me to study something practical. So I did aerospace engineering, and he said that wasn’t what he meant.” She smiled a little. “He never saw me in the suit. He died in my second year. I joined the authority after I graduated.”

“He’d have seen it on you this morning,” said his father, “if he’d been standing where my wife was. I suspect he’d have done the same thing she did.”

Song-Zhu looked at him.

“Not because of the job,” he said. “Because you’ve made a life that asks a great deal of you, and you keep giving it. That’s harder than any of the things on these shelves.”

For a moment she couldn’t say anything at all. Then she said, “Thank you, Professor.”

“You’re very welcome.”

His mother reached across from the sofa and squeezed her hand. “And next year you’ll come earlier. We need more time with you. We’ve hardly started.”

“I’d like that,” said Song-Zhu, and found she meant it more than almost anything she’d said all year.

✦ ✦ ✦

Sunday came too fast. The flight was at two.

She stood in the blue room folding clothes into her case, the snowflake against her shirt. Ren Hao came in and leaned in the doorway.

“Ready?”

“No.”

“Neither am I.”

She sat down on the bed beside her case. “I liked your parents.”

“They liked you.”

“I know.”

He raised an eyebrow. “How do you know?”

“Your mother’s hugged me three times since breakfast.”

“She hugs everybody.”

“Your father gave me a book with his own notes in it.”

“He gives everybody books.”

“With his own notes in?”

He paused. “No,” he admitted.

She looked down at the pendant, and touched it. “Your mother cried at my flight suit.”

He came and sat beside her. “She told me afterwards she’s been wanting to say that to you since September.”

“She said my father would be proud of me.” Song-Zhu turned the chain in her fingers. “Nobody’s said that to me before. They say they’re sorry. I think I liked hearing it from her.”

He took her hand, and didn’t say anything, because he’d learned there were things she needed to hear said and things she needed to say into silence, and this was the second kind.

“I didn’t expect to feel at home here,” she said eventually.

“Good.”

“Your mother says I can come back whenever I want.”

“That’s because you can.”

“Your father says he’ll send me his reading list.”

“He will. It’ll be eleven pages.”

She leaned her head on his shoulder. “Thank you for bringing me.”

He put his mouth to her hair. “Thank you for coming.”

“Would you bring me again?”

“Every Christmas, if you want.”

“Don’t promise things you can’t control.”

He thought about it. “Then I’ll ask you every year.”

She considered that. “That’s better,” she said, and he kissed her, there on the edge of the case, with the snow still coming down past the window.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the gate she went through the photographs on her phone.

Him under the old tree, loaded with snow. His mother laughing at the stove. His father pretending, badly, not to be smiling while she photographed him. And one his mother had taken through the kitchen window without either of them knowing: the two of them in the hedge, in the red scarves, her bare hand on his face, kissing. She looked at that one a long time.

He leaned over. “Which one?”

She showed him. He went quiet. “Send it to me,” she said.

“I’ll send you all of them.”

“Not the one where I’m eating.”

“That one first.”

“Hao.”

He laughed, and she put her head on his shoulder. Outside the big windows, snow was falling across the runway in the floodlights, and the de-icing trucks were going out to the aircraft, spraying orange.

She’d come to Vancouver to meet his parents. She was going home with a book of honest poems, a pair of gloves, a silver snowflake, a dozen photographs, and the knowledge that a garden at minus twelve was the quietest place on earth.

“Cold?” he said.

“No.”

“You’re lying.”

She slid her fingers between his. “A little.”

He tightened his hand. She closed her eyes. For once she didn’t mind the cold at all.

chapters.title: The Loud Client
chapters.desc: He hires FENCE, two rooms above Auntie Au’s, to test his own firm, and pays triple. In the second week Eliana Lin finds his first hire copying client files at two in the morning. Song-Zhu sits with him till dawn.
chapters.epigraph: “But let the evidence finish talking first.”
chapters.content:
The staircase was the thing that did it.

Ren Hao stood at the bottom of it on Monday the thirteenth of April at four minutes to ten, on Terrace Road, a short walk from the ferry pier, with the smell of frying garlic and steamed dough coming out of the shop beside him, and looked up. It was steep and narrow and built for one person at a time. The paint was coming off the handrail. At the top, on a door with a pane of frosted glass, somebody had stuck a yellow sticky note that said, in capitals, FENCE.

He’d had a staircase exactly like it once. Seven years ago, in his last year at university, above a print shop on the other side of the harbour: two rooms, two second-hand desks, one printer that jammed if you looked at it, and a sign on the door that Isla had made for him out of a cereal box because he couldn’t afford a real one. Six people, by the end of that first year. He’d shouted up those stairs every morning so that everyone knew he was coming and had time to look busy.

“Sir?” said the junior from records behind him, holding three archive boxes and looking at the stairs with dread.

“Up,” said Ren Hao, and went up them two at a time, and opened the door, and announced himself to the entire building.

“HELLO! IS THIS THE SECURITY COMPANY?”

At a desk by the window a young woman with her dark hair pulled tight back looked up from a laptop. At the other desk a second young woman shut her eyes. Downstairs, somebody dropped something metal.

“Ren Hao,” he said. “I have an appointment. I think. Someone downstairs said come up. Is this the right place?”

“Mr. Ren, your appointment’s at ten,” said the woman at the laptop.

He looked at his watch. “Excellent. I’m early.”

“You’re two minutes early.”

“That’s what I said.”

He came in and looked round. Two rooms and the door between them. Second-hand desks. A wall that had been painted grey and somehow still managed to be two different greys. A whiteboard of diagrams. A kettle that predated both of the women. And the yellow sticky note on the glass, which he read aloud from the inside, backwards.

“FENCE. Good name. Short. Memorable. Slightly threatening.”

“That’s what we were going for,” said the second woman, opening her eyes.

He laughed, loudly, and shook the first one’s hand hard enough to slop her coffee. “I’ve heard about you. You’re the one who found the hole in the Calder business.”

“I did part of the assessment,” said Eliana Lin, more carefully, wiping her wrist.

“And now you’ve got your own firm. Wonderful. I love independent businesses. I love women who know what they’re doing. I love a good dumpling.” He turned and went back to the top of the stairs and put his head over the rail. “WHO MAKES THE DUMPLINGS?”

From below: “ME.”

“I LOVE YOU!”

A pause. “THEN BUY SOME!”

“I WILL!” He came back in, glowing. “I like this building.”

“I think we’ve found our target market,” murmured the second woman. That would be Yen Si-Wei, then. Business student, fifteen percent of the company, according to the one-page summary his assistant had found. She was looking at him as if he were an interesting new kind of weather.

He sat down. He lasted about four seconds before he stood up again, because he thought better on his feet and always had.

“My firm advises private clients on risk,” he said. “We have a good reputation, an expensive office and an IT department that tells me everything’s fine. Which is exactly why I don’t believe it. Test us. Everything you’re legally allowed to test. The systems, the procedures, the people, the habits. I want to know where we’re soft before somebody else tells me. No courtesy reports. No pretending something’s fine because somebody senior might be offended. If there’s a hole, tell me. If someone’s incompetent, tell me. If I’m incompetent, tell me that too.”

“It won’t be comfortable,” said Eliana.

“Wonderful.”

“It’ll disrupt your operations. We’ll need a written scope, signed authorisation and named contacts. We won’t go anywhere outside what we agree. We don’t promise to find everything. And we don’t claim anything we can’t back up.”

“Good. Good.”

“How many people have administrator access to your systems?”

“Six.”

“Why?”

“Operational requirements.”

It wasn’t an answer, and they both knew it.

He stopped pacing and looked at her properly. She looked back. She was twenty-three, according to the summary, and sitting in a two-room office with a dumpling shop underneath it, and she was looking at the head of a firm on three floors of a tower in exactly the way he had once looked at a bank manager who had told him to come back when he was older.

“You’re very direct,” he said.

“You’re paying for an assessment. Not a compliment.”

He sat down again, and this time stayed down. “Ask your questions.”

She asked them for forty minutes. Network structure, permissions, devices that went home in people’s bags, how long they kept logs and who could read them, who let contractors in, what happened to a person’s access when they changed jobs inside the firm. She interrupted him every time he said something that sounded like an answer and wasn’t. When he said, with some pride, that the firm had never had a significant security incident, she put her pen down.

“How do you know?”

“We have monitoring.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

He looked at her. “You’re asking whether we know we’ve never had one. Or whether we just haven’t noticed.”

“Yes.”

Si-Wei, at the other desk, ate a dumpling out of a paper bowl without a sound.

“Now I understand why you came recommended,” said Ren Hao.

“How much?”

She told him. He listened to the whole figure.

“Triple it,” he said.

“That’s not how we price.”

“Then price properly. You’re taking responsibility for my company for six weeks. I want you to have the time to do it right. I’m not paying for a cheap report that tells me what I want to hear. Besides,” and he beamed at her, “I like your face.”

“That’s not a pricing metric,” said Si-Wei.

“It should be.” He stood up. “Thank you. I love you already.”

He said it the way he said everything he meant, at full volume and without the slightest embarrassment, and for one second Eliana Lin plainly didn’t know whether to laugh. He shook both their hands. He picked up his briefcase. He was halfway down the stairs, with the junior and the archive boxes coming carefully after him, when he stopped and came back up.

He put his head round the door. “Where are the dumplings?”

✦ ✦ ✦

The woman downstairs was round-faced and floury and somewhere past sixty, and she looked at him across her counter with the expression of a person who had heard everything he’d shouted and was reserving judgement.

“So. You’re the loud one.”

“I’m the loud one.”

“You look hungry.”

“I’ve had breakfast.”

“That doesn’t mean you’re not hungry.”

He looked at the trays. “What do you recommend?”

“Everything.” She pointed. “Chive and prawn. Egg and chive. Mushroom and cabbage. The ones with the pleats are the prawn.”

“Four boxes. Mixed. I’m feeding an office.”

She began to pack them, and asked whether he had a girlfriend, and when he said yes, asked whether he fed her properly, and when he said he tried but she ate rice balls out of convenience stores standing up, Auntie Au put two extra dumplings in the top box and said, “Then you take these to her, and you tell her an old woman said.”

He paid. He took the bags. And then, because she had somehow made him feel in four minutes like a nephew she’d been feeding for years, he came round the end of her counter and hugged her.

She stood stiff in his arms for one second. Then she patted his back with a floury hand, twice, hard.

“Go away, handsome. You’re too much.”

“Everyone says that.”

“Then everyone’s right.”

He promised to bring the entire thirty-second floor for lunch. On his way out he passed Si-Wei on the stairs, coming down for more napkins, and told her she was obviously the brains of the operation, and she said, “Obviously,” without breaking stride. He signed the proposal on the bonnet of the car before he’d got into it, and handed it to the junior, who carried it back up.

He’d got as far as the end of the road when he remembered something and rolled the window down.

“KEEP THE RECEIPT, AUNTIE,” he shouted. “I’M CLAIMING THESE.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Song-Zhu was on her living-room floor when he let himself in that evening, sitting cross-legged in the middle of a ring of photographs of a bent landing-gear leg, with a pen in her mouth.

She looked up. “What’s that?”

“Dinner.”

She took the bag and looked inside, and her whole face changed. “Dumplings. From where?”

“Auntie Au’s.”

She took the pen out of her mouth. “Who’s Auntie Au?”

“The woman under my new security firm.”

Song-Zhu put the photograph she was holding down on the carpet slowly. “You hired a security firm.”

“Yes.”

“To protect you from what?”

“From us. To test my own people. My own systems.” He sat down on the floor with her, inside the ring of photographs, careful not to kneel on the landing gear. “We’ve grown too fast. A hundred and twelve people. Three floors. Clients I don’t know by their first names any more. The department that runs our security is the department that tells me our security’s excellent. I wanted someone outside it to look.”

She studied him. “And this someone is above a dumpling shop.”

“Two rooms. A two-hundred-metre walk from the ferry.” He took a dumpling out of the box with his fingers. “Eliana Lin. Twenty-three. Her partner’s a business student called Yen Si-Wei who owns fifteen percent and said obviously to me on the stairs.”

“Was she terrifying?”

He looked at her. “How did you know?”

Song-Zhu laughed. “What did she do?”

“Wouldn’t let me finish a sentence. Told me operational requirements wasn’t an answer. Then she told me her price, and I tripled it, and she said that wasn’t how they priced.”

“Oh, I like her.”

“I thought you might.”

She reached into the box. “Did you tell her you love her?”

“Why would you ask that?”

“Because you did, didn’t you.” She pointed the dumpling at him. “And the woman in the shop.”

He considered lying. “Her name’s Auntie Au. She sent you these two. With the pleats. She says you’re to eat them sitting down.”

Song-Zhu stared at him, and then at the two dumplings, and then burst out laughing so loudly that her neighbour knocked on the wall.

“You were in that building less than an hour,” she said, “and you’ve got another family.”

“I have a large capacity.”

“Unfortunately.” She ate one of Auntie Au’s dumplings, sitting down, as instructed. Then she looked at him over it, more carefully. “Why that one? There are big firms who do this. Firms with lifts.”

He was quiet. “Because my first office had stairs like that,” he said. “Two rooms over a print shop. Isla made the sign out of a cereal box. When I went up to banks in my one suit they told me to come back when I was older. I promised myself that one day I’d be the person who walked up somebody’s stairs and paid them what they were worth.” He shrugged. “And she’s good. Everyone I asked said so. Desmond thinks I’m wasting money.”

“Desmond?”

“Desmond Chai. One of the partners. My first hire.” He smiled a little. “He thinks anyone under thirty is a liability. I’ve told him that includes me. He says that’s what he means.”

She leaned against his shoulder. “How was your day? Apart from the dumplings.”

“Busy.”

“Anything interesting?”

He thought about it. “Not yet,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

FENCE started on the Tuesday.

They came to the tower with two laptops, a hard case, a printed list of requirements and a signed scope, and by Wednesday afternoon half his staff were afraid of them. Eliana had a habit of appearing silently at somebody’s elbow and asking a question they didn’t want to answer. Why was that cabinet open. Why had a visitor gone past reception without anybody walking her. Why had a man who’d moved from research to sales eighteen months ago still got access to the research drive. Why did the managing partner have administrator rights to a system he never used.

“For contingencies,” said Ren Hao.

“Which contingencies?”

“I’ll send you a written explanation.”

“That’s not an answer either,” said Eliana, and wrote something in her notebook, and he began to understand why Si-Wei always looked.

He couldn’t stay away from them. He knew it was absurd. He had a firm to run and three clients in crisis and a girlfriend who’d started texting him Have you been up the stairs again at lunchtime. But he went up the stairs anyway. He turned up to their meetings without warning, and he never once turned up empty-handed. Pineapple buns on the Tuesday. Coffee for both rooms on the Thursday. A bag of oranges on the Friday, and a question about whether anybody had actually had lunch, and when nobody answered he went downstairs and came back with lunch. On the Friday afternoon he found that Si-Wei had drawn a table on the whiteboard headed REN HAO, UNPLANNED VISITS, with a column at the end marked Likelihood of food (%). Every row said 100.

“That’s slander,” he said.

“It’s data,” said Si-Wei.

He was loud. He knew he was loud. But he signed every approval they put in front of him, found them every person they asked for, and the one time a director tried to steer a meeting round to something flattering, he said “Let her finish,” and the director let her finish.

On the first Friday Eliana came into his office on the thirty-second floor with a printed list.

“Your staff are polite.”

“Thank you.”

“It’s not a compliment. They apologise before they lie.” She put the list on his desk. “One of them told me he never shares his passwords. I found three of them on a note under his keyboard.”

Ren Hao shut his eyes. “Who?”

She told him.

“Put it in the report,” he said.

“I was going to.” She turned to go, and then turned back. “Also, your coffee machine’s terrible.”

“I’ll have it replaced.”

“Don’t. It’s on the network. It’s the second-biggest risk in the building.”

“What’s the first?”

Eliana looked at him, and didn’t answer, and went out.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Wednesday of the second week he was in FENCE’s front room at ten past six, sitting on the corner of Si-Wei’s desk eating a dumpling, when Eliana opened the post. A cream envelope. Handwriting. A pressed flower under the ribbon.

“A wedding!” he said. “Whose? Yours? When’s yours?”

“It’s not mine.”

“When is it, though? Yours.”

“Ren,” said Eliana, and he put both hands up, one still holding the dumpling, and grinned, and noticed that she had gone pink right up to the hairline, and filed that away to tell Song-Zhu.

She didn’t look up for the rest of the evening. Neither did Si-Wei. They’d gone quiet, the two of them, in the last two days, in a way he’d started to notice: fewer questions in the corridors, longer hours, the door between their two rooms kept shut. When he asked how the assessment was going, Eliana said, “Fine.”

“That’s reassuring.”

“Do you want reassuring or accurate?”

“Accurate.”

“Then it isn’t finished. We’re still verifying something.” She looked at him across the desk, with an expression he couldn’t read. “You’re not going to ask me what?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because you said you’re still verifying.”

She studied him a moment longer. Then nodded once. “Good,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

His phone rang a little after two on the Friday morning, the twenty-fourth.

He was awake by the second ring, the way he’d been awake for every call at that hour since he’d started a firm whose clients’ worst nights didn’t keep office hours.

“Ren.”

“Mr. Ren. It’s Eliana Lin.”

He sat up. In the dark beside him, Song-Zhu turned her head on the pillow.

“What’s happened?”

“I need you at your office. We found something. I’d rather not say it on the phone.”

Her voice was flat. Too flat. He’d heard that voice from his own mouth, on calls to clients, when the news was the kind that changed the shape of a company.

“Is anybody hurt?”

“No.”

“Have you touched anything?”

“We’ve preserved what we can without changing it. We haven’t spoken to anyone.”

“Don’t. I’ll be there in twenty minutes.”

He was already out of bed and reaching for yesterday’s trousers on the chair.

Song-Zhu was sitting up. “Hao?”

“FENCE. They’ve found something.”

“Something bad?”

“She won’t say on the phone.” He found his shirt. “Which means yes.”

She watched him dress for a moment in the light from the street. Then she pushed the duvet off and got up and started dressing too.

“You don’t have to come.”

“I know,” she said, and pulled her jumper over her head.

He looked at her. He didn’t argue.

✦ ✦ ✦

At two forty-one he walked into the big conference room on the thirty-second floor, with the city dark and wet beyond every pane of the glass wall, and found Eliana Lin and Yen Si-Wei sitting on one side of his table with a laptop, a sealed drive in an evidence bag, and a short stack of printed pages squared off precisely in front of them.

Song-Zhu didn’t come in with him. She stopped by the glass at the end of the room, in her jumper, with her hands in her pockets, and let him go on alone.

He sat down at the head of his own table. He folded his hands on it.

“Tell me.”

Eliana told him.

It took her eleven minutes, and he didn’t interrupt once. Not a break-in, not a stranger. Client files opened in the small hours by an account that had no business being awake. Copies made, on three separate nights, at about two in the morning. Each of the three nights the night before an account moved to the same rival firm: three clients who’d left in the last five months, that he’d lost and written to personally and been told, each time, politely, that it was nothing to do with the quality of the work. Records showing the copies leaving by a route marked staff only, that nobody had approved. What could be proved and what couldn’t. The report on the table didn’t accuse anybody of anything the records didn’t show. It said that everything should be preserved and the rest left to lawyers.

She turned the first page round to face him, and put her finger beside the account name, and took it away. He read the name.

The room was quiet. Outside, a long way below, a single siren went along the harbour road and away.

“You’re sure?” he said at last.

“I’m sure the access broke your own policies. I’m sure files were copied and taken out by a route nobody approved. I can’t tell you everything that was taken. And I can establish which account did it. I can’t yet tell you whose hands were on the keyboard. That’s for an investigation.”

“Good. Keep that distinction.” He looked at the table a while. “His name’s on the wall downstairs,” he said. “He was here when we had six people.”

“I’m sorry,” said Eliana.

“Don’t be sorry for finding it.” He looked up at her. “Send me the final report. Nobody goes near him until the lawyers have it.” And then, because it was true, and because she was sitting at his table at three in the morning having done exactly what he’d paid her to do, which was to break his heart accurately: “You know what? I really do love you.”

He stood up. He smiled at her, worn out, meaning it.

Si-Wei looked at the ceiling. Eliana pressed her lips together. “Thank you, Ren.”

“Triple was worth it,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

When they’d gone into the small room next door to ring their lawyer and start the timeline, he sat down again.

He put his right hand flat on the table. It had started to shake, slightly, and he pressed it down on the wood until it stopped.

Song-Zhu came away from the glass. She didn’t say anything. She pulled out the chair beside his, the one at the corner of the table, and sat down in it, close enough that their knees touched, and waited.

“Desmond,” he said.

“I know.”

“He was the first person I hired. Not the first who worked for me. Isla did, for a summer, for nothing, and was terrible. The first one I chose. He answered an advertisement I put on a university noticeboard, and came up the stairs above the print shop in a borrowed tie, and told me my business plan had four mistakes in it. He was right about three.” He gave a short laugh that had nothing in it. “I paid him less than the printer cost. He stayed anyway. He slept on the floor of that office with me the night we nearly lost our first big client. He came to my parents’ for dinner. He’s known Isla since she was nineteen. When we moved into this tower he stood next to me in the lobby while they put the names up.”

She didn’t say maybe he didn’t do it. She didn’t say I’m sure there’s an explanation. She put her hand over his flat hand on the table and left it there.

“I trusted him with everything,” said Ren Hao. “Seven years.”

“I know.”

“Three clients. I wrote to all three. Personally. I asked what we’d done wrong.” He looked at the page with the name on it. “He helped me draft the letters.”

Her fingers tightened.

“How long?” he said. “How long has he been...?”

“You don’t know yet,” she said.

“No.”

“Then listen to me.” She turned in her chair so she was facing him. “I do this. This is my job. Somebody puts a page in front of you at three in the morning, and it’s got a name on it, and every part of you wants to decide the whole story right there, because not knowing is unbearable. That’s when you make the worst mistakes of your life.” Her voice was low and steady. “You can be angry. You can be hurt. You can hate him, if that’s where it ends up. But let the evidence finish talking first.”

He looked at her a long time. Then he turned his hand over under hers, and held on.

✦ ✦ ✦

She stayed with him through the night.

She didn’t try to make him go home. She didn’t fill the silence. When he rang his head of legal at ten past three and had a twelve-minute conversation in his quietest and most precise voice, she sat beside him and listened. When he arranged, without alerting anyone, to have the relevant systems locked down and the access records secured, she wrote the times on a notepad for him without being asked, because she couldn’t help herself. At half past three she went down forty floors in the lift and came back with two coffees and a paper bag from the convenience store on the corner.

“Eat something.”

“I’m not hungry.”

“I didn’t ask if you were hungry.” She put a sandwich in front of him. “You fed me for ten months. Eat.”

He looked at her. He ate half the sandwich. She watched him do it with deep satisfaction.

“You’re very bossy,” he said.

“Someone has to be. And it’s my turn.”

A little after four Eliana came back in.

“We’ve confirmed the three nights. I’ll have a timeline for you by six.” She hesitated. “There’s something else. There’s access from the same account going back further. Before the three dates. Older logs, some of them past your retention period, so I can’t tell you yet whether anything was copied.”

“How far back?”

“I’m checking.”

“Then I want the scope expanded. The whole firm. Every account with the same access. Every partner. Me included.”

“That’ll take longer. And cost more.”

“Send me the figure.”

She nodded, and went back out. Ren Hao looked at the closed door.

“She’s good,” he said.

“Yes.”

“I should have hired her years ago.”

“She’d have been sixteen,” said Song-Zhu, and he made a sound that was nearly a laugh, and put his face in his hands, and she put her palm flat on his back between his shoulders and kept it there.

At five he told her about the night above the print shop. Two of them on the floor on flattened boxes, eating cold noodles out of the carton, the client’s lawyer threatening to sue them out of existence by Monday, and Desmond saying, at four in the morning, if this goes under I’ll come and work for you at the next one. And at the next one, and the one after.

“I used to tell him,” said Ren Hao, “that when we made it, he’d never have to worry about money again.”

“Did he?”

“I thought so.” He turned the paper cup round in his hands. “I keep going back over the last few months. Meetings. Questions he asked about accounts. Things I thought were ordinary. I keep looking at every one of them to see if it’s a lie.”

“Stop doing that tonight,” she said. “You can do it on Monday with the lawyers and a timeline. Not now. Not on your own.”

“I’m not on my own.”

“No,” she said. “You’re not.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The light came up grey over the harbour at a little after six.

At six thirty Eliana came out with the timeline: printed, dated, every entry referenced to a record. The three nights, at about two in the morning, the night before each account moved. No evidence yet of payment. No evidence yet of anyone else. She stood at the end of the table while he read it.

“I know this is personal,” she said.

He looked up.

“But I need you to understand that our job isn’t to prove Mr. Chai did it. Our job is to find out what happened. If it turns out to be uncomfortable for him, it is. If it turns out to be uncomfortable for you, it is too.”

He looked at her. She was twenty-three, and had been awake for twenty-four hours, and was standing in his boardroom telling him the rules of his own trade.

“You’re right,” he said.

“Good.” She closed her notebook. “Then we’ll go on.”

“Eliana.”

“Yes?”

“Thank you.”

“Don’t thank me until the report’s finished,” she said.

“You’re very hard to please.”

“That’s why you hired us,” said Eliana Lin, and went back to her laptop.

✦ ✦ ✦

A little after seven Song-Zhu found him alone in his own office, standing at the glass, looking down through the internal window at the floor below: rows of empty desks, the lights coming on automatically, one by one, as the building woke up for a Friday that didn’t know anything yet.

She came up behind him and put her arms round his waist and her cheek against his back. He put both his hands over hers.

“How are you?” she said.

“I don’t know.”

“That’s allowed.”

“I thought if there was one person in this building I’d never have to question,” he said, “it was him.”

She held on tighter. He turned round in her arms. His face was grey with tiredness, and there was a line between his eyebrows she’d learned meant he was holding far more than he was letting anybody see.

“What if all of it was a lie?” he said. “Seven years.”

She put her hand on his cheek. “Then the lie’s his. Not yours. The years you worked, the things you built, the people downstairs who come in at nine and trust you. That was all real. You don’t have to turn your whole life into a mistake because one man in it might have been taking it apart.”

He looked at her. She kissed him. Not to distract him, not to make anything better. Only to remind him that he wasn’t standing in that office on his own, and when she drew back she kept her hand where it was.

“Come home,” she said.

“I’ve got work.”

“You’ve got a hundred and twelve people who can work. And a lawyer. And a twenty-three-year-old who frightens you.”

“I need to...”

“Hao.”

He stopped.

“You’ve been awake all night.”

“So have you.”

“Yes. And I’m telling you to come home.”

He looked at her a while longer. Then, for the first time since nineteen minutes past two, he nearly smiled.

“All right,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

At his flat she made him shower. He said he was perfectly capable of showering himself. She said she knew, but he’d been standing in the bathroom doorway looking at the tiles for two minutes.

When he came out, in clean clothes, with his hair wet, she was sitting on the end of his bed with his phone in her hand.

“Your report’s come. Eliana sent it to your email. I haven’t opened it.”

He looked at the phone. Then at her.

“You can read it after breakfast,” she said.

He took the phone from her, and looked at it, and then opened the drawer of the bedside table and put it inside, and shut the drawer. Song-Zhu’s eyebrows went up.

He sat down beside her. “Breakfast first.”

“Good boy,” she said, and he laughed, and put his face against her neck, and stayed there.

“Stay with me today?” he said into her skin.

“I texted Mabel at five. I’m not going anywhere.”

“I love you,” he said.

She put her fingers into his wet hair and held his head against her.

“Keep saying it,” said Song-Zhu.

And for a little while, in the grey morning, with the phone shut away in a drawer and the report unread inside it, he let himself be held.

chapters.title: Betrayal
chapters.desc: He dismisses Desmond Chai and sits in his car for two hours. She climbs into the back seat. Explicit, windows fogged: she makes him look at her.
chapters.epigraph: “Stay with me. All the way. Don’t go anywhere.”
chapters.content:
Desmond Chai arrived at seven minutes past nine, carrying two coffees.

One for himself. One for Ren Hao. Black, no sugar, from the cart on the corner that Desmond had insisted for seven years was better than anything in the building, which it wasn’t.

It was such an ordinary thing that for a moment Ren Hao couldn’t look at him.

“Black. No sugar.” Desmond put the cup down on the desk and loosened his tie and sat in the chair opposite, the one he’d sat in a thousand times. “What’s the emergency? You sounded very formal on the phone. And Kong’s outside your door, which is never a good start to a Monday.”

Kong was the head of legal. He was outside the door because Ren Hao had asked him to be, and because he’d spent most of the weekend with Eliana Lin’s final report and a copy of the partnership agreement, and had said on Sunday night, in his driest voice, Do it by the book, Hao, and do it once.

Ren Hao looked at the man across the desk.

He remembered him at twenty-two, coming up the stairs above the print shop in a borrowed tie, with a copy of the business plan he’d been sent marked up in red. There are four mistakes in this. He remembered him sitting on flattened cardboard on the floor of those two rooms at four in the morning, the night they nearly lost the Penrose account, saying if this goes under I’ll come and work for you at the next one. He remembered him in the lobby of this tower on the day they’d moved in, three years ago, watching the man with the ladder put their names up on the wall. Look at us, Desmond had said. We actually did it.

He had believed him. He looked down at the folder.

“There’s been an internal security review.”

“The new firm. Upstairs from the dumplings.” Desmond smiled faintly and took the lid off his coffee. “The young girl.”

“Eliana Lin.”

“She’s very young.”

“She’s also very good.”

“I’m sure.”

Ren Hao opened the folder and laid three printed records on the desk, side by side, facing the other way.

“Do you recognise these?”

Desmond leaned forward. His eyes went over the first page. The second. The third. His face hardly changed at all, and it was the not-changing that Ren Hao would remember for the rest of his life. Seven years, and he’d never once seen Desmond read anything without some flicker of opinion going across his face. He saw one now: nothing.

“Access logs.”

“Yes.”

“What’s this supposed to show?”

“Confidential client files copied from our systems on three nights. At about two in the morning.”

“By whom?”

Ren Hao turned the last page round so that the name at the top faced him. For a moment neither of them said anything.

Then Desmond sat back. “That’s my account.”

“I know.”

“Could be a compromised credential.”

“We considered that.”

“Then you should know better than to put this in front of me as if it proves something.”

“We’ve examined the access records,” said Ren Hao, “the device each session came from, the transfers, the authentication logs, and the badge records for the building on each of those nights. The device was your laptop. The badge was yours.”

Desmond gave a short laugh. “An independent firm you hired to look at your own systems, and it found something on me. That’s convenient.”

“They weren’t told to find you. They were told to find holes.”

“And the three accounts. That’s what this is about, isn’t it. Clients move, Hao. That’s business.”

“Not usually the morning after somebody’s copied their risk assessments and contact histories.”

Desmond’s jaw tightened. “You’re accusing me of stealing from you.”

“I’m asking you to explain the records.”

There was a long silence. Desmond looked at him across the desk, and then at the papers, and then at him again.

“Hao,” he said, gently. “We’ve known each other seven years.”

“I know.”

“Seven years. Do you really think I’d do something like that?”

And there it was. The sentence Ren Hao had been dreading since two forty-one on Friday morning. Not I didn’t do it. Not let me help you find who did. Only an appeal to everything between them, laid across the desk like a coat over a hole in the floor, as if seven years ought to be enough to make the records go away.

“That’s what I’ve been trying to understand,” said Ren Hao.

Desmond shook his head. “This is ridiculous. You’re letting a twenty-three-year-old consultant tell you how to run your company.”

Ren Hao’s eyes came up. “Don’t.”

“Don’t what?”

“Don’t make this about her age. She didn’t copy anything.”

Desmond looked away, at the window. Ren Hao closed the folder.

“On three nights your account accessed files you had no reason to open and copied them out of the firm by a route nobody approved. That’s a breach of the access policy you signed, and helped me write, and that alone is gross misconduct under the agreement. Whatever else those files were used for is for the lawyers now, not me. Your access ended at eight this morning. Your devices are secured. Kong has the formal notice. You’re dismissed, effective today, and your partnership ends with it.”

Desmond stared at him.

“You can’t be serious.”

Ren Hao said nothing. Desmond laughed once, a small disbelieving sound, and looked round the office. The desk. The glass wall. The framed photograph on the cabinet by the door: six young people on a staircase above a print shop, squinting, holding a sign made of cereal box. His eyes stopped there.

“We built this together,” he said.

“Yes.”

“I was there when you had nothing.”

“I remember.”

“I gave you seven years.”

“No,” said Ren Hao. “We gave each other seven years. That’s what I can’t...” He stopped, and found his voice again, quieter. “I’m not the one who copied the files, Desmond.”

For one moment something moved in Desmond’s face. Not guilt. Something nearer to calculation, as if he’d been playing a hand and had only just seen that the other man had turned his own cards face up on the table long ago.

Then it was gone. He stood up. He buttoned his jacket. He left his coffee where it was.

“You’re going to regret this,” he said.

“I’ve been regretting it since Friday,” said Ren Hao.

The door closed behind him at nine thirty-four. Through the glass Ren Hao watched Kong fall into step beside him, and the two of them go down the corridor towards the lifts, and not look back. He didn’t move.

The second coffee sat on the desk between the two chairs. After a while he picked it up. It was still warm. He took it to the small sink in the corner and poured it away, and rinsed the cup, and put it in the bin, because it was Desmond’s cup from Desmond’s cart and he couldn’t think what else to do with it.

Then he went back to his desk and sat looking at the empty chair.

He didn’t cry. He didn’t shout. He didn’t throw anything. That, he thought distantly, would have been easier.

✦ ✦ ✦

A little after ten Eliana knocked on the glass. Si-Wei was behind her.

“Come in.”

“His credentials are disabled and the records are preserved,” said Eliana. “Legal has everything. The expanded review’s started. I want to be clear that we don’t yet know the full extent of the copying.”

“I understand.”

She looked at him longer than a consultant looks at a client.

“Are you all right?”

“I’m fine.”

She didn’t believe him and didn’t argue. “We’ll keep going.”

“Eliana. Your work’s been excellent.”

“Thank you.” She turned to go, and then turned back in the doorway. “Don’t let this make you careless with the rest of your people.”

“Meaning?”

“Meaning one person can betray you without everybody else becoming a suspect. You’ve got a hundred and eleven people out there who didn’t do anything. Don’t start looking at them the way you looked at that log.”

He considered that. “Understood,” he said, and she went, and he sat with what she’d said a long time. She was twenty-three. She had walked up his stairs two weeks ago and refused to let him finish a sentence. Now she’d found something he’d spent seven years failing to imagine, and had stopped in his doorway to tell him how not to break himself on it.

He was grateful. He was also, in a way he couldn’t explain to anyone, furious with the world for making her necessary.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty past twelve he left the building.

He didn’t tell Joyce where he was going. He didn’t ring Mr. Yau. He took the lift to the basement and got into his own car, which he hardly ever drove, and drove it out of the building and round two corners and down into the underground car park of an office block that was half empty since its biggest tenant had moved out. He went down to the lowest level, because there was nobody on the lowest level, and parked in the far corner under a light that flickered, facing a concrete wall.

He turned the engine off. The silence settled round him like water.

His phone lit on the passenger seat at twelve forty. Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots). He watched it ring out. Not because he didn’t want to hear her voice. Because he didn’t know what he’d say if he heard it, and he was afraid of what it would sound like.

At ten to one he remembered a night above the print shop, in the rain. Damp carpet, noodles out of cardboard, Desmond complaining about a client who wanted the impossible by Thursday, and Ren Hao saying they should both get proper jobs. You’re not going to quit, Desmond had said.

No?

No. You’re too stubborn.

Ren Hao had thrown a napkin at him. Desmond had caught it, and said, We’ll make this work.

At five past one he remembered Desmond giving Isla a lift home in the rain from a university debate she’d lost, and coming back to the office and saying your sister is going to run the world and she’s going to be furious with all of us while she does it.

At twenty past one he remembered the first time someone had called them partners. A client, by mistake, in a meeting, you and your partner, and the two of them catching each other’s eye across the table and not correcting it.

At half past one he remembered the three letters he’d written to the three clients who’d left. We value your trust above everything. Please tell me plainly what we did wrong. Desmond had read every draft. Desmond had suggested a better word in the second paragraph.

At twenty to two he remembered the access logs.

Just after two he remembered Desmond’s face reading the name, and how nothing had moved in it at all.

At ten past two he finally turned the phone over. Three messages.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): How did it go?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Hao?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I’m not asking you to explain over text. Just tell me you’re all right.

He looked at the last one a long time. Then he typed.

Ren Hao: I fired him.

The reply came before he’d put the phone down.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Where are you?

He looked through the windscreen at the concrete, and the flickering tube, and nothing.

Ren Hao: In the car.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Which car park?

He sent her the location.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Stay there.

He almost smiled. He knew that tone. He’d heard her use it on a man from an operator who’d wanted to power up a cockpit before the recorder breaker was pulled.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty past two the rear passenger door opened.

He hadn’t heard her come down the ramp. She must have got a taxi to the top and walked. She was in her work clothes, a loose cream jumper and dark trousers, her lanyard pushed into her pocket, her hair coming out of its clip, and she leaned into the back of the car and looked at him in the driver’s seat over the headrests.

“Get in the back.”

He turned round. “What?”

“Get in the back, Hao. I’m not sitting with a gearstick between us.”

He looked at her for a second. Then he got out, and shut his door, and got in beside her, and pulled the rear door closed, and the car was quiet again, except now it had both of them in it.

She didn’t say anything at first. She took his hand.

“Did he deny it?”

“Not in so many words.”

“What did he say?”

“He said we’d known each other seven years. He asked me if I really thought he’d do that.” He looked down at their hands on the seat between them. “He never said he didn’t.”

She nodded slowly. She’d sat in enough rooms with enough people to know what that meant.

“And then?”

“And then he said we built the firm together.”

She was quiet.

“He wasn’t wrong,” said Ren Hao.

She rubbed her thumb across his knuckles. “No.”

“He was there from the first week.”

“I know.”

“I trusted him.”

“I know.”

He looked out of the side window at a concrete pillar with a painted number on it. “I keep remembering things. Small things. Stupid things. Things that meant nothing at the time. And I keep holding each of them up to see whether he was already doing it then. Whether he was doing it when he gave Isla a lift. Whether he was doing it when he helped me write those letters.”

She shifted closer on the seat. “You may never know when it started,” she said.

“I don’t know if the rest of it was real.”

“The rest of what?”

“Any of it. The friendship. The years.”

She thought about that, properly, the way she thought about everything that mattered.

“You can miss someone who hurt you,” she said. “You can be angry with him and still keep the good things. You don’t have to go back and make those years mean nothing just because the end of them is ugly. And you don’t have to forgive him to admit that he mattered.”

He sat still. Then he gave a small, exhausted laugh.

“You’re very good at this.”

“At what?”

“Knowing what to say.”

“I’m not,” she said. “I’m just listening. It’s the only thing I’m actually good at.”

Something in his face gave way. Not all at once. Just enough. He leaned forward and put his face against her shoulder, and she put both arms round him and held his head there with one hand, and a long time neither of them moved.

“I thought I’d feel relieved,” he said into her jumper.

“Do you?”

“No.”

“What do you feel?”

He took a long time. “Embarrassed.”

She drew back to look at him. “Why?”

“Because I didn’t see it. I trusted him with the business. With clients. With my people. With my family. I brought him to my parents’ table. I let him into everything.” His voice went low. “I’m supposed to be the person other people hire to see this coming.”

“You trusted somebody,” she said. “That isn’t something to be ashamed of. His choices are his. Not yours.”

“What if I should have known?”

“Then you’ll learn what you missed, when you know what it was.” She put her palm against his cheek. “But don’t punish yourself for not expecting it from someone you loved. That’s not a failure in you. That’s the thing he used.”

He looked at her. “Stay,” he said.

“I’m already here.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The car park hummed. A long way up, tyres went round the ramp and away.

She sat sideways on the seat, one leg tucked under her, and watched him. He looked at her, and some of the grey had gone out of his face.

“Have you eaten?” he said.

She gave him a look. “Don’t.”

“Sorry.”

“I had lunch.”

“What?”

“Food,” said Song-Zhu, and he laughed, low, and she touched the corner of his mouth where the laugh had been.

“You’ve been somewhere else all afternoon,” she said.

“I don’t know how to come back.”

“Then let me help.”

She leaned in and kissed him. Gently. He kissed her back, but slowly, his mouth hardly moving, his eyes going past her to the side window, to the pillar, to the number painted on it, and she felt the exact second he went away again.

She pulled back. She took his face in both hands.

“Hao.”

“Mm.”

“Look at me.”

He looked.

“Not at the window. Not at the phone. Not at him.” She waited until his eyes had come all the way back to hers and stayed there. “At me.”

He looked at her. She kissed him again, and this time he stayed.

It was slow. She kept it slow. She kissed his upper lip and then his lower one, and opened his mouth with hers, unhurried, and when his hand came up to the back of her neck she let it, and when he tried to take the kiss and deepen it, the way he always did, she drew back half an inch and made him wait, with her breath on his mouth and her thumbs on his cheekbones, until he understood that this was hers, and let her have it.

“Song-Zhu.”

“Yes?”

“I don’t want you to be the thing that makes me feel better.”

“I’m not.”

“I don’t want to use you to forget him.”

“I’m not asking you to forget him.” She stroked his hair back off his forehead. “I’m here because I want to be. Because you’re in a car park at the bottom of a building, on your own, and I want to be wherever you are.”

He looked at her, and nodded. She shifted on the seat and her knee hit the centre armrest, hard. She looked down at it, offended.

“This car is very inconvenient.”

He laughed. “That’s your professional observation?”

“It’s too expensive to be this uncomfortable.”

“I’ll write to the manufacturer.”

“Please do.” She put the armrest up out of the way with one hand and looked at him. “Can I?”

“You never have to ask me that.”

“I know. I’m asking.”

He put his hands on her waist. “Yes.”
