She swung her leg across him and settled astride his lap, facing him, in the back of his car, with her knees on the leather on either side of his hips and her head nearly touching the roof, and she put her hands on his shoulders and looked down at him.

“Better?” she said.

“Much.”

She undid his tie first. She took her time over it, the knot and then the long silk sliding out from under his collar, and dropped it somewhere behind her. Then the top button of his shirt, and the next, and the next, until she could put her hand flat inside it on his chest, on his skin, on his heart going hard under her palm. She kissed his jaw. His temple. The place between his eyebrows where a crease had been sitting since Friday. She kissed it until it let go.

He shut his eyes. She stopped.

“Look at me,” she said.

He opened them.

“Stay with me. All the way. Don’t go anywhere.”

“I won’t.”

She took his hands off her waist and put them under her jumper, on her bare back, and he breathed in sharply at the heat of her. She pulled the jumper over her head and let it fall onto the front seat. She was in a plain white bra and nothing about her was in any hurry. He looked at her the way he’d looked at the snow. He put his mouth against her collarbone and she let him, and when he reached round for the clasp she let him do that too, and then she was bare from the waist up in the flickering light, and he made a sound against her skin that she felt in her spine.

He kissed her breast. Slowly, open-mouthed, his hand spread on her back holding her to him, and she held his head there with her fingers in his hair and her eyes shut and her breath coming shorter. When he turned his head to the other side she rocked forward against him without meaning to, and felt how hard he was under her through his trousers and hers, and they both went still.

“Hao.”

“Yes.”

“Look at me.”

He looked up at her. His mouth was wet. His eyes had gone dark and focused, and every bit of him was there, in the car, with her, and nowhere else at all.

“Good,” she whispered.

She got his belt open. He got her trousers undone and pushed them down as far as he could, and she swore at the car, and he laughed against her throat, and she lifted herself off him and wrestled one leg free of the trousers in the space between the seats with her elbow against the window and her hair caught on the coat hook, laughing too, helplessly, and he held her steady with both hands so she didn’t fall into the footwell.

“This,” she said, breathless, “is the least dignified thing I’ve ever done.”

“You once fell out of a camp bed.”

“That was the bed’s fault.”

“This is the car’s,” he said, and she kissed him to make him stop talking, and got the leg free, and came back down astride him in nothing but her knickers and his open shirt hanging off his shoulders, and the windows had started to cloud at the edges.

She pressed down against him and moved, once, slowly, and his head went back against the seat.

“Don’t,” she said. “Don’t close your eyes.”

He opened them. He held her gaze while she pushed his trousers down off his hips, and while she pulled her knickers aside, and while she took him in her hand and held him there, against her, wet, and didn’t move.

“Song-Zhu,” he said, and it was barely her name, it was hardly a word.

“Watch,” she said.

And she sank down onto him, slowly, so slowly, all the way, with her hands on his shoulders and her eyes on his, and he watched her do it, and neither of them breathed.

When she was settled on him she stayed still. She let him feel it. She put her forehead against his and held him inside her and looked at him from an inch away, and felt him trembling under her hands with how badly he wanted to move.

“Not yet,” she said.

“Please.”

“Not yet. Stay here.”

He stayed. His hands were on her hips, gripping hard, and he didn’t move them. She could feel him holding himself back with everything he had, which was a great deal, and she loved him for it so much that it nearly frightened her. Then she began to move.

Slow. She rose and came down again, slow, the whole length of him, and his breath went out of him in a sound she’d never heard him make. She did it again. And again. She set the pace and kept it there, unhurried, deliberate, her hands on his shoulders, her eyes on his face, and every time his eyes started to slip shut she said Hao and they came back to her. The windows clouded over completely. The flickering light went soft and grey through the fogged glass. The car rocked, slightly, on its springs. The only sounds were their breathing and the small wet sounds of her moving on him and the leather creaking under her knees.

“Look at me,” she whispered.

“I am.”

“Keep looking.”

He looked. He looked at her. Somewhere in the middle of it his hands left her hips, one coming up to the back of her neck and the other sliding down between them, and found her, and touched her in time with her own movements, exactly as she liked it, and her rhythm broke for the first time and she gasped against his mouth.

“There,” he said, low. “There. Let me.”

She let him. She kept moving, slower than she wanted, slower than either of them could bear, and he kept touching her and kept looking, and she felt it building in her from far down, a long slow tightening, and she put her forehead on his and held his gaze and let him see it happen. When she came it went through her in long helpless waves, her thighs shaking on either side of him, her fingers digging into his shoulders, her mouth open on his name, and she didn’t close her eyes once, and neither did he.

He held her through it. When she’d stopped shaking he was still hard inside her, not moving, waiting, his hand at the back of her neck and his whole body taut as wire.

“Now,” she said against his mouth. “Now you.”

He took hold of her hips again and moved under her, up into her, and it was only a few strokes, deep and hard and helpless, his eyes on hers the entire time as she’d asked, before he came with a sound torn out of the bottom of his chest, holding her down on him with both arms, his face pressed into her neck at the last.

For a long time afterwards nobody moved.

She lay against his chest with her cheek on his bare skin, his open shirt round both of them, her hair stuck to her temple. His hand moved slowly up and down her back. The windows were completely white. Her trousers were in the footwell. His tie was somewhere under the front seat. Water was running in a thin line down the inside of the glass beside her head.

“Better?” she said eventually.

“Yes.”

“Good.”

He pushed the damp hair off her face. “Thank you.”

She lifted her head and frowned at him. “For what?”

He thought about it, honestly. “For coming. For finding me.”

“You told me where you were.”

“I didn’t ask you to come.”

“I know.” She put her hand on his cheek. “You don’t have to ask. Not every time. Not with me.”

“I don’t want you to feel you have to fix things.”

“I’m not fixing anything,” said Song-Zhu, and lay back down on his chest. “I’m keeping you company. That’s very different.”

He wrapped both arms round her. Somewhere on the front seat his phone buzzed. He looked towards it.

She didn’t lift her head. “Don’t.”

“It might be work.”

“It can wait five minutes. Kong can wait five minutes. The whole firm can wait five minutes.”

“You’re very strict.”

“Yes,” she said, and he didn’t reach for it.

✦ ✦ ✦

They stayed until the windows began to clear.

“Do you want to talk about him?” she said, while she was finding her trousers.

“Not yet.”

“All right.”

“Maybe later.”

“Whenever.” She fought one leg back into them in the footwell and gave up being dignified about it. “Ow.”

“What?”

“Your seatbelt buckle. It’s been in my knee for twenty minutes.”

“You didn’t say.”

“I was busy,” she said, and he laughed, a real laugh, tired and surprised, and she looked at him and smiled.

“I don’t know what happens now,” he said, buttoning his shirt. “With any of it.”

“The firm carries on. The review carries on. You’ll find out what happened, and then you’ll decide what you think about Desmond, when you know the whole story. Not before.” She pulled her jumper on and her head came out of it with her hair everywhere. “And tonight you’re going to come home, and eat something, and sleep.”

“Is that an order?”

“Yes.”

“Can I negotiate?”

“No.”

“You’re becoming very difficult.”

She leaned over and kissed his chin. “I learned from someone.”

Just after five he got out of the car into the cold concrete air. She climbed through to the front seat for her bag and her lanyard and his tie, which she found under the passenger seat and handed to him without a word. He put it in his pocket.

She looked up. “What?”

He shook his head. “Nothing.”

She came round the car and put her arms round his waist, and they stood beside it in the flickering light, and he held her.

“Come home with me,” he said.

“I thought I already was.”

“Good.”

She touched his face. “And Hao. Tomorrow you can be angry again. As angry as you like. But tonight you don’t have to be the managing partner.”

“Who am I tonight?”

“My boyfriend,” she said.

He kissed her. “That sounds manageable.”

“Don’t start.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening he didn’t open the report again. He didn’t ring Desmond, or write to him, or read the message Desmond sent at nine, which Kong had told him on Sunday he mustn’t answer and which he forwarded, unread, to Kong.

He ate dinner with her. He had a shower. He lay beside her in bed while she told him about a colleague who’d labelled an evidence box bits, just that, bits, and how she’d made him relabel every bag in it in front of Mabel. He laughed in the right places. He listened.

When she fell asleep he stayed awake a little longer, thinking about two rooms over a print shop. Two desks. A printer that jammed. A borrowed tie. A man on the floor at four in the morning saying we’ll make this work.

He didn’t know which of those memories were still safe to keep. He didn’t know whether the review would find more, or how far back it went. He didn’t know whether it had started months ago or years.

He knew one thing. He’d spent seven years building something with a man he trusted. He wasn’t going to let that man take the part of him that had been able to trust in the first place.

Beside him she moved in her sleep, and her hand found his on the sheet, and held on.

He held it back. For the first time since Friday, he let his eyes close.

chapters.title: Her Promotion
chapters.desc: Investigator-in-charge at twenty-six. He throws her a party she didn’t want; she forgives him in the kitchen. He invites himself to Yu Chen’s party and lifts the doctor off the ground.
chapters.epigraph: “Believing in me. Instead of deciding how it’ll turn out.”
chapters.content:
The call came at sixteen minutes past ten on Wednesday the thirteenth of May.

Song-Zhu was in the corridor outside the briefing room with a paper cup of coffee in one hand and a stack of maintenance records in the other, in the middle of telling Dexter that a timeline with a forty-minute hole in it wasn’t a timeline, it was a suggestion, when her phone went.

Director Kwan.

She stepped away from the door. “Good morning, Director.”

“Have you got a moment?”

“Yes.”

“Come up to my office, please.”

She looked at the records in her arm. “Is something wrong?”

“No.”

It came too quickly for her to believe it. “Then shall I bring the Kestrel file?”

“Leave it.”

She narrowed her eyes at the wall. “That sounds suspicious.”

A short laugh down the line. “Just come upstairs, Song-Zhu.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Director Kwan’s office was on the top floor of the authority’s building and looked east over the airport, so that every few minutes something large and white went past his window slowly and his visitors lost their train of thought. Song-Zhu had been in it often enough to know where he kept the good tea, which drawer had the spare pens, and which of the two visitors’ chairs had a loose leg.

She sat in the one with the loose leg.

“You know there’s another chair,” said Director Kwan.

“This one’s got character.”

“It’s got a loose screw.”

“Exactly.”

He shook his head, and looked at Mabel, who was standing by the window with her arms folded and the expression of a woman trying hard not to give anything away and failing at the corners.

Song-Zhu looked from one to the other. “Now I’m actually worried.”

“Don’t be.” The director put a folder on the desk between them, and didn’t open it. “From the first of June, we’re putting you on the investigator-in-charge roster for major occurrences.”

For a second she didn’t move.

“The roster,” she said.

“The roster.”

“Not deputy.”

“Investigator-in-charge. If something big comes in after the first of June and it’s your week, it’s yours. The whole investigation. The site, the recorders, the team, the families, the report.” He looked at her over his glasses. “Mabel recommended you. I agreed with her. So did the board, eventually, after a conversation I won’t repeat.”

She looked at Mabel.

“Don’t look at me like that,” said Mabel. “I’m sixty-one. I want a holiday.”

“Director, I’m twenty-six.”

“I’m aware of that.”

“Just checking.”

He sat back. “Your age isn’t why we’re having this conversation. Your work is. Your evidence handling is the best in the building. You don’t rush. You know that a technical finding has to survive people who’ll do anything to make it say something else. And you can make a room full of people who disagree with you work together, which is rarer than you’d think in this place.”

“That’s a very polite way of saying I’m difficult.”

“It is,” said Mabel.

“You won’t be doing it alone,” said the director. “You’ll have experienced people under you, and Mabel above you, for as long as she can be prevented from going on that holiday. This isn’t a test of whether you can do everything yourself. It’s whether you can direct it, decide, and carry it.” He paused. “Do you want it?”

Song-Zhu looked at the folder. She thought about a field outside the city with a twin turboprop on its back in it. She thought about a room in another country with a laptop on a table and fifty seconds of a voice. She thought about the training hangar and a little girl at a funeral in a yellow dress, holding a plastic aeroplane too big for her hand.

“Yes,” she said.

“Good.”

“Very much.”

He smiled then, properly, for the first time. “Congratulations, Investigator Xu.”

She laughed. It came out of her unexpectedly, bright and a little shaky, and Mabel turned away to the window so nobody would see her face.

“Don’t thank me,” said the director. “You’ll hate me by August.”

“That’s a very encouraging management style.”

“Experience.” He slid the folder across. “Read it. Ask questions. And don’t mistake being the youngest person in a room for being the least qualified one.”

At the door she stopped. “Director?”

“Yes?”

“Can I tell my boyfriend?”

He looked up. “You’re asking my permission to tell your boyfriend?”

“No. I’m asking whether I can leave this office before you give me anything else.”

“Go,” said Director Kwan.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ren Hao was in a meeting on the thirty-second floor, listening to his head of operations propose a new structure for client response, and had found three problems with it in the first four minutes, when the phone lit up beside his notebook.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I have news.

He looked at it. Then at the speaker. Then at the phone.

Ren Hao: Good news, or shall I come?

Three dots. Gone. Three dots again.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Good news.

Something in his face changed, and across the table Joyce, who’d learned long ago not to ask, looked down at her pad.

Ren Hao: Ring me when you’re free.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): No. Guess.

Ren Hao: A new case?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Warmer.

Ren Hao: A promotion?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Warmer.

He put his pen down.

Ren Hao: Song-Zhu.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Investigator-in-charge. From 1 June. The next big one is mine.

He read it twice. He forgot, for several seconds, that there was a meeting.

Ren Hao: At twenty-six?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I was there when they said it.

He laughed. Out loud, in the middle of somebody else’s sentence, a sudden delighted bark of a laugh that made the head of operations stop dead.

Ren Hao looked up. “Sorry. Carry on. It’s very good. It’s got three problems. Carry on.”

Joyce’s pen didn’t move on the pad, which was how he knew she was smiling. The phone buzzed once more.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Don’t make a big deal of it.

He looked at that a long time. He was absolutely going to make a big deal of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

By six that evening he’d arranged flowers, a cake from the bakery she’d mentioned once in passing in February, and a private room at the back of the noodle place behind the cargo terminal. By a quarter past six he’d invited six people. By twenty past, four more. By twenty-five past he’d ordered champagne, and was on the phone to a photographer Joyce had found, when his other line went.

“Why,” said Song-Zhu, “is there a cake?”

He looked at the cake, which had arrived early and was on his desk. It was an excellent cake.

“Because you’ve been promoted.”

“Why has Dexter just asked me what time he should come to my party?”

“Because...”

“And why did the man at the noodle shop ring me to ask how many chairs?”

He paused. “He wasn’t supposed to ring you.”

“Ren Hao.”

“Yes.”

“What have you done?”

He looked at Joyce, who was standing in the doorway with a clipboard and an expression of great neutrality.

“Nothing excessive.”

Joyce’s expression said otherwise.

Song-Zhu was quiet. “How many people?”

He considered lying. “Ten.”

“How many?”

“Eleven. Including the photographer.”

“Hao.”

“It’s a celebration.”

“I know.”

“You’re happy.”

“Yes.”

“Then...”

“I don’t want a party,” she said.

He stopped. There was no anger in it, nothing sharp at all; it was simply clear, the way she said things that weren’t going to change. He looked at the cake, and the flowers, and the list on Joyce’s clipboard, and something in him that had been running at full speed since half past ten came to a stop.

“Oh,” he said.

She sighed down the line. “I know you mean well.”

“I do.”

“I know you do.”

“All right. I’ll cancel it.”

She was quiet. “Thank you.”

He looked at Joyce. Joyce looked back, and lowered the clipboard, and took out her phone.

“What about the flowers?” said Song-Zhu.

He looked at the arrangement on the side table. “Do you want the flowers?”

“What flowers?”

“The flowers I ordered.”

“How many?”

“Enough.”

“Hao.”

“Too many.”

She laughed, low. “Keep one bunch. Give the rest to your floor.”

“All right.”

“And no party.”

“No party.”

“Promise.”

He hesitated, which she heard. “I promise,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t throw a party. He did, however, cook dinner at her flat, which was different, he reasoned, because there was no photographer, and no guests, and no champagne. There was only one bunch of white anemones in a jug on her counter and dinner for two on her stove.

She came in a little before eight, and put her bag down, and stood in the doorway of her own kitchen looking at him: sleeves to the elbow, a tea towel over his shoulder, stirring something.

“Hello,” she said.

“Hello.”

She looked round elaborately. “Where’s the party?”

“Cancelled.”

“The photographer?”

“Cancelled.”

“The eleven people?”

“Disappointed. Dexter, mainly. He’d bought a shirt.”

“Good,” said Song-Zhu, and came across the kitchen and put her arms round his waist from behind, and her cheek between his shoulder blades, and stayed there.

He turned the heat down and put his hand over hers on his stomach.

“Long day?”

“Long morning. Longer afternoon. Mabel cried. She says she didn’t. She did. She went and stood at the window.” Song-Zhu held on tighter. “I have to sign things now, Hao. Things with my name on, that other people do what they say.”

“I know.”

“It’s frightening.”

“I know.” He turned round in her arms. “Congratulations.”

“Thank you.”

He looked at her, and what was in his face was so open and so warm that she had to look at his collar instead.

“You’ve worked for this since before I knew you,” he said. “You care about doing it right more than anyone I’ve ever met. And you hate people making a fuss. I know all of that.”

“Correct.”

“But you’ll let me be glad.”

She smiled at his collar. “You’re allowed to be glad.”

“Investigator Xu.”

She groaned. “Don’t.”

“Shall I call you that now? Formally?”

“Only if you want a spoon thrown at you.”

He laughed, and turned back to the pan.

✦ ✦ ✦

She found the cake when she went to the fridge for water.

It was on the bottom shelf, behind a box of vegetables, as if somebody had tried to hide it and hadn’t tried hard. White, plain, beautiful. On the top, in dark chocolate, neat:

INVESTIGATOR XU

She looked at it. She shut the fridge. She turned round slowly. He was looking carefully at the pan.

“Hao.”

“Yes.”

“You kept the cake.”

“I did.”

“You said you’d cancelled everything.”

“I cancelled the party.”

“That’s not the same thing.”

“No,” he admitted.

She folded her arms. He looked at her.

“I thought you might still want the cake,” he said. “It’s from that place on Tanner’s Row. The one you said in February was the only good thing about the lab moving. The lemon one.”

She tried hard to keep her face straight. That was unfair. He knew it was unfair. He’d remembered one sentence from three months ago about a cake, and the street it was on, and that it was lemon. He’d simply mistaken her wanting to be celebrated for wanting to be surrounded.

“Turn that off,” she said.

He turned off the stove. “What?”

“Turn it off and look at me.”

He did.

“You really don’t understand,” she said, “the difference between making me happy and making an event out of making me happy.”

He looked down. “I know.”

“Do you?”

“I got excited.”

“I could tell. From the cargo terminal.”

“I wanted everybody to know.”

She softened, despite herself. “Why?”

He looked at her. “Because you’re brilliant,” he said. “Because you work harder than anyone I’ve ever met and come home exhausted and still tell me about chains of custody over dinner. Because you notice the thing nobody else notices. Because you keep asking questions when it would be so much easier to stop. Because they’ve finally seen what I’ve been seeing for eleven months, and I wanted to stand on a table and shout about it.”

Her face changed.

“I wanted to celebrate you,” he said.

She looked at him. Then she unfolded her arms and put her hand on his cheek.

“You do,” she said. “All the time.”

He didn’t say anything.

“You celebrate me when you listen to me talk about a mislabelled evidence box for forty minutes.”

“Forty?”

“Fifty. You asked questions.”

He laughed, slightly.

“You celebrate me when you remember I’ve got an early briefing and don’t ring me at midnight to ask if I’ve eaten.”

“I do ring you at midnight to ask if you’ve eaten.”

“Sometimes you don’t.” Her thumb moved on his cheekbone. “And you celebrate me when you let me come home and be tired, without trying to make me feel better straight away. That’s the one I like best.” She looked up at him. “I don’t need a room with eleven people in it to know you’re glad. I know. I’ve known all day. You laughed in the middle of a meeting. Joyce told Dexter, and Dexter told me.”

He breathed out. She went up on tiptoe, which she hardly ever had to, because he was already bending to her, and kissed him.

It was soft. Then it wasn’t. She kissed him slowly, against her own fridge, with her hand on his face and his hands coming round to the small of her back, and he made a low sound into her mouth and pulled her in close, and the kiss went deep and unhurried and warm, the kind that had nowhere to be. She bit his lower lip, gently, and he breathed in sharply through his nose. When she drew back, she stayed close enough that their noses touched.

“You’re forgiven,” she whispered.

“Already?”

“Don’t make me reconsider it.”

He laughed against her mouth, and kissed her again, and the pan sat cooling on the stove, forgotten, for some time.

✦ ✦ ✦

They ate at the counter. The cake came afterwards. He cut it with enormous care so that the lettering stayed whole on the first slice, and put it in front of her.

“You’re very serious about cake.”

“I’m serious about everything.”

“I know. It’s a condition.”

She ate a mouthful. Then another, and closed her eyes. He watched her.

“Good?”

She nodded, and held out her fork. “Try.”

He leaned across the counter and she fed him a bite, and he chewed, and considered.

“Good.”

“See?”

“You were right.”

Her eyebrows went up. “Say that again.”

“No,” said Ren Hao.

She laughed. He reached across and took her hand on the counter, and lifted his water glass with the other.

“To Investigator Xu.”

She lifted hers. “To no photographers.”

They touched glasses. In the jug on the counter, the white anemones leaned towards the light.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Wednesday the twenty-seventh, she was on her sofa reading the roster handbook with her feet in his lap when his phone went, and he looked at the screen and lit up like a lamp.

“Auntie Au.”

Song-Zhu lowered the handbook.

He listened. His eyebrows went higher and higher. “No. No. When? This Saturday? And she didn’t tell me? Of course she didn’t. Thank you, Auntie. Yes. I love you. Yes. I’ll buy some.”

He rang off and immediately rang someone else, and Song-Zhu, who was beginning to suspect, put the handbook face-up on her stomach and watched him.

“ELIANA!” he said, at a volume that made her neighbour’s dog start barking. “I HEARD! YU CHEN IS GOING TO EMERGENCY MEDICINE!”

A small voice on the other end said something.

“I’M COMING. I’LL BRING FOOD.”

The small voice said something else.

“Everything.”

A pause.

“It’s a promise,” said Ren Hao, and hung up, and looked enormously pleased with himself.

Song-Zhu looked at him.

“Did she invite you?”

“She will have.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

“She said what food. That’s practically an invitation.”

“Hao. Did you just invite yourself to a party at somebody else’s house?”

“I expressed enthusiasm.”

“Is that what it’s called?”

“Yes.” He looked at her. “You’ll come. You’ve wanted to meet her for six weeks.”

She had. She’d heard about Eliana Lin every evening since April. She’d heard about the triple fee and the passwords under the keyboard and two in the morning in his boardroom, and she’d read the final report herself, over his shoulder, and thought it was the most honest piece of work she’d seen from outside her own building in years.

“All right,” she said. “But you’re not making a speech.”

“Of course not.”

“And you’re not picking anybody up.”

He looked wounded. “Why would I pick anybody up?”

“Because I know you,” said Song-Zhu, and went back to the handbook.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday the thirtieth of May he stopped at Auntie Au’s on the way, because he couldn’t walk past it, and came out with three bags. Song-Zhu carried the cake. He went through the side gate into the garden behind Eliana’s house first, at full speed, three bags swinging, and she followed with the cake held level and a strong premonition.

It was a small garden with a persimmon tree in it and a wall at the back, and someone had strung warm bulbs through the branches and along the top of the wall so that the whole thing glowed in the dusk. There were cards propped on the table that said CONGRATULATIONS, DR. WANG. There was a great deal of Auntie Au’s food already, and more people than Song-Zhu had expected, and an expensive coffee machine on a trestle table that a tall, cheerful woman was defending from a tall, unsmiling man. And there, by the table, a quiet man in a dark shirt with his sleeves rolled up was talking to two friends and looking slightly overwhelmed.

“WHERE IS THE DOCTOR?” said Ren Hao. “EMERGENCY MEDICINE! YOU’LL SAVE LIVES!”

He put the bags down on the nearest chair, crossed the grass in three strides, and hugged Dr. Wang Yu Chen so hard that he lifted him clean off his heels.

Song-Zhu, at the gate with the cake, shut her eyes.

“That’s the plan,” said Yu Chen, winded, when he’d been put down.

Ren Hao had already turned. “ELIANA! YOU DID THIS? YOU’RE A WONDERFUL WOMAN!” And hugged her too, while she stood rigid in his arms with a plate in one hand and over his shoulder caught the doctor’s eye, and smiled at him.

Song-Zhu came across the grass and put the cake down on the table, next to a printed card. She read it.

18:00 Arrival. 18:30 Food. 19:00 Toast. 19:15 Unstructured celebration. 20:00 Cake.
No speeches longer than three minutes.

“Who’s the three minutes for?” she asked the young woman standing beside it, who had a business student’s tidy handwriting and an air of having seen everything twice.

“Ren Hao,” said Yen Si-Wei.

“Fair,” said Song-Zhu.

Si-Wei looked at her properly for the first time, and her face changed. “You’re Song-Zhu.”

“I’m Song-Zhu.”

“You’re real. He talks about you at FENCE. We assumed you were at least partly invented.”

“He does that,” said Song-Zhu, and Si-Wei laughed, briefly.

Eliana came over a minute later, extracted at last from Ren Hao, and looked at Song-Zhu with the same careful attention she seemed to give everything.

“Xu Song-Zhu. The crash investigator.”

“Eliana Lin. The security firm above the dumplings.”

“I read about you. Your authority published a paper on recovering a damaged recorder last year. The one from the river.”

Song-Zhu blinked. “Nobody reads those.”

“I read everything that tells you how to get data out of something that’s been in water,” said Eliana. Then she hesitated, and added, in a different voice: “I heard. About June. Congratulations.”

“Thank you.” Song-Zhu looked across the garden to where Ren Hao was now explaining something to the tall cheerful woman with both arms. “You heard.”

“He told Auntie Au. Auntie Au told Si-Wei. Si-Wei told me.” Eliana considered. “He also said not to make a fuss about it, because you don’t like fuss.”

Song-Zhu turned and looked at her.

“So I’m not,” said Eliana, and handed her a plate.

✦ ✦ ✦

At seven Si-Wei tapped a glass and held out a microphone, and Eliana stood looking at it.

“You said no speeches.”

“Three minutes.”

Eliana took it. She made a toast of exactly four sentences, about a man who’d spent a long time looking after other people and had forgotten he was allowed to want things for himself, and the garden went quiet for one beat at the end of it.

Then Ren Hao clapped like a firework going off, and everybody followed.

Song-Zhu, beside him, clapped too, and was watching the doctor’s face, which hadn’t moved. She saw him look at Eliana. She saw him walk over, and take the microphone out of her hand, and put it down. And she saw him go down on one knee in the grass, in front of everybody, and take Eliana’s hand and kiss the back of it, and then kiss it again.

“Oh,” she said, under her breath.

Ren Hao had gone completely still beside her. She glanced up. He looked as if he’d been struck by something.

“Get up,” Eliana was saying, scarlet. “Everyone’s watching.”

“I know. Thank you,” said Yu Chen, and stood up, and didn’t let go of her hand, and kissed her: slow and long, in front of her sisters and three triplets and the whole garden, with his hand at her waist and her fingers knotted in his.

Ren Hao made a noise that was probably heard at the ferry pier.

“THAT’S LOVE!”

Song-Zhu put her face in her hands.

✦ ✦ ✦

She found him later, after the cake, in Eliana’s kitchen, helping Auntie Au put dumplings onto a tray with great seriousness.

“Did you,” she said, leaning on the counter, “just pick up a grown man?”

“Yes.”

“Off the ground.”

“Only a little way.”

“I told you not to pick anybody up.”

“You told me on Wednesday. It’s Saturday. Things change.” He put the last dumpling in place and handed the tray to Auntie Au, who patted his cheek and took it out into the garden. “He got the job he wanted. He’s worked for years. And she was happy.”

“She was.”

He looked at her. “You’re laughing at me.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because you greeted him like he’d just come home from a war.”

He considered that. “That’s not inaccurate. Emergency medicine.”

She shook her head, and then reached out and took his hand on the counter, and they stood there for a moment in somebody else’s kitchen, with the noise of a party going on outside about somebody else’s good news.

“I’m glad we came,” she said.

“You wanted to.”

“I did. Thank you for bringing me.”

“You’d have come anyway. You’d have come on your own to see Eliana.”

“I would.” She looked at him. “She didn’t mention my promotion to anyone. She asked me not to tell her the details. She said you’d told her I don’t like fuss.”

He looked at her, a little anxious. “Was that all right?”

“It was perfect,” said Song-Zhu. “You worked it out. By Saturday.”

He breathed out. She went up and kissed him, quickly, warmly, against the counter, with the sound of the garden through the window. When she drew away he kept his hand at her waist.

“You’ll have to stop doing that,” he said.

“Doing what?”

“Making me want to throw another party.”

“Don’t you dare.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They left after ten. Her feet hurt. She’d eaten twice what she’d meant to. He carried her bag and his empty bags, folded, and she walked beside him under the streetlights with their shoulders touching.

“He’s nice,” she said. “The doctor.”

“He is.”

“She looked happy.”

“She did.”

She glanced at him sideways. “You like her.”

“I respect her.”

“That’s not what I said.”

He thought about it. “She’s very good at what she does. And she doesn’t flatter me.”

Song-Zhu laughed. “You like that?”

“I find it restful.”

“Because everyone else is afraid of you.”

He looked down at her. “Not everybody.”

“No,” she said. “Not everybody.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In the car she went quiet. The city went past, the lights stretching out in long smears on the glass. He reached across and took her hand, and she laced her fingers through his.

“I’m a bit frightened,” she said eventually.

He glanced at her. “Of June?”

She nodded. “It’s different. Being responsible for your own work and being responsible for everyone’s. I know how to investigate. I know how to read evidence. I know how to argue with someone who’s jumped to a conclusion. But now I’m the one who decides. If I’m wrong, it’s my name.”

He squeezed her hand. “You’re allowed to be frightened.”

She smiled faintly. “That’s your advice?”

“Yes.”

“Very helpful.”

He laughed. Then, at a red light, he looked at her properly.

“You don’t have to prove you deserve it every morning,” he said.

“You think I’ll try.”

“I know you’ll try.” He turned back to the road. “Don’t carry the whole thing because your name’s on it. Build a good team. Listen to them. Let them do their jobs. Ask the stupid question first, so they’re not afraid to. And when you decide something, decide it because the evidence says so. Not because you think you have to be right.”

She looked out of the window a long time. “That’s what I’m afraid of. Having to be right.”

“Then remember why they chose you.”

“Why?”

“Because you don’t rush to be right,” said Ren Hao. “You listen. You check. You ask again when something doesn’t make sense. That’s why they trust you with it.”

She looked down at their joined hands, and held on.

“Thank you,” she said.

At the next red light he lifted her hand and kissed her knuckles.

✦ ✦ ✦

At her flat she kicked her shoes off by the door and went straight to the kitchen for water, and he followed her and leaned in the doorway.

“What?” she said, over the glass.

“Nothing.”

“You’re staring.”

“I’m allowed.”

She put the glass down. “You’re very pleased with yourself.”

“I have a reason.”

“Which is?”

He came into the kitchen. “My girlfriend is an investigator-in-charge.”

She laughed. “Your girlfriend was a very good investigator before you started telling dumpling shops.”

“Still,” said Ren Hao.

She held her hand out. He took it, and she pulled him in, and put her arms round his waist and her cheek against his chest, and he held her, in the same kitchen where she’d forgiven him for the cake.

“You’ll be good at it,” he said into her hair.

“I hope so.”

“You will.”

She lifted her head and looked at him. “Don’t promise things you can’t control.”

He considered that, and nodded. “You’re right. I’ll say it differently.” He put her hair behind her ear. “I believe you can.”

That was different. She could take that. She reached up and kissed him. He kissed her back, one hand at her cheek and the other at her waist, slow, and when she drew away she stayed close.

“That’s better,” she whispered.

“What is?”

“Believing in me. Instead of deciding how it’ll turn out.”

“Noted,” he said.

She touched his jaw. And in her small kitchen, with the dishes in the sink and the anemones on the counter and the city going on beyond the window, Ren Hao held her and let her be exactly what she’d worked so hard to become. Not his responsibility, not a project. Not someone he needed to arrange the world round.

Just Xu Song-Zhu. Twenty-six. A little frightened. Entirely capable of it.

Two months later, at four in the morning, it would be her week.

chapters.title: Too Much
chapters.desc: She tells him he’s too much. He agrees, and goes quiet for a day: their anniversary. She calls him back with one word.
chapters.epigraph: “I just need to be able to breathe inside it.”
chapters.content:
Ren Hao sent her seventeen messages on Thursday. The first came at twelve minutes past seven.

Ren Hao: Morning. Did you sleep?

The second, four minutes later.

Ren Hao: Rain forecast from three. Umbrella.

At twenty-six minutes past:

Ren Hao: I’ve moved your car’s service to Saturday. You said you might need it on Friday.

A little before eight:

Ren Hao: Breakfast?

Song-Zhu read them in her bathroom with a toothbrush in her mouth, and answered with one thumb.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Eating.

Ren Hao: Eating what?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Food.

Ren Hao: Very informative.

She smiled round the toothbrush. Just after eight he sent a photograph of a small paper bag on the counter of the authority’s front desk.

Ren Hao: Left something at your reception. Don’t skip lunch.

Inside, she knew without looking, would be one of the egg tarts from the bakery by his building, because she’d said once in March that they were the only egg tarts in the city that weren’t lying about the custard. She sent a heart. He sent three back.

A little after eight he rang. She answered in the corridor, walking to the lift.

“Hello, boyfriend.”

“Hello.”

“You’re ringing me.”

“I am.”

“Why?”

“To hear your voice.”

“You heard it last night.”

“That was last night.”

She laughed. He asked about her morning, whether the revised evidence schedule had come through, whether she wanted picking up after work, whether the new handheld radios for the roster team had arrived or whether he should ring someone. She answered what she could. The lift doors opened.

“Hao, I’ve got to go.”

“Have a good day.”

“You too.”

“I love you.”

“Keep saying it,” she said, and went into the lift, and the doors closed on her smiling.

It was sweet. It was always sweet. That was the problem.

By Thursday night she’d answered seventeen messages, two calls, a voice note about the rain, and a photograph of her own lunch that she’d sent him as a joke and that he’d replied to, entirely seriously, with a question about whether there’d been any protein in it.

She loved the attention. She did. She loved that he remembered things she’d said once, months ago, in passing. She loved that he worried. She loved that he was loud about everything, including her. But for two weeks, since the first of June, since her name had gone on a roster that meant that when the phone rang at four in the morning it would be for her, she’d felt herself being wrapped, gently, in something soft, a layer at a time. And she couldn’t find the edge of it to unwrap.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday she was in the roster office just before nine at night, going through an exercise plan line by line, when her phone went.

“Hi.”

“Have you eaten?”

She shut her eyes. “Hao.”

“What?”

“I’ve eaten.”

“What did you have?”

“Rice.”

“And?”

She looked at the plan. “Vegetables.”

“And?”

“Do you want a photograph?”

He laughed. “Only if you’re hiding something.”

She smiled despite herself. “I’m working.”

“I know. I only wanted to check.”

“All right.”

A pause. “Are you going to be late?”

“Probably.”

“How late?”

“I don’t know yet.”

“I’ll come and get you.”

“No, it’s fine.”

“I don’t mind.”

“I know you don’t mind. I do.”

A silence on the line.

“Hao?”

“I’m here.”

“I’ve got a lot to finish. I’ll get a taxi.”

“I can book one.”

“I can book one too.”

Another pause. “All right.”

She softened. “Thank you.”

“Text me when you leave.”

She didn’t answer straight away.

“Song-Zhu?”

“Yes.”

“Please.”

She sighed. “All right.”

She went back to the exercise plan. Twenty minutes later her phone lit on the desk.

Ren Hao: Booked you a car anyway. Driver’s name below. He’ll wait as long as you need.

She looked at it a long time. Then she put the phone in her desk drawer and closed it, and finished the plan, and at twenty to twelve walked out past the waiting car to the taxi rank and got into a taxi.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was in her flat when she got home. He had her key now; she’d given it to him in March, on a ring with a small plastic aeroplane on it, and had been delighted by how carefully he’d used it ever since. He was on her sofa with his laptop open on her coffee table and his sleeves rolled up, and there was a plate on her counter under a second plate.

“You’re awake,” she said, taking her shoes off.

He looked up. “Of course.”

“You’ve got work in the morning.”

“So have you.”

“How long have you been waiting?”

“Not long.”

She looked at the clock on the oven. He smiled.

“Don’t look at me like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like you’re about to give me a performance review.”

She laughed, faintly. He came over and kissed her, and she leaned into him, and for a moment it was all right.

Then he touched her cheek. “You’re tired.”

“Yes.”

“You didn’t take the car.”

“No.”

“He waited for an hour, Song-Zhu.”

“I didn’t ask him to.”

“I know. I’m only saying...” He stopped himself. “Eat something. There’s chicken.”

“I’m not hungry.”

“You’ve hardly eaten all day.”

She stepped back out of his hands. “Hao.”

“What?”

“I said I’m not hungry.”

“I know. But you ought to have something.”

She looked at him. He looked back.

It was such a small moment. An ordinary one. But something in her had been collecting moments for two weeks, one at a time, like evidence: the umbrella, the car service, the egg tart, the calls, the reminders, the car outside the building with a man in it waiting, the plate on her counter under a plate. And all at once there were too many of them to hold.

“I need you to stop,” she said.

He frowned. “Stop what?”

“All of it.”

His face changed. “What do you mean, all of it?”

“The messages. The checking. The arranging. Ringing to ask if I’ve eaten. The cars. The umbrellas. The service on my car, which I didn’t ask you to move. The man outside my building, waiting, so that I have to walk past him and feel guilty.”

“I thought you liked those things.”

“I do.”

“Then...”

“Not all the time.”

He went quiet.

She pressed her fingers to her forehead. “I’m not angry that you care about me.”

“Then what are you angry about?”

“I’m tired,” she said. “Since the first of June I’m on the roster every third week. I sit in rooms all day where people wait for me to decide things. I’ve got a team who look at me to see if I know what I’m doing. I’ve got exercise plans and radios and a man from the operator who keeps calling me young lady in meetings. And when I come home I feel like there’s somebody else waiting to make sure I’ve done everything properly. That I’ve eaten. That I’ve slept. That I took the car.”

His jaw tightened. “That isn’t what I’m doing.”

“I know it’s not what you mean.”

“Then why are you saying it like that?”

“Because that’s what it feels like.”

He looked away, at the window.

She came a step closer. “I need you to know I can look after myself.”

“I know you can.”

“Do you?”

“I do. Most days I do.”

“Because sometimes it doesn’t feel like it.”

“I’ve never once said you couldn’t.”

“You don’t have to say it, Hao. You book the car.”

The silence stretched. And then she said it. She heard it come out of her mouth before she’d decided to say it, the way the worst things do.

“You’re too much sometimes.”

The words landed in the room between them and stayed there.

Ren Hao didn’t move. For one second he looked as if he hadn’t understood. Then his face changed. Not anger. Something much quieter than anger, and much worse.

“Too much,” he said.

She regretted it immediately. “Hao...”

“No. I heard you.” He nodded once, slowly. “You’re right. I am.”

“That’s not what...”

“It’s fine.”

“It isn’t.”

He closed the laptop and picked it up. “I’ll give you some room.”

“That’s not what I’m asking.”

He looked at her. “Then what are you asking?”

She opened her mouth. Nothing came out. Because she didn’t know how to say it. That she wanted him close without feeling watched. That she wanted all of his affection without the management. That she wanted him to love her loudly, the way he did everything, only not so loudly that she couldn’t hear herself think inside it.

“I just want to breathe,” she said.

He nodded. “Understood.”

He put his laptop into his bag. He put on his jacket. He came across the room to her, and she thought for one second he was going to argue, or hold her, or ask her again, and he did none of those things. He kissed her cheek, lightly, the way you’d kiss somebody at a station.

“Eat something if you get hungry,” he said, and then shut his eyes, because he’d heard himself. “Sorry. Goodnight, Song-Zhu.”

“Hao.”

He stopped at the door. “Yes?”

She looked at him. He waited. She couldn’t find a single word.

“Nothing,” she said.

He nodded, and went, and closed the door so quietly behind him that she didn’t hear the latch.

✦ ✦ ✦

She lay in bed and looked at the ceiling.

No footsteps in the next room. No voice asking whether she wanted water. No arm coming across the mattress in the dark.

A little after one she picked up her phone. Nothing. She opened their messages. The last thing he’d sent was the car.

Ren Hao: Booked you a car anyway. Driver’s name below. He’ll wait as long as you need.

She looked at it until the screen went dark by itself.

She’d wanted room. He’d given it to her. So why did it feel?

✦ ✦ ✦

Saturday was the thirteenth of June. She woke at seven, out of habit, and reached for the phone, out of habit. Nothing. No Morning. No weather. No question about breakfast.

She made coffee. She drank it standing up. She checked the phone.

At ten she went for a run along the harbour, and came back, and checked it. At twelve she did her laundry and checked it between the wash and the dryer. At two she found she’d opened their conversation so many times she’d stopped counting. By four she was composing messages in her head and throwing them away. Are you busy? Too casual. How’s your day? Too much like pretending.

I’m sorry. Not enough. She put the phone in the drawer of her bedside table, and then took it out again.

She’d never noticed how much of her day he filled until he stopped filling it. There was no photograph of something he’d seen and thought she’d like. No observation about a stranger’s dog. No voice note about a supplier who’d sent the wrong thing to the wrong floor. No call for no reason except that he wanted to hear her. She missed the noise. She missed him.

And it was only at six o’clock, sitting on her sofa with the light going gold on the wall, that she worked out what the date was, and put her hand over her mouth.

A year. A year ago tonight, she had walked into a French restaurant with fuel on her boots, and a man in a three-piece suit had told her to wash her face.

He would know. Of course he’d know. He’d have known for weeks. He’d have booked something. He’d have planned it down to the minute, with an agenda, typed. And then, last night, she’d stood in her own kitchen and told him he was too much, and he’d gone home and unbooked all of it, one line at a time, so that she’d never have to feel guilty about it.

She sat still with that.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ren Hao was in his office at eight o’clock on a Saturday night, because it was the only place he could think of to go.

He’d come in at nine that morning. He’d read two reports, and answered every email, and cleared the week’s approvals, and done everything he was supposed to do. He hadn’t messaged her.

His phone was on the desk beside the keyboard. He’d looked at it once, at eleven, and then turned his chair so that it was behind him.

He’d heard her. You’re too much sometimes. He’d heard the tiredness in it, and he’d heard that it was true, and he’d heard the part of it that went in under the ribs. He knew what he was. When he was worried, he organised. When he loved somebody, he got there first, before they’d asked, before they’d known they needed anything. When he couldn’t fix the thing that mattered, he fixed every small thing round it instead, so his hands had something to do. He’d always thought it was a kind of devotion. Sometimes it was. But he’d made himself so present in every hour of her day that he’d forgotten she needed space to move in it.

He understood that. He did. What he didn’t know was how to be less without becoming someone she didn’t want.

At four that afternoon he had rung the restaurant, the French one with the candles, and cancelled the table for two at eight. Then he had rung the florist and cancelled the flowers. Then he had taken a folded piece of paper out of his inside pocket, an agenda, typed, one year to the day, Item 1: Apologise for the soup, and put it in his desk drawer, and closed it.

Just after eight his phone rang. He turned the chair round. Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots).

He looked at it for two rings. He answered.

“Hello.”

She didn’t say hello. She didn’t say sorry. She didn’t say anything for a moment at all, and he could hear her breathing, and he could hear that she was standing in her kitchen, because her kitchen had a fridge that hummed in E flat.

“Come,” said Song-Zhu.

And rang off.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was at her door in twenty-three minutes. He didn’t use the key. He knocked. She opened it.

He was still in his work trousers and a pale shirt with the collar open and no tie, and he looked tired in a way she’d never seen him look tired before, all the brightness turned down. She was in an old T-shirt and soft trousers with her hair wet from a shower she’d had for no reason except to have something to do. They looked at each other across the doorway.

“Hi,” she said.

“Hi.”

“You knocked.”

“You asked me to give you room.”

Her eyes filled, all at once. “Oh, Hao.”

“Did you need something?” he said, carefully.

She swallowed. “Yes.”

“You,” said Song-Zhu.

His face changed.

“I’m sorry,” she said, before she could lose her nerve, standing there in her own doorway. “I shouldn’t have said it like that. What I meant is that I need room sometimes. I need to be able to say no to a car, or dinner, or a phone call, without feeling I’ve let you down. That’s what I meant. That’s all I meant.” She took a breath that shook. “I don’t want you to stop being you. I don’t want you to go quiet because I said you were too much. I didn’t know what quiet would sound like. Now I do and I hate it. I miss you.”

He looked at her. “You saw me last night.”

“I know.”

“That was twenty hours ago.”

“I know.”

A faint, exhausted smile. “Then you’ve had plenty of me.”

“Not like that,” she said. “Not the station kiss. Not goodnight, Song-Zhu.”

He didn’t come in yet. He stood in her doorway with his hands at his sides.

“I don’t want you to feel crowded,” he said.

“I know.”

“I don’t want you to feel managed.”

“I know.”

“I was trying to give you what you asked for.”

“I know.”

He breathed out. “But when you said I was too much...”

He stopped. She waited, the way she’d learned to wait.

“It made me feel,” he said slowly, “as though the way I love you is something you have to put up with.”

Her face crumpled. “Oh, Hao.”

He shook his head. “I know that isn’t what you meant.”

“No.”

“But it’s what I heard.”

She came out of the doorway onto the landing and put both hands flat on his chest.

“I love the way you love me,” she said. “All of it. The egg tarts. The weather. The ridiculous agendas. I just need to be able to breathe inside it.”

He shut his eyes. Then he nodded.

“And you need to tell me when something hurts,” she said. “You don’t have to disappear for a whole day to do it. You don’t have to cancel our anniversary on your own in your office so that I’ll never know.”

His eyes opened.

“I worked it out at six,” she said. “I’m an investigator. You’d booked the restaurant. The French one.”

He didn’t deny it. “I wasn’t trying to punish you,” he said.

“I know.”

“I thought you wanted me to stop.”

“I wanted you to stop doing some things. Not to stop wanting me.”

He looked at her, and something in his face came loose at last.

“That’s an important distinction,” he said.

“Yes.”

“You should put it in a report.”

“I’m putting it in a report,” said Song-Zhu, and pulled him in by his shirt.

✦ ✦ ✦

She kissed him on her landing. It wasn’t graceful. She was too relieved and he was too tired and their noses bumped, and she laughed against his mouth.

“What’s funny?”

“You’re in the way.”

“That’s unfortunate.”

She kissed him again, and this time he put his hands up to her face and held it, carefully, and the kiss slowed down. She felt the hesitation in him. The care. A question he wasn’t asking out loud. She drew back an inch.

“You’re allowed to touch me.”

“I know.”

“Then stop looking as if you’re waiting for written permission.”

He laughed, low, and the sound went through her. “I’ll work on it.”

“Work on it now.”

He did.

He walked her backwards through her own door and kicked it shut behind them with his heel, and put her against the wall of her little hallway beside the coat hooks, and kissed her. Deep, and slow, and then not slow at all. His hands went into her wet hair. Hers went into his shirt. He made a low rough sound into her mouth that she’d been missing since half past eleven the night before without knowing she’d been listening for it. She pulled him closer by his belt. He pressed her into the wall with the whole length of his body and held her there, his thigh between hers, his mouth on her jaw and then her throat and then back on her mouth.

“I missed you,” he said against her lips.

“I was right here.”

“I know. That was the worst part.”

She held his face in both hands and kissed him again, softly now, a long slow kiss with her eyes open, so that he could see it in her face. Everything she couldn’t say yet. Everything she’d nearly said in a kitchen in May. All of it.

He saw it. She watched him see it. He didn’t ask her to say anything.

He put his forehead down on her shoulder and stood there, breathing, holding her against the wall, and she put her arms round his neck and held him back.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, he sat on one of her kitchen stools and she stood between his knees with her hands on his shoulders.

“Can I ask something?” he said.

“Yes.”

“What would you like me to do differently?”

She thought about it properly. “Ask before you arrange things.”

“All right.”

“Don’t ring three times if I don’t answer once.”

“Fair.”

“And if I say I’m working, believe me.”

“I do believe you.”

She raised an eyebrow. He corrected himself.

“I’ll behave as though I believe you.”

She laughed. “Better.”

“Anything else?”

“Sometimes,” she said, “I want you to send me something stupid without expecting me to answer it.”

He blinked. “Something stupid.”

“A dog. A cloud that’s the wrong shape. Something you saw and thought was funny. Not a question. Not a reminder. Just you, telling me something.”

He smiled slowly. “I can do that.”

“And sometimes I want you to ask if I want help. Instead of helping.”

“All right.”

She ran her thumb along his jaw. “And tell me when you’re hurt. Don’t decide for both of us that silence is easier.”

“All right.”

She leaned down and kissed him. “Your turn.”

“My turn?”

“What do you need?”

He looked at her a long time. “I need to know you don’t resent me for caring,” he said.

“I don’t.”

“I need to know that when you want room, it doesn’t mean you want less of me.”

She took his face in her hands. “It doesn’t. It never does.”

“And I need you to tell me when I’m getting it wrong,” he said, “before it gets to the point where everything I do is unbearable.”

She nodded. “I can do that. I should have done it two weeks ago.”

He turned his head and kissed her palm. “Have you eaten?” he said.

She looked at him.

He held both hands up. “That was a joke.”

“I haven’t,” she admitted. “I’ve been waiting all day for somebody to ask me.”

He laughed, really laughed, the first time she’d heard it in twenty hours, and it filled her kitchen up to the corners.

✦ ✦ ✦

In bed, she lay with her back against his chest, his arm loose round her waist. She traced the bones of his hand.

“Hao?”

“Mm.”

“Are we all right?”

He kissed her shoulder. “We’re learning.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“It’s the honest one.” He was quiet a moment. “I don’t think loving each other means we’ll get everything right. We’ll annoy each other. We’ll say things badly. Sometimes we’ll need different things on the same night. But I don’t want to be afraid of telling you when something hurts. And I don’t want you to feel guilty for asking me for room.”

She turned in his arms and looked at him in the dark.

“Then don’t be,” she said. “And don’t make me.”

He smiled. She kissed him, slow and quiet, and turned back and tucked herself into him.

After a while his voice came from behind her ear.

“Song-Zhu?”

“Mm.”

“Can I send you a picture tomorrow?”

She smiled into the pillow. “Of what?”

“I haven’t found it yet.”

“Then yes.”

A pause. “And can I ask if you’ve eaten?”

She turned her head. “Hao.”

“Sorry.”

She reached back and found his hand. “Once.”

“Once?”

“Once a day.”

He considered it. “That’s very restrictive.”

“Goodnight.”

“Happy anniversary,” he said into her hair.

She was quiet for so long he thought she’d gone to sleep.

“Next year,” she said, “I’m booking the restaurant.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Just after seven the next morning her phone buzzed on the bedside table. He’d got up at six for a call and gone home to change. She opened one eye.

A photograph. A small, entirely round dog sitting upright in a supermarket basket, with an expression of grave responsibility.

Ren Hao: He looks like he runs a company.

She stared at it. Then she put her face into the pillow and laughed until her ribs hurt.

Ren Hao: No reply needed.

She typed anyway.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): He’s obviously the managing partner.

Ren Hao: I’d hire him.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): He’s better qualified than you.

Ren Hao: Unnecessary.

She smiled at the screen a long time. Then she sent him the round dog back, with one word under it, and put the phone down on the bedside table, face up, where she could see it.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Again.

chapters.title: The Last Quiet Week
chapters.desc: The day after the seven-all hacking contest on his floor, a beach house with no phones. A week before the crash. Explicit, every day: the shower, the deck, the sand, the sea.
chapters.epigraph: “There’s nobody for a kilometre.”
chapters.content:
He came home on the Saturday night at a quarter to ten, still talking.

“Seven-all,” said Ren Hao, in her doorway, with his tie in his pocket and his jacket over his arm and the expression of a man who’d just watched the best sporting event of his life. “Seven-all. After eleven hours. And then they both said rematch at exactly the same time, Song-Zhu, the same syllable, and Professor Szeto put her head on the table, and I laughed so much I had to hold on to a chair.”

“You told me.” She was on her sofa in shorts and a vest with her feet up on the bag she’d packed for the morning. “You texted me at six. In capitals.”

“And the doctor brought them both tea. Both. Eliana nearly bit him.”

“You texted me that too.”

“And at four o’clock she went and sat on the fire stairs, and he went after her, and she came back in and found two more.”

She looked at him over the back of the sofa, and couldn’t help smiling. “You love her.”

“I love everybody today.” He came round the sofa and dropped onto it beside her and pulled her feet into his lap. “I had two of the best security minds in the city at my boardroom table for eleven hours, legally. It’s the most fun I’ve had in years.”

“Better than me?”

He looked at her. Then down at her feet in his lap. Then at the bag under them.

“Ask me on Saturday,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

*Sunday* He had one rule for the week. No phones.

She had three. No work. No talking about work. No waking her up before nine. He agreed to all four.

The beach house was two hours out of the city along the coast road, at the end of a sandy lane, behind a line of pines bent all one way by the wind. It wasn’t grand. One big bedroom with a window onto the sea, a smaller one nobody needed, an open kitchen, a wide wooden deck with a sagging outdoor sofa on it, and a path through the dune grass down to a little curve of beach that belonged, for seven days, to nobody but them.

He’d chosen it because in November, in the dark, she’d said she wanted once in her life to wake up somewhere without traffic.

She stood in the doorway and looked out at the water. “Oh.”

He put the bags down. “Good oh?”

“Very good oh.”

He came up behind her and put his arms round her waist. “How much planning went into this?” she said, leaning back on him.

He considered lying. “Some.”

“Hao.”

“I drove out three weeks ago. I checked the road, the water pressure, the kitchen, the lock on the deck door and where the nearest hospital was.”

“Of course you did.”

“And whether the bed creaked.”

She turned round in his arms. “Does it?”

“No,” said Ren Hao. “I tested it.”

“On your own?”

“I sat on it. Thoroughly.”

She laughed and put a finger on his mouth. “Holiday.”

“Right.” He kissed the fingertip.

They put their phones in the drawer of the little table by the door, his and then hers, and she shut it with her hip.

“There.”

He looked at the drawer. “I might experience withdrawal,” he admitted.

“At least you’re honest.”

“Seven days.”

“Seven days,” she said. “Just us.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They walked the length of the beach until the light went soft. She carried her sandals. He rolled his trousers to the knee, and she warned him the sea would reach his knees anyway, and it did, and he stepped back from a wave with such outrage that she had to sit down on the sand.

“Managing partner afraid of the sea.”

“Of cold water.”

“It’s the same thing.”

She got up and ran. He went after her. She turned and walked backwards in front of him with her hair blowing across her mouth, laughing.

“Catch me.”

He caught her round the waist and lifted her clean off the sand, and she shrieked and kicked.

“Put me down!”

“You asked me to catch you.”

“Not abduct me!”

He put her down. She immediately put her arms round his neck. “Again,” she said.

They ate on the deck: fish he grilled, rice, a bottle of cold white wine. She sat with one leg folded under her and watched the water go dark, and he watched her, and when she caught him at it, he only shrugged, because there was nobody on the whole coast to see him do it. Afterwards he hummed something tuneless and held out his hand, and she said that was worse than no music, and took it anyway, and they danced barefoot on the warm boards with no rhythm at all until the first stars came out.

When they went in, the bedroom window was open and the room was full of the sound of the sea.

He undressed her slowly, by the window, in the dark, with the moon coming in pale on the floor. He took his time over it. Her T-shirt over her head. Her shorts down her legs, his hands following them. He stood behind her and kissed the side of her neck and held her back against him, his hands flat on her bare stomach, and she could feel him through his trousers, hard against the small of her back.

“Nobody can hear us,” he said against her ear. “Do you understand? For a whole week. There’s nobody for a kilometre.”

She shivered. “So?”

“So I want to hear you.”

He laid her down on the bed that didn’t creak and looked down at her for a long moment in the moonlight, as though he were memorising where everything was. Then he took her wrists in one hand and put them above her head on the pillow and held them there, gently, and kissed his way down her. Her throat. Her breasts, one and then the other, slow, until she arched up off the mattress into his mouth. Her ribs. The soft skin below her navel. When he reached between her legs she was already wet, and he made a low sound of satisfaction and let go of her wrists and pushed her thighs apart with both hands and put his mouth on her.

She didn’t hold back. She didn’t have to. She came the first time with her fingers knotted in his hair and his name going out of the window into the dark, louder than she had ever let herself be anywhere, and he didn’t stop, and the second time she was sobbing with it.

Then he came up over her and pushed into her in one long slow stroke and held there, looking down at her, his weight on his forearms either side of her head.

“Again,” he said. “Louder.”

He took her slowly, and then not slowly, and the bed didn’t creak once, and she was louder.

Afterwards they lay tangled in the sheet with the sea going in and out below the window.

“You tested it,” she said, into his chest.

“Thoroughly.”

“Five stars.”

“Only five?”

“I’ll review it again on Saturday,” said Song-Zhu, and fell asleep halfway through his laugh.

✦ ✦ ✦

*Monday* She woke to the smell of coffee and found him in the kitchen in yesterday’s T-shirt, reading the instructions that had come with the coffee machine.

“Having trouble?”

“Good morning. No.”

“You’re reading the manual.”

“It came with the machine.”

“That’s generally what manuals do.”

He gave her a look and poured her a cup, and watched her drink it, with the face of a man waiting for exam results.

“Hao. This is good.”

His whole face lit. “Really?”

“Really.”

“I followed the instructions.”

“I know you did,” she said, and kissed him, because he was so pleased with himself that it was unbearable.

They did nothing all morning. She read on the deck. He read beside her, and lasted twenty-three minutes before he asked what her book was about. She told him. He asked three questions. At the third she lowered the book.

“Are you reading yours?”

“Yes.”

“Then read it.”

Ten minutes later his hand closed round her bare ankle. She didn’t look up.

“What’s that?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re holding my foot.”

“It was there.”

She lasted another page. Then she put the book down open on the boards and climbed into his lap in the deckchair and kissed him until both books had slid off onto the deck and neither of them went to pick them up.

In the afternoon they swam. The water was cold enough to make her gasp. She stood waist-deep with her arms wrapped round herself, insisting she was adjusting, until he splashed her, and then it was war, and then he caught her round the waist in the deep water and she wrapped her legs round him and he held her up against him, both of them laughing, salt on their mouths.

That night the shower lasted a great deal longer than it needed to.

It was small, tiled in blue, with a window high up that showed the dark. He stood behind her under the hot water and washed the salt out of her hair, carefully, with his fingers working slow circles against her scalp, and she shut her eyes and leaned back on him.

“You’re treating me like glass,” she said.

“You’re precious.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

She turned round. Water ran down between them. She put her hands on his chest and ran them down, slowly, over his stomach and lower, and took him in her hand, and watched his face change.

“My turn,” she said.

She pushed him back against the tiles and went down onto her knees on the wet floor in front of him, with the water coming down on both of them, and looked up at him once through her wet lashes before she took him into her mouth.

He said her name, hoarse, and his hand went flat against the tiles. She took her time. She’d learned him by now, what made his breath catch and what made him swear, and she did all of it, slowly, until his other hand was in her wet hair, not pushing, only holding on, and his whole body was shaking with the effort of staying still.

“Song-Zhu,” he said. “Song-Zhu. Stop. Not like this. I want...”

She stood up. He turned her round before she’d finished standing and put her against the wall where he’d been, with her palms on the warm tiles and his body along the whole length of her back, and his mouth at her ear.

“Do you know what I’m going to do now?” he said, low, under the noise of the water.

She shook her head. She did know. She wanted to hear it.

He told her. In detail. Quietly. Every single thing, in order, while his hand slid down her stomach and between her legs and did the first of them, and she pressed her forehead to the tiles and moaned. And then he did every one of the rest, exactly as he’d said he would, holding her up when her knees went, until she came with her cheek against the wet wall and his arm locked round her waist, and he followed her with his teeth in her shoulder and the water going cold on both of them.

Wrapped in towels on the bed afterwards, she looked at him.

“That was a very good shower.”

“Five stars?”

“Four and a half.”

“Why the half?”

“The hot water ran out.”

“I’ll write to the owners,” said Ren Hao.

✦ ✦ ✦

*Tuesday* At ten past eight he broke her third rule.

She woke slowly, out of a dream about nothing, to the feeling of his mouth on the inside of her knee, and then a little higher, and then higher, and the sheet had been pushed down to the end of the bed and the morning sun was warm across her stomach.

“Hao,” she said, without opening her eyes. “It isn’t nine.”

“I know.”

“That’s a rule.”

“I’m not waking you up,” he said, against the inside of her thigh. “You can stay asleep. You won’t have to do anything at all.”

She opened one eye and looked down the bed at him. He looked back up at her with an expression of perfect innocence.

“You,” she said, “are a lawyer’s nightmare.”

“I’m a risk consultant. I find the loopholes.”

She shut the eye again. “Fine. Carry on. I’m asleep.”

He carried on.

He did it slowly. He held her hips down on the mattress with both hands so she couldn’t move, and kept her there, at the edge of it, long past the point where she’d stopped pretending to be asleep, until she was saying his name over and over to the ceiling and pulling his hair and begging, in a voice she didn’t recognise, and only then did he let her go over, and it went on and on, the sun on her and his mouth on her and the sea outside.

Afterwards he came up the bed and lay beside her and looked extremely pleased with himself.

“Ten past eight,” she said, when she could speak.

“Yes.”

“I’m going to sue.”

“You’ll lose,” said Ren Hao, and she rolled over on top of him and showed him what she thought of his loopholes.

They argued about breakfast at eleven. He wanted eggs. She wanted pancakes. He said they could have both.

“That’s how we end up with too much food.”

“We’re on holiday.”

“That isn’t a nutritional exemption,” she said, and he stared at her and then laughed, and made pancakes.

In the afternoon they walked into the village: one street, a harbour wall, a shop that sold everything. She bought a ridiculous straw hat. He told her it suited her. She asked if he was lying. He said no, and she wore it the rest of the day. They bought peaches and cold drinks and a small blue bowl from a potter by the harbour, and he carried everything except the bowl, because she wouldn’t let him.

“Do you think I can’t carry a bowl?”

“No.”

“Then let me carry the bowl.”

“Yes, ma’am.”

“Good boy,” she said, and took his free hand.

In the evening he cleaned as he cooked, and wiped the counter three times, and she watched him do it from a stool.

“You’re doing it again.”

“The counter’s wet.”

“It’s a kitchen.”

He looked at the cloth in his hand. Then, deliberately, he put it down and left it.

“Look at you,” she said. “Growing.”

On the deck after dinner, with her feet in his lap, she told him about a lecturer she’d had who would rather spend twenty minutes explaining why a question had been badly worded than admit he’d got something wrong.

“Sounds familiar,” said Ren Hao.

“Are you talking about yourself?”

“No.”

“Desmond?”

His hand stopped on her ankle. Only for a second. She saw it.

“Sorry,” she said.

“It’s fine.”

“Have you heard anything?”

“Nothing new. The review’s still going. Kong has it.” He looked at the water. “Not tonight.”

“All right.”

He looked at her. “I like that you ask.”

“Then I’ll keep asking,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

*Wednesday* She woke up alone, and for four seconds didn’t know where she was. Then there was a crash from the kitchen.

“Hao?”

“I’m fine.”

He was standing in the middle of the kitchen floor, barefoot, beside a plate in several pieces.

“What happened?”

“An accident.”

“Obviously.”

“I was making toast.”

She looked at the toaster, and at the plate, and at him.

“How,” she said, “does anybody break a plate making toast?”

“Poor coordination.”

She put her hand over her mouth. He looked at her with great dignity.

“Don’t laugh.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

“I am,” she agreed, and kissed him, and took the broom off its hook. “Sit down. Drink your coffee.”

“You’re managing me.”

“Somebody has to,” said Song-Zhu.

They spent the whole day on the beach. She collected shells. He collected her sandals, her towel, her hat, and the bottle of water she kept leaving behind on the sand.

“You’re carrying everything,” she said.

“You keep leaving it.”

“I think you like being useful.”

He considered it. “Probably.”

“You’re allowed to sit down.”

He put it all down in a heap and sat, and she sat between his knees and leaned back on him, and they watched the waves come in for an hour without saying anything.

At sunset she led him down to the edge of the water. She stood where it reached her ankles, in his old shirt with the sleeves rolled up, the light going red behind her.

“Take a picture.”

“No phones.”

She laughed. “Right.”

“I’ll remember it,” he said, and did.

That night was warm, the warmest of the week, with no wind at all. They didn’t go to bed. They lay on the sagging outdoor sofa on the deck under the stars, with the small lamps along the rail turned off and the sea a sound in the dark, and she was still wearing his shirt and nothing else.

“That’s mine,” he said.

She looked down. “Is it?”

“Yes.”

“Take it back, then.”

He undid the first button. And the second. He was slow about it, the way he was slow about things he wanted to remember. When he’d undone all of them he didn’t take it off her. He opened it and pushed it off her shoulders and left it lying under her on the cushions, and looked at her in the starlight.

“Hao. We’re outside.”

“There’s nobody for a kilometre.”

“There’s the sea.”

“The sea won’t tell,” he said, and kissed her.

She pulled him down. He went. He kept his weight on one arm beside her head and kissed her neck, and her breasts, slow, and she pushed his shorts down with her feet, impatient, and he laughed into her skin. When he came into her it was easy and slow and deep, and the sofa groaned under them, and she laughed out loud at the sound and put her hand over her own mouth.

“Don’t,” he said, and took her hand away and held it down on the cushion. “Don’t you dare. Not out here.”

So she didn’t. She let every sound come out of her into the warm dark, and he moved in her unhurried and relentless, looking down at her face in the starlight, telling her in a low voice how she looked, how she felt round him, what he was going to do to her before the night was over, and then doing it. At some point she turned him over on the narrow cushions so she was on top of him with the stars behind her head and the shirt hanging off one arm, and rode him slowly, her hands flat on his chest, and watched his face, and when he came it was with his hands tight on her hips and her name going out over the water.

They lay there afterwards under the blanket he’d brought out because he always brought a blanket, and watched the stars.

“That one,” she said, pointing.

“Which one?”

“That one.”

“That’s several.”

“You’re terrible at this.”

“I’m a risk consultant,” said Ren Hao. “I can’t see the stars. I can only see what could fall on us.”

She laughed into his neck. They fell asleep out there and woke at three, cold, and went in.

✦ ✦ ✦

*Thursday* It rained all morning. The beach vanished behind a grey sheet. The pines thrashed. She stood at the window in his jumper.

“Well. So much for our beach holiday.”

He came up behind her and put his arms round her. “It’s still there.”

“We can’t swim.”

“We could.”

“In that?”

He looked at it. “Perhaps not.”

“So what do we do?”

He kissed the side of her neck. “Anything.”

She turned round. “That’s a dangerous answer.”

“Is it?”

She took his hand and walked him back to the bedroom.

They spent the whole morning there, with the rain on the windows and no phones and nowhere to be. It was lazy and slow and full of laughing. She pushed him down on his back and sat astride him and took him into her by inches, teasing, lifting away again whenever he moved his hips, until he was gripping the sheets with both fists and swearing at the ceiling.

“Song-Zhu.”

“Mm?”

“Please.”

“You’re very quiet this morning,” she said, considering him from above. “That’s suspicious.”

“I’m not quiet. I’m begging.”

“Oh,” she said. “Is that what that is.”

She sank all the way down at last, and he groaned. And then she rode him the way the rain came down outside, steady and unhurried and endless, her hands braced on his chest, rocking, until his head was thrown back on the pillow and his hands were on her thighs and he’d stopped making words at all. When he was close she stopped dead and held still and looked down at him until he opened his eyes.

“Not yet,” she said. “Look at me.”

He looked at her. She started again, slower. She took him to the edge three times like that, and back, and on the third time she went over with him, both of them shaking, her hair falling down over both their faces.

Afterwards she lay across his chest and listened to his heart slow down.

“You’re quiet now,” she said.

“I’m enjoying myself.”

“That’s suspicious.”

“Why?”

“You’re usually talking.”

He ran his fingers through her hair. “Would you like me to talk?”

“Not especially.”

She settled. A while later she said, “I like you like this.”

“Like what?”

“Not in a hurry.”

“I’m not in a hurry.”

“Promise?”

“Promise,” he said, and she believed him, and didn’t know yet what that promise would cost.

He cooked lunch while she sat on the counter and ate the ingredients. He turned round to find her with half a tomato.

“That was for the salad.”

She ate it. “Was.”

He laughed and stepped in between her knees and she kissed him with tomato on her mouth. In the afternoon they played cards. He was competitive. She was worse. She accused him of cheating. He accused her of having no respect for the rules. She said the rules were badly designed. He said she was losing. She threw a cushion at him.
