He caught it, and put it over her face, and she laughed until she slid off the sofa onto the floor.

He let her win the last game. She knew. He knew she knew. Neither of them said so.

In the evening the rain stopped, and the air smelled clean, and they sat on the wet deck steps with a towel under them.

“Do you ever think about after?” she said.

“After what?”

“After this week.”

“Work.”

She laughed. “Yes. Work.”

“We go home. You go back on the roster on Monday. I go back to the office. And then we do this again.”

“That’s it?”

“What else?”

She shrugged. “Nothing.”

He turned her face to his. “Do you want something else?”

She looked at him a long time. There was something in her face he couldn’t read, and then something he could, and she didn’t say it, and he didn’t ask her to.

“No,” she said, and kissed him instead.

✦ ✦ ✦

*Friday* The sun came back. She woke early and found him already on the deck with a cup of coffee, watching the sea.

“Why are you up?”

“Couldn’t sleep.”

“Why?”

He shrugged. She sat beside him in his shirt and leaned on his shoulder.

“Tell me something,” she said. “Something you’ve never told me.”

He thought about it. Then he smiled.

“When I was fourteen I wanted to be a chef.”

She lifted her head. “What?”

“Not a famous one. I wanted a restaurant. Small. Twelve tables. Good food. A short menu, and it changed every week. No bookings after eight, so the staff could go home.”

“That’s very specific.”

“I had plans. I drew a floor plan on graph paper. My father found it and pinned it to the fridge.”

“What happened?”

“University. And then the firm.”

“Do you still want it?”

He looked at the water. “Sometimes.”

She put her chin on his shoulder. “Then one day.”

“Maybe.”

“What would you call it?”

He turned his head and looked at her. “Song-Zhu’s,” he said.

She stared at him. “Why?”

“Because you’d decide the menu.”

“I’d put dumplings in everything.”

“I know.”

“And you’d complain about the cost of the prawns.”

“I would not.”

“You absolutely would.”

He kissed her. She kissed him back, and didn’t say anything a while, because there were things in her throat she still couldn’t get out.

They swam in the afternoon, and lay on the sand, and he brushed sand off her shoulder, and she said it was a beach, and he did it anyway. In the evening they ate outside with the lamps lit. And then, at about eleven, with the moon three-quarters full and the tide going out, she took his hand and led him down the path through the dune grass to the beach.

“Where are we going?”

“You’ll see.”

At the bottom she let go of his hand and walked out onto the wet sand where the moon lay on it like a sheet of foil, and turned round to face him, and pulled her dress over her head and dropped it.

He stood quite still at the foot of the path.

“Song-Zhu.”

“There’s nobody for a kilometre,” she said. “You told me so on Sunday.”

“I meant the house.”

“The beach is closer to nobody than the house is.”

He came down onto the sand. She undressed him there, at the edge of the water, in the moonlight, slowly, button by button, the way she’d learned he liked it, and when he was naked she stood back and looked at him, silver all over, and he let her look. Then she pulled him down.

The sand was cool and damp and gave under them. She lay back on her spread dress and pulled him over her, and the sea came in further than either of them expected and washed over their feet, and she gasped and laughed and held on to him. He kissed her. He kissed the salt on her throat. He pushed into her slowly, and the next wave came in round his knees and her hips, cold, and she cried out and arched up into him and he held her there, inside her, the sea pulling out again under them, sand shifting under her back.

“Cold,” she gasped.

“I know.”

“Don’t stop.”

“I’m not going to stop.”

He didn’t. He moved in her slowly with the rhythm of the water, in and out, as if the sea were setting the pace and he was only following it, looking down at her in the moonlight, her hair spread out dark on the wet sand, and every time a wave came in over them she clutched at him and he pushed deeper, and every time it went out he drew back and she pulled him down again. There was sand in everything. Her hair, his knees, her mouth when she kissed him. She didn’t care. She’d never cared about anything less.

“Look at me,” he said.

She looked up at him with the moon behind his head.

“I’m going to remember this,” he said. “Every second. When I’m old I’m going to remember exactly this.”

“So am I,” said Song-Zhu.

He slid his hand under her and lifted her hips off the sand and held her against him and moved faster, and she came with the sea washing over both of them and her nails in his back and his name going up into the empty sky, and he followed her with his face in her neck, shaking, and held her there in the shallow water until the tide had pulled back off them altogether.

They lay on the sand afterwards, wrapped in her damp dress and his shirt, and looked up at the moon.

“There’s sand,” he said, “in places sand should never be.”

“It’s a beach.”

“I’m aware it’s a beach.”

“You’ll be finding it for a week.”

“Good,” said Ren Hao, and she turned over and kissed him with sand on her lips.

✦ ✦ ✦

*Saturday* Their last morning came too fast. She woke at six, before him, and lay and watched him sleep. Then she got up and went down to the sea on her own, in the grey light, and walked into it to her waist and stood there with her arms round herself, cold, watching the light come up over the water.

He found her ten minutes later. He walked into the sea in his shorts without a word and came up behind her and put his arms round her, and she leaned back against his chest, and a long time they stood in the water and watched the sky turn from grey to white to gold.

“I don’t want to go back,” she said.

“Neither do I.”

“Can we stay?”

He thought about it. “We could. Another night.”

She turned round in his arms. “Really?”

“Really.”

She looked at him a long time, salt water to her waist, and then shook her head.

“No,” she said. “If we stay another night I’ll never leave.”

“That’s a reasonable concern.”

“So it has to be now.”

She kissed him in the sea, slow, her arms round his neck, her body cold and then warm against his, and he lifted her and she wrapped her legs round him in the water, and they made love standing in the waves at dawn, slowly, almost without moving, her forehead against his, the sea holding them up, and neither of them said a single word the whole time. When she came she only breathed his name, once, into the cold air between their mouths.

He carried her out of the sea. She sat on the kitchen counter afterwards eating a peach while he packed.

“You fold clothes as if they’re going for inspection.”

“They’re going in a suitcase.”

“Exactly.”

“Would you rather I threw them in?”

“Yes.”

“Absolutely not,” said Ren Hao.

Before they left he checked the house twice. She stood in the doorway and watched him.

“The kitchen?”

“Yes.”

“The bathroom?”

“Yes.”

“The drawer by the door?”

He stopped. He went back. He opened it, and there they were, both phones, dark, exactly where they’d left them on Sunday.

He took them out and gave her hers without turning it on.

“Not yet,” she said.

“Not yet,” he agreed, and put his in his pocket.

He picked up both bags. She held her hand out. He looked at her, and then gave her one.

“Progress,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

She fell asleep in the car halfway back, with her head against the window and the straw hat in her lap and the blue bowl wrapped in a towel at her feet. At a red light on the edge of the city he looked across at her. Her mouth was a little open. She had sand on her neck.

He didn’t know that it was the last quiet week they’d have a long time.

He didn’t know that the days ahead were about to divide themselves into before and after. That in eight days the sea would stop being a place to swim in, for her, and become a place she’d stand beside for hours in a flight suit, looking at the water, listening to it, trying to make it give back what it had taken. That she’d learn to recognise the particular silence of a room full of families waiting. That he’d learn how little money, or influence, or planning, or love could do against certain kinds of loss.

For now he knew only that she was asleep beside him, and the week had been good, and he loved her. The light went green. He drove on.

✦ ✦ ✦

At her flat that evening she turned her phone on in the kitchen. It lit up and kept lighting: emails, messages, missed calls, the roster for Monday. The whole world had gone on without them. She scrolled through it once, and put it face up on the counter, and left it.

“Anything?” he said from the doorway.

“The roster. I’m on from Monday. Seven days.”

“Do you need to look at it now?”

“Tomorrow.” She held her hand out to him. “Can we have one more quiet evening first?”

He came and held her. “Of course.”

They stood in her kitchen and talked about nothing: the round dog in the village, the plate, the pancakes, the card game, a restaurant with twelve tables and no bookings after eight. At sixteen minutes past ten she said her legs were too tired for the hall, and he picked her up and carried her down it, and she protested and laughed all the way.

He put her down on the bed. She held on to his collar.

“Hao.”

“Yes?”

She looked up at him. He waited. She almost said it. He saw her almost say it.

“Keep saying it,” she said instead.

“I love you.”

“Again.”

“I love you.”

She pulled him down. Outside, the city went on. Somewhere phones rang and people worked through the night, and at an airport a long way from here an aircraft that would come home on the second of August was being serviced by a contractor in a hangar, under bright lights, by people who were tired and wanted to go home.

But in her bedroom, Ren Hao and Xu Song-Zhu were still living in the week they’d been given. They didn’t know it was the last quiet one. Perhaps that was the mercy of it.

chapters.title: The Crash
chapters.desc: A passenger jet goes into the sea on approach with 180 people. Her phone at 4 a.m. It’s his client’s airline. He builds the wall again before six, drives her, and stays out of the way.
chapters.epigraph: “Just don’t leave him alone with the waiting.”
chapters.content:
The phone rang at three minutes past four. Song-Zhu was awake before the second ring. For one moment she didn’t know where she was. Her bedroom, dark. The air conditioning humming. Ren Hao asleep beside her with one arm heavy across her waist, the sheet tangled round his legs.

Then it rang again, and she knew exactly where she was, and what week it was, and whose name was on the roster.

She reached across him for it. Duty Officer. Then, underneath, before she’d answered, a second call waiting: Director Kwan.

Director Kwan didn’t ring at four in the morning.

“Xu.”

“Song-Zhu. It’s Kwan.” His voice was perfectly level, which was how she knew. “We have an accident. A passenger jet, inbound, on approach to the main runway. It went into the sea about twenty minutes ago, two kilometres short.”

Her hand closed on the phone.

“How many?”

“A hundred and eighty on board. A hundred and seventy-four passengers, six crew. We have no confirmed survivors. We have nothing confirmed at all.”

For a second the room lost every sound in it.

“Whose is it?”

He told her the airline. She shut her eyes.

“I know,” said Director Kwan, before she could say it. “Mabel’s already on her way in. We’ll deal with the declaration this morning, properly, in writing, the same way we did in October. Until then you do what the roster says you do. It’s your week. It’s yours.”

“Understood.”

“Operations centre. Your team’s being called. We’ll brief when you arrive.”

“Yes, Director.”

“Song-Zhu.”

“Yes?”

“Drive carefully. Or better, don’t drive.”

The line went. She sat with the phone in her lap for exactly two seconds. Then she got out of bed.

✦ ✦ ✦

He woke when she switched on the lamp. “Song-Zhu?”

She was already at the wardrobe, pulling out trousers, a shirt, the flight suit in its bag from the hook on the door.

He sat up. “What’s happened?”

“An aircraft’s gone into the sea. On approach. A hundred and eighty people.”

He was wide awake in a second. She watched it go through him: the number, and then, because he was who he was, the next question.

“Whose?”

She said the airline’s name. He didn’t move. She saw him hear it. She saw him understand, all at once, everything it meant: the holding group, the man who’d rung him three times in October, the wall in his firm, the declaration in hers. She saw his face close over all of it, deliberately, like a man putting a sheet over furniture.

“I’m leading it,” she said.

“I know.”

“Kwan says the declaration’s this morning. In writing.”

“Then mine will be in writing by six.” He was already out of bed. “I’ll drive you.”

“You don’t have to.”

“I know.”

She looked at him a moment, buttoning her shirt with fingers that weren’t quite steady. Then she nodded.

“Thank you.”

He didn’t ask whether she was frightened. He didn’t tell her it would be all right. He went to find his clothes.

✦ ✦ ✦

A little after four they were on the road.

The city was almost empty. Wet streets, green lights for nobody, a delivery van, a single bus lit up inside like an aquarium with no one in it. He drove with both hands on the wheel. She sat beside him with the phone at her ear and her notebook open on her knee, writing.

“Confirm the roster. I want the first response group at the operations centre in an hour. No, don’t send anyone to the shore yet. One command point. We go through search and rescue, not round them.” A pause. “Air traffic. Everything. The tower tapes, approach, ground, radar, the weather observations for the last two hours, the flight plan, the movement records. Originals secured, copies only for working. Write down who touched what and when.” A pause. “Good. I’m twenty minutes away.”

She rang off. It rang again at once. She answered it. He drove.

At the long straight by the container port his own phone lit in its cradle on the dashboard. He looked at the name. It was the man who owned the holding group.

He didn’t answer it. He let it ring out on the dashboard and kept driving. She saw. She didn’t say anything, and neither did he, and that was its own kind of conversation.

At the next red light she finished a call and lowered the phone and said, looking straight ahead, “You’ll have to ring him.”

“I’ll ring Raymond and compliance first. Then him. In that order.” His voice was calm. “The wall from October. Same terms. Raymond takes the account and everything to do with this. I don’t see a file, a briefing, a draft statement. I don’t go near it.”

“And if he won’t accept that?”

“Then he can find another firm.”

She looked at him then, sideways, in the red light.

“Hao. He’s your biggest client.”

“I know what he is,” said Ren Hao. The light went green.

✦ ✦ ✦

A little after four he pulled up outside the operations centre.

It was a low building on the airport perimeter road that nobody looked at twice on an ordinary day. Every window in it was lit. Cars were arriving fast and parking badly. Beyond the barrier at the edge of the car park a television van was already raising its mast.

She undid her seat belt. He handed her the bag from the back seat before she reached for it.

“I’ll stay near,” he said.

“Don’t wait if you’ve got work.”

“I’ll wait.”

He corrected himself. “I’ll be near, and available. You tell me what you need. If you don’t need anything, I’ll still be near.”

She almost smiled. “All right.”

He reached across and put his hand over hers on the bag strap. “Song-Zhu.”

“Yes.”

“You’re the right person for this.”

She swallowed. “Thank you.”

He wanted to kiss her. He could feel the television mast going up beyond the barrier, and the cameras on it, and the man who’d been ringing him, and the declaration that wasn’t written yet, and he didn’t. He squeezed her hand once, hard, and let her go.

She got out and walked into the light without looking back, and he watched her go all the way in.

✦ ✦ ✦

At five past five he rang Raymond, who answered on the first ring because he’d seen the news, and said “I know,” before Ren Hao had said anything.

“Same wall as October,” said Ren Hao. “You lead. I’m out of it, completely, from now, and it’s in writing by six. Copy compliance. Copy legal.”

“He’ll want you.”

“He can want me.”

“Hao, it’s a hundred and eighty people.”

“I know how many it is,” said Ren Hao, low. “That’s why it can’t be me.”

A little after five he rang the owner back, and told him the same thing in fewer words, and listened to what the owner said about loyalty and five years and what was owed, and said, “Raymond will be with you in an hour. He’s the best I have. Look after your families,” and rang off.

Then he sat in his car outside the operations centre, at twenty past five in the morning, in the grey beginning of the light, and wrote down the time of each call and what had been said in it, the way she would have done, because nobody had asked him to.

✦ ✦ ✦

*Operations centre, 5:12 a.m.* The first briefing was standing up. There weren’t enough chairs and nobody wanted one.

One screen showed the last of the flight path in white: the long curve in from the south-west over the sea, the turn onto final, the line coming down towards the runway threshold and simply stopping, two kilometres short, over water. A second screen showed the search area, already widening. A third showed the manifest, still marked UNVERIFIED in red across the top.

She stood at the head of the table. Round it were investigators, engineers, an operations officer, a liaison from search and rescue, a woman from the airport authority with her coat still buttoned, two men from the operator’s safety department who had clearly been woken by the same phone call and dressed in the dark. Some of them were older than her by thirty years. Some had more investigations behind them than she’d had birthdays. She saw them look at her, and look at Mabel standing by the wall behind her, and look back at her.

Mabel didn’t move from the wall. Song-Zhu took a breath.

“What we know. Then what we don’t.”

The operations officer began. “Contact lost on final approach at three forty-two. Last radar return over water, two point one kilometres from the threshold, at...”

“Height?”

“Four hundred and twenty feet, decreasing.”

“Was there a distress call?”

“Tower reports a transmission, possibly an emergency call, about thirty seconds before contact was lost. We haven’t heard the recording yet.”

“Then it’s unverified. Nobody calls it a distress call until we’ve heard it. Write it as a transmission.”

He nodded.

“Search and rescue have floating debris,” said the liaison. “Some of it consistent with the type.”

“Main wreckage?”

“Not located.”

“Survivors?”

The liaison looked at the table. “None found.”

The room was absolutely quiet.

“Then we don’t say anything we don’t know,” said Song-Zhu. “No numbers to the press. No repeating what we’ve heard in a corridor. Nobody turns a guess into a fact because somebody asks them the same question three times. If you don’t know, you say you don’t know.” She looked round at them, one at a time. “Our first job is to support the search and preserve the evidence. We’re not here to find a cause this morning. We’re here to make sure that in a year’s time we still can.”

She turned to the screens.

“Preserve the flight path. All of it. Air traffic recordings, radar, weather, the flight documents, the load sheet, the technical log, the maintenance records for the last two years. We’ll ask the operator for what’s theirs,” and she looked at the two men from the safety department, who straightened, “and we’ll keep our own custody and our own record of everything we’re given. Recorders: we don’t know where they are or what state they’re in. Get the specialist search assets requested now. Nobody makes promises about timings. Nobody.”

To the operations officer: “Families. One channel. Coordinate with the airport and the operator. I want somebody at the terminal now, and I don’t want one single family to find out from a television that their mother was on that aircraft.”

She looked round the table.

“Questions.”

There were a great many. She answered them one at a time, and when she didn’t know, she said so, and wrote the question down.

When they broke up, Mabel came off the wall and stood beside her for exactly as long as it took to say, low, “Good,” and then went to find a telephone.

✦ ✦ ✦

*6:03 a.m.* The first pictures came through just after six, from a helicopter.

The sea was grey. The sky over it had begun to go white at the edge, but the water was still dark and heaving with the swell that had come in overnight. Boats were working in a loose line across it with their lights still on. On the surface, things.

A long curved sheet of something pale that had been part of a fuselage. Seat cushions, blue, a great many, scattered across a hundred metres like confetti after a wedding. A yellow life jacket, uninflated, its tapes trailing. A child’s rucksack. A suitcase, open, its clothes floating out of it in a slow fan. A section of something with a row of oval windows in it, floating upright for a moment and then rolling over.

The camera went down closer. Nobody in the room said anything.

“Can we identify the section?” said Song-Zhu.

“Not yet.”

“Mark the coordinates. Time. Source of the footage. Keep the original file.”

“Done.”

A boat moved slowly past the window section. Somebody on its deck pointed at the water. The camera turned.

There was a person in the water. A man, by his shirt, floating with his face in the sea and his arms out, a few metres from the wreckage, moving with the swell the way the cushions moved. Very still. The room didn’t breathe.

The helicopter held on him for a long second, and then the picture swung away.

Song-Zhu looked at the screen a moment longer. Then she turned to the coordinator.

“Has recovery been confirmed?”

“Not yet. The boat’s going alongside.”

“Document the position. Every person brought out of the water gets a position, a time, a condition and a chain of custody, and the recovery record stays separate from the debris inventory. Separate. Always.”

“Understood.”

She looked back at the screen.

The next picture was the boat. Two people in orange leaning over the side. Between them, being lifted, something heavy in a dark shirt, streaming water, arms hanging. They laid it on the deck. One of them knelt and put two fingers to the neck and stayed there, and then sat back on his heels, and the other put a grey blanket over all of it, head to feet.

Song-Zhu looked away. For one second. She looked at the wall above the screen, at a clock that said seven minutes past six. Then she looked back.

“Continue,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

*7:18 a.m.* The airport had opened a family assistance area in a conference suite above the arrivals hall. By the time she got there it was full.

People sat in rows of chairs that had been put out for a trade presentation. Some held phones. Some held passports, and printed booking confirmations, and photographs. Some were still in what they’d been wearing when the phone rang: pyjama trousers under a coat, slippers, a man in a dinner jacket with the tie undone. A small boy, five or six, was asleep across two chairs with his head in a woman’s lap. She was holding his shoes in one hand and her phone in the other, and every few seconds she looked at the phone.

By the door an old man was asking the same question of anybody who came near him.

“Has anyone heard from the flight?”

A young woman in an airport lanyard was answering him gently. “We’re waiting for confirmed information, sir.”

“But they said on the television it had been found.”

“Some wreckage has been located.”

“Then where are the people?”

The young woman didn’t answer straight away. Song-Zhu stopped walking.

A man was pacing the back of the room with his phone at his ear. “Ring her again. Ring her again.” He lowered it and looked at it and dialled, and lifted it, and it rang out, and he dialled again.

She knew the shape of this. She’d read it a hundred times, in transcripts, in the appendices to other people’s reports, in interviews with families after other accidents. She’d sat in a room like it once herself, in another country, aged nineteen, with a notebook.

Knowing the shape of it was nothing at all like standing in it.

A family liaison officer from the authority came over, a man she knew slightly from training days, grey in the face already.

“Investigator Xu.”

“How are the families being told?”

“Through the operator and the airport. Next of kin are being contacted from the manifest as it’s verified. Nobody’s been given an identification. Nobody’s been told anything we don’t know.”

“Keep it that way. Is there a single point for each family? I don’t want anyone telling their story four times to four people in four lanyards.”

“We’re setting it up.”

“Set it up faster.”

Across the room a man was holding up a photograph to every person who came close. A young woman, laughing, in a graduation gown. The photograph had been folded and unfolded so many times it had gone soft at the crease.

“Have you seen her?”

He turned and saw Song-Zhu’s lanyard, and came straight towards her.

“Are you from the investigators?”

“Yes.”

“Can you tell me whether she survived?”

She met his eyes. She’d known, since she’d taken this job, that one day somebody would ask her that question and she’d have to answer it honestly, and she’d thought about what she’d say. Not one of the things she’d thought of was any use at all.

“We’re still working to find out what’s happened and who’s been brought out of the water,” she said. “I won’t tell you anything that isn’t confirmed. I’m sorry. I won’t guess.”

He stared at her. “She’s twenty-three,” he said.

“I understand.”

He looked down at the photograph. “She rang me yesterday,” he said. “She said the plane was early and she’d be home for breakfast.”

There was no sentence in any language that could make that smaller. So she didn’t look for one.

“I’m sorry,” she said again, and asked the liaison officer to stay with him, and he did.

✦ ✦ ✦

*8:36 a.m.* He was still in the car park when her message came.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Have you gone home?

Ren Hao: No. Outside.

A minute.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Can you bring coffee?

Ren Hao: What kind?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Any.

Ren Hao: I’ll bring something to eat as well.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Hao.

He looked at the screen.

Ren Hao: Coffee only. Understood.

She met him at the staff door at the side of the building. He held out the cup. She took it in both hands.

“Thank you.”

He looked at her face. She hadn’t slept and wouldn’t, and there was a line between her eyebrows that hadn’t been there at four o’clock, and her hair was scraped back so tight that a few strands had come loose at her temples and stuck there.

“Have you...” he began, and stopped.

“Sorry,” he said.

“It’s all right.”

“Anything else?”

She shook her head.

“I’m here,” he said.

She nodded. He didn’t ask what she’d seen. He didn’t ask how many. He didn’t ask if she was all right. He understood that she couldn’t hand him the morning in a sentence by a fire door, and that if he made her try, it would cost her something she needed for the afternoon.

She drank half the coffee standing up. Then she said, looking at the lid:

“There’s a little boy in the family room.”

He waited.

“Five or six. His auntie brought him. He’s waiting for his mother.” Her voice was low. “He keeps asking when she’s coming. I don’t know what to say to him.”

He didn’t hurry to answer. “You don’t have to find a sentence that makes it better,” he said. “Just don’t leave him alone with the waiting.”

She looked up at him. Then she nodded, and finished the coffee, and gave him the empty cup, and went back in.

He stood holding it a long time after the door had shut.

✦ ✦ ✦

*10:14 a.m.* The main wreckage hadn’t been found. The search box had been doubled and then doubled again. The recorders were somewhere under forty metres of grey water.

In the technical room the specialist put up a diagram of the aircraft with two small orange boxes in its tail.

“They’re in the rear fuselage. But we can’t assume the rear fuselage is in one place any more.”

“No,” said Song-Zhu.

“The beacons should be transmitting. The navy’s survey vessel is two hours out. Visibility on the bottom is poor and the current’s running.”

“When they come up,” she said, “they’re photographed where they’re found, before anybody touches them. They come out of the water in a container of seawater from the same place. Nobody cleans them. Nobody dries them. Nobody plugs them into anything until we’ve done the condition assessment, and I’m in the room.”

“Agreed.”

“Log every sweep. What equipment. What time. What area. I want to be able to say in a year exactly where we looked and when.”

She looked at the two orange boxes on the diagram. She’d spent her whole working life with them. She knew everything they could say: height, speed, heading, the angle of every control surface, the warnings, the voices. The last thirty minutes of the people at the front. She knew what they couldn’t do, too. They couldn’t make the sea give anything back.

✦ ✦ ✦

*12:52 p.m.* The update came through on the operations channel. Recoveries were continuing. The number recovered was being verified. Each position was being documented, each transfer to the authorities recorded.

She read it twice. Then she put the tablet down and walked to the window.

Outside, it was a bright, ordinary, beautiful Sunday. Somebody was flying a kite on the grass beyond the perimeter fence, and it was red, and it climbed and dipped and climbed. Out past the end of the runway, past the kite, past the edge of the land, the boats were still working.

She pressed her fingertips flat on the windowsill until they went white. Then she went back to the table.

“Update the recovery map. Recovered persons separate from wreckage. I want every record cross-checked against two sources before anything leaves this room.”

“Yes, boss.”

“And the liaison team gets confirmed information before the next public briefing. Not after. Not at the same time. Before.”

“Understood.”

She sat down. The work went on.

✦ ✦ ✦

*3:26 p.m.* He rang her once. She answered on the fourth ring.

“Hello.”

“How are you?”

She looked at the table in front of her. A report. Three maps. A list of forty-one outstanding requests, eleven of them crossed off.

“I don’t know.”

He was quiet a moment. “Have you had a break?”

“A small one.”

“Do you need anything?”

“No.”

“All right.” He didn’t ask anything else. She heard him not asking, and understood what it cost him, and it went through her like heat.

“Hao?”

“Yes.”

“Can you stay? Near. I don’t know when I’ll finish.”

“I’ll be here.”

“Thank you.”

“Don’t thank me.” A pause. “Song-Zhu. Don’t try to carry all of it.”

She looked through the glass at her team: Dexter at the photographs, two engineers bent over the maintenance records that the operator’s men had brought in a box at eleven, the liaison officer on the phone with his hand over his eyes.

“I can’t promise that.”

“Then let them carry some of it with you.”

She was quiet. “All right.”

He hesitated. She heard him decide whether to say something.

“I’ve done it,” he said. “The wall. In writing, at six. Raymond’s got the account. I’m out of all of it. Compliance has signed it. Kong’s sent a copy to Mabel.”

She shut her eyes. “I know. Mabel told me at eleven. She said you’d sent it before she’d finished her coffee.”

“Good.”

“Hao...”

“Go back to work,” he said gently. “I’ll be here.”

✦ ✦ ✦

*6:41 p.m.* The evening briefing was in the same room as the morning one, with the same screens. The search box had grown to fill most of the second screen. A great deal more wreckage had been found and logged. Some of it had been matched to the aircraft. The main wreckage hadn’t been located. The recorders hadn’t been found. There were still no survivors.

The search-and-rescue liaison stood up and said, carefully, in the words that had been agreed, that the operation was moving from rescue to recovery.

Nobody in the room moved. A hundred and eighty people. One of the engineers took his glasses off and put his hand over his eyes and kept it there.

Song-Zhu let the silence go on for exactly as long as it needed to, and not a second longer.

“Overnight,” she said. “The priorities.”

“Main wreckage. The recorders. Recovery. Debris mapping.”

“Clean handovers between shifts. No gaps in the search log. If there’s a gap I want to know why.” She turned to her own people. “Tomorrow we start the detailed history. Technical records. Maintenance, back to the last heavy check and every contractor who touched it. Crew records. The operational history of this aircraft, this route, this approach. Weather. Air traffic.”

One of the older investigators, a man named Leong who’d been doing this since before she was born, said, “Have we got an early theory?”

She looked at him. “No,” she said.

He nodded slowly.

“We’ve got an aircraft in the sea. We’ve got a hundred and eighty people who didn’t come home. We’ve got wreckage, and a search, and two recorders somewhere on the bottom.” She looked round the table. “That’s all we’ve got. Our job is to find out what happened. Not to decide what happened because the whole world wants an answer tonight. If anybody in this room says the word pilot or the word weather to anybody outside it before we’ve got the recorders open, they’re off my team.”

Nobody argued. Leong, by the wall, looked at Mabel, and Mabel slightly inclined her head. She closed the briefing.

✦ ✦ ✦

*8:17 p.m.* He was standing by his car when she came out, under the floodlights at the edge of the car park, and he straightened up when he saw her.

She walked towards him with the bag hanging off one shoulder. He took it from her. He didn’t say anything except “Hello.”

“Hello.”

He opened the passenger door. She got in. He put her bag on the back seat and came round and got in, and for a moment neither of them said anything at all, and the engine wasn’t on.

“Home?” he said.

She looked through the windscreen at the floodlights. “Yes.”

He drove. The roads were busy now: Sunday night, people coming out of restaurants, buses stopping, a group of young men crossing on a red light, laughing at something one of them had said. It all looked exactly the way it had yesterday. That was the thing she couldn’t get past.

Several minutes went by before she spoke.

“I saw a person in the water this morning.”

He kept his eyes on the road.

“And then another one.” Her voice was flat. Not because she felt nothing. Because she had spent fifteen hours making sure that what she felt stayed underneath what had to be done, and it hadn’t come up yet, and she was afraid of what would happen when it did. “On the screen. From the helicopter. They were lifting them onto the boats. They put blankets over them. Grey ones.”

He nodded once.

“I kept thinking that they’d been on a plane this morning,” she said. “Someone probably asked for a blanket. Someone probably complained that it was too early. Someone was going home to see their family for breakfast. A girl rang her father yesterday and said she’d be home for breakfast.”

She stopped.

“A hundred and eighty,” she said.

“Yes.”

“I don’t know how many they’ve brought in.”

He didn’t ask.

She leaned her head on the window. “That little boy was still there at six. His auntie took him home at half past. He asked me if his mother was in the sea. He asked it just like that. Is my mummy in the sea.”

Ren Hao’s hands tightened on the wheel.

“I didn’t know what to tell him.”

“What did you tell him?”

“That I didn’t know yet. And that I’d find out. And that I’d tell his auntie the truth when I did, whatever it was.” She looked at the lights going past. “He said promise. So I promised.”

He swallowed. “Then that’s what you’ll do.”

He reached across the console, and she took his hand, and held it, and he drove one-handed until the road needed both, and then he gave it back to her, and she held it again at the next light.

✦ ✦ ✦

*9:03 p.m.* She went straight into the bathroom and stood under the shower a long time.

She washed her hands. Then she washed them again. Then a third time, carefully, between every finger, and she didn’t know why, because she hadn’t touched anything, it had all been on a screen, and her hands were perfectly clean.

When she came out he’d put a clean towel on the bed and a glass of water on her side, and he was in the kitchen standing over two bowls of plain rice with egg and spring onion on top.

“I made something simple.”

“Thank you.”

He turned round, and his face changed when he saw hers. She’d showered, and the day was still all over her, in her eyes and her mouth and the way she held her arms.

He didn’t say anything. He held his arms open, a little, at his sides. She walked into them.

He didn’t hold her tightly. He didn’t hold her as if he could keep any of it off her. Just enough. Just so she could feel there was somebody there. She put her face against his chest.

“I don’t want to talk.”

“All right.”

“I don’t want to explain anything.”

“You don’t have to.”

She shut her eyes. He put his mouth to her hair. They stood in her kitchen until she drew back.

“Can we eat?”

“Yes.”

They ate at the counter. He didn’t ask whether it had broken up in the air or on the water. He didn’t ask about the recorders. He didn’t ask what the families had said, or what the owner had said to him a little after five, or what Raymond was doing now. He let her eat. Halfway through she put her spoon down.

“Do you know what I hate?”

“What?”

“That tomorrow I have to go back and do it again. And they’ll all still be waiting. And the recorders will still be on the bottom. And there’ll be more meetings and more reports and more things we don’t know, and everybody will look at me.” She looked at him. “And I’ll have to be the one who tells them what happens next.”

He reached across and took her hand.

“You don’t have to know everything tonight.”

She made a sound that was almost a laugh. “You’ve said that before.”

“It was true before.”

She held on to his fingers. Later they sat on her sofa, her feet under a blanket, leaning on him. His phone was on the coffee table, face up, on silent. Her work phone was beside it, face up, not on silent. Neither of them pretended it was anything else.

A little before eleven hers buzzed, and she sat bolt upright. He didn’t move.

She read it. The survey vessel had found a larger section of wreckage on the bottom. Its extent was being assessed. Neither recorder recovered. She put it down.

“Anything?”

“They’ve found more of it.” She leaned back on him. “Not the recorders.”

After a while she said, “I need you to know something.”

He turned his head.

“When I’m working I might not answer. I might be gone for days. I might come home and not want to talk at all. And there are going to be things I can’t tell you.” She looked at him. “Things I’m not allowed to tell you. Above all now. With whose aircraft it is.”

“I know.”

“I don’t want you to think I’m shutting you out.”

“I won’t.”

She looked down at their hands. “And please don’t try to fix this for me.”

His face went soft.

“I can’t,” he said. “I know I can’t. Nobody can.” He brushed his thumb across her knuckles. “But I can drive you. I can bring you home. I can make rice with an egg on top. I can sit with you when you don’t want to talk. And I can get out of your way when you need to work.” He paused. “That’s what I can do. So that’s what I’ll do.”

Her eyes filled for the first time all day. She didn’t let them spill.

“That’s enough,” she said.

He kissed her temple, and she leaned on him, and neither of them slept a long time.

✦ ✦ ✦

*Monday, 3 August, 3:57 a.m.* She woke before the alarm, and lay still, and reached for the phone.

Messages from the operations centre. The search would resume at first light. The recovery teams had made progress overnight. The number recovered was being verified. Neither recorder had been found.

She got up. He woke when the mattress moved.

“What time?”

“Nearly four.”

He sat up. “Coffee?”

She nodded. He went. When he came back with the cup she took it in both hands, and he stood and watched her drink it.

“Ready?” he said.

She looked at her phone. Then at him. “No,” she said.

“All right.”

She finished the coffee and picked up her bag. He picked up his keys.

At half past four they were on the road again, in the dark, the same road, the same empty green lights. She looked out of the window. He drove. At the long red light by the container port he reached across, and she took his hand and held it, and neither of them said anything.

A hundred and eighty people. A hundred and eighty names on a manifest that had stopped being marked UNVERIFIED at nine o’clock last night and had been marked something else instead. A hundred and eighty seats. A hundred and eighty families who’d expected somebody to walk through the arrivals hall at a quarter past four on a Sunday morning, tired and crumpled and complaining about the coffee.

And somewhere past the end of the runway, under forty metres of grey water, the sea was holding everything they’d need to know.

She’d become an investigator-in-charge at twenty-six. She’d wanted the responsibility. She’d wanted to lead one properly, start to finish, her name on it. She’d wanted to prove she could. She had never wanted this.

He pulled up outside the operations centre. The television van was still there. There were three of them now.

She undid her seat belt. Before she opened the door, he touched her wrist.

“Song-Zhu.”

She looked at him. He didn’t say it would be all right. He didn’t tell her to be strong. He didn’t tell her she was the right person, because he’d already said it, and she already knew.

“I’ll be here when you’re done,” he said.

She looked at him. Then she leaned across, in front of the vans and the cameras and all of it, and kissed him, once, on the mouth, quickly, and held his face for a second afterwards in her hand.

She didn’t say anything. She didn’t have to. He saw it.

Then she got out, and went in, and he watched until the door shut, and drove away.

And out past the runway, the boats went on searching.

chapters.title: Thirty Days
chapters.desc: Both recorders stop eleven seconds early. She stops sleeping. He moves into her flat without asking, and won’t read one line of her draft.
chapters.epigraph: “I keep hearing the silence.”
chapters.content:
The first time Song-Zhu heard the eleven seconds, she thought the playback had failed.

The second time, she thought the technician had stopped it too early.

By the fifth, she understood that the silence was real. And by the ninth she’d begun to hate it more than anything she had ever heard.

✦ ✦ ✦

*Tuesday, 4 August, 10:16 a.m.*

The flight data recorder had come up the afternoon before, from forty-one metres, still bolted into a piece of the rear fuselage the size of a garden shed. The divers had photographed it where it lay before anybody touched it. It had come out of the sea in a plastic tub of its own seawater, labelled and sealed and signed for three times between the dive boat and the laboratory, and nobody had cleaned it or dried it or plugged it into anything until she was in the room.

The cockpit voice recorder had come up at dawn, two hundred metres away, on its own, out of a field of seat frames.

Both were dented. Both were scorched along one edge. Both memory modules were intact.

Now, in the secured room at the back of the laboratory, with the blinds down and the door locked and a sign on it that said NO ENTRY in two languages, she stood behind the specialist’s chair while the first verified flight data came up on his screen.

“Limitations first,” she said.

“The casing took a lot of damage. The crash-protected memory’s sound. We’ve downloaded, verified, made the working copy. The data’s good.” He hesitated. “Until it isn’t.”

“Show me.”

The traces came up across the screen in a long ribbon of coloured lines. Altitude. Airspeed. Heading. Pitch. Roll. Engine parameters, flap position, gear, the angle of every control surface, the radio altimeter counting down towards the sea. Two hours and nine minutes of an ordinary flight, and then the turn onto final, and the long steady descent, everything where it should be.

And then every line on the screen stopped. All at once. At the same instant. As if someone had drawn a ruler down through them.

“There,” said the specialist.

She leaned in. “How long before impact?”

“Our best estimate from radar and the tower is eleven seconds.”

“Eleven.”

“Eleven. Give or take a fraction.”

“Is it an abrupt stop?”

“Completely. No degradation. No noise. Every parameter’s clean up to the last frame and then there’s no next frame.”

“Could the aircraft still have been flying when it stopped?”

“Yes. Radar has it for another ten seconds at least.”

“Could the recorder have stopped while everything else on the aircraft was still working?”

“In theory.”

“Can we say what happened in those eleven seconds?”

“Not from this,” he said. “Not from anything I’ve got.”

She looked at the ruler-straight edge where the lines ended.

“The voice recorder,” she said.

He didn’t answer. He didn’t have to. She’d seen his face when she came in.

“Same place?” she said.

“Same second. Both of them.”

The room was quiet. Two recorders, on two separate pieces of wreckage, two hundred metres apart on the bottom of the sea, and both of them had stopped listening at the same instant, eleven seconds before the end.

She knew what that usually meant. Every investigator in the building knew what that usually meant. She also knew that usually had killed more truth than any fire.

“Then we write it exactly like that,” she said. “Both recorders end at the same time, approximately eleven seconds before the estimated impact. Cause of the termination: not determined. Nobody in this building uses the word power outside this room until we can prove it. Nobody.”

“Understood.”

She wrote it down in her notebook in block capitals and underlined the last two words twice.

NOT DETERMINED.

✦ ✦ ✦

They listened to the voice recording that afternoon, in sections, with the door locked: her, the specialist, two authorised investigators, four pairs of headphones, nobody else. It was never to be copied, never to leave the room, never to be described to anybody outside it in more words than the law allowed.

A cockpit. Two men at the end of a night flight, tired, professional, a little dry with each other, the way people get after two thousand hours side by side. The checklists. The tower. The captain asking for the runway lights to be turned up a step. The first officer making a joke about the coffee. The ordinary rhythm of two people doing a job they’d done thousands of times.

There was no great speech. There was no warning anybody could have put in a film. There was work, and questions, and answers.

And then, near the end, something in both their voices changed.

One of the investigators shifted in his chair. The specialist’s hand went to the pause.

“Continue,” said Song-Zhu.

A few words, fast. A sound in the airframe she couldn’t name. Another few words. And then nothing.

Not a scream, not a crash. Not the sound of the sea. The recording simply ended, mid-breath, as if someone had shut a door. Nobody moved.

“Again,” she said. “From two minutes before.”

They played it again. And again. By the fifth time she knew that the silence wasn’t a fault in the playback. By the ninth she knew every frame of the last thirty seconds before it, and could have drawn the waveform with her eyes shut, and still had no idea what happened in the eleven seconds after it stopped.

“We’ll need the sounds identified,” she said at last, taking the headphones off. Her ears rang. “Separately. Speech, background, airframe. Every uncertain segment stays marked uncertain. Nobody labels a sound until it’s been matched.”

“Agreed.”

She stood up. The chair scraped. For one moment she thought she might have to sit down again.

She didn’t. She collected her notes and walked out, and down the corridor, and into the women’s toilets at the end, and locked herself in a cubicle, and stood with her back against the door and her hands flat against it for four minutes without making a single sound.

Then she washed her face, and went back to work.

✦ ✦ ✦

*Thursday, 6 August, 2:43 a.m.* He woke to the sound of her key in the door.

He’d been asleep on her side of the bed, because it smelled of her, which he’d never tell anyone. He looked at the clock and lay still and listened. The lock. The door. Her bag going down on the floor. Her shoes coming off, one, two, in the dark, without the hall light. He got up.

She was standing in the hallway in the same clothes she’d left in at five the morning before. She went still when she saw him.

“I didn’t mean to wake you.”

“It’s nearly three.”

“I know.”

“Have you...” He stopped himself.

She gave him a look that was too tired to be anything.

“Sorry,” he said.

She went past him into the bedroom without touching him. He followed her and didn’t touch her either. She sat down on the end of the bed and looked at her hands.

“Bad day?” he said.

“Same day.”

He understood the difference. He went to the kitchen and brought her a glass of water, and she drank all of it and gave him back the glass.

She changed into an old T-shirt and got into bed. He turned out the lamp and lay down beside her, and didn’t reach for her.

She was still a while. Then she turned onto her back. Then towards the window. Then towards him.

At twenty-six minutes past three she got up. A little before four she came back. Just after four he heard the bathroom tap running, and running, and running.

At a quarter past four she was sitting on the end of the bed in the dark with her phone lit in her hands.

“Song-Zhu.”

“Mm.”

“Come and lie down.”

“I’m not sleepy.”

“That’s all right. You can lie down anyway.”

She hesitated a long time. Then she put the phone face up on the floor and came back and lay down against him, and he put his arm round her and stroked her hair, slowly, from the crown to the ends, over and over. She didn’t sleep. Neither did he.

✦ ✦ ✦

*Saturday, 8 August* The preliminary report was due within thirty days. The date had been fixed the morning after the crash and written on the whiteboard in the investigation room in red, and nobody had wiped it off since.

TUESDAY 1 SEPTEMBER.

It wasn’t the final report. It wouldn’t find a cause. It wasn’t meant to. It was meant to say, a month afterwards, what had happened as far as anyone could say for certain, and what was being done to find out the rest. Everybody in the building knew that.

But the date had got into every meeting like water into a fuselage. Every morning somebody asked what had been established. Every afternoon somebody asked what could go in. Every evening she went down the list of what was still unknown, and every evening it was longer than the list of what wasn’t.

At half past five on Saturday a senior investigator put a draft timeline on her desk.

“Preliminary sequence.”

She read it. “Some of these times are estimated.”

“Yes.”

“Then they say estimated. Every one.” She put her finger on a line. “This says the aircraft experienced an abnormal event eleven seconds before impact.”

“The recorders stop there.”

“That doesn’t establish an abnormal event.”

He frowned. “Well, something happened.”

“Something happened. We know that because the aircraft’s on the bottom of the sea. We don’t know what happened in those eleven seconds.” She looked up at him. “We can’t use the silence as evidence. It’s the absence of evidence. That’s all it is.”

He looked at the page. Then he nodded. “I’ll revise it.”

A little before six her phone buzzed.

Ren Hao: Still at the centre?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Yes.

Ren Hao: I’ll wait.

He waited until twelve minutes past eight. When she came out he was leaning on the car with his jacket over his arm, and he straightened up.

“You’re still here.”

“I said I would be.”

“You’ve got work.”

“I’ve done the part that needed doing.”

He opened the door for her. When she’d got in he handed her a paper bag. She looked inside it. A sandwich, egg and cress, from the place by his building.

“You’re trying again,” she said.

“Yes.”

She looked at it, and then gave him a small, worn-out smile. “All right.”

She ate half of it before they got to the flyover. It was the first thing she’d eaten since a biscuit at eleven. He didn’t say a word about it.

✦ ✦ ✦

*Tuesday, 11 August* He’d been sleeping at her flat for nine nights.

He hadn’t moved in. Nobody had said anything about moving in. There’d been no conversation, no question, no key cut. He’d simply never left. The first night was the night of the crash. The second, she’d come home at three and he’d been there, so he’d stayed. The third, he’d brought a clean shirt. The fourth, groceries. The fifth, his laptop charger. The sixth, his good coffee machine from his own kitchen, because hers was terrible and she was drinking six cups a day.

By the ninth, there were four of his suits in her wardrobe, pushed along the rail so that her flight suits had moved down to the end. His shoes by the door. His toothbrush beside hers. His watch on the bedside table. His shaving things on the shelf where her hair clips used to live. A box of the tea she liked, which she hadn’t bought. A list on the fridge in his handwriting, of things that had been done, bins, laundry, filter changed, ticked off.

She noticed all of it. She’d noticed it a day at a time, the way you notice water coming up round your ankles.

At twenty to seven she came out of the bedroom and found him in her kitchen in a white shirt and dark trousers, with his hair wet, making coffee with his own machine. She stood in the doorway.

“Why is your charger here?”

He looked at the counter. “I keep forgetting to take it.”

“And your shoes?”

“Same reason.”

“And four suits?”

He paused, holding the jug. “Because I keep staying.”

She folded her arms. “Do you?”

“Do I what?”

“Keep staying.”

He turned the machine off and looked at her properly. “Song-Zhu.”

“You’re living here, Hao.”

He didn’t deny it. “Is that a problem?” he said.

“Did you ask me?”

A small silence.

“No,” he said.

“Then why are you doing it?”

He put the jug down. “Because you’re not sleeping. Because you come in at three and go out at five. Because you forget to eat until I put something in your hand. Because on Sunday night you stood in this kitchen for ten minutes holding your phone without moving, and I don’t think you knew you were doing it.” His voice had gone quiet. “I don’t want to leave you alone like that.”

“I didn’t ask you to leave.”

“I know.”

“But you didn’t ask to stay, either.”

He looked down. She looked past him at the fridge, and the list on it, bins, laundry, filter changed, in his tidy capitals, ticked.

She should say it now. She knew she should. She could feel the shape of the conversation they ought to have, and how long it would take, and what it would cost, and what was left in her to pay for it with. And she had a briefing at eight, and a draft at noon, and three families at four, and nineteen days.

“We’ll talk about it,” she said. “After the first of September. Properly.”

He looked up at her. And she saw, in his face, exactly what he heard: not not yet, but yes. She was too tired to correct him.

“And don’t reorganise my cupboards,” she said.

“I haven’t touched your cupboards.”

“Your eyes have.”

He laughed, slightly. It was the first time she’d heard it in nine days. She took the coffee he held out, his coffee, from his machine, in her mug, and it was the best coffee she’d had in a month, and she hated that.

She drank it. She kissed his cheek on the way past him.

She didn’t say you can stay. She didn’t say go home. She went to work.

✦ ✦ ✦

*Friday, 14 August* The technical team had tried everything they knew.

They’d compared the flight data with radar, with the tower recording, with the airport’s surface cameras, with the engines’ own maintenance computers, two of which had been recovered and might yet give something up. Everything agreed with everything else, right up to the instant the recorders stopped. After that there was radar, a few blurred returns, and the tower calling the callsign. And nothing from the aircraft.

“Could the recording have stopped because the recorders lost power?” said Song-Zhu.

“It’s one possibility,” said the specialist.

“Damage? To the recorders, or the wiring to them?”

“Yes.”

“Can we tell the difference?”

“Not with what we’ve got.”

“Anything before they stopped? Any fault message? Any warning? Any sign at all that something was going?”

“Nothing conclusive.”

“Were they working normally until the last frame?”

“As far as we can tell, yes.”

“Then that’s what we say.”

He nodded. “Do you want us to keep trying? There are a few damaged sectors on the memory boards. I don’t think there’s anything on them. I can’t promise.”

“Keep trying. Inside the technical limits. Document every attempt, and every failure.”

On her way out she glanced back at the screen. The ribbon of lines, and the edge where they ended, perfectly straight, perfectly vertical.

She’d started to see it when she shut her eyes.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came home that night a little before two. He was asleep on her sofa, sitting up, his head tipped against the arm at an angle that would hurt in the morning, one hand on his chest, his phone lit on the cushion beside him with a document still open on it. He’d been waiting for her, and lost.

She stood in the doorway and looked at him a long time. Then she picked up the phone and locked it and put it on the table, and touched his shoulder.

“Hao.”

His eyes opened. “You’re home.”

“I’m home.”

He sat up at once. “What time is it?”

“Nearly two.”

He rubbed his face. “Did you...”

She looked at him.

He held up both hands. “Sorry.”

She sat down beside him. He looked at her sideways.

“How was it?”

She looked at the dark television. “Eleven seconds.”

He waited.

“We’ve tried everything we can. Both of them stop. Eleven seconds before. We don’t know why.” She leaned forward with her elbows on her knees. “Everyone asks me what happened in the eleven seconds. Every family. Every journalist. Kwan. The board. Everyone.”

He said nothing.

“I want to know too,” she said. She pressed her palms together, hard. “I want to know so badly that sometimes I think if I listen to it enough times, I’ll hear something we missed. Something underneath. If I just listen hard enough.”

“Have you?”

“No.” She laughed once, with nothing in it at all. “Of course not. It doesn’t change because I listen to it again. It’s a recording. It’s the one thing in the world that never changes.”

He reached for her hand. She let him take it.

“Then don’t listen to it tonight,” he said.

“I have to.”

“Not tonight.”

She turned her face away from him. He didn’t argue. After a long time she said, so quietly he almost didn’t hear it:

“I keep hearing the silence.”

He moved closer, and she leaned into him, and he held her until her shoulders stopped shaking, and then a long time after that.

✦ ✦ ✦

*Thursday, 20 August, 3:11 a.m.* He woke to an empty bed.

He found her at her dining table, in his old university sweatshirt, her hair knotted up with a pencil through it. Her laptop was open with three documents side by side on the screen. A notebook beside it, every page black with her small fast writing. A cup of tea, stone cold, with the bag still in.

“Song-Zhu.”

She didn’t look up. “Mm?”

“Come to bed.”

“In a minute.”

“How long have you been up?”

“I don’t know.”

He came round the table, and stopped, carefully, at the corner, where he couldn’t see the screen.

“Did you sleep at all?”

She scrolled. “Earlier.”

“When?”

She stopped scrolling. “After dinner.”

“For how long?”

She didn’t answer.

“Song-Zhu.”

She shut her eyes. “Please don’t.”

He stood still.

“I’m trying to finish the sequence,” she said. “For the report.”

“It’s three in the morning.”

“I know what time it is.”

“I didn’t say you didn’t.”

She turned in the chair to look at him, and her face was so tired that it frightened him.

“I’ve got eleven days,” she said. “Please stop asking me to sleep as if I can just decide to.”

He took a breath, and let it go. “All right.”

She turned back to the screen. He didn’t leave. He pulled out the chair on the far side of the table, opposite her, where the laptop’s lid was between them, and sat down in it.

After a while she looked at him over the top of the screen.

“Do you want to read it?” she said. “You could tell me if the sentences are too long. You’re good at sentences.”

He looked at her. “No,” he said.

She blinked.

“I can’t,” he said gently. “You know I can’t. Not one line. Raymond’s sitting in a room tomorrow with the people who own that aircraft. If I’d read a single word of your draft, at your table, at three in the morning, then nobody could ever be sure again what I knew and when. Not Kwan. Not the families. Not you.” He put both hands flat on the table. “I’m not going to be the reason anybody doubts that report.”

She stared at him. Then something in her face crumpled, slightly, and came back.

“I forgot,” she said. “I actually forgot. I’m so tired I forgot whose aircraft it is.”

“I know.”

“Thank you.”

“Don’t thank me. Just don’t show me.” He reached across, not to the laptop, to her hand on the table beside it. “I’ll sit here. You work. I’ll read my own book. I won’t look.”

He got his book from the sofa and sat back down opposite her and read it, or held it open and looked at it, for forty minutes, without once lifting his eyes above the lid of her laptop. She worked. She muttered. She deleted a whole paragraph and wrote it again. Once she said no out loud to the screen, quite fiercely, and he didn’t ask.

Just after four she closed the laptop.

He looked up. “Bed?”

She nodded. He stood. She stayed sitting. He waited. And then she reached up for his hand.

“Will you come with me?” she said.

He held on to her fingers. “Of course.”

✦ ✦ ✦

*Sunday, 23 August* He started a list.

Not a list of things she had to do. A list of things he could do without making her decide anything. Food in the fridge. Clean towels. Laundry. A spare charger in her work bag. Her car filled. The bins. The post. Her mother rung on Sunday afternoons, because her mother had rung him on the fourth of August from her sister’s in tears and said she won’t tell me anything, Ren Hao, she never does, please, and he’d said he’d ring every Sunday, and he had.

He didn’t schedule her. He didn’t set reminders on her phone. He didn’t make her tell him when she’d eaten.

He made the flat easier to come home to. That was all.

He learned to leave things alone. He didn’t touch the papers on her dining table. He didn’t move her bag. He didn’t close the notebooks she left open, and he didn’t read them either; he laid a clean sheet of paper over each open page without looking at it, so that she wouldn’t have to worry. When she came home, he asked her one question.

“Company or quiet?”

Sometimes she said company. Sometimes she said quiet. He took both without making either into anything. But he was frightened.

He watched her lose weight. Her rings started turning on her fingers. He watched her forget the names of people she’d been introduced to the week before. He watched her wake out of short, thin, broken sleeps and reach for her phone before her eyes were properly open. He watched her sit on the floor of the shower long after the hot water had run out, with the cold coming down on her, not moving.

He wanted to fix it. He’d never wanted anything so much. He wanted to take her away for a day. He wanted to ring Director Kwan and tell him she needed to be stopped. He wanted to make the whole world stop asking her questions she couldn’t answer.

He did none of it. Not because he didn’t want to. Because in June she’d told him not to turn worry into control, and he’d promised, and it was the hardest promise he’d ever kept.

He wrote the list on a sheet of paper and stuck it on her fridge, under the one that said bins, laundry, filter changed, and ticked things off it, and didn’t notice that the list on the fridge had become two lists, and then three, and that his shirts now took up more than half her wardrobe, and that she’d stopped being able to find her own hair clips.

She noticed. She didn’t say anything. Not yet.

chapters.title: The Families
chapters.desc: The families. His firm runs the family side for the airline, behind a four-page wall. A widow asks what the pilot said; Song-Zhu can’t tell her.
chapters.epigraph: “One more moment. With someone who isn’t here.”
chapters.content:
The first family asked her whether the aircraft had exploded.

The second asked whether the passengers had known they were going to die.

The third asked whether the pilots had tried to save them.

By the end of the morning she’d learned that there were a hundred ways to ask the same question, and that it was always the same question underneath. Did they suffer? And there wasn’t one answer she was allowed to give that would make the room any easier to breathe in.

✦ ✦ ✦

*Monday, 24 August*

The family assistance centre had moved, in the third week, from the conference suite above arrivals to a hotel on the airport road that the airline had taken over entirely. It had private rooms for meetings, a desk in the lobby, a quiet room for children with beanbags and a box of crayons, a nurse, a room where people could sit without anyone asking them anything, and on the second floor, behind a door with a keypad, the room where the belongings were.

Song-Zhu had read the briefing notes twice in the car. She knew the questions. She knew which answers were established, which were still being examined, and which she couldn’t give at all, because the law said so.

She also knew that the families wouldn’t care about any of those distinctions. Not because they were unreasonable. Because their people were gone.

A man stood up from a chair by the lobby door as she came through it.

“Are you the investigator?”

“I’m Xu Song-Zhu. I’m leading the investigation.”

He looked at her lanyard a long time, as if he could read something else on it. “My wife was on the plane.”

“I’m sorry.”

“She was coming home. We were going to have dinner.” He took out his phone and turned it round for her to see. A message, timed eleven minutes to two on the morning of the second of August.

Boarding now. Don’t forget to buy the fruit.

Song-Zhu read it. Then she looked at him.

“I didn’t forget,” he said. “I bought it that morning. Before anybody rang. It’s still in the bowl. I can’t...” He put the phone away. “Can you tell me if she knew?”

“I can’t. Not yet. We don’t have enough that’s been verified to answer that. I’m sorry.”

He nodded, as if he’d been expecting it, and sat back down.

The first session had seven families in it. The family liaison officer introduced the team and said what the meeting was for. Song-Zhu answered the technical questions. The recorders had been recovered. Both recordings ended at the same moment, about eleven seconds before the impact, and the reason hadn’t been established. The voice recording was still being examined, and its contents were protected by law. The team was going through the aircraft’s maintenance history, the crew records, the weather, the air traffic recordings, everything. A preliminary report would come out on the first of September. It would say what had been established. It wouldn’t give a cause.

A woman at the end of the table looked at her. “Then you don’t know.”

“Not yet.”

“How long?”

“I can’t give you a reliable date for the final report. Usually about a year. It’ll take as long as it takes to get it right.”

The woman looked down at the table. “Everybody keeps telling us to wait.”

“I know.”

“No, you don’t.” The room went still. The woman looked up. “You go home. You finish work and you go home. We go home and they’re not there.”

Song-Zhu didn’t defend herself. There was nothing to defend.

The woman wiped her face with the back of her hand. “I’m sorry.”

“You don’t have to be.”

Song-Zhu came round the table and sat down in the empty chair beside her, and stayed there for the rest of the meeting.

✦ ✦ ✦

That afternoon, at four, the identification team confirmed four more names. One of them was the little boy’s mother.

Song-Zhu didn’t have to be the one to tell them. There were people whose job it was, trained, careful, kind. But she’d made a promise in a room full of chairs on the second of August to a boy who’d asked whether his mummy was in the sea, and she’d made it to his auntie too, and so at half past five she was standing outside a door on the third floor of the hotel with the family liaison officer, waiting while he knocked.

The auntie opened it. She saw their faces, and her own face went still.

The boy was sitting on the bed watching cartoons with the sound off. He looked round.

Song-Zhu sat down on the carpet in front of him so she wasn’t taller than him. The liaison officer did the talking. She didn’t interrupt. She’d have got it wrong. But when he’d finished, and the auntie had sat down on the bed and pulled the boy into her lap, he looked over his auntie’s arm at Song-Zhu on the floor.

“You said you’d find out,” he said.

“I did say that.”

“Is she in the sea?”

“Not any more,” said Song-Zhu. “They brought her out. She’s on land now. She’s safe on land, with people looking after her, until your family can be with her.”

He thought about that a long time, in the silent flicker of the cartoons.

“Okay,” he said, and turned his face into his auntie’s shoulder.

Song-Zhu stayed on the carpet until the auntie looked at her and nodded, and then she got up and went out and shut the door without a sound, and stood in the corridor with her hand flat on the wall.

✦ ✦ ✦

*Tuesday, 25 August* Raymond came up to the thirty-second floor at eight in the morning and stood in Ren Hao’s doorway with his tie already loosened.

“I need to talk to you about the airline.”

“You can’t,” said Ren Hao, without looking up. “That’s the whole point of you.”

“Not the investigation. Not the statements. Not the lawyers. The families.” Raymond came in and shut the door. “It’s falling apart, Hao. The family side. People getting three phone calls in a day from three departments asking the same questions. People told by one desk their hotel’s paid for and by another desk it isn’t. A man in Room 214 asked four times for an interpreter for his mother and got a leaflet. A woman was rung on Friday about claims before anyone had rung her about her husband’s wedding ring. The airline’s people are drowning and ours are running behind them with buckets.” He sat down without being asked. “The owner wants you. Not on cause. Not on messaging. On the families. He says he’s heard you’re the only person in this city who can stand in a room full of people who’ve lost everything and make the hotel work.”

Ren Hao put his pen down.

“And you said?”

“I said I’d ask. And that if you said yes, it’d have to go to compliance and Kong first, and then to the investigators, in writing, before you set foot in that hotel.” Raymond looked at him. “And I said that if you said no, I’d understand.”

Ren Hao sat still a long time. He thought about the wall he’d built at five past five on the second of August. He thought about what he’d said to her at three in the morning across her dining table. He thought about Room 214 and a woman rung about claims before anybody had asked her about a ring.

“Get Kong,” he said.

By two o’clock it was on paper. Four pages. He’d lead the firm’s family-support work and nothing else: accommodation, transport, interpreters, belongings, the hotel, one named contact for every family, and the people who answered the telephones. Nothing about the investigation. Nothing about the cause. Nothing about what the airline said in public. Nothing about the lawyers or the claims. He wouldn’t be in any meeting where the investigation was discussed, wouldn’t see any document about it, and would leave any room in which it came up. Raymond kept everything else. Compliance signed it. Kong signed it. And at ten past three it went to Director Kwan, with a covering letter, and a request for any objection by close of business.

At ten to six Director Kwan wrote back. Two lines. No objection, on these terms. Ms. Xu has been informed.

He read Ms. Xu has been informed three times.

He rang her. It went to voicemail. He didn’t leave one. He wrote a message and deleted it and wrote it again.

Ren Hao: Kwan’s told you. I should have told you first. I’m sorry. The families only. Nothing else. I’ll explain tonight if you want me to. If you don’t, I won’t.

At twenty past nine she replied.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Mabel read it to me in the corridor. I read it again myself. It’s a good wall. Do the hotel properly.

He looked at it a long time. Do the hotel properly. Nothing else. No kiss at the end. No see you tonight.

He went to her flat anyway, because his suits were there, and his toothbrush, and because he no longer knew how not to.

✦ ✦ ✦

*Wednesday, 26 August* She saw him first through the glass wall of a meeting room on the ground floor of the hotel.

She was coming out of a private session with a family from the north who had flown in on Sunday, and he was across the lobby in a dark suit, standing with two of his own people and a woman in the airline’s uniform with a clipboard. He was listening. He asked a question. One of his people wrote something down. The woman from the airline nodded, and nodded again, and Song-Zhu watched her shoulders come down by about two inches.

He looked exactly the way he looked at work. Composed. Focused. Unhurried. A man who could walk into a building full of grief and broken logistics and make everyone in it believe, for the first time in three weeks, that somebody had a list. He turned his head, and saw her. Neither of them moved.

She looked at the woman in the airline’s uniform beside him. Then back at him.

He gave her a small nod. Not hello, not an invitation. Just: I see you, and I know where I’m standing.

She gave him the same one back. And walked on.

Twenty minutes later they met in the corridor by the lifts. He was on his own.

“Song-Zhu.”

“Hao.”

He glanced at the lifts. “Are you all right?”

She looked at him. “At work?”

He understood at once. “Sorry.”

She shifted her folder to the other arm. “You’re doing well. The man in 214’s got an interpreter. His mother told the nurse.”

“She told me too. In three languages, none of which were mine.”

Her mouth moved, slightly. Then it stopped.

“I didn’t know you’d be here today,” he said.

“I’m here every day.”

“I can have someone else do the lobby when you’re...”

“Don’t.”

He stopped.

She took a breath. “You’re allowed to do your job. You’ve got four pages that say exactly what it is. And I’m allowed to do mine.” She looked at the doors of the meeting rooms down the corridor, one after another, all of them shut, people behind every one of them. “So let’s do them.”

“All right.”

A pause. “Are you going home tonight?” he said.

She looked at him, and he couldn’t read it.

“Probably,” she said.

“I’ll see you there.”

She nodded. He stepped aside to let her past. Neither of them touched the other.

✦ ✦ ✦

*Thursday, 27 August* Her name was Ting Mei. She was forty-one. Her husband had been in seat 23C, on his way back from a three-day conference, and he had texted her from the gate, as he did every time he flew, a photograph of the departures board with their two initials typed underneath.

Song-Zhu met her in a small room on the ground floor with pale walls and two armchairs facing each other and a box of tissues on the low table between them that nobody had touched. A family liaison officer sat a little to one side, with a notebook he wasn’t writing in.

Mrs. Ting had brought her own notebook. It was a school exercise book, blue, and she held it in both hands on her knees.

“I’ve written them all down,” she said. “My questions. So I won’t forget any.”

“That’s all right.”

“I don’t want to waste your time.”

“You won’t.”

Mrs. Ting opened the book. There was a list, numbered, in neat small writing, down two whole pages. Song-Zhu could see that the first line had been written and crossed out and written again.

“The first one is about the cockpit,” said Mrs. Ting.

Song-Zhu folded her hands. “Go on.”

“What did the pilot say?”

The question was so direct that Song-Zhu felt her whole body go still in the chair.

“I know you’ve got the recorder,” said Mrs. Ting. “The one that records their voices. It was on the news.”

“Yes. It’s been recovered.”

“And you’ve listened to it.”

“An authorised team is examining it.”

“But you’ve listened to it.”

Song-Zhu took a breath. “Yes.”

Mrs. Ting leaned forward. “Then what did he say? Did he tell the other one something was wrong? Did he say he couldn’t control it? Did he say...” Her fingers pressed into the blue cover. “Did he say anything to us? To the people in the back? Did he tell them?”

The small room seemed to close in round the two chairs.

Song-Zhu remembered the recording. The two tired voices. The coffee joke. The runway lights up one step. The change, near the end, in both their voices. The words she still had in her head and would have in her head, she suspected, for the rest of her life. And then the door shutting.

She remembered the instruction she’d given her own team: nothing uncertain to be labelled as fact.

She remembered the law. The voice recording was protected. Not because anybody wanted to hide it. Because pilots all over the world had to be able to speak freely in their cockpits, knowing that what they said in the last minutes of their lives would be used to stop it happening to someone else, and not played on the news, or read out in a courtroom, or told across a low table in a hotel to a stranger. Anything that was ever released would be released properly, carefully, in the report, in the words the analysis could support, and not a syllable more.

She couldn’t tell her. Not because she wanted to keep anything from her, not because she thought Mrs. Ting couldn’t bear it. Because she had no right to turn protected evidence into a private answer in a hotel room. And because she couldn’t hand her an interpretation that nobody had established.

And underneath all of that, small, far down, a nineteen-year-old in another country with a notebook on her knee, asking the same question first on her list, and being told no.

“I’m sorry,” said Song-Zhu. “I can’t tell you what’s on the cockpit recording. Not now.”

Mrs. Ting stared at her. “Why not?”

“It’s protected by law. It has to be examined and handled in a particular way, so that whatever we eventually say about it is accurate, and so that it can’t be used for anything except stopping this happening again. Anything we can release will be in the report.”

“But you know.”

“We’ve examined parts of it. The analysis isn’t finished.”

“Then you know something.” Mrs. Ting’s voice dropped to almost nothing. “Did my husband hear the pilot tell them they were going to die?”
