Song-Zhu’s throat closed. She looked down at her own hands for one second. Then she made herself look up again, and meet the woman’s eyes, because it was the least she could do.

“I can’t answer that,” she said.

Mrs. Ting looked at her a long time. Then she closed the blue book.

“All right.”

“Mrs. Ting...”

“Please don’t.” She looked at the window. “I don’t want another explanation. Everybody has an explanation.”

The liaison officer moved slightly in his chair.

Mrs. Ting stood up. “Thank you for coming.”

Song-Zhu stood too. “I’m sorry I couldn’t give you what you wanted.”

Mrs. Ting looked at her.

“I didn’t want what I wanted,” she said, and her voice broke straight down the middle. “I wanted to know what he heard. Before.”

She picked up her bag and went out, and closed the door so gently that the latch didn’t click.

Song-Zhu sat down again in the armchair. The liaison officer looked at her.

“Do you want a minute?”

She nodded. He went out. She sat looking at the empty chair. The worst part wasn’t that Mrs. Ting hadn’t asked her for the cause. It was that she’d asked for so little. A few words. One moment. Something her husband might have heard, that she could take home with her and put somewhere.

And Song-Zhu had nothing she was allowed to give her.

✦ ✦ ✦

He found her at a quarter to seven outside the staff entrance at the back of the hotel, sitting on a low brick wall by the bins with her folder beside her.

“Song-Zhu.”

She looked up. “Hello.”

He sat down on the wall, not quite touching her. “Have you finished?”

“For today.”

They sat. A delivery van reversed into the bay and beeped and stopped and somebody unloaded crates of water.

“Did something happen?” he said at last.

She looked at the van. “A widow asked me what the pilot said.”

He turned to her.

“She asked if he knew they were going to die. If he told the other one. If he said anything to the people in the back.” She rubbed her forehead. “I couldn’t tell her.”

He didn’t ask what the pilot had said. He didn’t ask whether there was anything. She noticed that he didn’t, and noticed how carefully he didn’t, and something in her that had been clenched since Tuesday let go a little.

“She looked at me,” said Song-Zhu, “as if I was choosing not to.”

“Did you explain?”

“Yes. She said she didn’t want another explanation.” She laughed once, short. “Of course she didn’t. She doesn’t need another person in a lanyard explaining procedure to her. She needs her husband.”

He was quiet.

“I wanted to give her something,” she said. “Anything. That he wasn’t frightened. That he didn’t know. That he did know and he wasn’t alone. That someone in that cockpit was being kind. I wanted to give her one sentence to take home.”

“But you don’t know those things.”

“No.”

“And if you did, you couldn’t tell her.”

“No.”

He reached across the gap between them on the wall, and she let him take her hand.

“Then you did the right thing,” he said.

“It doesn’t feel like it.”

“I know.”

She pressed her lips together. “She was so polite. When she went. She thanked me.” Her eyes filled. “She thanked me for coming to tell her I couldn’t tell her.”

He moved closer on the wall, and put his arm round her shoulders, and she leaned her head against him, by the bins, in her lanyard, with a man unloading crates of water ten metres away, and didn’t care who saw.

✦ ✦ ✦

*Saturday, 29 August* They were in two different rooms in the same building, on two different floors, talking about the same people.

At fourteen minutes past three she was on the fourth floor with her team, going through what could and couldn’t go in the briefing on Monday.

A little after three he was on the ground floor with the airline’s family-assistance manager, reading a complaint. A family had been told by somebody on the airline’s helpline that the investigators would soon be announcing the cause.

“Who said that?”

“We’re finding out.”

“Find out by four. And then find every family that person spoke to this week, and ring them back, and correct it, in person, today.” He put the complaint down. “Nobody promises a finding we haven’t got. Nobody gives a family a convenient sentence when we haven’t got an honest one.”

A little after three, upstairs, she was saying to her team, “If we haven’t got an answer, we say we haven’t got an answer. Not we’re hopeful. Not we expect. We haven’t got one.”

Neither of them could see the other’s screen. Neither of them knew what the other was saying. They found out a long time afterwards that they’d said almost the same sentence, four floors and five minutes apart.

On opposite sides of the same thing. And neither of them able to make the other side any lighter.

✦ ✦ ✦

*Sunday, 30 August* She came in a little before ten. He was in the kitchen with his tablet, and he locked the screen the moment her key turned, before she’d got the door open, as he did every night now.

“Hello.”

“Hello.”

“How was your day?”

“Long.”

He nodded. “Mine too.”

She looked at him. “Families?”

“Families.”

She leaned on the counter. She looked round her kitchen. His coffee machine. His list on the fridge, the third one, dry cleaning, Mum (Sun) ✓, her car. His tea in her cupboard. His shirts, she knew without looking, in her wardrobe. Her hair clips, she knew without looking, in a little glass bowl he’d bought for them, on a shelf where she’d never have put them.

“Do you ever feel,” she said, “like you’re working for people who all want different things from you?”

He considered it. “All the time.”

“The families want answers. The airline wants to know what it can say. The investigation needs time. Everybody wants the same thing in the end, and they all want it in a different shape.” She looked at him. “And you’re working for the airline.”

“For the families. Through the airline.”

“While I investigate their accident.”

“Yes.”

“Does it bother you? That we’re on different sides?”

He thought about it properly. “I don’t think we’re on different sides,” he said. “My job is to make sure the people in that hotel are treated like people. Your job is to find out what happened to the people they lost. Those aren’t the same. But they’re not against each other.”

“And if the airline doesn’t like what I find?”

“Then my job’s still the same. And I’ll still be making sure the man in 214’s mother has an interpreter.”

She was quiet.

“And I don’t need to know what you’re finding,” he said. “I don’t want to. I’ve made sure I can’t.”

“Good,” she said.

He smiled faintly. “That sounded almost like a threat.”

“It was a reminder,” said Song-Zhu, and nearly smiled back, and didn’t.

He came round the counter and stood in front of her and didn’t touch her. She looked at him. Then she put her forehead against his chest, and he put his arms round her.

“How do you stop thinking about the people in a room,” she said into his shirt, “after you’ve left it?”

He took a long time to answer. “You don’t always,” he said. “But you don’t have to take every one of them home.”

“I don’t know how not to.”

“I know.”

She stood there, against him, in her kitchen that was half his kitchen now.

“We should stop pretending,” she said, “that we can keep our work in separate boxes all the time.”

He put his mouth to her hair. “We can keep the work separate. We don’t have to keep the feelings separate. You’re allowed to come home upset about a room. I’m allowed to tell you a day was bad. We just don’t make each other’s work our own.”

She thought about that. “All right,” she said.

But later, when he’d gone to have a shower, she stood in her bedroom in front of her wardrobe and opened it and looked at his four suits, six suits now, hanging on her rail, and her own flight suits pushed down at the far end in the dark, and she stood there a long time with the door open.

✦ ✦ ✦

*Monday, 31 August* The last family briefing before the report was smaller. Four families. Mrs. Ting was one of them. She sat by the window with the blue exercise book on her knee, and when Song-Zhu came in their eyes met, and Mrs. Ting nodded, politely, and Song-Zhu nodded back.

The update was nearly the same as the last one. Tomorrow the preliminary report would come out. It would set out what had been established. It wouldn’t give a cause. The recorders were still being examined. The eleven seconds were still not explained.

Afterwards Mrs. Ting waited until the others had gone.

“Mrs. Ting.”

“Investigator Xu.”

“How are you?”

Mrs. Ting gave a small worn smile. “People keep asking me that.”

“I’m sorry.”

Mrs. Ting looked at the empty chairs. “I’ve been thinking about what I asked you. On Thursday.”

Song-Zhu sat down opposite her.

“I understand you can’t tell me what’s on it,” said Mrs. Ting. “I don’t like it. I still don’t understand how there can be things that belong to the last minutes of my husband’s life that I’m not allowed to hear. But I understand that there are rules. And that you didn’t make them up on Thursday afternoon to get rid of me.”

“Thank you for saying that.”

Mrs. Ting turned the blue book over in her hands. “Do you think he knew? Not what’s on the tape. I know you can’t. I mean you. Do you think he knew something was wrong?”

“I can’t make that judgement without evidence.”

“I thought you’d say that.” Mrs. Ting looked down. And then, low, as if she were embarrassed to be saying it to a stranger in a hotel conference room: “I keep wondering if he was thinking about me.”

Song-Zhu’s eyes stung.

Mrs. Ting gave a small embarrassed laugh. “It’s a stupid question.”

“It isn’t.”

“There’s no way you could know.”

“No,” said Song-Zhu. “There’s no way I could know.”

Mrs. Ting nodded, and closed the book, and stood up.

“Thank you,” she said, “for not pretending.”

It wasn’t forgiveness. It wasn’t relief. It was only a woman saying out loud that another woman hadn’t lied to her.

Somehow it was heavier than the anger had been.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was outside when she came out, by his car, finishing a call with one of his people. He ended it when he saw her.

“Ready?”

She nodded. He opened her door. She got in. He shut it carefully and came round.

When he’d started the engine she said, looking straight ahead, “I saw her again.”

“The widow?”

“She asked me if her husband had been thinking about her.”

He didn’t move. “What did you say?”

“That I couldn’t know.” She looked through the windscreen. “She thanked me for not pretending.”

He reached across, and she took his hand, and they sat there with the engine running for a long minute before he drove.

At home she changed and sat on the sofa with her feet under her. He made tea, and brought it, and sat beside her. She held the cup in both hands and didn’t drink it.

“Every family has one question,” she said. “One they keep coming back to, whatever else they ask. Some of them ask if the pilots knew. Some ask if the aircraft was already broken when it took off. Some ask if it hurt.” She looked at the tea. “And she asks what her husband heard.”

He was quiet.

“They all want the same thing,” she said. “One more moment. With someone who isn’t here.”

He put his arm round her.

“I can’t give them that,” she said.

“No.”

“I can’t give any of them what they want.”

“You can give them the truth,” he said. “When you have it. All of it. And you will.”

She shut her eyes. The television stayed off. Neither of them looked at a phone. For the first time that day nobody was asking her a question, and nobody was asking him to fix a hotel.

Tomorrow the report would come out and say almost nothing. The families were still waiting. And somewhere, on a recording in a locked room that she’d listened to forty-one times, two tired men had said their last words, and the last eleven seconds of them were missing, and she couldn’t tell a woman with a blue exercise book what either of them had been.

She leaned against him, and held the cold tea, and didn’t sleep.

chapters.title: Equipment
chapters.desc: The preliminary report says almost nothing. He organises her life so she can work. She tells him she’s his girlfriend, not his equipment. For the first time, he asks before kissing her.
chapters.epigraph: “Not your equipment.”
chapters.content:
The preliminary report was published at nine o’clock on Tuesday the first of September.

At seven minutes past nine, somebody on the radio called it disappointing.

At twelve minutes past, a journalist asked online whether the investigators were hiding something.

At nineteen minutes past, the father of a passenger wrote that thirty days had gone by and he still didn’t know why his daughter was dead.

At twenty-four minutes past, the airline’s communications team asked for a paragraph to be clarified that had already been clarified twice.

And at half past nine, Song-Zhu read the report for the fourth time that morning, and it still said the same thing.

Facts. Only facts. No cause. Nothing to explain the eleven seconds. No finding about the crew. Nothing anybody could hold on to.

✦ ✦ ✦

*9:42 a.m.* The briefing room was full. Television cameras along the back wall, on a riser. Microphones taped in a bunch to the lectern. Director Kwan at it, with his reading glasses on. Song-Zhu to one side of him, beside the screen, in the dark blue suit she’d bought for exactly this and had hoped she would never wear.

He took them through it. The flight. The approach. The time contact was lost. The search and recovery, the hundred and eighty, the identifications so far. The recorders: both recovered, both recordings ending at the same moment, approximately eleven seconds before the estimated impact, cause of the termination not yet determined. The voice recording under examination. The maintenance and operational history under examination. The investigation continuing.

A man in the second row stood up before Kwan had finished the last sentence.

“Does the report say what caused the crash?”

“No. The investigation hasn’t reached a conclusion about the cause.”

“Then what does it tell us?”

“What has been verified at this stage. And what work has been done, and what work is still to do.”

A woman at the back. “Isn’t it unusual for both recorders to stop eleven seconds early?”

Kwan looked at Song-Zhu. She stepped up to the second microphone.

“The technical team is examining the recordings and the circumstances in which they ended. We won’t speculate about the reason until we can support it.”

“Could it mean the aircraft lost electrical power?”

“That’s one of the possibilities being examined. It hasn’t been established.”

“Could the pilots have lost control?”

“The report makes no finding about that.”

“Is there anything on the voice recorder that shows a problem?”

“The voice recording is protected by law. It’s being examined. We won’t release anything from it outside the proper process.”

The questions kept coming. They came in different shapes and they were all the same question. Was it the aircraft. Was it the pilots. Was there a warning. Was the airline to blame. Were the crew trained. Was the aircraft properly maintained.

She’d written most of the technical sections herself. She knew every qualifier in the document. She knew which sentences had been rewritten nine times, which figures had been checked against three sources, and which claims had been taken out because the evidence wouldn’t hold them up.

The report was accurate. It was also so incomplete that it hurt to stand next to it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her phone was full when she got back to her office. Kwan. Three colleagues. Two numbers she didn’t know. Her mother. And Ren Hao.

Ren Hao: It’s out.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Yes.

Ren Hao: You stood up there and didn’t guess once. I watched it in the hotel lobby with forty people. Nobody in the room breathed while you were talking.

She looked at it a long time. She didn’t know why it made her want to cry. She put the phone down and didn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

*11:16 a.m.* The first family rang before lunch. The second rang while she was in with the technical team. The third came in person.

A man in his fifties stood in front of her desk holding a printed copy of the report. He’d folded the pages so many times on the way there that the corners had gone soft as cloth.

“I’ve read this.”

She stood up. “Of course.”

“It doesn’t say why.”

“No. We haven’t established the cause.”

He put his finger on a line. “Eleven seconds. It says eleven seconds.”

“Yes.”

“What happened in them?”

“We don’t know yet.”

“Then what are you doing?”

She took a breath. “We’re going through everything. The recorders. The maintenance records. The crew records. The weather. Air traffic. And every piece of wreckage we can bring up. We’re still bringing it up.”

“But you don’t know.”

“Not yet.”

He looked down at the report in his hands.

“My daughter was on that plane,” he said. “Twenty-six. She was starting a new job next week. At a bank. She’d bought shoes.” He folded the report again along its soft creases. “I thought after thirty days there’d be something.”

Song-Zhu looked at the folded pages.

“There’s a great deal in it,” she said. “Everything we can stand behind. But I know it isn’t what you came here for.”

He stared at her. Then he nodded, once. “Thank you,” he said, and went.

She sat down and opened the report on her screen again, page after page. Accurate. Careful. Defensible. Not enough.

✦ ✦ ✦

*1:08 p.m.* At the hotel on the airport road, in a room on the ground floor with the blinds half down, Ren Hao was reading a draft letter.

It was his letter. It was the letter that would go from the airline’s family-assistance team to every one of a hundred and eighty families that afternoon, and the family-assistance team was his, all four pages of it, signed and countersigned. Under the heading and the condolences and the practical arrangements, somebody he hadn’t met had added a paragraph.

The airline notes that the preliminary report found no evidence of a technical defect in the aircraft.

He read it twice.

“Who wrote this?”

The airline’s family-assistance manager looked unhappy. “It came down from upstairs. With a request that you approve it.”

“I can’t approve it.”

“It’s only one sentence.”

“It’s one sentence about the cause,” said Ren Hao. “I’m not allowed to touch the cause. It’s written down that I’m not allowed to touch the cause, and Director Kwan has a copy.” He took his pen out. “And it isn’t true. The report doesn’t say there’s no evidence of a defect. The report says nobody knows yet. That isn’t the same thing. You can’t use a gap in what’s known as if it were a finding in your favour, and you can’t use it in a letter to a woman whose husband is dead.”

The manager looked at him. He drew a line through the paragraph. Then he wrote in the margin, in capitals: NOT IN MY REMIT. NOT TRUE. REFERRED TO RAYMOND UNDER THE WALL.

“The letter goes without that paragraph,” he said. “With a copy of the report itself, in full, so they can read what it actually says. And somebody rings Mrs. Ting in 306 before it arrives and tells her it’s coming, so she isn’t on her own when she opens it.”

“I’ll have to tell upstairs.”

“Tell them,” said Ren Hao. “And tell them it was me.”

He sent the paragraph, and his note, to Raymond, and copied Kong, and wrote down the time. Then he sat in the half-dark room a long time with his phone in his hand. He wanted to ring her. He didn’t.

Ren Hao: Have you eaten?

He looked at it. Then, before she could see it:

Ren Hao: Sorry. Don’t answer that.

He put the phone in his pocket.

✦ ✦ ✦

*9:46 p.m.* By the time she came home, he’d made dinner.

Rice in the cooker. Soup on the stove, turned low. A plate of greens under a plate. Her work shirts from the basket washed and hung on the airer. Her tea in the cupboard, a new box. A glass of water on her side of the bed. Her phone charger moved from the sofa to the bedside table. Her work bag, which she always dropped by the sofa, picked up and put by the front door, where she’d see it in the morning.

She noticed every one of those things. She’d been noticing them for a month.

And she noticed the sheet of paper by the kettle, in his capitals.

DINNER — STOVE.
CAR — 7:00 A.M.
DRIVER — CONFIRMED (MR. YAU).
SLEEP — PLEASE!

She looked at the last line a long time.

He came out of the bedroom. “You’re home.”

She was looking at the paper. “What’s this?”

He followed her eyes. “Just a few things.”

“A few things.”

“Dinner. Getting you in tomorrow. You’ve got the technical briefing at nine, and you were out at five today, so I thought if Mr. Yau...”

“I can book a car.”

“I know you can.”

She picked the paper up. “And the last one?”

His mouth moved. “That one’s a suggestion.”

“With an exclamation mark.”

“I was trying to make it friendly.”

She put the paper down on the counter. He smiled at her, tired and hopeful. “There’s soup.”

She didn’t move. He saw it.

“What’s wrong?”

She looked at the stove. Then at the charger on her bedside table, through the open door. Then at her bag by the front door, where she would never in her life have put it.

“How long have you been doing this? Arranging everything.”

He hesitated. “Since the report got close. Mostly.”

“Mostly.”

“Some of it before.”

He came a step towards her. “Song-Zhu, you’re exhausted. You’ve been exhausted for a month. I thought if I took the small things...”

“You moved my bag.”

“So you wouldn’t have to look for it at seven.”

“You moved my charger.”

“You keep leaving it on the sofa and then your phone dies at three.”

“You booked a driver.”

“Because you’ve got an early...”

“You made me a schedule.”

“Not a schedule. A reminder.”

She stared at him. He stopped. There was an expression on her face he’d learned. Not anger. The moment before she decided whether to explain something properly, or walk away from it.

“Song-Zhu?”

She put both hands flat on the counter. “Can we talk,” she said. “Now. It’s the first of September.”

His face changed. “Yes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She went to the dining table, and didn’t sit. He followed her, and didn’t sit either.

“Do you know what I feel like?” she said.

He waited.

“Every morning someone needs something from me. An answer. A decision. A signature. Someone wants to know what happened. Someone wants me to explain why I don’t know. A man came to my desk today with a report folded so many times it had gone soft, and asked me what happened to his daughter, and I didn’t know.” She looked at him. “And then I come home. And everything’s been arranged.”

“I thought it would help.”

“I know.” She held up a hand. “Let me finish. Please.”

He shut his mouth.

“I know you’re frightened,” she said. “I know you love me. I know you’ve been trying to make things easier for a month, and I know how hard you’ve tried, and how much you’ve stopped yourself.” Her voice was quiet. That made it worse. “But you make decisions about my life as if I’m not in it. You’ve decided what I eat. How I get to work. When I sleep. Where my things go. My hair clips are in a glass bowl, Hao. I don’t own a glass bowl. You moved in. You moved in, and I didn’t say yes, and I didn’t say no, because I was too tired to say anything, and you heard that as yes.” She looked at him. “And you watch me. All the time. To see if I’ve eaten. If I’m tired. If I’m about to fall apart. And I know you don’t mean it like this, but sometimes it feels like being monitored.”

His jaw had tightened. “I don’t want you to feel like that.”

“Then stop.”

He looked at her. She looked back.

“I’m your girlfriend, Hao,” said Song-Zhu. “Not your equipment.”

The words landed in the room between them and didn’t move. He didn’t move either.

“I’m not one of your clients,” she said, more softly. “I’m not a crisis you’re managing. I’m not a hotel. I’m not something you can optimise until every risk’s been accounted for and written on a sheet of paper by the kettle.”

His eyes went down. “I know.”

“Do you?”

He looked up at her. She was tired, he saw. Not only in her body. Tired of being watched, and measured, and got to first.

“I can be exhausted and still be capable,” she said. “I can be upset and still know what I need. I can miss lunch once without anybody building a whole system round me.” Her voice shook, slightly. “I need to be the one running my life, Hao. Even now. Most of all now. Because it’s the only thing I’ve got left that’s mine.”

He nodded slowly. “I thought I was helping,” he said.

“You are helping. Sometimes.” She paused. “And sometimes you’re making it harder to breathe.”

He took that in. For a long time he didn’t answer.

“I didn’t see it,” he said at last.

“I told you in June. Ask.”

“I know.”

“You said you understood.”

“I did. I do.”

“But you keep going back.”

He looked down at his own hands. She watched him. He wasn’t arguing. He wasn’t explaining. But she could see the instinct in him, rising: to lay out all the reasons, every single thing he’d done and why, the bag and the charger and Mr. Yau and the tea, to show her how much it had been for her.

She didn’t want the list. She wanted him to hear her.

“You’re right,” he said.

She breathed out.

“I’ve been treating your life like a problem I could organise.” He was quiet. “And I think I’ve been doing it because I don’t know what else to do. I can’t fix the crash. I can’t get you back those eleven seconds. I can’t give the families what they need. I can’t make you stop hearing what you’ve heard in that room.” He stopped. “So I’ve been fixing everything round you. Because it felt better than sitting here every night knowing I couldn’t do anything at all.”

Her face changed.

He gave a small, unhappy smile. “I sat in a hotel today and crossed out a sentence somebody wanted to send a hundred and eighty families, and it was the best I’ve felt in a month. Because it was something I could do. And then I came here and did it to you. All evening. With a list.”

She looked at him a long time. “Then sit with me,” she said. “When you can’t do anything. Don’t do anything. Sit with me.”

He lifted his eyes.

“Don’t turn me into one more thing you’ve got to manage,” she said. “I’ve got enough of those for both of us.”

“All right.”

“I want you here.” She stepped closer. “I want you here because you’re the person I want to come home to. Not because you’ve decided I can’t look after myself.”

He reached for her hand. She let him take it.

“And the flat,” he said. “I’ll take my things home. Tomorrow. All of it. And we’ll talk about it properly when this is over, and you’ll decide.”

She looked at him. She looked at the six suits she couldn’t see, on her rail, in the dark. She looked at the coffee machine.

“Not tomorrow,” she said. “I can’t do that tomorrow too. Just... stop adding to it. And ask.”

“I will.”

“And if I say no?”

“Then I’ll listen.”

She studied his face. “Even when you think you know better?”

A faint, rueful smile. “Above all then,” said Ren Hao.

✦ ✦ ✦

They stood close. He was still holding her hand.

He looked at her face. The shadows under her eyes, gone almost purple. The line between her eyebrows. Her hair coming out of its tie. He wanted to pull her into his arms. He wanted to kiss her. He wanted to wipe out the last fifteen minutes with the plain warm weight of holding her, the way he’d done after every argument they’d ever had. He stopped.

She noticed. “What?”

He hesitated. Then he said:

“Can I kiss you?”

She blinked. For a second she looked almost startled. Not because he’d never kissed her. He’d kissed her at taxi ranks and in car parks, against kitchen counters and office glass, on beaches, in hedges, in the middle of arguments to end them, and once, in July, simply because she’d walked past him in the kitchen eating a peach. But he had never once asked her.

Not after a fight, not when he wanted to make something better. Not when he didn’t know if she wanted him close.

“You’re asking,” she said.

“Yes.”

A small movement at the corner of her mouth. “Why?”

“Because I don’t want to assume,” said Ren Hao. “Not anything. Not any more. Not even this.”

Something in her face changed. The tiredness stayed. But something underneath it went soft.

She lifted her free hand and put it on his cheek.

“Yes,” she said.

He bent his head, slowly, giving her the whole time to change her mind.

The kiss was barely anything. His mouth on hers, light, and still. No hurry. No persuading. No trying to tell her through it that everything was all right. He kissed her once, and drew back an inch, and looked at her.

“All right?”

She nodded. “Yes.”

He kissed her again. And this time she came into it. Her fingers slid round to the back of his neck, and her mouth opened under his, and he held her waist with both hands and didn’t pull her one centimetre closer than she came on her own. She came all the way. She kissed him slow and deep and a little desperate, with her eyes shut and her hand tight in the hair at his nape, the way she hadn’t kissed him in a month, and he let her lead it, all of it, every second, and didn’t take one thing she didn’t give.

When she drew back she kept her forehead against his.

“That was different,” she said.

“I was.”

She laughed. A small, real laugh, the first in days, right against his mouth.

He shut his eyes. He’d missed that sound more than he’d known it was possible to miss anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

The sheet of paper was still by the kettle.

She picked it up. He watched her. She found a pen in the drawer and drew a line through SLEEP — PLEASE! Then through DRIVER — CONFIRMED (MR. YAU).

“Shall I cancel him?”

She nodded. He took out his phone and rang Mr. Yau, who was still up, of course, and apologised, and told him he could have a lie-in, and Mr. Yau said something that made Ren Hao laugh once, and put the phone down.

“He says thank goodness. He says he’s been driving you for a month and you never talk to him and he was running out of radio stations.”

Song-Zhu put her hand over her eyes. “I’ll talk to him. When this is over. I’ll buy him biscuits.”

“He’d like that.”

She looked at the list. “Dinner can stay.”

“Good.”

“The tea can stay.”

“Excellent.”

“The charger can stay. You were right about the charger.”

“Thank you.”

“But don’t move my bag.”

He looked at it, by the front door. “Understood.”

“And don’t ask me every hour if I’ve eaten.”

“Understood.”

“Once.”

“Once.”

“Unless I look like I’m about to faint.”

“That’s a different category.”

She gave him a look. He held both hands up.

She folded the list in half and put it in the drawer with the pen. Then she came and put her arms round his waist, and he held her.

“I know you’re frightened,” she said into his chest.

His arms tightened. “Yes.”

“So am I.”

He bent his head over hers. “I know.”

She looked up. “But I don’t need you to make my life smaller so nothing else can happen to it.”

He looked down at her. He put his mouth against her hair.

“I’ll remember,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

They ate at the table. He’d made enough for two. She finished her rice and went back for more soup, and he saw her go back, and said nothing.

She looked at him over the bowl. “You’re very quiet.”

“I’m eating.”

“You’re watching me eat.”

“I’m watching the soup.”

She narrowed her eyes. He gave up. “I was watching you.”

She shook her head. And then, slightly, she laughed.

He held his hand out across the table, palm up, and she put hers in it, and they talked about nothing for half an hour. A colleague who’d sent the whole floor an email with a photograph of his cat attached instead of the evidence schedule. The neighbour’s dog. A restaurant they’d walked past in May. He told her about a consultant of his who had that morning, under pressure, sent a meeting invitation titled Grief Workshop (Internal) to an entire external client list, and she put her spoon down and laughed with her whole face for the first time in a month, laughed until she had to wipe her eyes.

He watched her do it. Not the investigator-in-charge, not the woman at the second microphone. Not the person who had to explain to a man with a soft folded report that eleven seconds were missing. Only Song-Zhu. The woman who laughed with all of her face, and stole the best pieces off his plate, and was stealing one now.

He wanted, more than anything, to keep that safe.

He was beginning to understand that loving her didn’t mean deciding what safe looked like. Sometimes it meant leaving the door open, and sitting by it, and waiting.

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past ten she was in bed with a novel she’d given up on in July. He came out of the bathroom and put his watch on the bedside table and stopped.

“Do you need anything?”

She looked up.

He heard himself. He held up a hand. “That was a question. Not a plan.”

“No,” she said. “Thank you.”

He turned out the light and got in, and lay on his side facing her, not touching her. She closed the book.

“Hao?”

“Yes.”

“Come closer.”

He moved across the bed. She put her head on his shoulder. His arm settled round her.

“Are you still upset?” he said.

She considered it honestly. “A little.”

“All right.”

“But I’m not going anywhere.”

He went still.

“I don’t want you to think,” she said, “that every time I tell you something hurts, it means I’m getting ready to leave.”

“I don’t think that.”

She lifted an eyebrow in the dark.

He breathed out. “Sometimes I think that.”

“I know you do.”

“I’m trying not to.”

“I know that too.” She moved closer. “You’re allowed to get it wrong.”

“That’s very generous.”

“It isn’t. It’s just true.” She kissed his chin. Then his cheek. Then the corner of his mouth, and stopped there.

He smiled against her. “Are you asking?”

“I’m demonstrating,” said Song-Zhu.

He turned his face to hers. “May I?”

She looked at him in the dark. “Yes,” she said.

He kissed her. Slowly. And when she reached for him, he went where she led, and not one step further, and it was the gentlest he had ever been with her, and afterwards she lay with her cheek on his chest and her fingers spread on his heart.

“Tomorrow,” she said, nearly asleep, “I might be difficult.”

He smiled into her hair. “You’ve always been difficult.”

She pinched his side. He caught her hand and kissed her knuckles.

“Tomorrow you can be whatever you are,” he said.

“And you?”

“I’ll be here.”

“Not moving my things?”

“Not moving your things.”

She settled against him. “Good.”

He didn’t set an alarm for her. He didn’t plan the morning. He didn’t check whether there was enough in the fridge for her to take a lunch. He lay in the dark with her asleep on him and tried, for the first time in a month, to do nothing at all.

The report was out. It had answered almost nothing. The recorders still had their silence, and the families were still waiting, and six of his suits were still hanging in her wardrobe, and he knew it, and he knew that she knew it, and that it wasn’t over.

But in the dark he understood something he had been slow to learn. She wasn’t something fragile that had been given to him to look after. She wasn’t a crisis to be contained. She was a person who could stand in the middle of the worst thing he’d ever seen and still choose, every night, to come home to him.

He wanted to be someone she could come home to. Not someone she had to recover from.

chapters.title: The Break
chapters.desc: She asks for a break until the investigation’s done. He takes his toothbrush and leaves the fridge full. The flat goes very quiet.
chapters.epigraph: “You already did, at the table.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Song-Zhu noticed was that he’d stopped asking whether she’d be home for dinner.

The second was that she’d started to dread the sound of his key in her door.

Neither of them mentioned either. They’d got good, in eighteen days, at not mentioning things.

He still kissed her goodbye in the mornings, and asked first, every time, with his eyes if not out loud. She still sent him photographs of things she thought were funny, a pigeon on a fuel bowser, a sign in the canteen that said PLEASE DO NOT MICROWAVE FISH (THIS MEANS YOU, DEXTER). He still bought the groceries, and asked before he brought anything new into the flat, and had moved her hair clips out of the glass bowl and back to the shelf where she’d always kept them, and put the glass bowl away in a cupboard. She still slept beside him. Some nights with her back against his chest. Some nights on her own side, with a space between them that neither of them filled.

They were still together. They were also, a little more each day, becoming strangers in the gaps between their sentences.

The investigation was in its seventh week. The preliminary report had been out for eighteen days. The eleven seconds were still eleven seconds. The voice recording was still in its locked room, and the technical team was still working through what was on it, and none of it could be hurried because people wanted it hurried.

She was sleeping badly. She ate when she remembered. She’d begun to hate the sound of her own phone.

And Ren Hao, who had once been able to make her laugh with a toothbrush in her mouth, had started watching her as if every silence might be the one that meant something.

He was trying. She knew how hard. That was what made it impossible.

✦ ✦ ✦

*Saturday, 19 September, 7:18 p.m.* It was raining. She was standing at her kitchen counter reading a message from Director Kwan. The technical team wanted another review of a sequence. Two sets of recovered data didn’t agree with each other about something, by a fraction of a second, and they needed her to look at it before Monday’s internal briefing.

She read it twice. She put the phone down.

He was at the stove. “You’re not eating that?”

She looked at the bowl by her elbow. “I will.”

“It’s getting cold.”

“I know.”

He turned the heat off under the pan. “There’s more rice.”

She nodded. He waited. She picked up the spoon and ate two mouthfuls, and put the spoon down.

He was watching her. She could feel it on the side of her face like heat from a lamp.

“Is something wrong?” he said.

“No.”

He turned round.

She sighed. “Please don’t.”

He stopped. “Don’t what?”

“Look at me like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like you’re waiting for me to fall over.”

His face changed. “I wasn’t.”

“You were.”

He put the wooden spoon down on the side. “Song-Zhu.”

She shut her eyes. “I know. I’m sorry.”

He came a step closer, and didn’t touch her. “Did something happen at work?”

“No.”

“Is it the data? The sequence?”

“No.”

“Then tell me.”

She looked at him. And there it was again. The careful voice. The attention, turned all the way up. The questions that were meant to help, and that made her feel she had to produce a reason for every single thing her face did.

“I don’t know how to talk to you any more,” she said.

He went completely still.

She looked away at once. “That isn’t fair. I know it isn’t. I know you’re trying. I know you stopped doing every single thing I asked you to stop doing. You ask before you kiss me. You ask before you buy milk.” Her voice cracked. “But now I feel guilty every time I don’t answer you properly. I feel guilty when I don’t want dinner. I feel guilty when I come in and I don’t want to talk. I feel guilty when you ask if I’m all right and I say no, because I can see what it does to you.”

“You don’t have to feel guilty,” he said.

“I know I don’t.”

“Then why do you?”

“Because you look so frightened,” she said. “All the time. And I can’t...”

She pressed both palms flat on the counter.

“I can’t keep looking after your fear and do my job,” she said. “There isn’t enough of me.”

His face tightened. She saw it. She hated herself for it. But it was true.

✦ ✦ ✦

*7:43 p.m.* They sat at her dining table. The food went cold between them. He didn’t touch his. She folded her hands on the table.

“I think I need a break,” she said.

He looked at her. For a moment it was.

“A break.”

“Yes.”

“From work?”

She shook her head. “From us.”

The silence was so complete that she could hear the rain on the railing of the little balcony, one drop at a time.

“What does that mean?” he said.

“I don’t know. Not exactly.”

“Do you want to stop seeing me?”

“No.”

“Do you want me to move out?”

She looked down. “I want you to go home. To your own flat.”

He didn’t move.

She went on before she could lose her nerve. “Until the investigation’s done. Until I can think about something other than the aircraft and the recorders and the families and the eleven seconds. Until I can come in through that door without carrying the whole thing in with me, and you looking at me while I put it down.”

He listened to all of it.

“How long?”

“I don’t know.”

“Until the final report?”

She hesitated. It could be a year. It could be more. She knew what she was asking.

“I don’t know, Hao.”

He sat back, slightly, in the chair. “Are you asking me to wait?”

She looked at him. “I’m asking you to give me room.”

He nodded once. “All right,” he said.

She blinked.

He looked at the table. “All right.”

She hadn’t expected him to agree so fast. Not because she’d thought he’d refuse. Because she’d made herself ready for the argument. For the questions. For him to ask what he’d done, what he could change, what he could arrange instead, a list, a plan, a better plan. He didn’t. He just sat there.

She swallowed. “You don’t have to say yes straight away.”

He looked up. “Would you rather I argued?”

“No.”

“Then I don’t understand.”

She pressed her lips together. “I don’t want you to think this means I don’t love you.”

The word went between them across the table. She hadn’t said it before. Not once, not to him. Not like that, in a sentence, even sideways. She heard it leave her mouth and couldn’t take it back and didn’t want to, and it was the wrong moment, the worst moment, and she’d said it anyway, inside a don’t, folded small, where it would hurt least. He looked at her.

“Does it?” he said.

“No.”

“Then I believe you.”

Her eyes stung.

He looked down at his hands on the table. “How much room?”

“I don’t know.”

“Do you want no contact?”

She shook her head. “I don’t know that either.”

“Then we don’t have to decide all of it tonight,” said Ren Hao.

She looked at him. Even now, she thought. Even now he was giving her room.

“Can we just,” she said, “stop? For a while?”

He nodded. “Yes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

*8:06 p.m.* He went into the bedroom. She stayed at the table.

She heard the wardrobe door. A drawer. The sound of his overnight bag being lifted down off the top of the wardrobe, where it had been since August. She shut her eyes.

She hadn’t thought about the practical part. She’d thought about saying it. About the words, and how to get them out, and the relief she might feel afterwards, the room she’d have to breathe in.

She hadn’t thought about his toothbrush. Or the shirts. Or his slippers by the bed. Or the charger on his side.

She got up and went to the bedroom door.

He was taking clothes out of her wardrobe. Not many. Two shirts. Trousers. Socks. The grey jumper. He folded every single thing before he put it in the bag, precisely, corners to corners.

The six suits he left hanging on her rail.

She leaned on the door frame. “You don’t have to pack tonight.”

He looked at her. “I should take what I’ll need.”

“You can come back for the rest.”

“All right.” He went back to folding.

“You’re taking your running shoes.”

He looked down at them. “Yes.”

She nodded. He put them in the bag, soles together. Then he went past her, carefully, without touching her, into the bathroom. She followed him to the doorway.

He took his toothbrush out of the cup on the basin.

It was blue. Hers was white. They’d bought them together in a supermarket in March, the week she’d given him a key on a ring with a little plastic aeroplane on it, and she’d laughed in the aisle at how seriously he’d considered the colours.

He held it. Then he put it into a small washbag and zipped the washbag shut.

Something in her chest pulled hard, like a seat belt locking.

“You’re taking that,” she said.

He looked up. “Yes.”

“Right.”

She watched him put the washbag into the overnight bag. The toothbrush went inside it and was gone.

It was such a small thing. It shouldn’t have mattered at all.

It mattered more than anything else he’d packed. Because he wasn’t going on a business trip. He wasn’t going to his parents’ for a weekend. He wasn’t going to come back tomorrow and complain that she’d stolen his pillow while he was gone. He was going because she’d asked him to, and he was doing it properly, and he was taking his toothbrush because that was what leaving was.

✦ ✦ ✦

*8:31 p.m.* He came out of the bedroom with the bag and stopped by the kitchen.

“There’s food in the fridge.”

“I know.”

“I made enough for the week. They’re labelled.”

She didn’t say anything.

“The soup’s on the second shelf. The chicken’s in the small one. I’ve kept the greens separate so they won’t go soft...”

“Hao.”

He stopped. “Sorry.”

He looked at the fridge. And then, because he couldn’t help it, he opened it.

The shelves were full. Not like somebody stocking up for a typhoon. Like somebody who had spent the whole afternoon, while she was at work, making sure the person he loved would have something to eat on every evening he wasn’t there. Soup. Rice. Fish in a marinade. Greens. A tub of the yoghurt she liked. Her milk. And, in a paper bag on the bottom shelf, a dozen of the little mandarins she ate without thinking about it, one after another, the way other people ate crisps.

She looked at the full fridge and understood that he had cooked all of that knowing. Not knowing for certain. But knowing. He shut the door.

“You don’t have to finish it all,” he said.

She almost laughed. “Thank you.”

“And if there’s anything you don’t like, give it to Mrs. Kei next door.”

“Hao.”

He stopped again. He looked at the fridge door, and then at her, and gave a small, helpless smile.

“I’m still doing it,” he said.

“You’re still doing it.”

She came across the kitchen. She stood in front of him.

“Thank you for the food,” she said.

“You’re welcome.”

✦ ✦ ✦

*8:46 p.m.* His bag was by the door. His shoes were on. She stood a few steps away from him in her own hallway, beside the hooks where her coats hung and where once in June he’d kissed her against the wall until she couldn’t stand.

Neither of them knew what to do with their hands.

“Do you want me to ring you?” he said.

She shook her head. “Not tonight.”

“Tomorrow?”

“I don’t know.”

He nodded. “All right.”

He put his hand on the latch. Then he stopped.

“Song-Zhu.”

She looked up.

“I love you,” said Ren Hao. “I’m not saying it so you’ll feel guilty. I’m saying it so that you don’t think agreeing to this means I’ve stopped.”

Her face changed. She opened her mouth. He saw her try. He saw the word come up into her throat and stop there, the way it had stopped for fifteen months, the way it had stopped on a kitchen floor in September and on a beach in July and in a doorway in November. He saw her fight it. He saw her lose.

“You don’t have to,” he said gently. “You already did, at the table. Inside a don’t. I heard it.”

Her eyes filled all the way up. He looked as though he might come back the two steps across the hall. He didn’t. He picked up his bag. He opened the door.

“Hao.”

He turned. She wanted to say something. She didn’t know what. Don’t go. Please go. I’m sorry. I need you. All four of them were in her at once, all true, all of them pulling in different directions like the lines on the data, and none of them would come out.

What came out was: “Take care.”

His face went soft.

“You too,” he said.

And he went, and closed the door behind him, so quietly that she didn’t hear the latch.

✦ ✦ ✦

*9:02 p.m.* The flat was quiet. Not peaceful. Quiet.

She stood in the hall a long time listening to his footsteps going down the corridor. Then the lift. The doors opening, and closing. Then nothing at all.

She looked down. His slippers were by the shoe cabinet. He’d forgotten them.

She picked them up. She stood holding them. She thought about putting them in the cupboard. Then she put them back down where they’d been, beside hers, toes together, neatly.

She went into the bedroom. His side of the bed. His pillow. The shape of him still in the mattress. His charger, still plugged into the wall on his side, the lead coiled on the floor. She sat down on her side.

Her phone lit on the bedside table. Kwan again. The sequence. She read it, and put the phone in the drawer, and shut the drawer.

For the first time in seven weeks, nobody was waiting for her to answer anything. She had the whole evening. The whole flat. All the quiet she’d asked for. She hated it.

✦ ✦ ✦

*10:17 p.m.* She made tea and didn’t drink it.

She opened the fridge. The labels were in his capitals, on strips of masking tape.

SOUP — MON.
RICE — TUES.
FISH — COOK BY THURS!

She stood in the cold light of it a long time. Then she shut it.

His book was on the coffee table. Beside it was one of his work notebooks, the black ones he went through one a month. Not a diary. Meeting notes, dates, actions, his neat capitals marching down the page. She picked it up and opened it at the end.

On the last page there was a shopping list.

MILK. EGGS. MANDARINS. GINGER. HER TEA. SOUP THINGS. HER TEA (THE OTHER ONE).

She looked at the last line a long time. Then she put the notebook down, exactly where it had been, at exactly the same angle.

She sat on the sofa with the television off. There was no sound from the kitchen. No footsteps from the bedroom. No voice asking if she wanted anything. Nobody complaining that she’d left a spoon in the sink again. She’d wanted to be alone. Now she was.

She picked up her phone. She opened his name. She typed, Are you home? She looked at it. She deleted it.

✦ ✦ ✦

*Sunday, 20 September, 6:12 a.m.* She woke before the alarm and reached across the bed, and her hand found the cold empty side of it.

For a few seconds she didn’t remember. Then she did.

She went into the bathroom. The space in the cup where the blue toothbrush had been was much bigger than a toothbrush.

She brushed her teeth. She stood at the basin afterwards with her hands on the edge of it a long time.

She’d asked him to go. He’d gone. There was nothing unjust in it. Nothing anyone had done wrong. He’d done exactly what she’d asked, exactly the way she’d asked it.

She ran the tap and washed her face in cold water, and went to work.

✦ ✦ ✦

*Monday, 21 September, 8:40 p.m.* On the third evening she realised she hadn’t said a word to anybody outside work for nearly twelve hours.

She heated the soup. SOUP — MON. She sat at the table with it. It tasted exactly the way it had the night he’d made it, of ginger and too much care. She ate half and stopped. She looked at her phone. Nothing from him.

She wondered whether he was keeping to it on purpose. She wondered whether he was waiting. She wondered if he was eating. She wondered if he’d taken the blue toothbrush out of the washbag yet, or if it was still in there, in the bag, at the bottom of his wardrobe, because unpacking it would make it true.

She opened their conversation. The last message was his, from Saturday afternoon, before any of it.

Ren Hao: There’s a new box of your tea behind the old one. So you don’t run out.

She put her thumb on it. Then she locked the phone.

✦ ✦ ✦

*Wednesday, 23 September, 11:54 p.m.* She dreamed about the sea.

Not the accident, not the wreckage, or the grey blankets, or the boats. Only the sea. A long dark stretch of water under a low grey sky, moving, moving, and nothing on it at all.

She woke with her heart going so hard she couldn’t breathe. She sat up and pressed the heels of her hands into her eyes.

The room was dark. She reached for her phone. No messages. She didn’t know what she’d wanted. A photograph. A round dog. No reply needed.

She turned and looked at his side of the bed.

And for the first time since he’d gone, she cried. Not loudly, not for long. A few tears into the pillow, sideways, because she’d finally understood that the quiet wasn’t going to end by itself. It was what she’d asked for. And he was the only person in the world she knew for certain would give her exactly what she asked for, for as long as she asked.

✦ ✦ ✦

*Saturday, 26 September* On the Saturday afternoon, a week to the hour after he’d gone, Ren Hao was in his own flat on the other side of the harbour.

He’d unpacked. He’d made himself do it on the Sunday. The shirts in his wardrobe, where they’d always lived and where they now looked. The running shoes by the door. The blue toothbrush in a glass beside his own basin, where it looked like nothing at all. He’d been to work. He’d gone to meetings, and to the hotel on the airport road every day, and sat with a man from Room 214 while his mother told him a long story in a language Ren Hao didn’t speak, and nodded at the right places, because the interpreter said he was nodding at the right places.

He hadn’t rung her. Not once.

He’d nearly rung her on the Sunday morning, when a client had sent him a video of a dog falling into a swimming pool with enormous dignity. He’d nearly rung her on Tuesday evening, when his car went past the French restaurant with the candles. He’d nearly rung her on Thursday at three in the morning, when he’d woken and reached across the bed and his hand had found the cold, empty, enormous side of his own mattress, and he’d lain there for an hour with the phone on his chest.

But she’d asked for room. So he gave her room.

At night he opened their conversation sometimes and read the last few messages. He didn’t delete anything. He didn’t send anything. He didn’t ring Mabel to ask how she was. He didn’t ring Dexter. He didn’t ring Mr. Yau to ask whether she’d taken a taxi on Wednesday. He didn’t ring Isla, who was in Lima, and who’d have known from his voice in four seconds. He didn’t want to turn her asking for distance into one more problem he could find a way round.

He missed her. He loved her. And for the first time in his life, he had no plan for what to do with either of those things.

He sat on his own sofa, in his own flat, with nothing in his hands, and listened to his own fridge hum, and found out that it hummed in a different note from hers.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the seventh night she stood in her kitchen and opened the fridge.

It wasn’t full any more. Half a carton of milk. Two eggs. A small box of rice with THURS on it, which she’d have to throw away and wouldn’t. And in the paper bag on the bottom shelf, the last of the mandarins.

She took it out. She peeled it slowly at the counter, in one long spiral, the way her father had taught her when she was six, and looked at the empty shelf where the soup had been.

She thought about the blue toothbrush. The bag. The way he’d stood at the door and waited, and waited, and seen her try, and told her she’d already said it.

She had wanted quiet. She had wanted to hear her own thoughts. She had wanted to stop being watched. She’d got every single thing she’d asked for.

And the flat had gone so quiet that she could hear her fridge humming in E flat.

She sat down at the table with the mandarin. She ate one segment. Then another. Then another, slowly, until there weren’t any left, and there was nothing in her hand but the peel. Outside, it started to rain again.

She looked at the empty chair across the table.

And for the first time she understood that asking somebody to leave wasn’t the same as wanting them gone. She’d asked. And he’d listened, the way he always listened, all the way, to the end.

Now she’d have to work out what she wanted when she wasn’t asking out of exhaustion.

She didn’t know yet. She went into the bedroom, and opened the wardrobe, and stood there in the dark looking at six suits on her rail that nobody had come back for.

chapters.title: The Missing Eleven Seconds
chapters.desc: A cabin crew member’s phone from the seabed: the lights go out, the brace call, and the captain on the PA with his last words about his daughter. Alone in the laboratory, she finally cries.
chapters.epigraph: “Nobody calls these his last words.”
chapters.content:
At sixteen minutes past eight on Friday the ninth of October, a message came from the evidence laboratory. It was one sentence long.

A personal device recovered in the latest seabed search has completed initial assessment; your presence is requested for review.

She read it twice. Then she put the phone down on her desk and looked at the wall for several seconds without seeing it.

Sixty-eight days. The preliminary report had given no cause. Both recorders ended at the same instant, eleven seconds before the impact, and nobody in the building could tell her why. She had spent nine weeks going through timelines, comparing every source against every other, questioning every assumption anybody put in front of her, and refusing, over and over, to let anyone turn an absence of data into an explanation.

Now there was something else. Not a recorder. A phone. She picked up her notebook and went.

✦ ✦ ✦

*9:02 a.m.* It didn’t look like a phone any more.

It lay in a clear sealed box on the bench under the lights, its case bent into a shallow curve by the pressure of forty metres of water, the screen crazed into a hundred pieces, white salt crusted along every seam. The charging port was split. Part of the back had lifted away from the frame like a fingernail. A label beside it.

Device: personal mobile telephone.
Recovered: seabed sector 14, rear cabin debris field.
Found in: cabin crew uniform, inside jacket pocket.

She read the label before she looked at the phone again.

“Whose?”

Mr. Seto, the forensic specialist, a precise grey man who had been at the laboratory since before it had a name, looked at his notes. “One of the cabin crew. Au-Yeung Hiu-lam. Twenty-nine. Aft crew. Confirmed through the uniform and the identity card in the same pocket. Her family’s been told a device was recovered. Nothing about what’s on it.”

“Damage before impact?”

“Nothing I’d put my name to. It’s consistent with what the sea did. I won’t give you a sequence.”

“Preservation?”

“Photographed where it was found. Brought up in seawater. Never powered. Stabilised, dried under control, then the chips. Nobody switched anything on. I’ll give you every line of the log.”

“The storage?”

“Damaged. Some of it’s gone. We’ve taken a full forensic image of everything that can be read. The original’s sealed.” He moved to the workstation. “We found a video.”

She looked at him.

“Recorded during the flight. Damaged, but most of it can be put back together. Three minutes and nine seconds of picture. Then some sound after the picture stops.”

“Audio.”

“Recovered. We’re checking it against the original image.”

She pulled out a chair.

“Before you watch it,” said Mr. Seto, and didn’t open anything yet, “two things. The phone’s clock isn’t the aircraft’s clock. I can’t tell you it was right to the second. So whatever time it says on the file, that’s the phone’s opinion, not a fact. We’ll correlate it against the other evidence before we say anything.”

“Understood.”

“And it’s the cabin. Not the flight deck. It doesn’t show you a single instrument.”

“I understand.”

He nodded. Then he opened the file.

✦ ✦ ✦

*9:19 a.m.* Black, for the first two seconds. Then a picture, tilted. The ceiling of the aft galley, a curve of grey plastic and a strip of dimmed light. The image moved as though whoever held the phone had only just lifted it.

A woman’s voice, low, laughing. “Say it again. Say it for the camera.”

The picture turned. Two cabin crew on the rear jumpseats, side by side, strapped in for landing in their harnesses, the way they were supposed to be. The one on the left was holding a paper cup she should have given in twenty minutes ago. She was tired, and amused, and pretending to be offended.

“I said,” said the woman with the cup, “that if the captain wants a better coffee he can come back here and make it himself.”

The woman holding the phone laughed. Song-Zhu had heard the captain ask for coffee forty-one times. On the voice recording, twenty minutes before the end. Is there any chance of a coffee that isn’t burnt? And the first officer had laughed and said he’d ask the back. The back had answered.

For a moment Song-Zhu forgot what she was watching. There was a life in it. Two women at work at four in the morning, at the end of a long night, with a paper cup, making a joke for somebody’s sister to see later. A voice behind the camera saying it’s for Mei-mei, she says we never do anything fun. The cabin dim behind them, rows of sleeping heads in the gap of the curtain, a reading light on halfway down.

Then a sound. It came through the phone’s tiny microphone as a deep, short thump, more felt than heard, from somewhere under the floor. The cup jumped in the woman’s hand. Both their heads went up.

Song-Zhu knew that sound. She’d heard it forty-one times. The sound in the airframe she couldn’t name, on the voice recording, in the last second before it stopped.

“What was that?” said the woman with the cup.

The picture shook. And the lights went out. All of them. The galley strip, the cabin lights beyond the curtain, the reading light halfway down. For one moment the screen was nearly black. Then, a second later, small and low, the emergency lighting came on along the floor of the aisle, in a line of dull points like a landing strip at night. Song-Zhu sat absolutely still.

“Stop,” she said. “Go back. Five seconds.”

Mr. Seto went back. The thump. The cup jumping. What was that. The lights going.

“Again.”

He played it again.

“The lights,” she said. “The cabin lights. Every one. At once.”

“Yes.”

“And the floor lighting. A second after.”

“About a second. On the phone’s count.”

She didn’t say anything else. She didn’t need to. Everyone in the room had read the recorder installation diagram for this aircraft type. Everyone knew which electrical supply the cabin lighting was on, and which supply fed the two recorders, and which one the emergency floor lighting ran from instead. She wrote one line in her notebook, small, and boxed it.

Cabin lights + recorders: same moment? CORRELATE. DO NOT SAY IT YET.

“Go on,” she said.

The picture swung about in the dark. Somebody further down the cabin said something sharp. A child began to cry. The woman with the phone said, fast, Brace position, we’ll be told, we’ll be told, and the other woman said put that away, Hiu-lam, put it away and didn’t put her own cup down. Then a chime. The PA.

A man’s voice through the cabin speakers. The captain. Calm, with something underneath it, like a wire pulled tight.

“Cabin crew, this is the captain. Brace, brace, brace.”

The crew on the jumpseats shouted it at once, both of them, the words they’d been trained to shout a thousand times and never once had to. Brace! Brace! Heads down! Stay down! The camera fell, pointing at the floor, at the dull line of the emergency lights, at the woman’s black shoes braced against the floor.

And the picture broke up into blocks of grey and green, and froze, and stopped. The room didn’t breathe.

“That’s the end of the picture,” said Mr. Seto. “Three minutes nine.”

“Is that the end of the file?”

“No.” He brought up a second window. “After the picture stops there’s damage. The video’s gone. But some of the audio packets survived, further on in the file. They belong to the same recording. I can’t tell you yet that there are no gaps in them.”

“How long?”

“Twenty-two seconds. With holes.”

“Play it.”

He did. Noise at first. A roaring, rushing, enormous noise that wasn’t any one thing. Then, inside it, the cabin. The two crew still shouting, hoarse now, heads down, stay down. The child crying. Somebody praying, in a language Song-Zhu didn’t speak. Something falling and striking the floor again and again. And then the PA chime. Again. The captain.

“Brace. Brace. Stay down.” A breath. Close to the microphone. Much closer than before.

And then, low, underneath the roar, a sentence that wasn’t an announcement at all. A sentence that sounded. Or remembered, and not taken it off.

“Tell my little girl...”

The rest went under a long rasp of distortion. Mr. Seto stopped it. Song-Zhu didn’t move.

“Again,” she said.

He played it.

Tell my little girl...

Distortion.

She leaned towards the speaker. “There’s more.”

“There’s more,” Mr. Seto agreed. “In the packets after. Damaged.”

“Can you separate it?”

“I can try. I won’t make it clearer than the data is.”

“I’m not asking you to.”

He looked at her. “Do you want a minute?”

“No,” said Song-Zhu. “Get the audio specialist.”

✦ ✦ ✦

*10:07 a.m.* They went through it the proper way, the only way, with the audio specialist in the third chair and every step written down as they took it.

The raw packets first. Then the isolated channel, the PA speaker separated as far as it would separate from the cabin around it. Then the processed version, with the specialist explaining every filter, what he had taken out, and what he had left alone.

The sentence came up out of the noise a piece at a time. A few words. A breath. A gap where the data simply wasn’t. Then his voice again, close, tired, gentle, a voice she’d heard asking for a coffee that wasn’t burnt.

“Tell my little girl...”

The specialist moved a slider by a millimetre.

“...Daddy tried.”

Then the roar. Then nothing. The end of the file. The room had no air left in it.

The specialist took his hand off the controls and put it in his lap.

“That’s the best we’ll get from what’s there,” he said.

Song-Zhu looked at the waveform on the screen. A small dense cluster. Two words.

“Can you confirm those words?”

“I can tell you the processed audio is consistent with that reading. I can tell you I’ve heard it fifty times this morning before you came in, and I hear the same thing each time. But the segment’s damaged. The processing has to be documented, and the original kept, and nobody gets to call what I’ve made a clean recording. It isn’t one.”

She nodded. “Understood.”

She wrote, in the notebook, slowly, in the plainest words she had.

Recovered cabin audio contains speech over the PA, attributed to the captain. Processed audio consistent with: “Tell my little girl . . . Daddy tried.” Reading subject to further verification. Original preserved.

She stopped. She read it. She added a line underneath.

Timing relative to end of recorders NOT YET ESTABLISHED. Correlate via airframe sound (CVR / phone) and cabin lighting.

The specialist looked at her notes over her shoulder. “That second line matters.”

“Yes.”

“Do we know this is the last thing he said?”

“No,” said Song-Zhu. “We know it’s the last thing that can be heard on this phone. We don’t know what he said on the flight deck after that. We may never know.” She looked at the screen. “Nobody calls these his last words. Not in this room, not in a report. Not until we can prove there was nothing after.”

“Agreed.”

She saved the notes. Her handwriting was perfectly neat. Her face was perfectly still. She’d spent her whole working life learning that an investigator couldn’t afford to mix up what she felt with what the evidence showed. She knew exactly where the line ran. She knew the limitations. She knew what could be said and what couldn’t. She couldn’t stop hearing it.

Tell my little girl.

Daddy tried.

✦ ✦ ✦

*10:41 a.m.*

“Song-Zhu.”

Mr. Seto was standing by the bench with a clipboard. “I need your signature on the review record. The extraction report goes round in the usual way when the technical assessment’s done.”

She took it. She read every line. Device reference. Recovery. Examination dates. Method. Integrity. Limitations. She checked each one twice, because that was the job, and signed at the bottom.

He looked at her. “Are you all right?”

It was an ordinary question. She looked back at him.

“Yes,” she said.

He didn’t believe her. He didn’t push. The laboratory went back to its own rhythm round her: keys clicking, low voices, a printer, the soft hum of the drying cabinets. The audio specialist was already talking to Mr. Seto about the next packets. She picked up her notebook and walked out.

She got as far as the corridor before she stopped.

She looked down at the open page in her hand. The sentence was there, in her own writing.

It looked so much smaller than it had sounded.

✦ ✦ ✦

*11:16 a.m.* There were three emails in her office. The technical lead. Director Kwan. The family liaison officer.

She answered the technical lead first. Two corrections, one question about the processing method. She answered Kwan second: a short summary, and a request, in plain words, that nothing about the recording, no interpretation of anything on it, go one inch beyond the authorised team until it had been formally documented and correlated. She opened the third.

The liaison officer wanted to know whether there was anything on the recovered device that could be shared with Au-Yeung Hiu-lam’s family. She looked at it a long time.

She thought about a voice behind a camera saying it’s for Mei-mei, she says we never do anything fun. She thought about a younger sister somewhere in the city who had been waiting since August for a clip of two tired women and a paper cup. She began to type.

The device contains recoverable personal material. Some of it may be returned to the family once it has been examined and separated from material relevant to the investigation. Please let them know, gently, that there is a short recording made by Ms. Au-Yeung for her sister during the flight, and that when we can, we will make sure her sister receives the part of it that was meant for her.

She sent it. She sat back in her chair.

Her eyes went to the notebook. She opened it. Tell my little girl. Daddy tried. She closed it. She opened it again. She couldn’t seem to stop.

✦ ✦ ✦

*12:03 p.m.*

Dexter put his head round her door. “You coming down?”

She looked up. “Sorry?”

“Lunch. It’s Friday. It’s the fish. You like the fish.”

“No. Thanks.”

He looked at her longer than Dexter ever looked at anything. “Eat something, boss.”

“I will.”

The door closed. She looked at the container on her desk that she’d brought from home. Rice, an egg, greens. She’d made it herself last night at eleven, in her own kitchen, standing up, the way he’d shown her in August.

She opened it. The smell made her feel sick. She closed it again.

She went to the window. The city was carrying on exactly as it did. Traffic. People on the crossings. A delivery rider waiting at the lights with his foot down, looking at his phone. Somewhere someone was late for a meeting.

Somewhere a little girl was waiting for her father to come home. Song-Zhu put her fingertips on the glass.

She had the crew file. She could have looked. She could have found out the girl’s name, her age, which school. Whether he’d promised to bring her anything back. Whether she’d sent him a message that night before he flew, and whether he’d read it in the crew room, and whether he’d answered.

She didn’t look. She had no right to know any of it yet, and no right at all to invent it. She went back to her desk, and worked.

✦ ✦ ✦

*3:38 p.m.* By the afternoon she had the first correlations.

The airframe sound on the phone and the airframe sound on the voice recorder were the same event. The specialist was certain of it, and could show why. On the voice recorder, the sound came nine-tenths of a second before both recorders stopped. On the phone, the cabin lights went out a little under a second after the same sound.

Within the margin of the phone’s clock, the cabin lights and the two recorders had gone at the same moment.

Which meant that for the eleven seconds after that moment, she had something nobody had had for sixty-eight days. Not the flight deck, not a single instrument. But the inside of the aircraft. The dark. The floor lights. The crew shouting the brace. And the captain on the PA, which ran from a different supply, still there, still talking, still doing his job, all the way down.

It didn’t give a cause. It didn’t tell her what had made that sound under the floor, or why the power had gone, or whether anything could have been done in eleven seconds at four hundred feet over the sea. It didn’t tell her what the two men on the flight deck had said to each other once their own recorder had stopped listening.

But for the first time, the eleven seconds weren’t empty.

She wrote the next steps into her notebook. The electrical supplies. The wiring in the area under the floor. The components from that area that had been brought up, and the ones that hadn’t. The maintenance history of every single part in it, back to the last heavy check, and who had signed for each one. At the bottom of the page she wrote:

Can the PA speech be attributed to the captain with enough confidence for the investigation record?

She underlined it once. Then again. Her phone buzzed.

Director Kwan: I’ve seen your summary. Take what time you need with it this weekend. We’ll talk on Monday. Well done.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Understood. Findings and limitations are documented. Notes will be with you before the briefing.

She put the phone down. She could still hear him. Not the brace, not the roar. Just the two words at the end.

✦ ✦ ✦

*6:27 p.m.* The building had mostly emptied. She went back down to the laboratory for her copy of the review record.

Mr. Seto was still there. He handed her a sealed envelope.

“Everything’s logged. The processing record’s attached. The original audio’s preserved separately. Nothing in the processed version will ever stand in for it.”

“Good. Thank you.”

He took his coat from the hook. He stopped at the door, with it over his arm.

“Song-Zhu.”

“Yes?”

He seemed to choose the words carefully.

“I know you hear a great deal in this job. I’ve watched you hear it for four years. But you don’t have to take every sentence home.”

She looked at him. For a moment she couldn’t answer.

“I know,” she said.

He nodded, and went, and the door sighed shut behind him on its closer, and she was alone in the laboratory.

✦ ✦ ✦

She should have gone home. She’d been in the building since seven. The notes could wait till Monday. The next review was booked. The evidence was preserved and the findings written down, every one, in the right words. There was nothing else that needed doing tonight.

She didn’t go. She sat down in the third chair, the specialist’s chair, in front of the dark workstation, with the sealed box on the bench beside her and the crumpled phone in it under the lights. She opened her notebook to a clean page.

She wrote: The recovered cabin audio contains speech attributed to the captain.

She stopped. The pen hung over the page. She tried again.

The captain’s last words were

She crossed it out. That wasn’t what the evidence showed. She knew better. She’d told a room full of people that morning that she knew better.

She wrote: The last identifiable speech on the recovered device

Her hand had started to shake. She put the pen down. She looked at the page. At the phone in its box. At the dark screen where the waveform had been.

Daddy tried.

Something in her face went. She pressed her lips together hard. She tried to breathe through it, the way she’d breathed through sixty-eight days, through the helicopter footage and the grey blankets, through the little boy on the bed and the man with the soft folded report, through Mrs. Ting’s blue exercise book. It had always worked. It didn’t work. She put her hand over her mouth.

The first sound that came out of her was so small she hardly recognised it as hers. Then another. She bent forward over the bench until her forehead was almost on it, with her hand pressed over her mouth, and her shoulders started to shake, and she couldn’t make them stop.

She wasn’t crying because she’d found the cause. She hadn’t.

She wasn’t crying because it was over. It wasn’t over.

She was crying because, after nine weeks of listening to silence, she had heard a father talk about his daughter. A man with a hundred and seventy-nine other people behind him in the dark, still on the PA, still saying brace, still doing everything he’d been trained to do with eleven seconds and no power and the sea coming up. And at the very end of it, still someone’s father. Still somebody’s person. A man with a little girl at home, who had known, at four hundred feet, that he wasn’t going to get there.

And had tried anyway. And had wanted her told that he had.

And underneath that, much further down, a nineteen-year-old in a room in another country, with fifty seconds of her own father’s voice on a laptop, listening as hard as she had ever listened to anything, for her name. And not hearing it.

He hadn’t said her name. He’d been flying an aeroplane. But maybe he’d thought it.

She cried until her throat hurt. She cried with her face on her arm on the laboratory bench, under the bright lights, beside a crumpled phone in a sealed box, for the captain, and for the little girl, and for Au-Yeung Hiu-lam’s sister who’d been promised something fun, and for a hundred and eighty people, and for her father, and for herself, because there was nobody in the building to see her.

No family waiting. No colleague needing her to know what it meant. No Director Kwan needing her composed at a lectern. No Ren Hao standing in a doorway trying not to ask whether she’d eaten.

Only the bench. The notebook. The box. And the sentence.

✦ ✦ ✦

*8:02 p.m.* When she lifted her head the laboratory lights had gone to their night setting, half-dim.

She wiped her face with the heel of her hand, and then with a paper towel from the dispenser by the sink, and her eyes were swollen and her breath kept catching.

She sat a long time. Then she took out her phone.

She opened his name. Their last messages were still there, exactly as they’d been. There’s a new box of your tea behind the old one. Her photograph of a pigeon. The ordinary conversation from before she’d asked him to go. She looked at his name.

She wanted to ring him. Not so he’d fix anything, not so he’d tell her what to do. She wanted to hear his voice. She wanted to tell him what she’d heard. She wanted him to know she’d cried, at last, after sixty-eight days, on her own, on a bench, and that she’d needed to, and that it had been the first honest thing her body had done since August.

But she remembered the break. She remembered him packing the blue toothbrush. The full fridge. The door. You don’t have to. You already did.

She’d asked him for room. He’d given her every inch of it.

Her thumb hung over his name. Then it moved away. She opened a message instead.

I heard something today.

She looked at it. She deleted it.

There was a father on that plane.

She deleted that too. She couldn’t put it in a message. She didn’t know yet whether she could put it into words at all.

She locked the phone and put it on the bench beside the notebook and sat in the half-dark with both.

✦ ✦ ✦

At a quarter to nine she left the building. The corridor lights were dimmed. She carried her bag in one hand and the sealed envelope in the other.

Outside, the rain had stopped. She stood under the canopy over the entrance and breathed the wet air.

She looked at her phone. Nothing. She hadn’t expected anything. She hadn’t asked for anything.

She put it away and walked towards the road.

At home the flat would be quiet. The cup on the basin would still have one toothbrush in it. The other pillow would still be empty. Six suits would still be hanging on her rail. She’d open the fridge and heat something and probably not finish it.

Tomorrow she’d go back in, Saturday or not. She’d check the audio. She’d chase the electrical supplies and the components under that floor and every signature on every one of them.
