She’d make sure nobody in the building said one word more about any of it than the evidence would hold. She’d do her job.

But tonight she’d heard a father try to say goodbye to his little girl. And for the first time since the second of August, she’d let herself cry about it. Not as an investigator, not as the person in charge. Only as a woman who had heard a father miss his child, and had wished, for one terrible minute in an empty laboratory, that she could have given him back eleven seconds. Or eleven more.

And who had heard, at last, what was in them.

chapters.title: The Report
chapters.desc: The interim statement names a maintenance failure. The airline’s owner asks Ren Hao to ring her; he refuses and reports it. His client turns on her in the press. Two days earlier he paid for Wei Long’s seat to Lima.
chapters.epigraph: “Then don’t help it happen by pretending the finding isn’t there.”
chapters.content:
At forty-two minutes past six on Monday the nineteenth of October, a message came in from the man who owned the airline.

We need to speak before the statement is released.

Ren Hao was already awake. He’d been awake since seventeen minutes past four, in his own kitchen on the wrong side of the harbour, with a cup of coffee in his hand that had gone cold an hour ago. Outside, the city was still dark.

He knew there was going to be a statement this morning. Everybody in the city who read a newspaper knew there was going to be a statement this morning. The authority had announced it on Friday: an interim statement, ten weeks after the accident, a little after nine.

He didn’t know what was in it. He’d made sure he didn’t. Under the rules, the operator would have been sent the draft over the weekend, in confidence, to check for factual errors, and the operator was a client of his firm, and the draft would be sitting at this moment on Raymond’s desk, and on Kong’s, and on the desks of three people on the twenty-ninth floor whose names he knew. It wasn’t on his. He’d built the wall himself at five past five on the second of August and tightened it on the twenty-fifth, and he hadn’t put a finger through it once in ten weeks.

His phone buzzed again.

Ring me. Now.

He looked at the clock. Forty-four minutes past six. He rang.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You’re up.”

“I’m here.”

“You’ve seen it.”

“No,” said Ren Hao. “I haven’t. I’m not permitted to see it. Raymond has it. You know that. You signed the letter.”

“Then I’ll tell you what it says.” The voice on the line was the same voice that had rung him three times in October a year ago, and a little after five on the second of August, and it had lost every ounce of its usual ease. “It says maintenance failure. It says a part was put into our aircraft at its last heavy check that wasn’t what the paperwork said it was. It says that’s why the power went. It says that’s why the recorders stopped. It will be on every screen in the city by ten o’clock, Ren, with our name in the same sentence.”

Ren Hao said nothing. He hadn’t known. Now he did. He wrote down the time, and owner told me content of draft, unsolicited, on the pad by the kettle.

“We’ve co-operated with them for ten weeks,” said the owner. “We’ve given them every record. Our people have sat in their rooms. And now they’re going to put the whole airline on trial in front of the world before they’ve even finished.”

“It’s an interim statement. It’s what they’ve established so far.”

“Don’t give me vocabulary.”

“Vocabulary matters,” said Ren Hao, “when you’re talking about an investigation.”

“Ren.” The voice changed again. It wasn’t a client asking for advice any more. It was a man looking for anyone at all who could stop a thing he couldn’t. “Ring her.”

Ren Hao looked at the window. The first grey was in the sky over the water.

“Who?”

“You know who. You know her. Ask her to hold it. Two days. Twenty-four hours. Ask her to look at the wording again. Just ask her.”

“No.”

A silence on the line.

“I’m sorry?”

“No. I won’t ring her about the investigation. Not this morning, not ever. I won’t ask her to hold anything, look at anything, change anything. I’m not going to use a person to lean on an independent report. And I’m going to tell Kong, and Raymond, and the authority, before nine o’clock, that you asked me to.”

“You’ll what?”

“That’s what the letter you signed in August says I have to do if anyone approaches me about the investigation. Including you. Above all you.”

“I’m not asking you to interfere...”

“You’re asking me to use the woman I love to change the timing or the content of a statement about the deaths of a hundred and eighty people,” said Ren Hao, and his voice had gone quiet. “I’m not going to do it.”

“Then what am I paying you for?”

“For the families. That’s what I’m on your account for. That’s all I’m on it for. Raymond’s on it for the rest. He’ll tell you what he told you on Saturday, I imagine, because I’ve worked with him for six years and I know what he’d tell you: acknowledge it. Don’t dispute what you can’t disprove. Say what you’ve done. Say you’ll co-operate. Look after the families first.”

“And if the finding’s wrong?”

“Then you challenge it the proper way, with evidence, later. Not at a lectern this morning.”

“And if we’re destroyed before later comes?”

“Then don’t help it happen by pretending the finding isn’t there.”

The line was silent.

“I hope you understand,” said the owner at last, precisely, “what this does to our relationship.”

Ren Hao looked at the clock on the oven. Two minutes to seven.

“I do,” he said.

He rang off. He sat for a few seconds without moving.

Then he wrote a full note of the call, timed, word for word as nearly as he could remember it, and sent it a little after seven to Kong and to Raymond and to the compliance head, and, under the terms of the letter of the twenty-fifth of August, to Director Kwan, with one line above it.

Reported as required: an approach this morning from the client asking me to contact the investigator-in-charge. Declined. Full note below.

Then he picked up the cold coffee and poured it down the sink and went to have a shower, and stood under it a long time, and thought about Saturday.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday he had rung Wei Long at a quarter past one.

He’d been awake since five. He’d spent the morning on the phone to two people at the ministry, one airline, and a man in a call centre who seemed to believe the operating status of an airport was a state secret, because his sister was in Lima, where on Thursday the ground had moved and a city had come down, and Isla had rung Wei Long at last on Friday from a satellite phone in the embassy’s shelter, two minutes and eleven seconds, and was alive, and wasn’t coming home, because she was the consulate and the consulate was needed.

And Wei Long was going. Of course he was going. And hadn’t, by a quarter past one on Saturday, booked anything at all.

“Where are you?”

“Home.”

“Don’t move. I’m coming over.”

He’d been there in twenty-three minutes, with a laptop and a coffee, and had walked into Wei Long’s flat and seen the dining table: the travel advisories, the pad, the itineraries in that small square handwriting with every connection time underlined. Three routes, compared. Not one booked.

There’d been one seat. One. Business class, five to midnight that night, through the Pacific hub, into Lima at half past twelve the next afternoon, their time. He’d found it at eleven and been watching it since, like a man watching a glass on the edge of a table.

“I can go economy,” Wei Long had said.

“Then go economy next time. I’m paying.”

“I can pay for my own ticket.”

“I know you can. I’m paying.”

And Wei Long had put out his hand and caught Ren Hao’s wrist over the laptop keys, and held it, and neither of them had said anything at all.

“Let me do this,” Ren Hao had said. “Please. I need to fix something. Let it be this.”

He’d heard his own voice go quiet, the way it never went. Wei Long had let go.

And afterwards, sitting at that dining table with the booking reference on the screen and his own phone lighting up twice beside his coffee, the owner’s name both times, and both times turning it over on the table so he wouldn’t have to see it, he’d told Wei Long. He hadn’t meant to. He’d told nobody. Not Isla, who was in a shelter in an earthquake and didn’t need it. Not his parents, not Raymond, though Raymond knew.

Song-Zhu and I are on a break. Since the nineteenth of September.

And Wei Long hadn’t asked why. And Ren Hao had told him anyway. The crash. The eleven seconds. The organising. She told me she was my girlfriend and not my equipment. She was right. It sounds familiar, Wei Long had said.

And Ren Hao had laughed, once, for the first time in a month, at a dining table covered in a careful man’s itineraries, because it did.

✦ ✦ ✦

*9:23 a.m.* Song-Zhu was in the main conference room at the authority when the statement went out. She’d read it for the last time at eleven the night before, and again at seven that morning, and she knew every word.

She knew what it said. She knew, even better, what it didn’t.

It said that the investigation had established that the aircraft’s normal electrical power had been lost approximately eleven seconds before impact, and that this was why both flight recorders had stopped at the same instant. It said that evidence recovered from the cabin, and from the wreckage, had made that possible to establish. It said that a component of the electrical distribution system, recovered from beneath the cabin floor, had been installed at the aircraft’s last heavy maintenance check, eleven months before, and that the component recovered didn’t match the record of its installation, and showed signs of previous service that the record didn’t mention. It said that this was a significant finding concerning the maintenance of the aircraft. It said that the investigation was continuing, into the component, into how it had come to be fitted, into the organisation that had fitted it, and into everything else.

It didn’t say that the investigation had established every factor. It didn’t say why the component had failed when it did. It didn’t say what had been said on the flight deck after the recorders stopped, or anything about the voice recording at all beyond the fact that it existed and was being examined. It didn’t mention a cabin crew member’s phone, or a paper cup, or two words at the end of a long roar.

It didn’t give the families everything they needed. But it was the first time anyone with the authority to say it had named a failure. And she knew the word failure would travel faster and further than every careful clause she’d built round it.

Director Kwan stood at the head of the table. “Before we talk about the media, I want this clear in every head in this room. This isn’t the final report. We aren’t blaming any individual. We’re saying what we’ve established. That’s all.”

“Understood,” said Song-Zhu.

“Will the airline dispute it?” said Leong, by the wall.

“Almost certainly.”

“And if they say the maintenance records we were given are incomplete?”

“Then they can show us, through the formal process. We don’t run this investigation through the newspapers.” Kwan looked at her. “Song-Zhu.”

She looked up. “The wording stays the same in every briefing, from everyone. A maintenance finding has been identified. That isn’t the same as everything’s been explained, and we can’t let the public conversation squash the two together. It’ll try.”

“Agreed. And the cabin recording?”

“It’s in the evidence inventory and nowhere else. The personal material on it stays out of the public domain. There’s a woman’s sister who’s going to get a clip of a paper cup, and a little girl who’ll be told something by somebody kinder than a newsreader, and neither of those things is going to be in a headline.” She heard her own voice and was surprised how steady it was. “Not while I’m in charge of it.”

Kwan held her eye. “Good.”

✦ ✦ ✦

*9:47 a.m.* The first headline came up twenty-four minutes later.

CRASH INQUIRY FINDS MAINTENANCE FAILURE

The second was sharper.

180 DEAD: AIRLINE’S MAINTENANCE IN THE DOCK

The third had given up on the difference between a finding and a verdict altogether.

WHO PUT THE FAULTY PART IN FLIGHT 7-?

She read them on her screen. She didn’t open any of them. Her phone started going. The press office. A colleague. The press office again.

She put the phone in the top drawer of her desk and closed it.

Kwan appeared in her doorway. “The airline’s holding a press conference.”

“When?”

“Eleven.”

She nodded.

He looked at her. “Don’t watch it.”

“I need to know what they say.”

“You need to know what they say about the investigation. You don’t need to sit through every accusation they make on the way.”

“I’ll monitor what’s relevant.”

He looked as though he might say something else. Then he said, instead: “He reported it. Did you know? At eleven minutes past seven this morning, in writing. Mr. Ren. The owner rang him before six and asked him to ring you and ask you to hold the statement. He refused. And then he sent me the whole call, word for word, timed, before I’d had my breakfast.”

She went still.

“I thought you ought to know that,” said Director Kwan, “before you see whatever you’re going to see today.” And he went.

She sat at her desk a long time looking at the closed drawer.

✦ ✦ ✦

*10:58 a.m.* At the hotel on the airport road, there was a television in the lobby on the wall above the reception desk, and somebody had turned it to the news channel at a quarter to eleven, and turned it up.

Ren Hao was in the lobby, by the desk, with two of his people and the airline’s family-assistance manager, going through the morning’s room changes. By five to eleven nobody in the lobby was going through anything. There were forty people in it. Most of them were families. They had stopped where they were standing and turned to the screen.

Mrs. Ting was by the window with her blue exercise book.

The man with the fruit was in a chair by the door.

On the screen, the airline’s chief executive stood at a lectern with two directors beside him. And at the back of the stage, half in shadow, not speaking, the owner.

Ren Hao looked at the owner’s face on the screen. Then at Mrs. Ting’s.

The chief executive began with the airline’s commitment to safety. It was a good paragraph. Raymond’s team had written it. Ren Hao recognised the rhythm of it.

Then he turned a page that Raymond’s team hadn’t written.

“We are deeply concerned by the interim statement released this morning. While we respect the work of the investigating authority, we believe the public should be cautious about accepting conclusions before the full investigation is complete.”

Ren Hao shut his eyes.

“We have provided extensive maintenance documentation. We are confident that our maintenance programme followed every established procedure.”

A journalist: “Are you disputing the finding?”

“We are questioning whether the finding is complete enough to be presented as an explanation.”

“Did your maintenance fail?”

A pause. “We don’t accept that characterisation.”

The lobby had gone completely silent. And then a journalist near the front asked the question that Ren Hao, if he’d been allowed anywhere near the preparation, would have spent three days making sure nobody on that stage would answer.

“Do you believe the investigators have been influenced by pressure from the victims’ families?”

The chief executive frowned. “We believe any investigation must remain independent of public emotion.”

In the lobby, somebody made a sound.

“Are you saying the families influenced the finding?”

“I’m saying that the investigation must be based on technical evidence, and not on public pressure.”

By the window, Mrs. Ting closed her blue exercise book. She stood up. She didn’t say anything. She walked across the lobby, past the reception desk, past the television, past Ren Hao, and out through the glass doors into the car park, and didn’t look back.

The man with the fruit put his face in his hands.

A woman by the lifts said, quite clearly, to nobody, “Public emotion.”

Ren Hao stood in the middle of the lobby with his list of room changes in his hand. Ten weeks. Interpreters, hotels, belongings, one named person for every family, a hundred and eighty letters with the report enclosed so nobody had to read a summary, every phone call returned. Ten weeks of making that building into somewhere people could bear to be.

The chief executive had taken it apart in nine words.

“Turn it off,” he said.

The airline’s manager looked at him. “Mr. Ren...”

“Turn it off.”

Somebody turned it off. He walked out of the glass doors after Mrs. Ting. He found her standing by the low brick wall at the back, by the bins, where Song-Zhu had sat in August. She was holding the exercise book against her chest with both arms.

“Mrs. Ting.”

She looked at him. She knew exactly who he was. Everybody in that hotel knew who he was.

“Don’t,” she said. “You work for them.”

“I work for you,” said Ren Hao. “In there. That’s all I’ve done for ten weeks. And I didn’t write that. And I’m sorry that anybody said it in a room you were standing in.”

She looked at him. “Is it true?” she said. “What they said this morning? The investigators? About the part?”

“I don’t know what’s in the investigation,” he said. “I’ve made sure I don’t. But I know who’s leading it. And she has never once in her life said a thing she couldn’t prove.”

Mrs. Ting looked down at the exercise book.

“No,” she said at last. “She hasn’t.”

✦ ✦ ✦

*11:34 a.m.* The owner rang before the press conference had finished. Ren Hao answered by the bins.

“That,” said Ren Hao, before the owner had spoken, “was not what Raymond advised.”

“I know what Raymond advised.”

“Then why...”

“Because I won’t stand there and take the blame for something we haven’t been given the chance to answer.”

“You weren’t asked to take the blame for anything. You were asked to acknowledge a finding.”

“They’re blaming us.”

“They’ve identified a maintenance failure.”

“It’s the same thing.”

“No,” said Ren Hao. “It isn’t. And you’ve just told forty families in my hotel that their grief is contaminating the evidence. One of them walked out. I’m standing beside her bin.”

The owner’s voice rose. “Don’t lecture me.”

“I’m not lecturing you. I’m telling you what you’ve done. You’ve made your airline look as though it won’t face what’s been found. You’ve questioned the independence of the people investigating it. You’ve told the families they’re the problem. And you’ve thrown away ten weeks of work by people who were trying to look after them in your name.”

“You’re protecting her.”

The car park was quiet. A plane went over, low, coming in on the approach, and the noise of it filled everything for several seconds and then went.

“Don’t,” said Ren Hao.

“Don’t what?”

“Bring her into this.”

“She is this. She’s the one who issued it.”

“She’s the investigator-in-charge. She isn’t your communications problem.”

“She’s made us look incompetent in front of the whole world.”

“She’s issued a finding based on evidence.”

“Your girlfriend.”

Ren Hao’s hand closed on the phone. “Don’t use my relationship with her to discredit that report.”

“Perhaps you should have thought of that before you took our money.”

There was a silence.

“Everything about it was declared,” said Ren Hao. “In writing. To you, to her authority, to my firm, on the morning of the crash. You’ve got copies. You signed them.”

“Don’t be clever.”

“I’m not being clever.”

“Your firm was supposed to stand with us.”

“My firm,” said Ren Hao, slowly, “is here to advise you. We are not here to manufacture a version of events that the evidence doesn’t support. And I’m not here at all except for the people in that building.”

The owner hung up. Ren Hao kept the phone at his ear for one more second. Then he lowered it, and wrote down the time, and went back inside to find a family-assistance manager and forty people who needed lunch.

✦ ✦ ✦

*12:18 p.m.* Raymond rang him a little after twelve.

“Have you seen it?”

“Seen what?”

“I’m sending it now.”

It came through. A website first; two of the papers would have it by the evening editions.

CRASH INVESTIGATOR IN RELATIONSHIP WITH AIRLINE’S CRISIS CONSULTANT
Questions over possible conflict of interest

Ren Hao read it standing in the hotel corridor.

There was no evidence in it that she’d ever shared anything with him. There was no evidence that he’d influenced anything. There was no evidence that either of them had ever done anything wrong at all. It rested entirely on the two facts that they had been together, and that his firm had been retained by the airline. There was a photograph of the two of them at the taxi rank outside the French restaurant, kissing, that someone had taken on a phone in June 2025 and kept. And there was one line, three paragraphs down, that he read four times.

A person close to the airline said the relationship “raised obvious questions about the timing and tone of this morning’s statement.”

He knew who that person was close to. He’d stood in the man’s kitchen at his daughter’s wedding.

“Hao,” said Raymond’s voice in his ear. “Are you there?”

“I’m here.”

“What do you want to do?”

“Don’t deny it. It’s true. We’re together.” He heard the word together and didn’t correct it, though it was the nineteenth of October and she’d asked him to leave on the nineteenth of September. “Say the relationship was declared, in full, on the morning of the accident, to everyone it should have been declared to, and that it was walled off on both sides from the first hour, and that the record of that is with the authority and has been since the second of August. Say I’ve had no part in anything but family support. Say we won’t discuss her investigation. And don’t let anyone, anyone, imply that she’s ever had one word from our client work through me, because she hasn’t.”

“Understood.”

“And don’t put it out yet.”

“Why?”

“Because if we put it out within an hour of his statement, he’ll make it look like we’re fighting about me. It isn’t about me.” Ren Hao looked down the corridor at the closed doors of the meeting rooms. “And don’t ring her. Nobody from this firm contacts her. Not today.”

“I wasn’t going to,” said Raymond.

“Good,” said Ren Hao.

✦ ✦ ✦

*1:06 p.m.* Song-Zhu saw it during the media review.

She read the headline once. Then again. She looked at the photograph of the taxi rank a long time. Her fist in his waistcoat. Fuel on her boots. Sixteen months ago. Somebody had been standing on that pavement, and taken it, and kept it, and found it this morning.

Her first feeling wasn’t anger. It was a tiredness so deep it felt like falling.

She’d expected the airline to fight. She’d expected its lawyers to go through every word. She’d expected the papers to turn ten weeks of careful work into three words in capitals.

She hadn’t expected to see his face next to hers.

She opened the declaration file. The one she’d written at eight in the morning on the second of August with Mabel sitting beside her, and signed, and had countersigned. She read it. She checked every date. She checked his letters, the one from the second and the one from the twenty-fifth, and Kwan’s two lines of reply. She saved copies of all of it in three places.

She wasn’t going to let a website make her careless.

Her phone buzzed in the drawer. She took it out. A number she didn’t know.

How much did your boyfriend tell you before you wrote it?

She looked at it. She took a screenshot. She forwarded it to the building’s security contact. She didn’t reply.

✦ ✦ ✦

*2:22 p.m.* Director Kwan had the article printed out on his desk. He didn’t ask her to sit.

“You’ve seen it.”

“Yes.”

“The relationship was declared at the start. Fully.”

“At eight a.m. on the second of August. You have it. Mabel countersigned.”

“Has anything changed since?”

She hesitated, for half a second. “We’ve been on a break since the nineteenth of September. That’s all.”

He looked at her over his glasses. “That’s not a change in the conflict. That’s a change in your life. I’m sorry.”

“Thank you.”

“Have you had any information from him about the airline’s response?”

“None.”

“Have you discussed the investigation with him?”

“Not one word. Not since the morning it happened. He wouldn’t let me. At three in the morning in August I offered him my draft to read for typos, and he wouldn’t look at the screen. He sat on the other side of the table for forty minutes with a book.” She stopped. “I forgot whose aircraft it was. He didn’t.”

Kwan was quiet.

“Any contact today?”

“No.”

“Good. We’ll go over the declaration again and make sure the record’s complete. You don’t speak to the press. Not a word. Not a no comment.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

“If the airline contacts you?”

“The press office.”

“Good.” He looked at her a long time. “How are you?”

She understood what he meant. Not the investigation, not the article. Her.

“I’m working,” she said.

He nodded, as if that were an answer, and let her go.

✦ ✦ ✦

*4:48 p.m.* Kong came up to the thirty-second floor at a quarter to five with a printed letter from the airline’s lawyers.

It asked the firm to issue a public statement distancing itself from the interim finding. It asked the firm to say that its earlier advice had been based on incomplete information. And it asked, in the last paragraph, in the politest words that could carry it, whether the firm’s managing partner’s personal circumstances were consistent with the firm’s continued role.

Ren Hao read it twice. He put it down on the desk.

“No,” he said.

“To which part?”

“All of it.”

“We can say we have no involvement in the investigation. That’s true.”

“Then say it.”

“They want us to say our advice was based on incomplete information.”

“It was based on what anybody had. It was right on Saturday and it was right this morning and they didn’t take it. We won’t say anything that suggests the finding is wrong. We don’t know if it’s wrong. Neither do they.”

Kong nodded. “And the account?”

“Review the contract.”

“Termination?”

“Possibly.”

“There’s a great deal of work outstanding. And two of our other engagements sit under the same holding group.”

“I know.”

Kong looked at him. “If we walk, it’ll look like an admission the advice was compromised.”

“If we stay,” said Ren Hao, “they’ll expect us to defend what that man said at eleven o’clock in front of Mrs. Ting. And we won’t.”

“That’s the choice.”

Ren Hao looked down at the letter.

For seven years he had built a firm on one belief: that good crisis work meant standing between people and their worst decisions when they were frightened. He’d watched chief executives take a bad day and turn it into a catastrophe because they couldn’t bear not knowing. He’d watched people shoot the messenger rather than open the message. He’d believed this client understood the difference. He’d believed it for five years.

He’d been wrong.

“Prepare the withdrawal assessment,” he said. “Everything. What we owe them, what they owe us, every engagement in the group, what it costs us, who it costs. On my desk on Wednesday.”

“And until then?”

“Until then the families still get their lunch.”

Kong collected the letter. At the door he stopped.

“One more thing. Our own board’s asked whether your relationship with the investigator affects your ability to advise the airline.”

Ren Hao looked up.

“Tell them it hasn’t affected one word of the advice. Every word’s on file.”

“And if they ask whether it affects your judgement?”

Ren Hao gave a small, tired smile that had nothing amused in it at all.

“My judgement,” he said, “is exactly why I won’t let that man use her name to get out of his own responsibilities.”

✦ ✦ ✦

*7:12 p.m.* She came home later than usual and put her bag down by the sofa, where she’d always put it, and took her shoes off, and turned on the kitchen light.

The flat was quiet. It had been quiet for thirty days. She’d got used to it, or to the shape of her evenings inside it.

She opened the fridge. Milk. Eggs. Greens. A box of rice she’d cooked herself on Saturday and labelled, in her own small writing, SAT.

She washed the greens. She heated the pan. Her phone was on the counter. She looked at it once. Nothing.

She knew he’d seen it. She knew his client had stood at a lectern that morning with families watching and called her finding premature. She knew there was a photograph of the two of them at the taxi rank on every phone in the city.

She knew he’d reported the owner’s call before seven, in writing, to Kwan.

She wondered if he was angry. Then she stopped herself. She had no right to ask him to look after her feelings about something she hadn’t even decided how to talk to him about.

She turned the heat down. She ate, at the table, by herself.

The phone lit with a headline. AIRLINE CALLS INTERIM FINDING PREMATURE, DEMANDS FURTHER REVIEW. She turned it over and finished her greens.

✦ ✦ ✦

*8:36 p.m.* He was still in his office. The withdrawal assessment didn’t exist yet, but a page had: four lines in his own capitals, headed WHAT IT COSTS. He looked at it. Then he looked at the window, at the harbour, at the lights going on along the airport road on the far side, and the hotel among them.

At twenty to two that morning a message had come in from the Pacific hub, then another from Lima at half past one in the afternoon, Lima time, which was half past two in the morning here. He hadn’t been asleep for either.

Wei Long: Landed. Going to her now.

And then, at half past eight this evening, another.

Wei Long: She’s eaten. Finally. She says to tell you she doesn’t need you to send another plane.

Ren Hao smiled for the first time all day.

Ren Hao: I wasn’t planning to.

Wei Long: She says you were.

Ren Hao: She’s reading my mind from Lima.

Wei Long: She says you have a very readable mind.

Ren Hao: Stay with her. Don’t let her work all night.

Wei Long: I’ll try.

A pause. Then:

Wei Long: Thank you for the ticket. I mean it.

Ren Hao put the phone down on the desk.

He was glad. He was glad Wei Long was there and that Isla was eating and that somewhere in the world, at least, two people who loved each other weren’t separated by anything any more.

He picked the phone up again. He opened her name.

He typed: I saw the article. I’m sorry they’ve dragged you into it.

It sounded like an apology for something he’d done. He deleted it.

My client’s statement wasn’t what my firm advised. Everything’s on file. We’re reviewing the account.

Too much work. Too much explanation. Too much of the thing she’d asked him not to bring home. He deleted it.

I hope you’re all right.

He looked at it a long time. She’d asked for room. He’d agreed. He’d promised himself, in a doorway with his bag in his hand, that he would never turn her silence into something he could manage.

He deleted that too. He put his coat on and turned the lights off and went home to his own flat, on the wrong side of the harbour, and the fridge that hummed in the wrong key.

✦ ✦ ✦

*11:28 p.m.* She was still awake, sitting up in bed with the interim statement on her tablet.

She knew every word of it now. Every qualifier. Every limitation. Every sentence that had been fought over in a room till midnight.

She’d signed it because it was what the evidence supported. Not because she wanted to blame anybody, not because she wanted to hurt anyone. Not because of who his client was, or in spite of it. Because a part under a floor hadn’t been what the paperwork said it was, and the power had gone, and two recorders had stopped listening, and a man had gone on talking to his passengers in the dark until the end.

She’d done her job. She put the tablet down. She looked at the other side of the bed.

She wondered whether he was home. Whether he’d eaten. Whether the man who owned the airline was making his life a misery. Whether he’d seen the photograph of the taxi rank, and what his face had done when he saw it.

And then she wondered whether he was lying awake somewhere on the far side of the harbour, wondering about her. She turned the light off.

In the dark the city went on passing the headlines round. The maintenance finding was public. The families had something new, and terrible, and true. The airline had a problem it had chosen to make worse. His firm had a decision to make. The investigation still had a long way to go.

Tomorrow she’d go back to the laboratory. She’d look at the component again, and the paperwork, and the signatures. She’d answer every question through the proper channels. She wouldn’t take back one word of the finding because a company didn’t like what it showed. She wouldn’t soften the truth to protect a man she loved.

She heard herself think it. A man she loved. In the dark, on her own, it came out whole.

And she wouldn’t ask him to choose between his work and hers.

They’d been apart for thirty days. That had been hard. This was something else. For the first time, the two separate halves of their working lives had walked into the same room, in front of everyone, and neither of them could simply get up and leave it. Not yet.

chapters.title: He Chooses Her Report
chapters.desc: He drops the airline, his biggest client, and doesn’t tell her. Ruby rings her from the coat room. She kisses him by the reception desk.
chapters.epigraph: “The coat room isn’t technically the building, Mr. Ren.”
chapters.content:
At twelve minutes past eight on Thursday the twenty-second of October, Ren Hao asked Kong to shut the door.

There were three documents on the table between them. The agreement with the airline’s holding group, five years old, forty pages, his signature on the last one. The correspondence of the last three days, including the letter asking his firm to distance itself in public from the interim finding. And a termination notice, two pages long, already drafted, waiting for a date.

“Before we do this,” said Kong, “I need to be sure you’ve understood what it costs.”

“I have.”

“They’re our biggest client.”

“I know.”

“Not just in fees. The whole crisis-response division was built round them. Fourteen people on the account. Two other engagements under the same group. There’ll be a hole in the year.” He named the figure.

Ren Hao nodded. “All right.”

“That isn’t a small number.”

“I didn’t think it was.”

“And the board’s going to ask why now. Straight after a public fight. It’ll look like temper.”

“Then we’ll tell them it isn’t.”

Kong folded his hands. “Hao. I have to ask you this, because somebody else will. Is this about Song-Zhu?”

Ren Hao looked up.

“No,” he said.

Kong waited.

“It’s about the client. We told them to acknowledge the finding. We told them not to question the independence of the investigation. We told them not to say anything at all that suggested the families had tainted the evidence. They ignored every word of it, in front of forty families in a hotel lobby, and then they wrote to ask us to stand up and say we’d been wrong to tell them.” He put one finger on the letter. “We can’t. And then they put a photograph of me at a taxi rank in a newspaper, so that everybody would talk about that instead of a part under a floor.”

“We’ve documented the separation.”

“Everything’s documented. That’s why I can sleep.” He looked at the draft notice. “I won’t have this firm used to discredit her work. I won’t sign a statement that says an investigation is unreliable because a client doesn’t like what it found. And I won’t pretend our advice was anything other than what it was.”

Kong was quiet.

“Then it’s straightforward,” he said.

“It should have been straightforward on Monday.”

“Do you want to give them a chance to withdraw the request?”

“No.”

“You’re sure?”

Ren Hao picked up his pen and dated the notice.

“Prepare it,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

*9:06 a.m.* The owner came himself, with two of his directors, which Ren Hao had expected.

He met them in the main conference room on the thirty-second floor, where the light came in flat off the harbour across a long table. He’d sat at the head of it six months ago at three in the morning and listened to Eliana Lin tell him about Desmond. He sat at the side of it now, not the head, and let the owner have the end.

The owner put his phone face up on the table and didn’t sit.

“I understand you’ve drawn up a notice.”

“I have.”

“You’re walking away.”

“Yes.”

“After five years.”

“After Monday,” said Ren Hao.

The owner laughed, short. “You can’t be serious.”

“I am.”

“You’ve had my people in your rooms for ten weeks. You’ve seen my crisis plans. You know exactly what’s at stake for us.”

“I do.”

“And now, when I need you most...”

“We advised you to respond responsibly to the finding. You chose not to. Then you asked us to say in public that our advice had been mistaken. It wasn’t. We won’t.”

“I have a right to challenge a finding.”

“Yes. Through the proper process. With evidence. Not by telling the families in that hotel that their grief is contaminating the investigation.”

The owner’s face hardened.

“You’re doing this for her.”

Ren Hao didn’t move. “I’m doing this because of what my firm is for.”

“Don’t hide behind your letterhead.”

“I’m not.”

“She issued that statement.”

“She’s the investigator-in-charge. Her work has nothing to do with mine. That’s been on paper since five o’clock on the morning of the second of August, with your signature under it.”

“And I’m supposed to believe you’ve no personal interest in protecting her?”

Ren Hao looked at the two directors beside the owner. Neither of them said anything. One of them was looking at the table. The other was looking at the window with the expression of a man who had advised exactly what Ren Hao had advised, and been overruled, and hadn’t been permitted to say so.

“Your maintenance records were examined,” said Ren Hao. “A component in your aircraft didn’t match the paperwork that came with it. If the finding’s wrong, you have a process. What you can’t do, with my firm’s help, is put a photograph of the investigator’s private life in a newspaper as though it were evidence against her.”

The owner leaned on the table. “You’re choosing her.”

“No.”

“Then what are you choosing?”

“The advice we gave you,” said Ren Hao.

There was a long silence. The owner looked down at the notice in front of him, and then back up, and for a moment Ren Hao saw him search for another version of the conversation: a compromise, a delay, a softer word, a way to keep it. There wasn’t one.

“You’re making a mistake,” said the owner.

“Perhaps.”

“Your board won’t thank you.”

“They’ve been told.”

“You’ll lose more than the account.”

“That’s possible.”

The owner picked up his phone. He didn’t offer his hand. He walked out, and the director who’d been looking at the window held the door for him, and on his way through it turned and looked back at Ren Hao, and gave him one small, tired nod.

Ren Hao stood until the door had closed. Then he looked at the notice on the table. He’d already signed it.

✦ ✦ ✦

*10:32 a.m.* The statement went out just before eleven. It was five sentences long.

It didn’t mention her. It didn’t mention a taxi rank or a relationship or anything personal at all. It didn’t criticise the airline. It said that the firm had ended its engagement with the carrier’s holding group, with immediate effect, following a review of the firm’s professional obligations in the light of the client’s public communications. It said that the firm wouldn’t comment on the investigation, its findings, or the personal circumstances of anyone connected with it. That was all.

Kong had approved every word. No adjectives. No accusations. Nothing that made anyone look noble. Just a decision. By eleven it was everywhere.

CRISIS FIRM DROPS AIRLINE OVER CRASH STATEMENT
REN HAO WALKS AWAY FROM BIGGEST CLIENT
CONSULTANCY REFUSES TO DISTANCE ITSELF FROM CRASH INQUIRY

He read the coverage once and closed it. He had a firm to run. Fourteen people whose work had been that account. Invoices. Obligations. Worry, going round three floors like a draught.

He rang his head of operations. “Everybody. The big room. Now.”

✦ ✦ ✦

*11:18 a.m.* He didn’t use slides.

“You’ll have seen it,” he said. “We’ve ended our work with the airline. It was our largest client. Some of you have spent ten weeks on it, and some of you five years. Losing it will hurt this year’s numbers and it’ll change who works on what. I’m not going to pretend it won’t.”

A hand went up at the back. “Are there going to be redundancies?”

“No decision’s been made about anybody’s job. We’ll look at the numbers properly first. I won’t give you reassurance I can’t back up, because you’d remember it if I did.”

“Was it because of what they said on Monday?”

“Yes. The client asked us to say something in public that contradicted our own advice. We said no.”

A pause. A younger voice, carefully: “Is it because of the investigator?”

He looked at whoever had asked it. A woman from research, in her first year, who looked as if she wished she hadn’t.

“No,” he said. “It’s a fair question and I’ll answer it properly. My relationship was declared on the morning of the accident. It’s been walled off on both sides from the first hour. Nobody in this building took part in the investigation and nobody in it has seen a word of it, including me. The client’s entitled to disagree with our advice. The client isn’t entitled to make us say we don’t believe it.”

Nobody spoke.

“I know this makes the next few months uncertain,” he said. “I’ll be straight with you about the numbers as we go. If you’re worried about your job, come to me, or come to your head of department. Don’t read the papers to find out what’s happening to you. Come and ask.”

When they’d gone, his head of operations stayed.

“The board’s going to ask you whether it was worth it.”

“Yes.”

“What’ll you say?”

Ren Hao picked up his notebook.

“That I’d do it again on Monday,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

*11:51 a.m.*

Ruby had been on the front desk on the thirty-second floor for six years. She had cake on her birthday every year because he made sure of it. She’d been in the room at eleven eighteen, at the back, by the door, and she’d heard every word. And she had heard, the day before, through the glass of his office, on the phone to Kong, a man say, low, And nobody tells her. Not from this building. She doesn’t need one more thing to carry.

At eleven fifty-one she went into the small room behind reception where the coats were, and shut the door, and rang a number she’d had in her phone since July of last year, when a woman in a flight suit had stood at her desk and asked her, quite seriously, what her boss was like when nobody was looking. It rang four times.

“Xu.”

“Ms. Xu. It’s Ruby. From Mr. Ren’s office. I’m sorry to ring you at work.”

There was a silence on the line. “Ruby. Is he all right?”

“He’s fine. He’s at his desk.” Ruby took a breath. “He’ll be furious with me. He told everybody yesterday that nobody from this building was to tell you anything. So I’m not telling you from the building. I’m in the coat room.”

“Tell me what?”

“Have you seen the news this morning?”

“I’ve been in the laboratory since seven.”

“He dropped them. The airline. All of it. This morning. They came up here and shouted at him and he signed it anyway. It was the biggest thing we had.” Ruby’s voice wobbled, and she was annoyed with it. “And he hasn’t told you, because he doesn’t want you to think you owe him anything. I’ve worked for him for six years, Ms. Xu, and I know what his face looks like when something’s cost him. It looks like this morning. I just thought somebody should tell you. That’s all. I’m going to hang up now before he finds me in here.”

“Ruby...”

“I’m hanging up,” said Ruby, and did.

✦ ✦ ✦

*12:38 p.m.* Song-Zhu hadn’t planned to go.

She’d sat at her desk for twenty minutes after Ruby rang, with the statement open on her screen. Five sentences. She’d read them six times. She’d rung the press office and asked them to confirm, in writing, that the firm’s withdrawal had no bearing on the investigation’s independence or its findings, and they’d confirmed it. She’d opened a document and read the same paragraph three times without taking in a word of it.

He’d dropped them. His biggest client. For seven years he’d built that firm out of two rooms over a print shop, and this morning he’d let a fifth of it go. And he hadn’t told her. She’d stood up.

Director Kwan had looked up as she went past his door. “Where are you going?”

“Out. For an hour.”

“Is everything all right?”

She’d hesitated. “Yes.”

He’d looked at her over his glasses. “Don’t discuss the investigation.”

“I won’t.”

“Good,” he’d said, and gone back to his screen, and she’d seen the corner of his mouth move.

Now she stood in the lift going up the tower to the thirty-second floor, in her work trousers and a dark blouse, with her lanyard in her pocket and her hair coming out of its clip, and watched the numbers change. Her hands were steady. Nothing else about her was. The doors opened.

Ruby was at the front desk. She looked up and saw who it was and went pink to the ears, and put down her pen.

“Ms. Xu.”

“Ruby.”

“I didn’t ring you,” said Ruby.

“No. Of course you didn’t.”

“He’s in his office.”

Song-Zhu didn’t move. Because the door to the inner corridor had opened, and Ren Hao had come out of it, with his jacket off and his sleeves rolled up and his tie pulled loose and a folder in one hand, saying something over his shoulder to somebody behind him, and he turned and saw her standing by the reception desk, and stopped dead. The folder hung in his hand.

For a second neither of them moved at all. The phones on Ruby’s desk rang and nobody answered them.

She’d imagined it in the lift. She’d thought she might ask him why he hadn’t told her. She’d thought she might be angry. She’d thought she might tell him that he had no right to make a decision like that without letting her see what it cost.

What she said was, “Hello.”

His face changed. “Hello.”

He didn’t come towards her. She saw him not do it. He stood in the doorway to the corridor with the folder in his hand and let her have the whole distance across the reception floor, every metre of it, to decide what to do with. She crossed it.

She walked past Ruby’s desk and up to him and took the front of his shirt in her fist, the way she’d taken his waistcoat at a taxi rank sixteen months ago, and pulled him down, and kissed him. The folder hit the floor.

For one second he didn’t move. Then his hand came up to her face, and the other one went round her back, and he kissed her back, not carefully, not with any of the restraint he’d been practising since September, but like a man who’d missed her every single day for thirty-three days and had spent every one of them refusing to make his missing her into something she had to carry. She held on to his shirt. He held on to her. Somewhere behind them a phone rang and rang and rang, and Ruby picked it up without a sound and said “Please hold,” and put it down again.

When Song-Zhu drew back he kept his forehead an inch from hers, and neither of them said anything.

From behind the reception desk came a deliberate sound of papers being shuffled. Song-Zhu shut her eyes.

Ren Hao’s mouth moved. “Ruby,” he said, without looking round.

“Yes, Mr. Ren.”

“Did you ring her?”

“No, Mr. Ren.”

“From the coat room?”

There was a pause. “The coat room isn’t technically the building, Mr. Ren.”

Song-Zhu began to laugh. She couldn’t help it. She laughed against his chest with her fist still in his shirt, really laughed, for the first time in so long that it hurt, and he looked down at her as though he’d been waiting thirty-three days to hear it, and Ruby said, to nobody, “I’ll make some tea,” and went away towards the pantry with enormous dignity.

✦ ✦ ✦

In his office she didn’t sit down. She stood by the glass with her arms folded, and he stood by the desk, and the door was half open, because neither of them had thought to shut it.

“You dropped them,” she said.

“Yes.”

“Your biggest client.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Would you like to sit?”

“No.”

“All right.”

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

He was quiet. “Because I didn’t want it to be something you had to answer. It was my decision. My firm’s. It wasn’t a message to you. It wasn’t asking you for anything.”

“You could have told me.”

“Yes.”

“I found out from your receptionist. In a coat room.”

“I know.”

“Do you know what that felt like?”

“I can imagine.”

“No,” she said. “You can’t.”

He didn’t argue.

She looked out at the harbour. “I spent the first twenty minutes after she rang thinking you’d done it because of me. Because of the newspaper. Because you couldn’t stand it.”

“I didn’t.”

“I know that now. I read it six times. You did it because they asked you to say your own advice was wrong.”

“Yes.”

“And because they tried to use me to get out of a part under a floor.”

“Yes.”

She turned round. “You didn’t have to lose the account.”

He gave her a small, worn smile. “I know.”

“That’s a great deal of money, Hao.”

“I’ve seen the numbers. Kong read them to me twice, slowly.”

She almost laughed. It came out as a breath.

“Are you angry?” he said.

She thought about it honestly. “Yes.”

His face went still.

“Not with you,” she said. “With them. With the newspapers. With whoever stood on a pavement sixteen months ago and kept that photograph. With the fact that they made it about us, when it should only ever have been about the evidence.” She looked at him. “And with you for not telling me. A bit.”

“That’s fair.”

“I don’t want you to make decisions about your life because you think I need protecting.”

“I didn’t.”

“Because I don’t.”

“I know you don’t.” He looked at her. “I didn’t leave that account to protect you from a newspaper. I left it because I wouldn’t stand up and defend something I knew was wrong. And because I told you, at your table at three in the morning in August, that I’d never be the reason anybody doubted your report. I meant it then. It cost more this morning. That’s all.”

She looked at him. She thought about a toothbrush going into a washbag. A full fridge. A man at her door who’d seen her try to say it and told her she already had.

He hadn’t asked her to change her mind. He hadn’t made her responsible for his sadness. And this morning he’d done the most expensive thing he’d ever done, and hadn’t asked her to carry any of it.

“You kept your word,” she said.

“I tried.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Ruby brought the tea, put it on the low table, looked at nobody, and went out and shut the door this time.

Song-Zhu sat down on the sofa at last. He took the chair opposite.

“How bad is it?” she said. “Properly.”

He told her. The number. The fourteen people. The two other engagements in the group that would almost certainly follow. A board meeting at half past two.

“Are you worried?”

“Of course I’m worried. There are people downstairs whose work was that account. We’ll have to change things. Some of it won’t be pleasant.” He put his cup down. “But I don’t regret it. I regret that it got to the point where it was the only honest thing left. I regret that the families had to watch people argue about vocabulary while they waited. I don’t regret saying no.”

She looked at him over her tea. “I didn’t come here to ask you for anything,” she said. “I want to be clear. I’m not coming back because you dropped a client. I haven’t changed my mind about the break. The investigation isn’t finished. I’m not ready to go back to how it was.”

“I know.”

“I still need time.”

“Then you’ll have it.”

She looked at him. He was tired. There were shadows under his eyes she’d never seen there, and his collar had turned in on one side, and nobody had told him. He looked like a man who’d been working too long and sleeping in the wrong key.

He also looked like somebody she had missed so badly that she’d had to sit down.

“Aren’t you going to ask why I came?” she said.

“I thought you might tell me.”

“I came because I saw what you’d done. And because I wanted to see you.” She swallowed. “I missed you, Hao.”

His face changed, slowly, all the way through.

“I missed you too,” he said. “Every day.”

“Even when I was being difficult?”

“Most of all then. That was when I knew it was you.”

She shook her head at him, and her eyes were wet, and she laughed. “That’s a terrible answer.”

“It’s an honest one.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past one she stood by the glass again, looking down at the street.

“I’ve got a technical review at three.”

“Do you want a car?”

She turned.

He heard himself. He held up one hand. “Sorry. Old habit. I’ll ask properly. Would you like me to arrange a car?”

“No. Thank you. I came on my own.”

“All right.”

She studied him. “You really are learning.”

“I’m trying.”

“I can’t promise when it’ll be over,” she said. “Or what I’ll feel when it is. And I don’t want you sleeping at my flat because we kissed by Ruby’s desk.”

“Understood.”

“I mean it.”

“I know you do.”

He came a step towards her, and stopped. She noticed. This time she was the one who reached out and took his hand.

“I’m not asking you to disappear,” she said. “I’m asking us to be careful.”

“We can be careful.”

“Can I see you again?” she said. “Not tonight. I’ve got work. But soon.”

He looked down at their hands. “You’re asking me?”

“I’m asking you.”

“Yes,” said Ren Hao.

✦ ✦ ✦

He walked her to the lifts. Ruby was on the phone, and finished the call, and looked up with an expression of impeccable professionalism.

“Ms. Xu. Mr. Ren’s half past two has arrived early.”

“Already?” said Ren Hao.

“They’re the board, Mr. Ren. They’re always early when it’s bad.”

He looked at Song-Zhu. “I have to...”

“Go,” she said. “You’re running a business. Go and tell them you’d do it again.”

The lift came. She stepped in. Then she put her hand on the door to hold it and looked back at him.

“Hao.”

“Yes?”

“Don’t forget to eat lunch.”

He stared at her. Then he laughed out loud in the middle of his own reception.

“That’s my line.”

“Not today,” said Song-Zhu, and let the doors close.

Ruby waited five seconds. Then, without looking up from her screen:

“Shall I move your half past two by fifteen minutes, Mr. Ren?”

“Why?”

“Because you look as if you need to sit down.”

He breathed out a laugh. “Do I?”

“A little.”

“You’re very observant, Ruby.”

“Thank you, Mr. Ren. It’s in my job description. Under coat room.”

✦ ✦ ✦

*2:04 p.m.* Her phone buzzed in the taxi.

Ren Hao: You left your folder.

She looked down. The folder was on her knee.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): No, I didn’t.

Ren Hao: I know. I wanted a reason to message you.

She looked at that a while.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): You could just message me.

Ren Hao: I didn’t know if I was allowed.

Something in her face went soft.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): You’re allowed. Don’t expect an answer when I’m working.

Ren Hao: I won’t.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): And don’t send me a driver.

Ren Hao: I wasn’t going to.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): You were thinking about it.

Ren Hao: I was assessing the risk.

She laughed out loud in the back of the taxi, and the driver looked at her in the mirror.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Eat lunch.

Ren Hao: Yes, Investigator.

For the first time in thirty-three days, the silence after the last message didn’t feel like a wall. It felt like room. The kind two people could learn to share.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night, in her own flat, she sat at her table with her phone beside a bowl of rice she’d made herself.

Ren Hao: Home?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Yes.

Ren Hao: Good. The board was bad. I told them I’d do it again on Monday. Nobody resigned. Goodnight, Song-Zhu.

She looked at it a long time.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Goodnight, Hao.

Nothing was mended. The investigation wasn’t finished. The airline was still furious. His firm had lost a fifth of itself. The papers would go on writing about the two of them for a week.

His toothbrush was still gone. His slippers were still by her shoe cabinet. Six of his suits were still on her rail.

But he’d kept his word when it cost him. He hadn’t asked her to reward him for it. He hadn’t even told her. And when she’d walked across his reception floor, he’d let her decide, every metre of the way, how close she wanted to stand.

She turned the light off and lay in the dark, and found she was smiling.

chapters.title: Not Yet, Still
chapters.desc: One dinner, no agenda. She still can’t say it. At the taxi rank, again, she asks before she kisses him.
chapters.epigraph: “That’s all tonight has to be.”
chapters.content:
The first time he asked her to dinner, he did it without making it sound like a question with consequences.

It was a Tuesday, the tenth of November. She was at her desk at seventeen minutes past eight at night with three documents open, one of them a table of torque values she’d been staring at so long the numbers had begun to look like decoration, when her phone lit up beside the keyboard.

Ren Hao: Have you eaten?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Define eaten.

Ren Hao: That’s concerning.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I had a biscuit.

Ren Hao: A biscuit isn’t dinner.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): It was a large biscuit.

A pause.

Ren Hao: Then I won’t interfere with your culinary achievements.

She smiled at the screen, despite everything.

Ren Hao: Would you like to have dinner with me one evening this week?

She looked at it. Not I’ll pick you up. Not I’ve booked somewhere. Not You need to get out of that office. A question, with nothing hidden behind it.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): What kind of dinner?

Ren Hao: The kind where we eat.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Very informative.

Ren Hao: I could elaborate, but I don’t want to overwhelm you with the concept.

She laughed, alone in the office.

Then she looked back at the torque values. There was still a great deal she hadn’t finished. There was still a great deal she couldn’t talk about. The investigation was moving, but slowly, and the interim finding had opened a dozen new rooms of questions: who had fitted that component, where it had come from, who had signed for it, who had signed for whoever had signed for it. The families were still waiting. She was tired of being asked how much longer.

And she was tired, in a way she couldn’t quite admit, of having to decide every single evening what to do with the gap between her and him.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Thursday?

Ren Hao: Thursday.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Somewhere ordinary.

Ren Hao: I can do ordinary.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Don’t book somewhere ridiculous.

Ren Hao: I wasn’t going to.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): You once rang a restaurant because they’d run out of the pudding I liked.

Ren Hao: That was a quality-control matter.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): It was a tart.

Ren Hao: A disappointing tart.

She put the phone face up on the desk before she could smile any more, and spent the rest of the evening looking at the clock more often than she needed to.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday he was there seven minutes early. He stood under the awning of a small place two streets from the authority, hands in the pockets of his dark coat, watching the traffic. It was squeezed between a stationer’s and a chemist. Wooden tables. Warm light. A menu chalked on a board that changed with whatever the kitchen had been sent that morning. He’d eaten there once, alone, in October.

He’d chosen it because it was near her office, because the noodles were good, and because there was nothing memorable about it whatsoever. No private room. No view. No candles. No occasion.

He’d tried hard not to make dinner into something that had to be remembered.

She came along the pavement with one hand on her bag strap and her phone in the other, her hair half up, a dark jumper under her long coat. She looked tired. Not ill, not fragile. Tired. He saw the line between her eyebrows before she saw him. Then she looked up.

The line went. Her mouth moved, a little, at one corner. It was enough to make him forget, for half a second, what he’d been about to say.

“You’re early.”

“Seven minutes.”

“That’s early.”

“I was near.”

“Have you been standing out here for seven minutes?”

“Possibly.”

“Why?”

He thought about it. “So you wouldn’t have to come in and look for me.”

She gave him a look of pure disbelief. “Hao. You could have sat down.”

“I could.”

“But you didn’t.”

“No.”

She shook her head, but the corner of her mouth stayed where it was. He held the door. She went in first.

There were no flowers on the table. No wine waiting. No card with her name. Two glasses of water and a small dish of pickled radish.

She sat down and looked round. “This is nice.”

“Good.”

“Very normal.”

“That was the plan. I mean,” he corrected himself, “that was the hope.”

She looked at the board. “Did you choose it because you know I like noodles?”

“Partly.”

“And the rest?”

“Because nobody here will look at you.” He paused. “And because the noodles are good.”

“Much better answer.”

She ordered the noodles she liked and a plate of dumplings, prawn and chive. He ordered rice and greens. When the waiter had gone there was a silence, and a while it wasn’t uncomfortable: cutlery at the next table, a couple talking low by the door, a bus going past outside. She turned her water glass round and round.

“How’s the review?” he said.

She looked up. “Do you want the professional answer or the complaining one?”

“Whichever you want to give me.”

“Professional: it’s ongoing.”

“Understood.”

“Complaining: I’d like to throw the whole thing in the sea.”

He nodded gravely. “That seems inconvenient, given where the aircraft already is.”

She stared at him. And then she laughed, a short sudden burst that made her put her glass down.

“That was terrible.”

“I know.”

“Really terrible.”

“I’d prepared myself.”

She shook her head, still laughing a little. He watched her. Not the woman in the laboratory with headphones round her neck. Not the person at the second microphone answering a room full of people who wanted certainty she couldn’t give them. Not the woman who’d stood in his office three weeks ago and told him she still needed time. Just Song-Zhu, laughing at a bad joke.

He’d missed her laugh more than anything. He didn’t say so.

“What else would you throw in the sea?”

“My inbox.”

“Understandable.”

“My laptop.”

“Expensive.”

“Director Kwan.”

He hesitated. “Let’s keep that one hypothetical.”

She grinned. “You’re no fun.”

“I’m protecting your career.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The food came.

For a while they talked about ordinary things. She told him about a junior investigator who’d sent an internal timetable to an entire distribution list, including a deputy minister who’d been trying to book the same meeting room for a fortnight. He told her about the firm. He kept it factual: two accounts moved, fourteen people found new work inside the building, a forecast rewritten three times. He’d spent most of Wednesday in meetings that could have been emails, and most of this morning explaining to a director that a company couldn’t replace its largest client by wishing hard.

“Did you say that to him?”

“Not in those words.”

“Shame.”

“I considered it.”

“Look at you. Being diplomatic.”

“How’s it going, from where you’re sitting?”

“Badly.”

He laughed. She reached for a dumpling.

“Is the firm all right?” she said. “Really.”

He took a moment. “It’s adjusting.”

“That’s not the same thing.”

“No.”

She waited.

He put his chopsticks down. “We’ll be all right. But there are decisions coming, and some of them won’t be nice, and I can’t pretend nothing’s changed.”

“Are you worried?”

“Yes.”

Just that. She looked at him with more attention.

“I’m not panicking,” he said. “I’ve got good people. Raymond’s been extraordinary. But it’s going to be a hard winter.”

“You’re allowed to say it’s hard.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

He gave her a small smile. “I’m working on it.”

She looked down at her bowl. There was something so familiar about it, the measured careful answer with the human part sitting just behind it where she could see it if she looked. She knew he was frightened. She knew he wasn’t asking her to make him less frightened.

That mattered more than she could have told him.

“You’re good at this,” she said.

“At what?”

“Knowing when to tell me something. And when to leave it.”

His face went soft. “I’m not always good at it.”

“No. You’re not.” She pushed the dumplings across the table towards him. “But you’re getting better. Eat. You’re being sentimental.”

“I didn’t know sentiment affected appetite.”

“It affects mine.”

“Then I’ll be quiet.”

“That would be a medical emergency,” said Song-Zhu, and he laughed out loud, and the couple by the door looked round.

✦ ✦ ✦

They stayed far longer than either of them had meant to.

Not because there was anything to discuss, not because they were trying to solve anything. They talked about a film she’d seen on a flight years ago and could never remember the end of. He told her about a man in his office who had spent twenty minutes arguing that the printer on the twenty-ninth floor was sabotaging him personally.

“Does the printer have previous?”

“Not that I know of.”

“Then you shouldn’t make assumptions. Investigate first.”

“I’ll make a note.”

She told him she’d started listening to music again on the bus home. He asked what.

“Nothing you’d know.”

“That’s unnecessarily hurtful.”

“You asked.”

“Send me something.”

“Why?”

“So I can listen to it.”

“That isn’t a reason.”

“It’s an excellent reason.”

She looked at him. Then she picked up her phone and sent him a song. His phone buzzed on the table. He looked at the title, and at her.

“I don’t know this.”

“That’s the point.”

He put the phone in his pocket without playing it.

She noticed. “You’re not going to listen?”

“I will.”

“When?”

“Later.”

“Why not now?”

He tipped his head. “Because I’d rather hear you talk.”

It was said. Not polished, not offered in the hope of anything back.

She looked down at her glass. Heat came up into her face.

“That’s not fair,” she said.

“What isn’t?”

“You can’t just say things like that.”

“I can.”

“Unfortunately.”

He smiled, and didn’t push it. She went back to her noodles. It was strange, she thought, how easily it came back. His hand resting by his glass. The way he listened without cutting in. The small movement of his eyebrows when she said something absurd. The way he looked at her as though there were nobody else in the room. She’d missed all of it.

But missing something wasn’t the same as being ready to have it back. That was the part she couldn’t explain to him. Or perhaps she could, and simply didn’t know how to say it without making it sound like wait for me.

She didn’t know what she was asking him for.

✦ ✦ ✦

Outside, the air had turned cold. The owner waved them off from behind the counter. She put her hands in her coat pockets. He walked beside her: not too close, not so far that she had to turn her head to talk to him.

They came to the taxi rank on the corner. A short queue under the streetlight. A cab at the front with its light on.

She stopped. “That’s me.”

“All right.”

Neither of them moved.

“Thank you for dinner,” she said.

“Thank you for coming.”

“It was nice.”

“I’m glad.”

She fiddled with the strap of her bag. He watched her fingers on the leather, then looked back at her face. There were things he could have said. When can I see you again. I want more evenings like this. Has anything changed. He said none of them.

“Would you like me to wait till you’re in?” he said.

She gave him a look. “I can get into a taxi on my own.”

“I know you can.”

“Then why ask?”

“Because I don’t mind waiting.”

She studied him. Then she nodded. “All right.”

The people ahead of her moved forward. When it was her turn, she didn’t reach for the door. She turned round.

“Hao.”

“Yes?”

She looked at him a second too long. He was standing under the streetlight in his coat with his hands in his pockets, perfectly calm. He didn’t look like a man waiting for an answer. He looked like someone who had learned that wanting something didn’t give him the right to ask for it before she was ready. That was what made it so hard. She wanted to say something.

I missed you. True. I want to do this again. True.

I don’t know how to come back. The truest of the three.

And underneath all of them, the one she’d said once in September folded small inside a don’t, and hadn’t been able to say since. It was right there. She could feel the shape of it in her throat like a stone. It wouldn’t come.

He saw her try. His face changed only a little. The softness stayed, but she could see him understand that she was reaching for something she couldn’t hold yet.

“You don’t have to say anything,” he said.

“I know.”

He nodded. And then she took a step towards him. A small one. He didn’t come to meet her. He waited until she’d reached for the front of his coat with one hand and closed her fingers in the wool.

“Can I?” she said.

His eyes went down to her hand, and back up to her face.

“Yes.”

She kissed him.

Not fast, not the way she’d kissed him by Ruby’s desk three weeks ago, all relief and fistfuls of shirt. This one started unsure, and found its way, slowly, to something she knew. His hand came to rest at her waist, lightly, and didn’t pull. When she leaned in, he leaned with her. When she tipped her face, he followed it. His thumb moved once against her coat. That was all. She kissed him a long time under the streetlight at the taxi rank, the same streetlight, sixteen months later, and when she stopped he stayed close enough that their foreheads nearly touched, and neither of them said a word.

Behind her the cab gave a short, impatient toot.

She shut her eyes. “That’s my taxi.”

“I know.”

She didn’t let go of his coat straight away. Then she did.

He stepped back. “Get home safely.”

“You too.”

“That isn’t how taxis work.”

“Don’t ruin it.”

“Sorry.”

“No, you’re not.”

“No,” he admitted. “I’m not.”

She got in. Before she pulled the door shut she looked at him once more. He was still there. Not waving, not asking her to stay. Only watching her with that quiet, whole attention.

She shut the door. The taxi pulled out. He stood at the rank until its tail lights had gone.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t text her. He walked to the main road with his hands in his pockets and the cold on his face.

He could send thank you for tonight. He’d already said it.

He could tell her he’d liked seeing her. She knew.

He could ask her to tell him when she was home. He’d decided, a long time ago, in a doorway, not to turn caring into an obligation. So he walked. At the crossing, his phone buzzed.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Nearly home.

Ren Hao: Good.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Dinner was nice.

Ren Hao: It was.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I liked that we didn’t talk about anything important.

Ren Hao: We discussed a criminal printer.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): A serious matter.

Ren Hao: I’ll open an investigation.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Don’t. You’ll start managing it.

He laughed, alone, at a crossing. The dots came, and went, and came.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I don’t know when I can do this properly.

He read it once. Then again. Not a no, not a promise. The truth, in the only shape she could get it into.

Ren Hao: I know.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I don’t want you to misunderstand tonight.

Ren Hao: I won’t.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I don’t want you to wait for something I can’t promise.

The lights changed. He didn’t move.

Ren Hao: Then don’t promise me anything. We had dinner. It was good. You kissed me. I kissed you back. That’s all tonight has to be.

He sent it before he could make it longer.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): You’re being very reasonable.

Ren Hao: It’s a horrible experience.

She sent a row of laughing faces. Then:

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Goodnight, Hao.

Ren Hao: Goodnight, Song-Zhu.

He put the phone away and crossed the road.

✦ ✦ ✦

She stood in the middle of her flat with her coat still on. She’d turned on the lights and put her bag down and taken off her shoes, and then stopped, by the door, and gone no further.

It was the same flat she’d had before him. The same shelves, the same sofa, the photograph on the side table that leaned slightly and that she kept meaning to straighten. Nothing had changed.

Except that now she knew exactly what the room sounded like with nobody else in it.

She hung up her coat. She went into the kitchen for water. She opened their messages and read his last one again.

We had dinner. It was good. You kissed me. I kissed you back. That’s all tonight has to be.

He hadn’t asked her to come back. He hadn’t asked her to decide. He hadn’t even asked when they could do it again. She should have been relieved.

What she felt was a small aching disappointment she couldn’t justify. Because she’d wanted him to ask. And she hadn’t wanted him to ask. Both of those were true at once, like the lines in the data.

She sat down on the stool and put her forehead in her hand.

She loved him. That hadn’t changed. It hadn’t changed in September or in October or tonight under the streetlight.

But loving him wasn’t the same as being ready. She could kiss him at a taxi rank. She could laugh at his terrible jokes. She could miss his voice and want his hand at her waist. She could do all of that.

She still couldn’t tell him she was ready to come home. And she still couldn’t say three words to his face.

She typed: I miss you.

She looked at it. She deleted it. Not because it wasn’t true. Because it wasn’t the answer to anything yet.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was home by ten. He stood in his own kitchen without turning the big light on.

His flat had always been quiet. He’d spent years arranging his life so that silence was comfortable, so that every object had a place and every evening could be accounted for. Then she’d arrived and made a mess of all of it. Hair ties in places with no logical reason to contain a hair tie. Cups on his desk. Windows opened when the air conditioning was perfectly adequate. Conversations begun while he was reading a contract, and carried on.

He’d never in his life been so happy to have his routines wrecked.

He missed her. He didn’t need to pretend he didn’t.

He sat on the arm of the sofa and opened his phone and looked at her name. He thought of the taxi rank. Of her hand in his coat. Of her asking can I?. As if it were the first one again, and she wanted it to be.

He played the song she’d sent him. Twice. Then he locked the phone.

It wasn’t a reconciliation. It wasn’t a return. It was one dinner, and one kiss under a streetlight.

And for now, that was enough. Not because he wanted so little. Because he wanted her to be the one who chose what came next.

✦ ✦ ✦

A little before midnight, one more message.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Home.

Ren Hao: Good. Sleep well.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): You too.

She put the phone down. So did he. Neither of them said I love you. Neither of them said come back. Neither of them said wait for me.

But the kiss stayed. A small warm thing between two people who still knew exactly how to find each other, and still didn’t know what to do once they had. Not yet. Still.

chapters.title: The Widow
chapters.desc: The captain’s widow and daughter, and six words in ordinary writing. He waits outside in the rain for three hours. She tells him the last thing her father ever said to her.
chapters.epigraph: “Night, Zhu-zhu. Back Thursday.”
chapters.content:
The request came through the family liaison office on Wednesday the ninth of December, in a single typed line.

Mrs. Yuk Wai-ling, widow of Captain Yuk Kam-fai, asks whether the investigator-in-charge would be willing to meet her privately.

Song-Zhu read it at her desk and didn’t move a long time.

She knew what Mrs. Yuk wanted. Everybody on the fourth floor knew. Three weeks ago, after a month of argument in rooms Song-Zhu had sat in and rooms she hadn’t, Director Kwan had decided that the speech recovered from the cabin crew member’s phone, the words over the PA attributed to the captain, wasn’t the cockpit voice recording, wasn’t protected in the same way, contained nothing that bore on the cause, and was, in his words, a message addressed to his family that has been in our evidence store for two months too long. The captain’s next of kin would be told, privately, before the final report. By the investigator-in-charge, if the family wished it.

The family wished it.

She wrote back: Yes. Saturday. Whenever she likes.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday night she took the black zip case out of her bedside drawer.

She hadn’t opened it since December last year. Since the night she’d sat on her sofa with Ren Hao’s hand under hers and listened to four minutes of a controller calling her father’s callsign. She’d put it away afterwards and not taken it out again.

She unzipped it now on her bed, on her own, in the lamplight. The silver recorder in its grey foam. And beside it, in the little pocket in the lid, the thing she had never once touched in seven years. His card. The one that had been in the recorder on his desk on the morning he flew. The last things he’d said into it.

She’d told Ren Hao a year ago, on that sofa: I’ve never played anything he recorded on it. Not once. I can’t.

Tomorrow she was going to sit across a table from a woman whose husband had said six words to his daughter in the dark at four hundred feet, and give them to her. She was going to hand a stranger her husband’s voice.

She didn’t think she could do that honestly if she’d never been able to do it for herself.

She took out the card she’d copied the air traffic recording onto and put it in the lid. She took out his, and pushed it into the slot until it clicked. Her fingers were shaking so badly that it took her three tries.

She sat with the recorder in her lap for nineteen minutes. Then she pressed play.

✦ ✦ ✦

His voice came out of the little speaker so close and so ordinary that she put her hand over her mouth.

Tuesday, oh-four-hundred. Block time six forty. Fuel figures on the sheet. Number two pack running warm again, tell engineering, they won’t believe me, they never believe me.

A pause. A rustle, paper. Then the voice changed, the way it had always changed, the way she’d forgotten it changed.

And this is for Zhu-zhu. Hello, Zhu-zhu. Bumpy over the sea tonight, tell your mother I’m fine, I’m always fine. It’s raining on the apron and the coffee’s terrible and I’ve bought you something from the shop here, it’s ugly, you’ll love it. Did you finish that problem set? I’m checking when I’m back. Don’t stay up. You never listen. Night, Zhu-zhu. Back Thursday.

A click. That was all. He’d said her name.

Twice. In the first fifteen seconds. Her name, the one only he had ever called her, that nobody had said out loud since the funeral, that she hadn’t heard in his voice for seven years.

She’d sat in a room in another country at nineteen with a notebook on her knee and listened as hard as she had ever listened to anything for fifty seconds, waiting for him to say it, and he hadn’t, because he’d been flying an aeroplane.

He’d said it here. In the last thing he’d ever recorded. On an ordinary Tuesday, with the coffee terrible, telling her not to stay up.

She didn’t cry a long time. She sat on her bed holding the recorder and played it again. And again.
