On the fourth time, at it’s ugly, you’ll love it, she began to laugh, and then the laughing turned over into something else, and she curled up on her side on top of the duvet with the little silver thing held against her chest and cried until two in the morning, and nobody was there, and for the first time that didn’t feel like the point.

At ten past two she picked up her phone.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I’m seeing the captain’s widow tomorrow. At eleven. At the authority. I don’t know how long.

She looked at it. She added a line.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): You can wait nearby, if you want to. You don’t have to.

The answer came in under a minute, at ten past two in the morning, as if he’d been lying awake on the other side of the harbour with the phone on his chest.

Ren Hao: I’ll be there.

✦ ✦ ✦

*Saturday, 12 December* Mrs. Yuk was standing by the window in the reception area when Song-Zhu came down.

She was small and neat and about forty, in a grey coat with a grey cardigan under it, and a thin silver chain at her throat. She was thinner than the woman in the photograph in her husband’s crew file, the one Song-Zhu had looked at only once, in August, and then closed. Beside her, holding her hand, was a girl of about twelve with her hair in a long plait, in a school coat, with a pale ribbon tied round her wrist.

“Investigator Xu.”

“Mrs. Yuk. Thank you for coming.”

“This is Bo-yee.”

The girl looked at Song-Zhu with an expression Song-Zhu knew from the inside. Ready for the worst. Pretending not to be.

“Hello, Bo-yee.”

“Hello.”

“Would you like Bo-yee in the room with us?” said Song-Zhu gently, to her mother. “Or would you like to hear it first, and then decide?”

Mrs. Yuk’s hand tightened on her daughter’s. “She wants to be there. I said no. She said she was twelve and it was her father.”

“I’m twelve,” said Bo-yee. “And it’s my dad.”

Song-Zhu looked at her.

“Then you should be there,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The meeting room was small, with pale walls and three chairs, and a box of tissues on the table that nobody had moved. A liaison officer sat a little apart, by the door. Song-Zhu didn’t bring a laptop. She didn’t bring headphones. She brought nothing but a single sheet of paper, blank side up. They sat.

“I want to explain exactly what this is,” said Song-Zhu, “before I tell you anything. So that you know what you’re being given, and what you’re not.”

Mrs. Yuk nodded.

“It’s not from the cockpit. The cockpit recording’s separate and protected, and I can’t tell you anything about it. This is from a phone. A member of the cabin crew was recording a video, a short one for her sister, when the power went. The phone kept recording after the picture failed. It picked up an announcement over the cabin speakers. It’s damaged. Parts of it are missing. We’ve had it examined and processed by specialists, and every step of that is written down, and the original has been kept exactly as it was.”

“I understand.”

“The voice on it has been identified as your husband’s. On the PA. To the passengers.” Song-Zhu kept her eyes on Mrs. Yuk’s. “After the brace call, there’s a short piece of speech we’ve been able to make out. It isn’t an announcement. I can’t tell you what he knew at that moment, or what he was thinking. I can’t tell you whether it was the last thing he said, because I don’t know what he said on the flight deck afterwards. I can only tell you the words.”

Mrs. Yuk had gone still. Bo-yee was holding her mother’s hand in both of hers.

“Please,” said Mrs. Yuk.

Song-Zhu didn’t turn the paper over. She didn’t need to. She’d heard it more than fifty times.

“He said,” she said, slowly and clearly, “Tell my little girl. Daddy tried.”

For a moment nothing happened at all. Then Mrs. Yuk’s face changed. Not all at once. First her eyebrows drew together. Then her mouth moved. Then her free hand came up and pressed flat against her lips. But it was Bo-yee who spoke.

“Little girl,” she said. Her voice cracked straight down the middle. “He said little girl?”

“Yes.”

“I told him not to call me that.” Her face crumpled. “I told him on the phone. On the Saturday. Before he went. I said I’m twelve, Daddy, I’m not little, it’s embarrassing, and he laughed and said you’ll always be my little girl, it’s the law, and I hung up on him.” She was sobbing now, openly, the way children did, with her whole body. “I hung up on him. That was the last time. And he said it anyway. He said it anyway.”

Her mother pulled her in. The two of them held each other in the small pale room, and the liaison officer looked at the floor, and Song-Zhu sat absolutely still across the table and let them.

She didn’t say it would be all right. She didn’t say he’d have forgiven her. She didn’t say anything at all, a long time, because the room was full of the one thing nobody in it needed her to add to.

When Mrs. Yuk could speak, she said, into her daughter’s hair, “He always did that. Called her that. Every time she told him not to. She used to pretend to be furious. She was never furious.”

“I was a bit furious,” said Bo-yee, into her mother’s coat.

Mrs. Yuk laughed, wetly, helplessly. “A bit.”

Then she looked up at Song-Zhu over the girl’s head.

“Daddy tried.”

“Yes.”

“He wanted her to know he tried.”

“Those are the words,” said Song-Zhu. “That’s all I can tell you about what he meant. But I can tell you, because it’s in the report, and it’ll be in the final one, that the evidence shows the crew did everything they could have done with what they had. And I can tell you that he was still on the PA to his passengers after the power went. He didn’t stop. He kept talking to them all the way down.”

Mrs. Yuk shut her eyes. Bo-yee lifted her face from her mother’s coat. It was blotched and wet and furious and twelve.

“Did he sound scared?”

Song-Zhu looked at her. She had promised herself on the bed at two in the morning that she wouldn’t lie to this child about anything, not by one syllable, not to make it easier.

“He sounded like a man doing his job,” she said. “And then, for those words, he sounded like your dad.”

Bo-yee looked at her a long time.

“Okay,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the door, Mrs. Yuk turned back.

“Investigator Xu.”

“Yes?”

“Did he sound like himself?”

It was so quiet Song-Zhu almost didn’t catch it.

She thought about the roar, and the distortion, and the two words that came up out of it like something surfacing.

“It was his voice,” she said.

Mrs. Yuk nodded slowly, as though that were enough. Perhaps it was.

“Thank you for not making it prettier than it was,” she said.

“Thank you,” said Song-Zhu, “for letting me be the one to tell you.”

Bo-yee, at the door, looked back over her shoulder.

“Miss Xu? Is it written down? What he said? Somewhere?”

“It’s in the evidence record. It’ll be in the final report, in the proper words.”

“Can I have it written down? In ordinary writing. Not report words.”

Song-Zhu looked at the sheet of paper still lying blank side up on the table. She turned it over. On it, in her own small handwriting, in the middle of the page, there was nothing but the six words, and a date. She held it out.

The girl took it in both hands and looked at it, and folded it once, carefully, and put it inside her school coat, against her chest. And then she and her mother went out, and the door closed behind them so gently that the latch didn’t click.

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d been outside the building since ten to twelve.

It had started raining at half past, lightly, and then not lightly, until the pavement was dark and the cars went by with a hiss. The building had a narrow overhang over its side entrance, deep enough for one person if that person stood straight against the wall.

At one o’clock the rain got heavier. At twenty-five to two he bought a coffee from the kiosk across the road, and it was cold before he remembered he was holding it. At ten past two he stepped further under the overhang to let an old woman with a shopping trolley go by, and the rain got the backs of his legs. At twenty to three he answered two messages from Raymond about the restructuring, and one from Ruby that said only Is she all right?, and that he didn’t answer, because he didn’t know.

He could have gone in. He could have asked at the desk. He could have rung. He didn’t.

He’d learned, in a doorway with a bag in his hand, that waiting and being useful weren’t the same thing. Sometimes waiting was the whole of what you’d been asked to do.

At twelve minutes past three the glass doors opened, and she came out.

She was holding her coat shut with one hand. The other hand was empty. She stopped on the step and looked at the street, and then. She saw him.

He was soaked from the knees down. The shoulders of his good coat had gone black with rain. His hair had come out of its shape and was stuck to his forehead. She stared.

“Hao.”

“Hello.”

“How long have you been standing here?”

“Not long.”

“How long?”

He looked at his watch. “About three hours and twenty minutes.”

“Three hours?”

“You said nearby.”

“You could have gone somewhere dry!”

“I did. Briefly. I bought a coffee.”

She looked at the paper cup on the wall beside him.

“That coffee’s dead, Hao.”

“Yes,” he agreed.

She came down the step under the overhang and took hold of his wet sleeve and looked at it.

“Why didn’t you go in?”

“You didn’t know how long you’d be. So I didn’t know when you’d come out.”

“That doesn’t mean standing in the rain.”

“I wasn’t standing in the rain. I was standing next to it.”

“Your shoes are ruined.”

He looked down. “They are.”

She looked up at him with an exasperation so complete that he nearly smiled. And then her face went, all at once, and the exasperation was gone, and what was underneath it was something he’d seen on her only twice before. On a kitchen floor. In a laboratory, though he hadn’t been there to see it.

“How was it?” he said.

“I told her.”

He didn’t ask what.

“She brought her daughter. She’s twelve.” Song-Zhu’s voice wobbled and she let it. “Her father used to call her his little girl. She told him not to, on the phone, on the Saturday, before he flew. She hung up on him. She’s carried that since August.” She pressed her lips together. “And now she’s got it written down. In ordinary writing.”

He didn’t move. And then she stepped forward and put her forehead against his chest, against his wet coat, and stood there. He went still.

It wasn’t something she did when she was hurting. She usually needed to put herself back together first, alone, before she let anybody close. He knew that. He’d learned it.

He didn’t put his arms round her. His hand hung for a moment in the air by her back. Ask. Don’t assume. Don’t make her body one more thing to solve. Then her fingers closed in his coat.

He understood. His arms came round her, and she breathed out, a long shaking breath, and he held her under the narrow overhang with the rain coming down a few centimetres behind her back, and put his cheek against her hair.

“Three hours,” she said into his coat.

“And twenty minutes.”

“You’re an idiot.”

“Possibly.”

“You could have gone home.”

“You asked me to wait.”

She was quiet for a long moment against him.

“Yes,” she said. “I did.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They found a café two streets away, small and steamed up, and he ordered her tea and himself something hot, and she sat opposite him and watched him wrap both hands round the cup.

“You’re shivering.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

“It’s the air conditioning.”

“It’s December.”

“Air conditioning isn’t seasonal.”

She reached across the table and touched the back of his hand. It was like ice.

“Hao.”

“Your assessment is accurate,” he said, and she laughed, slightly, for the first time that day.

For a while they watched the rain go down the window.

“I didn’t tell you before,” she said, “because I couldn’t. It was evidence. It wasn’t mine. It still isn’t mine. It’s hers now, and Bo-yee’s. So I’m not going to tell you what he said. I’m sorry. I don’t think I should.”

“You don’t have to be sorry. I’d never ask you.”

“I know you wouldn’t.” She turned her cup round. “But there’s something else. Something that is mine. And I want to tell you.”

He put his cup down.

“Last night,” she said, “I played my father’s card.”

He went still.

“Not the air traffic. His. The one that was in the recorder on his desk the morning he flew. The last things he said into it. I’ve had it seven years. I told you I’d never played anything he recorded, and I hadn’t. I couldn’t. And last night I thought: tomorrow I’m going to sit across a table from a woman and hand her husband’s voice to her. And I’ve never once been brave enough to take my own father’s.” She looked down at her tea. “So I did.”

He didn’t say anything. He reached across the table, slowly, and she let him take her hand.

“It’s mostly his logbook,” she said. “Fuel. Block time. A pack running warm. Complaining that engineering never believed him. And then at the end, there’s a bit for me.” She took a breath.

“He said, Hello, Zhu-zhu. He said Bumpy over the sea, tell your mother I’m fine. He said he’d bought me something ugly from an airport shop and I’d love it. He asked if I’d finished a problem set. He said don’t stay up, you never listen. And then he said Night, Zhu-zhu. Back Thursday.”

Her eyes had filled. She didn’t stop.

“He said my name, Hao. Twice. At nineteen, in that room, with the fifty seconds, I listened for my name with everything I had, and he didn’t say it, and I’ve spent seven years thinking that the last time he spoke he didn’t think of me. And he did. He had. Two days before. On a Tuesday. About homework.”

The tears ran down, and she let them.

“That’s what he said. That’s his last words to me. Night, Zhu-zhu. Back Thursday.”

Ren Hao held her hand across the café table and didn’t say anything a long time. Because there wasn’t anything he could say that would be bigger than that, and he knew it now, and he’d learned not to try.

“Thank you,” he said at last, low. “For telling me.”

“Nobody calls me that. Nobody’s said it since the funeral. My mother can’t.”

“I won’t,” he said. “It’s his.”

She looked at him then, across the table, with her eyes wet and her hand in his, and something went through her face that he couldn’t read and then could. She opened her mouth.

He saw it come up. The word. Right there, the closest it had ever been, closer than at the door with his bag, closer than at the taxi rank. He saw her reach for it.

And he saw it stop. Not because it wasn’t true. Because she wasn’t ready to say it into a café on a wet Saturday afternoon.

She shut her mouth again, and pressed her lips together, and looked at him helplessly.

“I know,” he said gently. “You don’t have to. Not today. Not here.”

“I want to.”

“I know you do. That’s enough, for today. Truly.”

She put her other hand over his, so that his was held between both of hers on the table.

“I still can’t come back yet,” she said. “I don’t want you to think because I let you hold me in the rain, or because I told you that...”

“I don’t think anything. You told me your father said your name. That’s what today is.”

“I don’t want to hurt you.”

“Song-Zhu,” he said. “I can be hurt without you having done anything wrong. I miss you. I’m not going to pretend I don’t. There are days I want to ring you because something absurd happened at work and you’re the first person I think of. There are days I want to ask whether you’ve eaten and I have to remind myself that you’re a grown woman with a canteen.” He looked at her steadily. “But I don’t want you to come back because you feel responsible for how much I miss you. Ever.”

Her fingers tightened round his.

“I don’t want that either.”

“Then we agree,” said Ren Hao.

✦ ✦ ✦

The rain had eased by the time they left. She made him take her umbrella, and he held it over both of them as far as the taxi rank on the corner.

A cab drew in. She didn’t go to it.

“Go home,” she said. “Dry your shoes. Not on the radiator.”

“Is that an instruction?”

“Yes.”

“Understood.”

“And have something hot.”

“Yes, Investigator.”

She looked at him under the umbrella. Then she reached up and pushed his wet hair off his forehead, and her hand stayed there, on his cheek.

“Thank you for not asking me to promise anything,” she said.

“I don’t need a promise. I’ve got your father’s voice saying your name. You gave me that. That’s more than a promise.”

She kissed him then, under the umbrella, at the corner, quickly, gently, with her hand still on his face, and it wasn’t like the taxi rank in November. That one had been a question. This one was something heavier, and older, and she held it longer. The cab sounded its horn, once. She got in. He watched it go.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night she sat at her kitchen table with the lights low and her hair wet from the bath. The black case was on the table in front of her, shut. Her phone buzzed.

Ren Hao: Home. Shoes drying. No radiator involved.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Good.

Ren Hao: I followed instructions.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): A historic day.

She looked at the screen a long time. Her thumb hung over the keys. Three words. She typed the first one. She looked at it. She deleted it, and typed something else instead.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): He’d have liked you. He’d have said your shoes were too shiny. Then he’d have liked you.

The answer took a minute.

Ren Hao: You told me that last December. I’ve been trying to deserve it ever since.

She put the phone down beside the black case.

They were still living apart. They still weren’t back together. The final report was eight months away.

But that afternoon she’d given a twelve-year-old her father’s words in ordinary writing. And last night her own father had said her name to her, twice, after seven years.

Neither of those things had mended anything. Neither of them had brought anybody home.

But they were true. And for tonight, that was what she had.

chapters.title: The Crumpled List
chapters.desc: A crumpled list in his coat: eighty-one reasons, crossed out and rewritten for a year. On his kitchen counter, explicit, she says I love you in the middle, and he stops dead, and then doesn’t.
chapters.epigraph: “Some things don’t have to be written down.”
chapters.content:
His coat was on the wrong chair. That was the first thing she noticed, on Saturday the ninth of January, standing in his flat for the first time in four months.

Ren Hao had a system for coats. She’d laughed at it in the summer of 2025 and he’d explained it to her anyway, at length, with diagrams in the air. Work coats in the wardrobe on the left. Weekend coats on the right. Anything he meant to wear again the next morning on the chair in the bedroom. Never, ever, on a dining chair.

His good dark wool coat was over the back of a dining chair, still damp at the hem from last night’s rain, when he’d met her outside the authority at half past seven and walked her to the noodle place and then to the taxi rank, the third Friday in a row.

She’d come for lunch. He’d asked on Wednesday. Would you like to come over on Saturday? I’ll cook. You can leave whenever you like. She’d said yes before she’d finished reading it.

She picked the coat up. “Your standards are slipping,” she called towards the kitchen.

“I heard that.”

“Good.”

“I’m making coffee.”

“That doesn’t answer the charge.”

“It wasn’t a question,” he called back, and she smiled, on her own, in his living room, and carried the coat towards the bedroom to put it on the right chair, because somebody had to.

Something crackled in the inside pocket. She stopped.

It was a wad of paper, folded small and soft at the corners from being handled. She hadn’t meant to take it out. She’d meant to put her hand on it, through the wool, the way you’d check for a phone. But it was so thick, and so worn, and as her fingers closed on it the outer fold came loose and opened a little, and she saw his handwriting.

His narrow capitals. Cramped. Black ink and blue. She looked towards the kitchen.

“Hao?”

“Yes?”

“What’s this?”

A pause. “What’s what?”

She unfolded it. There were six sheets of paper, from a notebook, torn out and folded together into one square. At the top of the first one, underlined twice:

REASONS. (FOR S-Z, WHO SAYS I WON’T GET PAST FIVE.)

Underneath, smaller, a date. Sun 11 Jan 2026. A year ago, nearly to the day.

She sat down on the arm of his sofa.

1. She laughs at her own jokes before she gets to the end of them.
2. She says she isn’t hungry and then eats half of what’s on my plate.
3. She has no idea how loud she is when she’s excited about a weld.

“Excuse me,” she said, out loud.

“What?” from the kitchen.

“Nothing.”

4. She can listen to the worst thing a person ever says and still remember to ask the man who brought her the tape whether he’s eaten.
5. She argues with traffic lights.
6. She doesn’t own an indoor voice and has never wanted one.
7. She can turn a ten-minute phone call into forty, and at the end of it I still feel short-changed.

She turned the page. There were more. A great many more. Some numbered. Some numbered and then crossed through. Some written again in the margin underneath, in different words, as if he’d sat with the sentence and decided it wasn’t true enough yet.

12. She’s kind when nobody’s watching. Most of all then.
13. She can tell when people are lying and she gives them time to stop.
14. She doesn’t mistake gentle for weak. In anybody.
15. She looks at me when she thinks I’m reading.

She stopped on fifteen. She read it again.

She remembered January 2026. The flat, his sofa, three months in, nearly four. She’d been tired and cross after cancelling a dinner at the last minute for a call-out, and she’d made a joke that wasn’t one, about how he’d get tired of her eventually, everyone got tired of her eventually, she was a lot. And he’d said he wouldn’t. And she’d said, how could he possibly know that. And he’d said he’d make a list. And she’d laughed at him and said he wouldn’t get past five.

He’d got past five.

19. She makes ordinary places into somewhere I want to stay.
20. She’s brave in ways she won’t give herself credit for.
21. She tells me when I’m being an idiot.

And beside twenty-one, small:

Frequently. With evidence.

She laughed out loud. Then she turned the page and stopped laughing.

22. She makes me want to be better and has never once asked me to be somebody else.

There were eighty-one of them. She knew because the last page had the number written at the bottom and circled.

Some were funny. Some were so particular that she could remember the exact minute he must have written them: the night of the cake, the camp bed, the snowball. Some were so private she felt she’d opened a door into a room he’d never meant her to walk into. And some had been written later.

She could tell from the ink. From the hand. The first pages were neat and nearly playful. The later ones were cramped, the letters pressed too hard into the paper. There were dates in the margins now. March. May. June (after “too much”). August. September. October.

And there were the crossings out. On the fourth page there was a line struck through so many times that the pen had nearly torn the paper.

~~47. She lets me look after her.~~

And underneath, in blue:

47. She lets me look after her when she wants it, and tells me when she doesn’t. I am learning the difference. Slowly. She is patient. She shouldn’t have to be.

Song-Zhu sat still on the arm of his sofa.

~~53. She trusts me with the things that frighten her.~~
53. She trusted me with the things that frightened her. I’d like to earn it again, without asking her to hand it over before she’s ready.

~~61. She makes me laugh.~~
61. I miss making her laugh.

~~62. She is home.~~
62. I miss being let into her home.

She stopped breathing.

63. I love her when she needs me to stay away. I didn’t know that was possible until 19 September.

She put the paper down on her knee. The kitchen had gone quiet. She could hear the coffee machine finish, and then nothing.

He’d written these while they were apart. Not as a letter, not as a plea. Not for her. He’d written them for himself, in a coat pocket, for a year, and crossed them out when they stopped being true, and written something truer underneath.

She turned to the last page. Black ink again.

77. She is still the first person I want to tell when something good happens.
78. She is still the person I look for when something goes wrong. Even in a hotel lobby. Even in a car park.
79. I love who she is. Not the version of her that’s easiest for me.
80. I want to be next to her. I don’t want being next to me to be one more thing she has to carry.

And at the bottom:

81. I love Xu Song-Zhu. Not because she makes my life easier. Because she makes it mine.

And a date beneath it, the ink still dark.

Sat 9 Jan 2027.

Today. He’d written the last one this morning.

“Song-Zhu?”

She looked up. He was standing in the doorway with two cups of coffee, in a grey jumper with the sleeves pushed up, and he’d taken one look at the paper on her knee and gone completely still.

His eyes went from the pages to her face.

“Ah,” he said.

She held them up. “Ah?”

He put the cups down on the nearest bookshelf, carefully.

“I was looking for that.”

“Clearly.”

“I thought I’d left it in my desk drawer.”

“You wrote eighty-one reasons.”

He shut his eyes, briefly. “Yes.”

“Eighty-one.”

“I can count.”

“Apparently you can also write.”

He looked at her warily. “Are you upset?”

She stared at him. “Why on earth would I be upset?”

“I don’t know. You’ve got a face...”

“The face of a woman reading eighty-one reasons.”

He was quiet. “It was private,” he said at last. “I wasn’t hiding it from you. I just didn’t write it for anyone to read. I didn’t write it to make you do anything.”

“I know you didn’t.” She looked down at the first page. “You did it because I said you wouldn’t get past five.”

His mouth moved. “Yes.”

“On your sofa. In January. After the call-out.”

“You remember.”

“I remember everything, Hao. It’s my job.” She turned a page. “Number one. I laugh at my own jokes before I finish them.”

“You do.”

“Number two. I eat half your food.”

“You do that too.”

“You could order more.”

“I do order more. You eat half of that as well.”

She almost laughed. She turned the pages.

“Twelve. I’m kind when nobody’s watching.”

His face changed. “That’s true.”

“Twenty-two.”

“That’s true too.”

“Forty-seven,” she said, and stopped, and read it aloud, the blue one. “She lets me look after her when she wants it, and tells me when she doesn’t. I am learning the difference. Slowly. She is very patient. She shouldn’t have to be.”

He looked at the floor. “That one was later.”

“I can see that.”

“I didn’t know whether to keep it. It isn’t a reason. It’s a thing I needed not to forget.”

“Sixty-three,” she said, quieter.

He didn’t say anything.

“I love her when she needs me to stay away. I didn’t know that was possible until nineteenth September.”

His jaw moved.

“Eighty,” she said. She could hardly get it out. “I want to be next to her. I don’t want being next to me to be one more thing she has to carry.”

He came away from the doorway.

“I didn’t mean you to find it.”

“I know.”

“It isn’t a request.”

“I know.”

“I don’t want you to think you have to...”

“Hao.”

He stopped.

“You kept the crossed-out ones,” she said. “All of them.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

He thought about it, properly, standing in the middle of his living room.

“Because I don’t think they were wrong,” he said. “They just weren’t finished.”

She couldn’t say anything. “And eighty-one,” she said. “This morning.”

“I was making coffee,” he said. “And I saw your mug. The one you left on the draining board three weeks ago. The ugly cat.”

“The cat isn’t ugly.”

“It’s got one eye.”

“It’s a design choice.”

“And I thought about how you leave things here now. Not because you live here. You don’t. You come over, and forget something, and come back for it. A mug. A hair tie. A scarf on Tuesday.” He looked at her. “And I realised I didn’t want to treat those things as evidence that you were halfway back. As a tally. I wanted them to be exactly what they were. You came round. You left your mug. That’s all. And I was happy. So I wrote eighty-one. It’s the only one I’ve written in the present tense since August.”

She looked down at the page a long time.

Then she folded the pages carefully, not along the old soft creases but new ones, and smoothed them flat with her palm.

“Can I keep it?” she said.

“It’s yours. It’s always been yours.”

She put it in the pocket of her own coat, on the hook by his door, and came back, and picked up her coffee from the bookshelf, and drank some, and pulled a face.

“It’s cold.”

“You’ve been reading for twenty minutes.”

“Seventeen is missing,” she said.

He blinked. “What?”

“You go sixteen, eighteen. There’s no seventeen. I counted.”

He came and looked over her shoulder at the page she’d taken out again. She was right. Sixteen, and then eighteen, and between them a gap the width of one line.

“I couldn’t get it right,” he said. “I wrote it nine times. I couldn’t find a way that didn’t sound embarrassing.”

“Try.”

He looked at her. Then he said, low, “I love the way you look at me when you’re half asleep. Because you haven’t remembered to keep anything back yet.”

Her fingers closed on the paper. She looked away, out of the window.

“That’s seventeen,” she said. “Don’t write it down.”

“I won’t.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They made lunch. Or rather, she announced that she was making lunch, and he was permitted to assist on condition that he didn’t touch the arrangement of anything.

“You’ve put the knife in the wrong place.”

He looked at it. “It’s next to the board.”

“Exactly.”

“Where should it be?”

“Nearer me.”

He moved it.

“Too near.”

He moved it back.

“Fine,” she said.

“Thank you for your generous approval.”

Noodles, greens, eggs. Nothing complicated. He washed the greens and made remarks she ignored. She kept looking at her coat on its hook by the door, where the list was.

“You’re going to read it again,” he said.

“Maybe.”

“You’ve read it.”

“Maybe I missed something.”

“You didn’t miss anything. You’ve never missed anything in your life.”

She went and got it anyway, and read him thirty-four, she talks to animals as though they’ve been fully briefed, while the water boiled.

“That’s slander.”

“You explained to a cat in the car park why it shouldn’t sit on a hot bonnet.”

“It was a safety matter.”

She went on reading. She came to sixty-two again, the crossed-out one, and the one underneath. I miss being let into her home. She touched it with one finger. He’d turned back to the sink.

“Do you regret writing any of them?” she said.

He turned the tap off.

“No.”

“Not even the hard ones?”

He dried his hands, slowly. “Those least of all,” he said. “Because I don’t want to only remember the easy parts of loving you. I used to think loving somebody meant knowing how to make them happy. If I saw what you needed before you did, and arranged it, and cleared everything out of your way, I’d be doing it right.” He leaned on the counter. “I know now I can make your life harder by trying to make it easier. I don’t want to forget that. So I kept the crossings-out.”

She looked at him a long time across his kitchen.

She put the list down by the fruit bowl.

She came round the counter and stood in front of him and put her hand flat on his chest.

“Can I kiss you?” she said.

His face changed. Not surprise exactly. The sudden, total, careful attention he always gave her when she was the one who moved first.

“Yes.”

She kissed him.

His hands came to her waist, and stayed there, and let her decide how close. She came close. She put her other hand round the back of his neck and opened her mouth against his and kissed him the way she hadn’t since July, not since the beach, slow and deep and certain, and she felt him make a sound into her mouth that was almost nothing and almost everything, and his fingers tightened on her waist, and still he didn’t pull.

When she drew back she stayed close enough to feel his breath.

“Your noodles,” he said, rather unsteadily, “are going to boil over.”

“You’re ruining it.”

“I’m saving lunch.”

“Let lunch suffer,” said Song-Zhu, and reached past him and turned the hob off without looking, and kissed him again.

This time he didn’t mention the noodles.

✦ ✦ ✦

He lifted her onto his counter.

He asked first, with his hands on her hips and his eyes on hers, and she said yes into his mouth, and he lifted her, and she was sitting on the cold stone edge of his kitchen counter in her jeans and a soft jumper with her knees either side of him and the fruit bowl at her elbow and the list folded beside it.

He stood between her knees and looked at her.

“Song-Zhu.”

“Mm?”

“Are you sure?”

She knew what he was asking. Not about the counter.

She looked at him for a long, long moment. At his face, tired and careful and so full of hope that he was trying with every muscle in it not to show her.

“Yes,” she said.

“Not because of the list?”

She gave him a small, incredulous look. “Hao. I’m not having some sort of romantic emergency because you wrote eighty-one sentences.”

“All right.”

“I’m here because I want to be here. I’ve wanted to be here every Friday at that taxi rank for three weeks.”

“All right.”

“Stop asking questions.”

He smiled against her lips. “I’ll try.”

She pulled his jumper over his head. He let her. She put both hands flat on his bare chest and ran them down, slowly, learning him again, the way she’d learn a piece of wreckage she thought she knew: the same, and not the same, and every centimetre to be checked. He was thinner. She could feel his ribs. He’d been sleeping badly in the wrong key on the wrong side of the harbour for four months, and she could feel every week of it under her palms, and she leaned forward and put her mouth on his collarbone where it stood out, and kept it there.

He breathed in sharply.

He undressed her slowly. Her jumper first, over her head, and he had to stop for a moment and just look. Then he kissed her throat, and her shoulder, and the top of her breast above her bra, and unhooked it with one hand and let it fall into the fruit bowl, and she laughed, helplessly, with her head back against his kitchen cupboard, and he laughed too, into her skin, and then neither of them was laughing.

He took her breast in his mouth, slow and warm, and she arched off the counter into him and put both hands in his hair. He took his time. He’d always taken his time with her, but this was different; this was a man who had thought for four months that he might never be allowed to again, and was going to do it properly, every single part of her, in order. He kissed his way down her stomach. He undid her jeans and she lifted her hips off the cold stone and he drew them off her, and her knickers with them, and dropped them on his kitchen floor.

Then he went down on his knees in front of the counter.

“Hao...”

“Let me,” he said. “Please. I’ve missed this. I’ve missed you. Let me.”

She let him.

He put his mouth on her and she made a sound she’d never made in his flat before, because his flat had always felt like the place where she was looked after, and nobody had ever made her sound like that in a place where she was looked after. He held her thighs open with his hands. He was slow, and then he wasn’t, and then he was slow again, deliberately, every time she got close, until she was gripping the edge of the counter with both hands and saying his name to the ceiling, and saying please, and he lifted his head for one second and looked up at her with his mouth wet and his eyes nearly black.

“Not yet,” he said. “Not until I’m inside you. I want to be there. Please.”

“Then get up here,” she said, and he laughed, hoarse, and stood.

She got his belt open with hands that wouldn’t work properly. He pushed his trousers down. She wrapped her legs round him and pulled him in against her and they both stopped, his forehead on hers, breathing.

“Look at me,” he said.

She looked. He pushed into her slowly. All the way. Until there wasn’t any space left between them at all, anywhere, and she was full of him, and he was holding her up against his chest with one arm round her back and the other hand flat on the counter beside her hip, and neither of them could breathe properly. He didn’t move. Neither did she.

“Four months,” he said, so low she barely heard it.

“I know.”

He began to move.

Slowly. Deep. Each stroke unhurried and whole, her heels locked behind him, her arms round his neck, his face an inch from hers so she could see everything it did. The fruit bowl rattled on the counter. Something rolled off it and onto the floor and neither of them cared. He held her gaze, and she held his, and it built in her slowly, a long rising tightness, and she didn’t want it to end, she wanted it to go on all afternoon, in his kitchen, with the light coming in across the floor and the noodles going cold and the list folded by her hip.

He was looking at her the way he’d looked at her in the snow. The way he’d looked at her on the beach in the moonlight. As if she were the only true thing he’d ever seen. She held his face in both her hands.

“Hao.”

“Yes.”

“I love you,” said Song-Zhu.

He stopped. Completely. Dead still, inside her, his whole body gone rigid against hers, his breath caught somewhere halfway in. His hand on the counter closed into a fist. He stared at her from an inch away, and his face did something she had never seen any face do.

“Say it again,” he whispered.

“I love you.”

“Song-Zhu...”

“I love you. I’ve loved you since the camp bed broke. Since before. Since you sent me minutes of our date at fourteen minutes past midnight. I couldn’t say it. I tried at your door with your bag in your hand and in the café and at the taxi rank every Friday, and I couldn’t, and I can now. I love you, Hao. I love you. I’m saying it into your face, in your kitchen, with you inside me, because I want you to know it isn’t folded up inside anything. It’s just true.”

His eyes had filled. They spilled over. He didn’t wipe them. He didn’t move at all except that he was shaking, all through, against her.

“I had things prepared,” he said, hardly a voice. “For when you said it. I had them ready for a year. I can’t remember any of them.”

“Good,” said Song-Zhu, and kissed him, and tightened her legs round him, and pulled him deeper. “Then don’t stop.”

And he didn’t.

He held her face, and kissed her, and moved in her again, and it wasn’t slow any more. It was something that had been held back for sixteen months, and it broke, and she broke with it. He drove into her against his kitchen counter with his face in her neck and her name and I love you and her name again going into her skin, over and over, and she held on to him with everything she had and said it back, every time, I love you, I love you, until the words weren’t words any more, and she came with her nails in his shoulders and her head back against the cupboard door and his mouth on her throat, crying, laughing, saying it, and he came a moment later holding her so tight against him that she couldn’t breathe and didn’t want to, with one long broken sound that was the closest she’d ever heard him come to silence.

For a long time afterwards neither of them moved.

He stayed inside her, holding her, his forehead on her shoulder, both of them breathing like people who’d come up from deep water. She stroked the back of his neck. He was still shaking, slightly. So was she.

“I’m going to have to clean this counter,” he said eventually, into her shoulder, in a wrecked voice.

She laughed so suddenly that he slipped out of her, and they both gasped, and then they were both laughing, helplessly, naked in his kitchen, with her bra in the fruit bowl and an orange on the floor.

“I love you,” he said, when he could. “I know you know. I wanted to say it now. After. When you’d said it.”

“I know.”

“Say it once more. I’m sorry. Once more.”

She took his face in her hands and looked at him.

“I love you, Ren Hao,” she said. “I didn’t say it because of the list. I didn’t say it because you waited. I said it because it’s true, and it’s been true for a very long time, and I’ve finally stopped being frightened of the shape of it in my mouth.”

He shut his eyes. “I know, sweetheart,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The afternoon went into evening. They didn’t go out.

She borrowed one of his shirts and wore it over her own jeans, and he made tea, and she sat on his sofa with her feet under her and read the list again. He came and sat beside her with the cups.

“Which number?”

“Eighty-one.”

“That’s a good one.”

“There’s something missing,” she said.

“Seventeen. I know. You told me not to write it.”

“Not seventeen. Something else.”

“What?”

She took his hand and put it flat against her cheek and held it there.

“You didn’t write she loves me back.”

He smiled, slowly, the whole way across his face. “I didn’t know she did.”

“That’s not an excuse.”

“I’ll add it.”

“No,” she said, and folded the list. “Some things don’t have to be written down.”

She leaned against his shoulder. For a while they listened to his flat hum round them. His fridge. His heating. A different key from hers, and she found she didn’t mind it.

“I want to come back,” she said.

He didn’t move at all.

She lifted her head. “Not because everything’s finished. It isn’t. The investigation isn’t. There’s the contractor, and the signatures, and seven months of work. I’ve still got things to work out.” She looked at him. “But I don’t want to keep pretending that loving you and being with you are two separate problems I have to solve one after the other. I want to try again. Properly. Slowly, if we have to. But together.”

His face changed. Not dramatically. His eyes first, then his mouth, then the rest of him, like a man who’d been holding a breath so long he’d forgotten he was allowed to let it go.

“Are you sure?”

She gave him a look. “Hao.”

“Sorry.”

“Yes. I’m sure.”

He lifted her hand and kissed the knuckles. “I want that. I want you.”

“I know.”

“But not how it was.”

“No,” she said. “Not how it was. Differently.”

“Can I come home with you tonight?” he said.

She looked at him. Then round at his flat. Then back at him.

“You can come round,” she said. “To my flat. But you’re not moving your toothbrush back in without asking. And you’re not rearranging my kitchen.”

“I’ve never rearranged your kitchen.”

“You moved my coffee machine in August.”

“It was blocking a socket.”

“It was where I wanted it.”

“All right.”

“And no scheduling my meals. No tracking my phone. No sending a car because it looks like rain.”

He hesitated, slightly.

She narrowed her eyes. “Ren Hao.”

“Agreed.”

“Good.” She put her forehead against his. “One more thing. You can still ask if I’ve eaten.”

“Can I?”

“Once a day.”

“Even if you say you’ve had a biscuit?”

“Then twice,” said Song-Zhu.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty-four minutes to nine his phone rang. He looked at it, and then at her.

“Isla.”

“Answer it.”

It was half past seven in the morning in Lima. His sister’s voice came through loud enough for the whole room.

“Are you busy?”

He looked at Song-Zhu. “Not especially.”

“You’re lying.”

“Why ring if you’ve already decided I’m lying?”

“Because I want to hear you admit it.”

Song-Zhu laughed.

There was a silence from Lima. “Is that Song-Zhu?”

“Yes.”

“Is she there?”

Song-Zhu leaned in towards the phone. “Hi, Isla.”

A sound came down the line from eighteen thousand kilometres away that was somewhere between a gasp and a shriek.

“Oh.”

Ren Hao shut his eyes. “Don’t.”

“Oh, my God.”

“Isla.”

“Are you back together?”

Song-Zhu looked at him. He looked back at her. She smiled.

“Yes,” she said.

Isla went quiet. Then, low, all the way from the other side of the Pacific: “Oh.”

“Yes.”

“Really?”

“Really,” she said, and wiped her eyes, and laughed at herself.

“Okay,” said Isla, and her voice was wobbling. “Okay. I’m not going to ask anything else. I’m going to be extremely respectful.”

“Since when?” said her brother.

“Since now. Don’t ruin it. I’m happy for you. Both of you. Wei Long’s right here, he says he’s happy for you, he’s doing his face, the small one.” A pause. “Hao?”

“Yes?”

“Don’t mess it up.”

“I’ll try not to.”

“Don’t try. Do. Love you. Goodbye,” said Isla, and rang off before anybody could say anything else.

Song-Zhu was laughing. He put the phone down and looked at her.

“She’ll be insufferable for a week.”

“Two.”

✦ ✦ ✦

When they were ready to go, she took the list out of her coat pocket one last time and unfolded it, there in his hall.

Eighty-one lines. A year of loving her in small exact observations. A year of changing his mind about how to say things, crossing out the words that had stopped being true and writing something truer underneath them. She ran her thumb over the last one.

Then she folded it, carefully, and put it in the inside pocket of her own coat, against her heart, where he’d kept it.

“Ready?” he said.

“Yes.”

“Taking it?”

“Obviously.”

She held her hand out. He took it. “Hao,” she said, at his door. “Next year. Make it eighty-two.”

He laughed. “Why?”

“Because you missed one.”

“Which?”

She kissed him, in his doorway, with her coat on and his list against her heart.

“Because I love you too,” she said against his mouth.

“I’ll write it down.”

“No, you won’t.”

“Why not?”

“Because I want you to remember it,” said Song-Zhu.

“I will,” he said.

And this time, when they left, neither of them was leaving the other one behind.

chapters.title: Back In
chapters.desc: Seven conditions on a noodle-shop napkin, and a clause about six suits. He signs, adds an eighth, and keeps every one. Signed with a kiss.
chapters.epigraph: “We remember we’re on the same side.”
chapters.content:
The napkin had come from the noodle place behind the cargo terminal, the one where they’d eaten on the nineteenth of June 2025 and she’d told him what she listened to for a living. It had the shop’s name printed in red in one corner and a grease spot in the other, and she’d brought it home in her coat pocket on Friday night without knowing why.

On Sunday the seventeenth of January, at her kitchen counter, she found out.

He was at her stove, making tea, because she’d asked him to come round for lunch and he’d asked whether he could make the tea and she’d said yes. He heard the scratch of her pen behind him. Then the scrape of the salt pot being moved out of the way.

“What are you writing?”

“Something important.”

“Should I be worried?”

“Possibly.”

He looked over his shoulder. She was sitting at her counter in his old university sweatshirt, which she’d never given back, with her hair in a clip and a napkin flat in front of her and an expression of enormous seriousness.

He turned off the kettle. “Is that a contract?”

“Not yet.”

“That sounds worse.”

She didn’t look up. “Bring the tea.”

He brought it, and put the cups down, and she slid the napkin across the counter to him. At the top, in capitals:

TERMS AND CONDITIONS FOR REN HAO MOVING BACK INTO MY FLAT

He read it. He looked at her.

“Moving back?”

“Don’t get excited. Read it first.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“Your face has.”

He looked down at the napkin again. There were seven conditions, numbered, in her small fast hand, crammed in round the grease spot.

1. Not all at once. A few nights first. Then we see.
2. You ask before bringing anything. Clothes, toiletries, chargers, coffee machines, and any suspiciously large box you say is “just something useful”.
3. My kitchen stays my kitchen. You can cook. You can wash up. You may not rearrange anything. This includes the coffee machine.
4. You can ask if I’ve eaten. Once a day. You may not monitor, remind, or send food to my building without asking.
5. No tracking my phone. Ever.
6. If either of us is upset, we say so. No going quiet for a day. No pretending it’s fine to be considerate.
7. I get a life outside us. So do you. Not every evening has to be together.

And at the bottom, squeezed in under the grease spot:

The six suits can stay. They’ve been here since August. I’ve got used to them.

And under that, smaller still:

Breach of any of the above may result in immediate eviction and the loss of kitchen privileges.

He read the whole thing twice. Then he put the napkin down carefully on the counter, as if it were something that might break.

“Kitchen privileges,” he said.

“Yes.”

“That’s the worst penalty?”

“Don’t underestimate me.”

He looked at her. She was trying hard to look stern, and the corners of her mouth weren’t managing it.

“May I ask a question?”

“One.”

“Are you asking me to move back in?”

She looked at him across her counter. “Yes,” she said.

The smile went out of his face, and something quieter came into it.

“Properly?”

“Properly. Slowly. But properly.”

He looked down at the seven conditions and the suits.

“Ren Hao,” she said, and he looked up. “I want you back in my life. Not just for dinner on Fridays. Not just a kiss at a taxi rank. I want to wake up and hear you in my kitchen making coffee in my terrible machine. I want to complain about your meetings. I want you to complain that I leave cups everywhere.”

“You do leave cups everywhere.”

“There. You’ve started already.”

He laughed.

“But I don’t want what we had in August,” she said, more quietly. “I don’t want you to think being together means you’re responsible for everything. And I don’t want to feel managed in my own flat. Ever again.”

“I understand.”

“I need you to mean it.”

“I mean it.”

She studied his face a long time. Then she pushed the pen across the counter to him.

“You’re supposed to sign it.”

“Where? There’s no room.”

“Write smaller.”

He laughed under his breath. He found a space along the right-hand edge, between condition five and the printed shop name, and wrote in his narrowest capitals:

I agree to all seven, and to the suits. I’ll ask when I’m not sure. I’ll listen when you say no. I’ll tell you when something’s wrong, instead of trying to manage it on my own. REN HAO.

She read it upside down. “Very formal.”

“I take contracts seriously.”

“Good. There may be penalties.”

“I assumed.”

She reached for the napkin. He held it back.

“Wait. I’d like to add something.”

“You’re not adding an eighth condition.”

“It isn’t a condition.”

He turned the napkin over. On the clean side, in the middle, he wrote one line.

8. We remember we’re on the same side.

She read it. All the teasing went out of her face.

“I’d like that one to bind both of us,” he said.

She looked at him. “Agreed.”

He wrote, underneath: Initialled by both parties. And his initials. And held out the pen.

She took it and wrote hers beside his. X.S.Z. Then she put the pen down.

“Done.”

He looked at it. Seven conditions on one side, a clause about suits, one shared promise on the other, two signatures and two sets of initials, on a greasy napkin from a noodle shop. It was worth more than any contract he’d signed in seven years.

“Now,” she said. “Sign it properly.”

“I’ve signed it.”

“Not with a pen.”

He looked up at her. She’d come round the counter. She was standing right in front of his stool, in his sweatshirt, with her hands on her hips.

“Contracts in my flat,” said Song-Zhu, “are signed with a kiss. It’s in the small print.”

“I didn’t see any small print.”

“It’s very small.”

He stood up. She put both her hands on his face and kissed him. Slowly, thoroughly, standing in her own kitchen, the way you’d put a seal on something with your whole weight so that it would never come off. He held her waist and kissed her back, and it went on so long the tea went cold on the counter, and neither of them cared.

When she drew back she kept her hands on his face.

“Signed,” she said.

“Witnessed,” said Ren Hao.

He folded the napkin into a small square and put it in his wallet, behind his cards.

“You’re keeping a napkin in your wallet?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“So I don’t forget.”

“You’ve got a perfect memory.”

“I know.” He looked at her. “I don’t want to forget what it took for you to ask me back.”

She went quiet.

“Thank you,” he said. “For letting me try again.”

She reached for his hand. “Don’t make me regret it.”

“I won’t take it lightly.”

“I know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The first night wasn’t moving in. It was a trial. She insisted on the word.

He arrived at quarter past seven on Monday with one small overnight bag.

She opened the door and looked at it. “That’s all?”

“One change of clothes. A toothbrush. Nothing else.”

“No charger?”

“My phone’s charged.”

“No spare shoes?”

“No.”

“No suspicious boxes?”

“No suspicious boxes,” said Ren Hao.

She stepped aside. “You’re learning.”

He came in and stood in her hall and looked round. It was exactly as it had been. Shoes by the door. Books on the side table. A cardigan over the back of the sofa. The photograph that leaned. The smell of her washing powder. His slippers, still beside hers by the shoe cabinet, toes together, exactly where she’d put them on the nineteenth of September.

He looked at the slippers a long time. He didn’t straighten the shoes. He didn’t pick up the cardigan. He put his bag down by the sofa and stood there.

She shut the door. “Well?”

“Well what?”

“How does it feel?”

He thought about it honestly. “Like being invited somewhere I missed.”

Her face went soft. “That’s a very careful answer.”

“I’m trying to be respectful.”

“You can be honest.”

“It feels,” said Ren Hao, “very good.”

He looked at the kitchen. “May I make dinner?”

“Yes.”

“May I use your chopping board?”

“Yes.”

“May I...”

“Hao.”

She came over and kissed his cheek. “You can cook. You don’t need permission to breathe. Just don’t move anything.”

“I remember.”

He made noodles. She sat on the counter and talked about work and swung her feet. When she mentioned a review that had been moved to next week, he looked up.

“Do you want to talk about it?”

“Not tonight.”

“All right,” he said, and went back to the pan, and she watched him go back to it, and smiled to herself. It was such a small thing. It was so different.

Afterwards he washed and she dried, and he put each plate where she pointed even when he obviously thought another cupboard made more sense.

“You want to move that,” she said.

“I do.”

“But you won’t.”

“No.”

“Good.”

“May I say one thing?”

“Go on.”

“Your cupboard arrangement is objectively inefficient.”

She laughed out loud. “You’re welcome to leave.”

“I’ve only just got here.”

“Then behave.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At bedtime he put his bag down by her wardrobe and didn’t unpack it.

She noticed from the bed. “You’re not putting your things away?”

“You said a few nights. I thought I’d wait.”

“There’s a drawer. The bottom one.”

He looked at her. “Are you sure?”

“I’m sure.”

He opened it. It was empty. She’d cleared it on Sunday afternoon, after he’d gone home with the napkin in his wallet.

“You made room.”

“One drawer.”

“One drawer,” he said, and his voice wasn’t quite steady.

“Don’t get ambitious.”

“I wouldn’t dare.”

He put his folded things inside it, and took out his toothbrush, and stood holding it. It was the blue one.

She looked at it from the bed. He looked at her.

“There’s a cup,” she said. “On the shelf. Next to mine.”

He went into the bathroom. She heard him put it down. She heard him stand there a long time without moving. Then he came back, and didn’t say anything about it, and neither did she.

He got into bed and lay on his side facing her, and didn’t reach for her. She closed her book.

“What?”

“I’m looking at you being here.”

“In my bed.”

“In your bed,” he agreed. “With my toothbrush next to yours. I’m allowing myself one minute to look.”

She put the book down and moved across the bed into him. He put his arm round her. She could hear his heart, and it was a sound she’d known for eighteen months and hadn’t heard for four, and she lay with her ear against it and didn’t say anything a while.

“Hao?”

“Mm.”

“Don’t make this perfect.”

He looked down at her. “What?”

“Don’t try so hard that you stop being you. We’ll get things wrong. We’ll argue. I’ll leave cups everywhere. You’ll annoy me about something stupid. Some nights I’ll want to be on my own. Some days you’ll come home and not want to talk.”

“All of that’s fine.”

“We have to be allowed to be ordinary.”

“I want ordinary,” he said. “With you. I’ve wanted ordinary for four months more than I’ve ever wanted anything.”

She lifted her face and kissed him. Quietly. No hurry. No declaration. Just the two of them, in her bed, with one drawer occupied and a blue toothbrush standing next to a white one on the shelf.

“Goodnight, sweetheart.”

“Goodnight,” she said, and fell asleep on his chest before he’d finished breathing out.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first week was a negotiation. Not a hard one. A series of small adjustments, one a day.

On the first morning he asked whether he could leave a second shirt. She said there were six suits in the wardrobe already and a shirt was hardly going to tip the balance.

On Tuesday he nearly moved her coffee machine. She caught him with his hands on it. He put it back without a word, and she kissed him for it.

On Wednesday he asked whether she wanted him to cook or order. She said she wanted to cook. He asked what she needed. She handed him a knife.

On Thursday she came home late and found him reading on the sofa.

“Long day?”

“Very.”

“Do you want food?”

She dropped her bag by the sofa, where she’d always dropped it, and he didn’t look at it. “Yes.”

“All right,” he said, and got up. No questions about why she hadn’t eaten. No remarks about the hour. Just food.

On Friday he had a bad day. She heard it in how he shut the door. He stood in the hall with his coat on.

“Bad day?”

“Yes.”

“Do you want to talk?”

He thought about it. “Not yet.”

“All right.” She patted the sofa beside her. “Then sit.”

He sat. She leaned on him. After a long while he said that one of the directors had disagreed with the restructuring, and had been partly right, which was the worst kind, and that he thought he’d made the wrong call on one of the people.

“Do you want to go through it?”

“Yes,” he said, which he had never once said to her before, about his own work, in eighteen months.

So they went through it. He explained. She asked three questions. On the third one he went quiet.

“That,” he said, “is actually useful.”

“I know.”

“You’re very modest.”

“One of my many qualities.”

In bed he told her he’d been afraid she’d think less of him for getting it wrong.

She turned to him in the dark. “Why would I?”

“Because I usually know what I’m doing.”

“Hao. You’re allowed to be a person.”

He was quiet a long time. “All right,” he said.

On Saturday morning she found the napkin on his side of the bed, unfolded, flattened under his watch.

“You brought it out?”

He was in the bathroom. “I read it every night.”

“Every night?”

“Before I sleep. It takes forty seconds. It’s a good way to end the day.”

She looked at it. Two signatures. The ink had smudged a little at one corner, over the grease spot. She folded it again along his creases, and went and slid it into the inside pocket of the jacket he’d hung on the back of her bedroom door. He came out and watched her do it.

“Somewhere safe,” she said, and straightened his collar, although he wasn’t wearing a shirt with a collar. “You’re officially allowed to stay another week.”

“Another week?”

“Don’t push your luck.”

He laughed. She reached up, and he bent, and she kissed him, and he held her and smiled against her mouth. She tapped the pocket with the napkin in it.

“That’s your contract.”

“I intend to keep every line.”

“Good,” she said, and kissed him again, longer.

When she drew back he looked at her the way he’d looked at her across the counter with the pen in his hand. A little disbelieving. A little overwhelmed. Very happy.

“What’s that face?”

He touched her cheek. “I used to think coming back would feel like getting back something I’d lost. It doesn’t. It feels like being invited somewhere new.”

“Maybe it is,” said Song-Zhu.

“Then I’m glad you asked me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, at the supermarket, he opened his wallet to pay, and the napkin was in it, folded small behind his cards. He unfolded it while the woman at the till scanned the eggs, and read it once, and folded it again.

Song-Zhu was by the fruit, holding up two oranges.

“Which?”

He looked. “The left one.”

“Why?”

“It’s smaller.”

“That’s not a reason.”

“It’s easier to carry.”

She stared at him. “You’re optimising oranges.”

“I’ll stop.”

She put both in the basket. “Good.”

They walked to the till together. No announcement. No grand anything. Groceries, an ordinary Saturday, and knowing that when they got home they’d be going to the same place.

Not because one of them had moved into the other’s life and taken it over.

Because they’d both made room. And this time they both knew exactly where the edges were.

At least until she decided to move the coffee machine herself.

chapters.title: Her Terms
chapters.desc: She runs the schedule now, under a yellow duck. He loves it. Explicit in the training hangar after hours, against a wing strut, on his suit jacket.
chapters.epigraph: “My schedule’s optimistic.”
chapters.content:
Ren Hao discovered, on a Tuesday morning in February, that his girlfriend was a great deal more frightening with a calendar.

Not that Song-Zhu had ever been disorganised at work. She could rebuild a sequence of events from a field of wreckage, tell you to the second when a witness had changed one word in a statement, and spot a mismatched part number in a maintenance log while eating noodles standing over a sink.

At home, her schedule had always been less a schedule than a set of ambitious suggestions. She would get up at six, run, finish a report, shop, ring her mother, and learn at last to pleat a dumpling. By nine she would have got up at half past seven, forgotten the run, found something new in a completely different case, eaten half a packet of crackers for breakfast, and decided dumplings were a problem for her next life.

He had once tried to help. He’d learned. Now, apparently, she’d decided to help herself.

He found the evidence on her fridge, under a magnet shaped like a yellow duck. A sheet of paper ruled into neat columns. Dates. Times. Notes in the margins. Some things highlighted. Some crossed out, hard. At the top, in her capitals:

FEBRUARY. OURS.

He stood in front of it with his coffee.

MON: work. Work. Dinner together if neither of us is dead.
TUES: work. Work. H. not to order food until S-Z has decided what she wants.
WED: walk. H. picks the route. No complaints about hills.
THURS: H. late meeting. Don’t wait up. (You can ring if you miss me.)
FRI: Isla on video, 9 a.m. Lima = 10 p.m. here. Both of us.
SAT: shopping, washing, and something.
SUN: NOTHING. DO NOT MAKE PLANS. THIS MEANS YOU.

He took a photograph of it.

From the bedroom: “If you’re photographing my schedule I want royalties.”

“I’m documenting a historic event.”

“You’re documenting a piece of paper.”

“A piece of paper that has successfully organised your life.”

“Don’t sound so impressed. It’s embarrassing.”

She came to the bedroom door fastening her watch, hair wet from the shower, in black trousers and a white shirt, with the face of a woman who had already done three things in her head before breakfast.

“Morning,” he said.

“Morning.”

“Is this binding?”

She looked at the fridge. “Legally?”

“Emotionally.”

“Unfortunately, yes.”

“Then I submit to your authority. Do I get a copy?”

“You get to look at it whenever you like.”

“That isn’t the same.”

“It’s my schedule.”

“Ours,” he said gently, pointing at the top of the page.

She looked at it, and at him. She came over and straightened the collar of his shirt, which didn’t need straightening. “Ours,” she agreed.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the end of the week he was its most devoted supporter.

Not because she’d become punctual. She still left the flat with one shoe in her hand and a piece of toast in her teeth. She still lost her keys, despite a bowl she’d bought specifically for keys. She still announced she was leaving in five minutes when she hadn’t yet decided what to wear.

The difference was that now she was deciding before the chaos arrived.

She decided which evenings belonged to work and which belonged to them. She decided when she wanted company and when she wanted a book and tea and the particular silence she liked. She decided where they’d eat. And she told him.

It was, Ren Hao found, an almost unbearably attractive quality.

On Thursday night he was in her kitchen reading an email when she came in and put a container on the counter in front of him.

“Dinner.”

“You made dinner?”

“I acquired dinner. I went to the shop, chose it, paid for it, carried it. That’s practically cooking.”

He opened it. It was the dish he liked from the place by her building, the one he’d mentioned once, in March last year.

“You remembered.”

“I have an excellent memory.”

“You left your passport in a taxi in October.”

“That was a test.”

“Of the driver’s honesty?”

“Of the universe.”

He put his phone down on the counter, face up, and didn’t look at it again.

She noticed. “You’re not going to finish your email?”

“You scheduled dinner. I’m attending.”

She looked pleased with herself and tried to hide it behind a glass of water.

He loved that look. The small satisfaction of a plan going right. The way she stood a little straighter when something she’d organised worked. He’d spent so long trying to make her life easier that he’d nearly missed how much she liked deciding what her life looked like.

Now she was doing it. And he was happy to be told where to stand.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday the hangar was dark after nine.

It was the training hangar on the far side of the airfield, the one where in October 2025 he’d worn a laminated VISITOR pass with more pride than anything he’d ever worn to a board meeting. The old regional jet the authority had bought for a dollar from a scrapyard still sat in the middle of it under the high roof, half its panels off, its insides labelled in yellow for trainees. No evidence in it. Nothing in it that belonged to anybody but the authority and whoever was learning.

The day’s course had finished at six. The instructors had signed out. The tools were in the cage. Song-Zhu had stayed to finish marking twenty-two written assessments from a class of fire crew, because she’d promised them back on Monday.

He’d come to collect her. He wasn’t on the schedule.

That was the first thing she told him, when she looked up from the trestle table under the wing and saw him standing just inside the side door with his suit jacket over his arm.

“You’re not on the schedule.”

“Good evening to you too.”

She looked at her watch. “You were supposed to be at home. Watching the duck.”

“I was at home.”

“And?”

“I missed you.”

She narrowed her eyes. “That isn’t a valid reason for entering a controlled area.”

“I signed in. The man on the gate knows me. He said her again?”

“That’s a procedural reason. It isn’t a valid emotional one.”

He came across the concrete. “Would you rather I said I’d come to admire the aircraft?”

“No.”

“To learn about aviation safety?”

“Absolutely not.”

“To see my girlfriend?”

Her face changed. “That’s acceptable.”

She’d taken off her work jacket. She was in a dark shirt tucked into her trousers, with the sleeves rolled up and her hair knotted up with a pencil through it, and some had come down round her face, and there was a long smear of red marking ink on the side of her hand.

He took her hand and looked at it. “What’s this?”

“Evidence of hard work.”

He rubbed his thumb over it. It didn’t come off.

“How much longer?”

“Ten minutes. Three papers.”

“Your schedule says you finished at half past eight.”

“My schedule’s optimistic.”

“Whose fault is that?”

“Mine,” she said, and he looked so surprised that she lifted her chin. “Don’t look so pleased. I know when I’m wrong.”

“I wasn’t going to say anything.”

“You were.”

“I was going to say you’re beautiful.”

“That’s a completely different conversation.”

“I can have two.”

She laughed, and marked the last three papers while he sat on an upturned crate and watched her do it, and when she’d done she slid them into a folder and stood up.

“Come and see. I want to show you something.”

He followed her under the wing to the main gear leg, where a long strip of light from one of the high lamps fell across the floor.

“This is what I was teaching today. Look.” She showed him a fitting, and the paperwork for it, laminated, on a stand. “The inspection notes don’t match the maintenance record. On purpose. I put it there. Half the class didn’t see it. One of them did, a woman from the airport fire station, in four minutes.”

He listened. He didn’t pretend to follow every word. He asked a question when he didn’t, and she answered it with the easy certainty of somebody who knew her work right down to the bolts.

“You’re very good at this,” he said.

“I know.”

“There’s that modesty.”

“I’ve been told not to undersell myself.”

“By whom?”

“Me,” said Song-Zhu.

The hangar hummed round them. Far off, past the shut doors, a vehicle went along the perimeter road and was gone. The high lamps lit the long curve of the wing above them and left the space underneath it in soft shadow. She looked at him.

“You’re staring.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because I like looking at you.”

“You’ve looked at me before.”

“Frequently. It’s turned into a habit.”

She came a step closer. “An expensive one?”

“One of my better investments.”

She reached for his tie.

He looked down at her fist round it. “Is this on the schedule?”

“No.”

“Should I be worried?”

“Very,” she said, and pulled him down.

✦ ✦ ✦

She kissed him the way she’d always kissed him when she’d decided something: without hesitation and without asking permission of anything, including gravity. She held him by the tie and kept him there and kissed him slow, and then less slow, until his hand had come round the back of her waist and was holding her against him.

When she let him go he looked at her as though he’d been hit.

“Hello,” he said.

“Hello.”

“Have you finished work?”

“Yes.”

“You’re sure?”

“Hao.”

“Sorry.”

She put her hand on his face. “You’re allowed to ask. I’m allowed to say yes.”

He turned his head and kissed her palm, over the red ink. “Then yes?”

“Yes.”

He kissed her again, and she walked backwards as he kissed her until her shoulders met the wing strut, the big angled leg of steel that came down from the underside of the wing to the floor, cold through her shirt, and she gasped against his mouth.

He stopped and looked round. “Are we on our own?”

“Everybody signed out at ten past six. The main doors are locked. The side door’s locked behind you, I heard you do it, you always do it. I’ve checked the cage. Nobody’s coming in before seven.” She held his face. “And before you ask, it’s a training airframe. There’s nothing in here that’s anybody’s evidence. We’re not touching anything we shouldn’t.”

He looked at her. “Did you plan this?”

Her mouth curved. “I planned to mark twenty-two papers and go home and have a bath.”

“And?”

“And then I saw you come in the side door with your jacket over your arm. And the schedule changed.”

“An amendment.”

“An urgent one,” said Song-Zhu, and took his jacket off his arm.

She shook it out. Dark grey, beautifully cut, made in another country by a man who’d measured him for an hour. She spread it out on the clean padded mat under the wing that the trainees used to lie on to look at the undercarriage. She looked back at him over her shoulder.

“Your jacket,” he said.

“Expensive?”

“Very.”

“Then you’d better be careful with it.”

“You’re the one who put it there.”

“Because I know you,” she said.

He came to her. He put his hands on her waist from behind and his mouth against the side of her neck, below the knot of hair, and she shut her eyes.

“Tell me what you want,” he said into her skin.

The teasing went out of her. What was underneath it was plain.

“You,” she said. “Here. Against that.”

He turned her round and put her back against the cold steel of the strut, and held her there with the whole length of his body, and looked down at her. She knew that look. She’d been missing it in her body for months without knowing what it was she was missing.

“Do you know what I’m going to do?” he said, low.

She shook her head, although she did. He told her.

He told her slowly, against her ear, while his hands did the first of it: her shirt, button by button, until it hung open, and his palm flat on her bare stomach, sliding up. He told her what he’d been thinking about since half past eight, sitting on the sofa watching the duck. He told her what he was going to do to her against this strut, and then on his jacket, and in what order, and how long he was going to take over each part, and what sound he wanted to hear her make, and then he began to do every single one of those things exactly as he’d said.

He undid her trousers and pushed them down and she stepped out of them. He knelt on the concrete in front of her and kissed the inside of her knee, and her thigh, and the cold steel was at her back and his warm mouth was on her and she put her head back against the strut with a dull clang and laughed, breathless, and then didn’t laugh, because he’d put his mouth between her legs and she couldn’t do anything at all but hold the strut above her head with both hands.

“Hao...”

“Not yet,” he said, against her. “I said not yet. I told you the order.”

He kept her there, at the edge, until her legs were shaking and her knuckles were white on the steel and she was saying his name up into the dark under the wing like something she was trying to get out of a recorder. Then he stood, and lifted her, and she wrapped her legs round him, and he held her up against the strut with her back to the cold and her front to him and pushed into her in one long slow stroke, and the noise she made went all the way up into the roof of the hangar and came back.

He held still. “Look at me.”

She looked at him.

“That’s the sound,” he said. “That one.”

He moved. Hard and slow against the strut, with his hands under her and her arms locked round his neck and her heels in the small of his back. The steel rang faintly behind her every time he moved, and she could feel it in her spine, and she didn’t care, she’d never cared about anything less. She kissed him with her teeth. He said her name into her mouth. Somewhere above them the old wing creaked on its stands.

“Your jacket,” she gasped. “You said. On your jacket. That’s next.”

“I know what I said.”

He carried her, still inside her, three steps to the mat under the wing, and knelt, and laid her down on his own grey jacket, on the silk lining, and came down over her, and she pulled him in.

On the jacket it was slower. He was over her with his weight on his forearms, and the underside of the wing was above his head, grey, with yellow trainee labels on it, CONTROL CABLE RUN and DO NOT STAND, and she looked up past him at it and started to laugh again in the middle of everything, helplessly.

“What?”

“Do not stand.”

He looked up. He looked back down at her. “I’m not standing.”

“I know you’re not.”

“I’m very much not standing,” he said, and moved in her, deep, and her laugh broke in half.

He took his time. He’d said he would. He took her slowly on his jacket under the wing, watching her face, talking to her in that low voice, telling her how she felt and what she looked like with her hair coming down out of its pencil and red ink on her hand on his shoulder, and when she got close he slowed further, and when she said please he kissed her and didn’t speed up at all, and when at last she came it went on a long time, under the wing, on the lining of a jacket that had cost more than her first year’s rent, with her fingers knotted in his shirt and his name going up into the dark. He followed her, holding her tight against him, with his face in her neck and a sound that was nearly hers.

They lay there afterwards a long time. The hangar went on humming. The high lamp threw its long strip of light on the floor a metre from them and didn’t reach.

She was lying on his chest. He was looking up at the wing.

“You’re thinking,” she said.

“Yes.”

“About work?”

“No.”

“About your jacket?”

“A little.”

She lifted her head. “You’re worried about it.”

“I’m deciding whether it goes to the cleaner or gets retired with full honours.”

She laughed, and lay back down on him.

“Are you cold?” he said.

“A bit.”

He reached for his shirt, and stopped himself with his hand on it. “May I?”

She smiled with her eyes shut. “Yes. You may give me your shirt.”

He put it round her shoulders and she put her arms into the sleeves and looked down at herself.

“It’s too big.”

“That’s generally how my clothes work.”

“You say it as if it’s a feature.”

“It is.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They dressed. She checked the doors, and the cage, and the side door, and turned off the lamps over the section they’d used, one by one. He waited by the door with his jacket over his arm, rumpled beyond saving, and didn’t hurry her once.

Outside the air was cold and clear. Mr. Yau was in the car by the gate, reading a paperback under the interior light. He’d driven Ren Hao there. Ren Hao hadn’t told him when to go.

Song-Zhu looked at the car. “You asked him to wait?”

“I asked him to bring me. I didn’t tell him when to leave.”

“Then tell him we’re leaving.”

Ren Hao went and knocked on the window. Mr. Yau wound it down, looked at the two of them, at the shirt, at the state of the jacket, and wound it up again without a single word, and started the engine.

She got in. Ren Hao stood by her open door.

“Song-Zhu.”

“What?”

“You’re enjoying this.”

“Immensely,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

At home she went straight to the fridge and took the February sheet out from under the duck.

“What are you doing?”

“Amending.”

Under Saturday’s shopping and washing and something, she wrote a new line in capitals.

FRI 9 P.M. HANGAR. (UNSCHEDULED. APPROVED RETROSPECTIVELY.)

He read it over her shoulder and laughed so much that he had to hold on to the counter.

She put the sheet back under the duck. He put his hands on her waist.

“May I ask something?”

“Of course.”

“May I have a copy?”

“Why?”

“So I know when I’m allowed to miss you.”

Her face went soft. “You don’t need a schedule for that.”

“No?”

“You can miss me whenever you like. Tell me whenever you like. I might not answer straight away.”

“I know.”

“But I’ll read it.”

“I know.”

She touched his face. “You’re getting better at this.”

“So are you.”

“At what?”

“Making room for me,” he said, “without making room for everything.”

She was quiet. Then she put her forehead on his chest.

“I like having you here,” she said.

“I like being here.”

“Even when I make you live by a sheet of paper under a duck?”

“That’s the part I like best.”

“You’re strange.”

“I’m in love with you.”

“That isn’t a defence.”

“It wasn’t meant to be one,” he said, and kissed her, once, and then again.

His girlfriend was running the schedule now. He loved it. And judging by the line she’d just written in capitals under a yellow duck, he suspected he was going to love February.

chapters.title: The Final Report
chapters.desc: A year on, the final report names the cause: a reused part signed off by a contractor. A hundred and eighty names read by the sea; he holds her hand in the front row. Then she times his toast at eleven minutes fourteen.
chapters.epigraph: “Eleven minutes, and fourteen seconds.”
chapters.content:
