The report was published at nine o’clock on Monday the second of August 2027. Song-Zhu had been awake since four.

No early meeting. No phone call. No bad dream. She simply opened her eyes in the dark and knew what day it was, the way she’d known a year ago, before the phone had rung.

She lay still and listened to the flat. Her fridge humming in E flat. A car going by below. Beside her, Ren Hao asleep on his side with one arm bent under the pillow, breathing slow. Seven minutes past four.

She shut her eyes. At eleven minutes past she opened them again.

At sixteen minutes past he stirred, and didn’t say anything, and reached across the bed and found her hand under the duvet and held it.

“Morning,” he murmured.

“Not yet.”

He opened one eye. “Is it still night?”

“Technically.”

“Then why are you awake?”

She looked at the ceiling. “Today.”

He was awake all the way at once. He turned onto his back and looked at the ceiling with her.

He didn’t say it would be fine. He didn’t say it would give the families answers, because some answers couldn’t give anybody back what they’d lost. He knew she’d spent a year walking towards this morning. Not because she wanted to get to the end of it. Because she owed it to a hundred and eighty people who would never be able to ask the questions themselves.

He rubbed his thumb across her knuckles.

“Do you want me to come?”

She turned her head on the pillow. “Yes.”

“All right.”

“You don’t have to stay all day. You’ve got work.”

“Raymond’s got work. I’ve got you.”

“Hao.”

“I’ll come because you asked me,” he said. “I’ll stay as long as you want me there. If you need me to go, I’ll go. If you want me next to you, I’ll be next to you.”

She looked at him for a long moment in the dark. Then she moved across the bed and put her face against his chest.

“Next to me,” she said.

“Next to you.”

He held her until the alarm went.

✦ ✦ ✦

The final report wasn’t dramatic. It didn’t arrive with a fanfare or a room full of people waiting for a revelation. It went up on the authority’s website at nine, with a summary for the public and four volumes of appendices: diagrams, metallurgy, maintenance records going back eleven years, photographs, timelines, the laboratory findings on a crumpled phone, and two hundred and twelve pages of analysis that had been argued over, sentence by sentence, by people who knew that one careless word in it could matter for twenty years.

The title was plain.

Final Report: Loss of a passenger aircraft on approach, 2 August 2026.

She was at her desk at eighteen minutes to nine. Her team were in. Nobody was saying much. A printed copy lay beside her keyboard, squared off. The live page was open on her screen, not yet live.

She’d read every word of it, more times than she could count. She’d checked every reference, every conclusion, every limitation. She’d sat in rooms where each sentence was turned over by an engineer, a lawyer and a pilot, and turned over again. She knew exactly what was in it. That didn’t make it any easier to open. Just before nine her phone buzzed.

Ren Hao: I’m downstairs.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Don’t come up yet.

Ren Hao: All right.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I’ll come down when I’m ready.

Ren Hao: Take as long as you like.

She put the phone face up beside the keyboard. At nine the page went live.

For a moment she didn’t move. Then she opened it.

The first pages were what they always were. The aircraft. The flight. The crew. The weather: rain, low cloud, a crosswind well inside the limits. The approach. The search. The recovery. The recorders.

And then, on page ninety-one, the section she’d written most of herself.

Maintenance and component history.

A component in the aircraft’s main electrical distribution system, under the cabin floor, had been fitted at the aircraft’s last heavy maintenance check eleven months before the accident, by a contracted maintenance organisation. The component had come through that organisation’s supply chain with paperwork showing it as new.

It wasn’t new. It had been removed from another aircraft, in another country, five years before, at the end of its approved service life. It had been refurbished by a supplier further down the chain. Its identifying plate had been replaced. The records that came with it didn’t show where it had been.

A traceability check required by the contractor’s own procedures, and by the regulations it worked under, hadn’t been carried out to the standard required. The contractor’s inspector had signed for the part. The airline’s maintenance system had accepted the signature. The part had gone into the aircraft.

At four hundred and twenty feet on final approach, in the dark, in rain, it had failed. The failure had taken out the aircraft’s normal electrical power in less than a second. The recorders had stopped. The cabin had gone dark. The crew had been left, at night, over water, at the lowest and slowest point of the whole flight, with eleven seconds and almost nothing.

The report named the cause. Not a maintenance irregularity, not an unexplained technical event. Not a combination of factors.

A reused part, presented as new, signed off by a contractor whose checks had failed.

It named the other failures too, because there were other failures: traceability controls that relied on paperwork nobody could verify; a contractor’s quality system that had been audited and passed twice; oversight that should have caught the mismatch and hadn’t. It didn’t pretend that one man’s signature explained everything. It didn’t blame the dead.

It said, on page one hundred and four, in a sentence she’d fought for in four separate meetings, that the evidence didn’t support any finding that the actions of the flight crew had caused or contributed to the accident, and that in the time and conditions available to them after the loss of power, their options had been extremely limited.

And it said, in a footnote on that page, that the captain had remained on the cabin address system to his passengers after the loss of normal power, until the end. She read the conclusions twice. Then she shut her eyes. A chair moved behind her.

“Boss?” said Dexter.

She opened them. “Yes.”

“It’s live.”

“I know.”

“Are you...”

“I’m all right.” She looked down at the printed copy. “Has the liaison team got the family packs?”

“Since eight.”

“Translations?”

“Checked against the report, not the press summary. Three times.”

“Good. The press conference is at eleven. I want the technical people in the room for the supply chain, and nobody, nobody, is to speculate about who knew what at the supplier. That’s for the police and the regulator.”

“Understood.”

She stood up. Her legs felt wrong, as if she’d been sitting for a year.

One year. One year since four o’clock in the morning. One year since the sea had turned into a place where people waited for names.

She squared the printed report against the edge of her desk and picked up her phone.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Coming down.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was by the entrance in a dark suit with no tie, holding two coffees. He’d thought about flowers, briefly, on the way, and decided that flowers would be an attempt to decorate a day that didn’t need decorating.

He looked at her face first. Then at the report in her hand.

“Hello,” he said.

“Hello.”

He held out a cup. “Black. No sugar.”

“Thank you.”

“How is it?”

“It’s published.”

“I saw.”

“The cause is established.” She took a breath. “A part under the floor. It came off another aircraft at the end of its life, five years ago. It got a new plate and new paperwork and went round again. The contractor signed it in. Their checks failed. The airline’s system took their word for it. It failed at four hundred feet.”

He listened.

“The physical evidence holds,” she said. “The metallurgy holds. The phone holds. The timing holds. And it wasn’t one signature. There were people who should have seen it at three different points and didn’t.”

“Does the report say that?”

“It says that.”

“Good.”

She looked at the lid of her coffee. “The families will know now.”

“Yes.”

“They’ve waited a year. And some of them will read it and still not understand why it had to be their person on that aircraft.”

He didn’t answer straight away. There was no professional answer to that. No sentence that could make it less cruel.

“I don’t think they should have to understand it,” he said at last, “for it to be true.”

She looked up at him.

“You’ve told them what happened,” he said. “You’ve told them what the evidence holds. You haven’t handed them one word you couldn’t stand behind. That’s what you promised a little boy on a bed a year ago.”

Her mouth tightened.

“I wanted it to be more,” she said. “I wanted it to be complete.”

“It’s as complete as an investigation can be. That doesn’t mean the loss is.”

She looked away down the road. He reached for her hand, and stopped, a few centimetres short.

She saw him stop. She slid her fingers into his.

“Come on,” she said.

“Where?”

“There’s a briefing. And then there’s the sea.”

“Am I invited?”

“You’re holding my coffee.”

“That’s an important role.”

“Don’t get above yourself,” said Song-Zhu, and took him in.

✦ ✦ ✦

The press conference was at eleven. She stood beside Director Kwan at the second microphone and answered for forty minutes.

She explained the contractor’s role. The component’s history. How the metallurgy had shown it was worn beyond anything it should ever have been allowed to carry. How the paperwork had said otherwise.

A journalist asked whether the contractor had falsified the records on purpose.

“The report sets out that the documentation was inaccurate and that the contractor’s verification and sign-off failed. Questions of intent, or of criminal or civil responsibility, are for the police and the regulator. They have the report. Our job is to find out what went wrong so that it doesn’t happen again. Not to decide who goes to prison.”

Another asked whether the pilots could have done anything differently. She was quiet before she answered.

“The report examines everything the crew did, as far as the evidence allows. It doesn’t support any finding that the crew caused or contributed to this. After the power was lost, at that height, at that speed, at night, over water, they had very few options and very little time. And the captain stayed on the cabin address to his passengers until the end.”

A third went back to the eleven seconds. “Can you say for certain that the missing data didn’t hide a chance to prevent the crash?”

“We can’t recover data that was never recorded. But this report doesn’t depend on those eleven seconds. Its findings rest on the physical evidence, the component, the recorded data up to the loss of power, the cabin recording, and the wider technical analysis. And we now know why the recorders stopped. That was the first thing we found.”

Her voice didn’t break once. She didn’t hurry. She didn’t let one technical finding be turned into a headline it couldn’t carry.

When the last question had been taken she thanked the room and stepped away from the microphone, and went out through the side door.

He was there. He’d been sitting at the very back, out of the way, and hadn’t spoken to a single journalist, and hadn’t gone near any of the families. He stood up when she came through the door.

“Did I go too fast?” she said.

“No.”

“Too slow?”

“No.”

“You’re not being objective.”

“I’m being entirely objective.”

“You think everything I do is excellent.”

“Not everything.”

“Name one thing.”

“You put the milk in the cupboard on Saturday.”

She stared at him. Then she laughed, small and tired and real, for the first time that day.

He held the door open. “Are you ready?”

She looked down the corridor that led to the family briefing room.

“No,” she said. “But I have to go.”

“I know.”

She took his hand. “Come with me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The memorial was that afternoon, by the sea.

The families had chosen it. A long grass headland above the water, two kilometres from the end of the runway, where on clear days you could see the approach lights coming on one after another across the bay. A hundred and eighty white chairs in rows facing the sea, with a space between each row. A long table under an awning, covered with photographs. And on a wooden board at the front, in plain black letters, a hundred and eighty names.

Some families had brought flowers. Some had brought photographs in frames. A woman in the third row held a child’s drawing against her chest. A man in the second row had his hands knotted together so tight the knuckles had gone white. Two old sisters sat side by side, shoulders touching, neither looking at the other.

There were children. Parents. Husbands, wives, partners, friends, colleagues. People who had flown in from the other side of the world because somebody they loved had been on that aircraft.

Song-Zhu came with the investigation team. Ren Hao walked beside her in black.

A woman from the families’ committee met them at the end of the rows.

“Ms. Xu.”

“Yes?”

“The front row is for the investigators, and for the families who asked to sit at the front.” The woman looked at Ren Hao, and then back at her. “And for your guest. The families asked.”

Song-Zhu stopped.

“They asked?”

“Mrs. Ting asked,” said the woman. “She said he was the one who rang everybody back.”

Song-Zhu looked at Ren Hao. His face had gone still.

“Thank you,” she said.

They sat in the front row. She reached for his hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

It began with silence. Not the kind she knew from laboratories and recorder rooms and the hours after midnight. This silence was made of people. People breathing. People holding hands. People trying not to make a sound.

Then the names were read. One by one. A hundred and eighty. Each followed by a pause the length of a breath.

Some families bowed their heads at a name. Some looked up at the board. Some cried at once. Some went still, as if moving would make it more real than they could stand.

Song-Zhu sat with her hands in her lap, and her right hand in his.

She knew these names. A year ago they’d been lines on a manifest marked UNVERIFIED in red. Then they’d been recovery records. Identification forms. Family liaison notes. Files. She’d learned to say every one of them properly. She’d learned which families wanted a phone call in the morning and which couldn’t bear the phone at all. Which mothers wanted every technical detail and which needed it in small pieces with a long pause between. She’d sat across tables from them and been shouted at, and thanked, and asked the same question a hundred different ways.

She’d never once forgotten that the report was about people, even when every sentence in it had to be about systems and parts.

Now the names were being read out loud by the sea.

Au-Yeung Hiu-lam. Two rows back, a young woman with her face in her hands, and a phone held against her chest.

Ting Ka-chun, seat 23C. In front of her, Mrs. Ting, upright, with a blue exercise book on her knee, closed.

Song-Zhu’s fingers tightened. He felt it. He didn’t look at her. He moved his hand so that his palm lay flat against hers. She turned hers over. He held it. Not tight enough to hurt, not so loose she could mistake it for anything else. Just enough.

Two names before the end, the reader said, “Captain Yuk Kam-fai,” and further along the front row, a girl with a long plait and a pale ribbon round her wrist put her hand inside her school blazer, flat against her chest, where she had kept a folded piece of paper for eight months, and held it there.

Song-Zhu couldn’t breathe. Ren Hao’s thumb moved once across the back of her hand.

When the last name had been read, nobody moved. Nobody clapped. Nobody announced that anything was over. A minute went by. Then another. A long way out across the bay, the approach lights came on, one after another, in a line on the water.

Then the woman from the committee stood and invited the families to the table with their flowers. Song-Zhu stood with everybody else.

She’d spent a year making sure that what lay behind those names wouldn’t be forgotten, or repeated. The report was out. The findings were made. The work had got to its end.

And every person on that headland was still going to go home without somebody.

She looked down at his hand. He was still holding hers. She squeezed once. He squeezed back.

✦ ✦ ✦

Mrs. Yuk found her afterwards, by the end of the awning. Bo-yee was beside her, taller than in December, the plait gone, her hair cut short to the jaw.

“Ms. Xu.”

“Mrs. Yuk.”

“I read it. Last night. They let us read it last night. All of it.” Mrs. Yuk held up a photograph, the one from his crew file. “I didn’t understand half the engineering. But I understood the part about the component. And I understood the footnote.”

Song-Zhu waited.

“He checked the locks twice,” said Mrs. Yuk. “He read the instructions before he built a shelf. He told Bo-yee that if you’re responsible for something, you do it properly, every time, even when nobody’s looking.” Her voice shook. “He’d have been so angry. If he’d known somebody signed for a part like that. He’d have been so angry.”

“Yes,” said Song-Zhu. “I think he would.”

“At least now we know. I know what happened. I know why. I know it wasn’t anything he did.” Mrs. Yuk wiped her eyes with the back of her wrist. “Thank you.”

Song-Zhu couldn’t find an answer straight away. She’d heard families thank her before. It had never once felt like something she could just take.

“I’m sorry,” she said at last. “That this is what the answer cost.”

Mrs. Yuk looked at her a long time. Then she reached out and touched Song-Zhu’s arm.

“You didn’t cause it.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

Song-Zhu didn’t answer.

Mrs. Yuk’s face softened. “Thank you for staying with it. For a year.”

Bo-yee stepped forward. “Miss Xu.”

“Yes?”

“Did you find out everything?”

Song-Zhu bent a little, so their eyes were level. “We found out what caused it, and how all the failures happened. There are some things the evidence couldn’t tell us, and I won’t pretend it could.”

The girl looked down. Then up.

“Will you remember him? Now it’s finished?”

Song-Zhu’s throat closed.

“Yes,” she said. “Every name. That’s what finishing means, for me. Not forgetting.”

Bo-yee nodded. Her mother took her hand. They walked away together across the grass towards the sea.

Song-Zhu stood where she was. And then Ren Hao was beside her, and didn’t ask what had been said, and she reached for him, and he let her hold on.

✦ ✦ ✦

It ended slowly. People stayed by the photographs, or by the board, or at the edge of the grass looking at the water. Some left in silence. Some stood in small knots, talking low, not ready to go back to ordinary life.

She helped the committee pack the printed programmes. She told a family where to find the appendices. She checked that no photographer had come past the rope into the families’ part of the headland. Only when everything was done did she sit down at last, on one of the white chairs in the empty front row. He put a bottle of water beside her.

“Thank you.”

He sat down next to her.

“It’s finished,” she said, after a while.

“The investigation?”

“The report. The briefings. The families. All of it.”

“How does it feel?”

She thought. “Strange.”

“Good strange or bad?”

“Neither.” She looked at the empty rows. “I thought I’d feel relieved. I thought there’d be a moment where I could put it down.”

“I don’t think there is one,” she said.

“No,” he said gently. “Perhaps not.”

“I’ve been carrying it a year. And now I have to remember what I did before.”

He smiled, slightly. “You made a mess of my kitchen.”

She turned and looked at him, outraged.

“I did not.”

“You did.”

“Your kitchen was too tidy.”

“My kitchen was perfectly organised.”

“It was sterile.”

“It was efficient.”

“It was depressing.”

He laughed. She leaned her head on his shoulder.

“Perhaps I’ll make a mess of yours again,” she said.

“I’d welcome it.”

“Don’t say that now. You’ll regret it.”

“I’ll take my chances,” said Ren Hao.

He didn’t tell her to go home. He didn’t tell her to sleep. He didn’t suggest a holiday or a change of scene or a new project. He sat beside her in the empty front row by the sea until the approach lights were all on across the bay, and when she was ready she stood up.

“Let’s go,” she said.

He took her bag.

She looked at it. “That’s mine.”

“I know.”

“I can carry it.”

“I know,” he said, and gave it back, and held out his hand instead, and she took it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Twelve days later, on Saturday the fourteenth, he gave the toast.

He’d called it a small family dinner. Isla, home from Lima since March, had believed him. It was in the top-floor private room of a restaurant by the harbour, with a table for twelve and flowers down the middle and a seating plan in a silver frame on an easel by the door with eleven names on it, and he’d put himself between his sister and her inspector.

Song-Zhu sat opposite him. She laughed less than anybody at the table, which Isla noticed. She ate slowly, and listened, and once, when Hao was in the middle of a story about a sailing camp, she reached across the table and straightened his collar without either of them stopping.

At some point, inevitably, he and she argued about a soup.

“It was supposed to be cold,” said Song-Zhu.

“It was too cold.”

“That isn’t a thing.”

“It is a thing. I’m a man of standards. Inspector, were my expectations reasonable?”

And Wei Long looked at her, and at Hao, and at the tablecloth, and said with great care, “What kind of soup?”, and she heard Hao laugh.

At a quarter past nine, with the pudding on the table and nobody yet brave enough to touch it, he stood up.

“Sit down,” said Isla.

“No.”

“Hao. Sit down.”

“Everyone,” said Ren Hao, and lifted his glass.

Across the table, Song-Zhu took out her phone, and set it face up beside her plate, and touched the screen.

“Are you recording this?” said Isla.

“No, I’m timing it,” said Song-Zhu.

The table laughed. He gave her a look of deep betrayal and carried on.

She’d heard it twice already. In her kitchen, on Tuesday and on Thursday, with him standing by her fridge with the duck on it holding a glass of water instead of wine. On Tuesday it had been eight minutes. On Thursday, nine.

He went back to the beginning. Vancouver. A four-year-old who wanted to do everything herself and fell off everything and got up and said she was fine. French out of spite. The northern language for their grandmother. Lima. The stairwell on the thirty-second floor where he’d gone so nobody would see his face.

And then October. He didn’t tell it well. He kept stopping. He said that for a day and a night nobody could tell him whether his sister was alive, and that the only person who’d answered every single one of his calls was a police inspector he’d once tried to have investigated. And then he said the line about the plane ticket and the boat, which he hadn’t said on Thursday.

That was the new bit. She looked at the timer.

When he’d finished, and the table had erupted, and somebody at the far end had shouted about time, she looked at the screen and said, “Eleven minutes, and fourteen seconds.”

“That’s not bad,” said Hao.

“It’s longer than a state banquet,” said Isla.

“Then I should go into public speaking.”

“No,” said the entire table.

Song-Zhu put her phone away and leaned towards Isla under the noise.

“He practised it on me,” she said. “Twice. On Thursday it was nine minutes. He added the boat.”

And across the table, through the noise and the flowers and the eleven names, he caught her eye, and she saw in his face that he’d seen her laugh, properly, all the way, for the first time since the morning of the report, and that it was the thing he’d wanted most out of the whole evening, and it hadn’t been in the speech at all.

chapters.title: His Firm, Her Rules
chapters.desc: He makes Raymond managing partner and comes home at seven. Isla gets engaged. At Eliana and Yu Chen’s wedding he takes the microphone uninvited, and lasts one minute fifty-two.
chapters.epigraph: “Go home, Hao.”
chapters.content:
The first time Ren Hao came home at seven, Song-Zhu thought something had happened to him.

She was in the kitchen on a Monday at the start of September, trying to decide whether the greens in the fridge were still legally greens, when the front door opened.

She looked at the clock on the oven. Three minutes past seven.

She looked at the door. She looked back at the clock.

He came in with his briefcase, wearing the face of a man who had just pulled off an extremely complicated negotiation.

“Hello,” he said.

She stared at him. “Hello.”

He put the case down. “What’s wrong?”

“You’re home.”

“Yes.”

“It’s seven.”

“That’s what the clock says.”

She narrowed her eyes. “Are you ill?”

He laughed. “No.”

“Has the building closed?”

“No.”

“Has somebody sacked you?”

“Not today.”

She put down the knife. “Ren Hao.”

He came across the kitchen and kissed her cheek. “Good evening.”

She didn’t move. “You’re home. At seven.”

“Would you like me to go out and come in again?”

“Don’t be ridiculous.”

“Then I’ll take my shoes off.”

She watched him do it. She looked at the clock again. Four minutes past.

“You’re very interested in the time,” he said.

“I’m interested in the fact that my boyfriend has appeared before I’ve had a chance to get cross with him for not appearing.”

He put his arms round her waist from behind and his chin on her shoulder. “Get used to it.”

She turned her head. “Is this permanent?”

“That’s the intention.”

“Why?”

“Because I’ve decided,” he said, “to run my firm. Instead of letting it run me.”

She was quiet. Then she smiled. “Good,” she said.

“That’s all?”

“What else do you want?”

“A little admiration.”

“You’re getting dinner.”

“Unbelievable.”

“You’re welcome,” said Song-Zhu, and when he reached for the chopping board she took it away from him and pointed at a stool. “Sit. I want to look at you being home.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It hadn’t been decided in an afternoon. It had taken nine months, a long hard look at how the firm worked, and more than one conversation in which he’d had to admit, out loud, to people who’d been waiting years to hear it, that being good at something didn’t mean he had to do every part of it himself.

The firm had grown up round his habit of taking responsibility. When a client was in trouble, he took the call. When a negotiation went bad, he walked into the room. When a decision would be unpopular, he made it himself, so nobody else had to carry it. He’d built his whole name on being the one you could rely on when everything went wrong.

It had made him successful. It had also made him necessary in ways that had stopped being any use to anybody.

Losing the airline had shown him. Not the money, though the money had been bad, and the winter had been worse. What it had shown him was how much of the firm hung on a handful of relationships, most of them his, and how little authority had ever been allowed to reach the floors below him.

He’d spent the spring and summer rebuilding. Not just replacing what the airline had paid. Rebuilding the shape of it.

The first change was the easiest to explain and the hardest to accept. He stopped being where every problem went. The second was harder. He made Raymond managing partner.

Not a title. A job. Raymond, who’d taken the airline account on the morning of the second of August at five past five without being asked twice, and run it behind a wall for ten weeks, and never once let a single page of it cross onto Ren Hao’s desk, and had been right on the Saturday before the interim statement, and been overruled, and said nothing. Raymond, who’d wear a bow tie to a board meeting and who argued with Ren Hao in meetings in a way that made junior staff go pale.

Equity. A real share. Authority over the client portfolio and the operating decisions, without waiting for anybody’s signature.

When Ren Hao told him, in his office, Raymond looked at the papers for nearly a full minute without saying a word.

“You’re serious.”

“Yes.”

“You’ve looked at what it costs you?”

“Twice.”

“The partnership deed?”

“Three times. Kong read it to me slowly.”

“And the...”

“Raymond.”

Raymond looked up.

“I’m not asking you to marry me,” said Ren Hao. “I’m asking you to run this place with me. Properly. Not as my deputy. As my partner.”

Raymond finally laughed. “That’s considerably more complicated.”

“Probably.”

“Why now?”

“Because you’ve been doing the job for a year and a half. The title ought to catch up.”

“And because you want to go home at seven.”

He didn’t deny it. “That too.”

Raymond studied him. “Can you, though? Go home at seven?”

“I intend to.”

“Then you’ll have to stop answering email at eleven.”

Ren Hao stared at him.

Raymond pushed the papers back across the desk, signed. “Just a suggestion. Partner.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was announced at the staff meeting the following Monday.

Ren Hao stood at the front and explained the new structure, who now decided what, where problems now went, and made it plain that Raymond’s role wasn’t ornamental. Then he said the other thing.

“From this month, I’ll generally be leaving this building at half past six. My working day isn’t measured by how late the lights are on in my office.”

There was a pause. Somebody looked down at their notebook. Somebody else looked at Raymond.

“That doesn’t mean we stop answering real emergencies,” said Ren Hao. “We work in a business where some things can’t wait till morning. But there’s a difference between an emergency and a client who’s discovered that emailing at five to seven gets them an answer at six minutes past.”

People laughed.

“We’ve got very good people in this building. I intend to let them do their jobs.”

Raymond, beside him, folded his arms. “That would be a welcome development.”

The room laughed louder. The first month wasn’t perfect. There were evenings when a client rang at twelve minutes to seven and insisted it couldn’t wait. There were mornings when he came in to find an email thread that had gone on past midnight. There was one Thursday when he got as far as the lifts and turned round because he’d remembered something he hadn’t told Raymond.

Raymond was in his office with the door open. He didn’t look up.

“No.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“You were going to.”

“I need to tell you...”

“Email me.”

“It’s important.”

“Then email me.”

Ren Hao stared at him. Raymond pointed at the lifts without lifting his eyes from his screen.

“Go home, Hao.”

He went home. And the next evening, he didn’t go back to the office after dinner. And the evening after that.

He started to learn the difference between being available and being responsible for everything. He still took the hard calls. He still went to the meetings that mattered. He still had bad days and clients who wanted more than anyone could give them. But he’d stopped treating every delay as a failure of his own. He’d stopped believing the only safe hands in the building were his.

And slowly, the firm got better for it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dinner at seven became a ritual. Not an instruction, not a performance. A habit they both wanted.

Sometimes she cooked. Sometimes he did. Sometimes they ordered noodles and ate them at the counter because neither of them could be bothered to lay the table. For the first fortnight he’d look at the clock while they ate, as though he was faintly astonished to be allowed to be there. She noticed.

On the third Monday she put two bowls on the table and found him standing in the kitchen with his phone.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“That’s a suspicious answer.”

He showed her. A client asking for an update.

“Does it need an answer tonight?”

“No.”

“Then?”

“I thought I’d reply.”

She took the phone out of his hand and put it on top of the fridge, beside the yellow duck, where he’d have to reach.

He looked at her. “Song-Zhu.”

“Dinner.”

“You’re very authoritative.”

“Thank you.”

“Should I be afraid?”

“Only if you haven’t washed your hands.”

He laughed and went to the sink. They ate. She told him about a colleague who’d written obviously defective in a draft report without one single reference to support it.

“Who?”

“Someone who’s going to regret it.”

“Did you say anything?”

“I asked him to define obviously.”

“What did he say?”

“That the defect was apparent.”

“And?”

“I asked him to define apparent.”

He put his chopsticks down. “You’re terrifying.”

“I’m thorough.”

“Is there a difference?”

“Several,” said Song-Zhu, and took the best piece off his plate while he was laughing.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday the fourth of October, at ten past eight in the evening, his phone rang on top of the fridge beside the duck.

He got it down. “Isla.”

He answered it on speaker. His sister’s face came up on the screen, in her flat across the harbour, with Wei Long behind her shoulder doing the small face, the one that meant he was trying hard not to have an expression.

“Hao,” said Isla. “Are you sitting down?”

“No.”

“Sit down.”

“Why?”

She held up her left hand to the camera.

There was a ring on it. One clear stone. He went completely silent.

Song-Zhu, beside him, put her hand over her mouth.

“He asked?” said Ren Hao at last, in a voice that wasn’t quite his.

“Yes, Hao.”

“And you said yes?”

“No. I’m ringing to complain.”

He stared at the screen. She laughed until the picture shook.

“Of course I said yes! This afternoon. He wrote seventeen paragraphs and I said yes before he’d got to the end of any of them.”

Ren Hao stood up so fast the stool went over behind him.

Song-Zhu watched his face. She’d never seen it do exactly that before: every guard on it come down at once, so that he looked about nineteen.

“Congratulations,” he said. “Isla. Congratulations.”

Her face went soft on the screen. “Thank you.”

“Put him on.”

Wei Long’s face came closer.

“Inspector.”

“Ren Hao.”

“You’ll go on treating my sister well.”

“I intend to.”

Ren Hao nodded, seriously. And then, because he was Ren Hao: “Is the ring insured?”

“Hao!” said Isla, from out of the frame. “I’m hanging up!”

“I’m asking a reasonable question!”

“Goodbye!”

“It’s a risk question! It’s my job!”

The screen went dark. He stood in the middle of the kitchen holding the phone and laughing, with his eyes wet, and Song-Zhu picked up the stool and set it on its legs and put her arms round him from behind and held on.

“She’s engaged,” he said.

“I know.”

“To the glacier.”

“I know.”

“I tried to have him investigated.”

“I know you did.”

“I’m so happy,” said Ren Hao, “I don’t know what to do with my hands.”

“Put them here,” said Song-Zhu, and took them, and put them round her.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three weeks later, on Saturday the twenty-third of October, Eliana Lin married Dr. Wang Yu Chen across two back gardens.

There were two houses on the street with their gardens side by side behind them, and between them a wall, and in the wall, now, a gate, freshly cut and hung, so that you could walk from one garden into the other under the branches of an old persimmon tree that leaned over both. There were lights strung along the top of the wall and through the branches. Chairs in rows on the grass. A celebrant. A great many people who had clearly known each other a long time, and three triplets in a row like exclamation marks, and an old woman in dark blue in the front row with a walking stick, who used it, before anyone could stop her, to rearrange the chairs.

Song-Zhu stopped at the side gate and looked at all of it.

“Eliana did this?”

“Yes.”

“It’s beautiful.”

“Don’t tell her. She’ll be unbearable.”

“She’s already unbearable.”

“That’s why we like her,” said Ren Hao.

Eliana was in white, at the window of the house on the left, looking down at the garden, and when she saw Ren Hao come in through the gate she pointed straight at him through the glass. He waved. She mouthed something. Song-Zhu was fairly sure it was behave.

“She’s asked you to behave,” said Song-Zhu.

“She has.”

“Are you going to?”

“I’m going to make a good-faith effort.”

She looked at him sideways. “You’re not taking the microphone.”

“Of course not.”

“Hao.”

“I said of course not.”

“You said of course not about Yu Chen’s party in May last year, and you picked him up off the ground.”

“Only a little way.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The ceremony was short. There were no long speeches. Eliana and Yu Chen stood together under the persimmon, by the new gate, with the people round them who’d watched them for six years.

Song-Zhu sat beside him and held his hand the whole way through.

When the celebrant got to and so, by the authority vested in me, Yu Chen leaned in.

“Wait...” said Eliana, laughing.

He kissed her before the celebrant got to the end of the sentence.

Both gardens erupted. The old woman in the front row banged her stick on the grass and laughed out loud. And Ren Hao, beside Song-Zhu, made a noise they probably heard at the ferry pier.

“I was going to say you may now kiss,” said the celebrant.

“Sorry,” said Yu Chen.

“He’s been waiting,” said Eliana.

Song-Zhu looked at the man beside her. His eyes were wet.

“You’re crying.”

“I’m not.”

“Your eyes are wet.”

“It’s the wind.”

“There isn’t any wind.”

He looked at her. She smiled at him. “Don’t start,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The reception was loud. Song-Zhu had expected loud. She’d been to a party in this garden before.

After the meal, when the speeches were done and the music hadn’t started yet, she looked round at her table and found his chair empty. She closed her eyes. Of course.

She opened them again and he was at the little table by the gate where the microphone was, saying something charming to the man in charge of it, and the man was handing it to him.

At the top table, Eliana saw. Her face did something complicated.

“Ren Hao,” she said, across the whole garden.

“Good evening,” said Ren Hao into the microphone.

People began to laugh. Song-Zhu sat back in her chair and folded her arms. Then she took out her phone and opened the stopwatch.

“First,” he said, “I’d like to apologise to the bride. She asked me to behave. I’ve failed.”

She pressed start. He glanced across the garden at her. She lifted one eyebrow. He saw it. He smiled.

“I’ll be very quick,” he said. “I’ve been timed before.”

The garden laughed.

“I want to say three things. One: Yu Chen is the luckiest man in this city. I’ve met most of the men in this city. I’m confident about this.” He looked at the bride. “Two: Eliana is terrifying. In the best possible way. She is the most terrifying twenty-four-year-old I’ve ever hired, and I’ve hired several, and she’s the only one who’s ever told me my coffee machine was a security risk and been right.”

Eliana put her face in her hands.

“And three,” said Ren Hao, “I personally have no idea how anybody survives six years in love with a woman who can take apart a bank’s entire security in an afternoon and still loses her phone in her own kitchen.”

Eliana picked up her napkin, balled it, and threw it at him across the grass. He caught it with one hand.

“See?” he said into the microphone, holding it up. “Terrifying.”

The two gardens fell about. Yu Chen, beside his wife, didn’t stop smiling. Ren Hao lifted his glass.

“To Eliana and Yu Chen. And to the gate.”

“To the gate,” said everybody, and drank.

Song-Zhu stopped the stopwatch. He handed the microphone back to the man, and came back across the grass with Eliana’s napkin in his hand, and sat down beside her, looking extremely pleased with himself.

“Well?” he said.

She turned the phone round so he could see it.

1:52.

He stared at it. “One minute fifty-two.”

“One minute fifty-two.”

“That’s the shortest I’ve ever been.”

“It’s the shortest anyone’s ever been. It’s a medical event.”

“Was it all right?”

She looked at him. Uninvited. At a wedding he’d been asked to behave at. Three things, and a napkin, and a toast to a gate.

“It was perfect,” she said. “It was all theirs. You didn’t put one word of yourself in it.”

His face went soft. Eliana came over twenty minutes later with Yu Chen behind her, and stood in front of their table, and pointed at him.

“You.”

“Me?”

“You took the microphone.”

“I did.”

“Without asking.”

“Yes.”

“At my wedding.”

“Yes.”

“After I specifically asked you not to.”

“Correct.”

She stared at him. Then she burst out laughing, and Yu Chen put his hand on her waist and said, “Thank you. That was lovely,” in his quiet way, and Eliana said, “I hate him,” and Ren Hao said, “That isn’t what your face says,” and she said, “I can hate you and like the toast,” and he said, “That’s fair.”

Eliana looked at Song-Zhu. “Did you know he was going to?”

“I told him if he did, I’d leave him there.”

“Did you?”

“No. I timed him.”

“How long?”

Song-Zhu held up the phone. Eliana read it, and looked at Ren Hao with real respect for the first time all evening.

“One fifty-two. You can come to the next one,” she said, and pulled Yu Chen off towards the music.

✦ ✦ ✦

They got home before midnight. He hung his jacket on the right hook. She kicked her shoes off and left them in the middle of the hall.

He looked down at them. “Resting?”

“Exactly.”

He stepped over them.

“See,” she said. “You’re learning.”

He brought her a glass of water and sat down beside her on the sofa, and she looked at him.

“Can I ask you something?”

“Always.”

“Do you miss it? Being the one who has to be everywhere. Every call. Every room.”

He thought about it. “Sometimes,” he said. “I liked being needed. I liked knowing that if something went wrong I could walk into a room and take it on my back.”

“And now?”

“Now I know the firm doesn’t fall down if I’m not in it. And it turns out I don’t fall down either.” He turned the glass in his hands. “I think I mixed up being indispensable with being good at my job.”

“And now?”

“Now I think being good at it means building something that stands up without me holding every corner.”

She looked at him a long time. “I’m proud of what you’ve done,” she said. “With the firm. With Raymond. With seven o’clock.”

He went still. She said it simply, without teasing, without turning it into anything. He looked at her.

“Thank you,” he said.

“You built something. And now you’re letting other people help you keep it.”

“You helped.”

“I’m not running your firm.”

“No. You’re running dinner.”

“Somebody has to,” said Song-Zhu, and stood up, and held out her hand. “Bed.”

“Is that on the schedule?”

She looked back at him over her shoulder. “Not everything has to be,” she said.

Behind them, on top of the fridge, beside the yellow duck, his phone lit up once with an email, and then again. Neither of them looked.

chapters.title: Vancouver Again
chapters.desc: Vancouver again, with Isla and Wei Long. In the little study she asks the professors how to propose to their son. His mother cries again.
chapters.epigraph: “Make it a question.”
chapters.content:
He asked her on the eleventh of November, at the kitchen counter, with the yellow duck watching.

“Will you come to Vancouver for Christmas?”

She looked up from her noodles. “You asked me that two years ago,” she said. “In the blue room. In the dark. You said next year you’d book a hotel.”

“I said I’d ask you every year.”

“You didn’t ask me last year.”

“Last year,” said Ren Hao, “I wasn’t allowed to ask you anything.”

She put her chopsticks down. She looked at him a long time across the counter.

“Yes,” she said. “Ask me again next year, too.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They landed on the twenty-fourth in the dark of the afternoon, and he hired a car at the airport, and drove, and talked the entire way. About the traffic. About his father’s latest letter to a newspaper. About Isla and Wei Long, who’d flown out the day before. About whether Wei Long had ever seen proper snow, which he hadn’t, and what his face would do when he did, which Ren Hao had been looking forward to since October.

“You’re going to be unbearable,” said Song-Zhu.

“I’m going to be delighted.”

“Those aren’t different.”

He was still talking when they pulled up outside the house at the end of the street of wooden houses, with the wreath on the door and the porch light on and the snow coming down, and he was out of the car and up the steps with both bags and a bottle of wine before she’d undone her seat belt.

The door opened. He was in the hall before anybody had said anything.

“I’m here! I missed you!”

He hugged his sister and lifted her clean off the floor.

“You saw me a week ago,” said Isla, from somewhere under his chin.

“I’ve missed you since then.”

There was a bag on the bottom stair. Wei Long took it off the step before Ren Hao could fall over it.

“Still carrying everyone’s things, Inspector? Good. You’re useful,” said Ren Hao, and went to find his father.

Song-Zhu came up the steps behind him with the snow on her shoulders and kissed Isla’s cheek.

“He’s been like this since the airport,” she said. “I nearly left him at a petrol station.”

Isla laughed. Wei Long, holding the bag, looked at the hall where her brother had disappeared, with the expression of a man reassessing a weather system.

Within an hour Ren Hao was in the kitchen arguing with his father about a novel neither of them had finished. His mother was making tea and crying slightly into it, as she did every Christmas Eve, because both her children were under her roof. And Wei Long had been given a box of decorations to carry upstairs, and had gone.

✦ ✦ ✦

His mother found her in the hall, taking off her boots.

“My dear.”

“Professor.”

She was hugged. She’d known she would be. She smelled oranges and cloves and the same soap as two years ago.

“Your face is cold. Have you eaten?”

“On the plane.”

“That doesn’t count.”

“He told me you’d say that.”

“He’s right, for once,” said his mother, and held her at arm’s length and looked at her properly. At her face. At whatever was in it that hadn’t been there two Christmases ago. Song-Zhu didn’t know what that was. She suspected his mother did.

“You look well,” said his mother. “You look better than the photographs.”

“He’s still sending photographs?”

“Every week,” said his mother, with deep satisfaction. “He thinks we don’t know he’s doing it on purpose.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She waited until the kitchen was loud. Until she could hear him and his father arguing about a narrator, and Isla laughing at both of them. Then she went up the narrow stairs.

The little study at the end of the upstairs hall had its door half open. His parents were both in it. His father at the desk with a pencil. His mother on the arm of the sofa with a cup of tea, looking at a book he was holding out to her. They both looked up.

“Professor?” said Song-Zhu, in the doorway. “Both of you? Can I ask you something? It’s private.”

There was a pause. Then his mother, with enormous interest: “Oh?”

Song-Zhu came in. She didn’t shut the door. The house was old and the hall was narrow and she didn’t think about it.

She stood in the middle of the small room with its books up to the ceiling and its reading lamp by the old armchair, where she’d sat two years ago and been told by his father that she’d made a life that asked a great deal of her and kept giving it.

“I want to propose to Hao,” she said.

The room went still.

“Oh,” said his mother. “Oh, that’s lovely.” And her voice had gone thick all at once.

“I didn’t know if you’d think it was strange.”

“Why would it be strange?” said his father.

Song-Zhu looked at the floor, and then made herself look up.

“Because we stopped. Last year. For four months. I couldn’t say it to him, and he couldn’t stop trying to fix it, and we stopped.” She swallowed. “We’re better now than we’ve ever been. I know I want my whole life with him. But I don’t want him to think I’m asking to make up for that. I don’t want it to be an apology. I want it to be the start of something.”

Her voice had gone lower and lower. She heard it go.

“Then don’t make it an apology,” said his mother. “Make it a question.”

“I thought that’s what a proposal was.”

“You’d be amazed,” said his father, dryly, from the desk, “how many people turn it into a lecture on their own history.”

His mother put her tea down and leaned forward and took both of Song-Zhu’s hands.

“Ask him,” she said, “because you want to begin something. Not because you want to prove you’d have chosen differently. He’ll hear the difference. He’s always heard everything.”

And then she began to cry, properly, the way she’d cried in the kitchen two years ago with her hand on the mend in Song-Zhu’s knee.

His father said something gentle to her, too low to hear, and put his hand on her back.

And Song-Zhu laughed, wetly, helplessly, standing in the middle of the little study with both her hands held, because she’d done it, she’d said it out loud to someone, and nobody had told her it was strange.

✦ ✦ ✦

Out on the landing, a box of Christmas decorations had been put down on the table at the top of the stairs. She didn’t notice it. Nobody did. Later it was gone, carried to the end of the landing by a man who had heard every word through a half-open door in a narrow old house, and who never told anybody, and never would.

✦ ✦ ✦

“How?” she said, when his mother had found her a tissue and herself three. “That’s the bit I don’t know. I don’t know how.”

“What would he want?” said his mother. “Not the ring. Start with him.”

Song-Zhu thought about it.

“Nothing big. He thinks he wants big. He doesn’t.”

“No.”

“He likes things that mean something. Things with a reason.”

“Yes.”

“He remembers everything.”

“Above all the things people say when they think he isn’t listening,” said his mother. “He was like that at four.”

Song-Zhu smiled. “Exactly.”

“Then give him something that belongs to the two of you. Somewhere that’s yours. He’d rather it was private. He’s loud, and he thinks everybody should know everything, but the things that matter most to him he’s always kept very close.”

“I thought so.”

“And don’t worry about whether it’s traditional.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

“Good. He’s traditional enough for both of you,” said his mother. “He’ll want to have asked first. He’ll get over it.”

His father looked up from the desk.

“What does he love most?” he said. “Of all the things about you. If you had to guess.”

Song-Zhu thought about a list in a coat pocket, eighty-one lines and one missing. She thought about a man on a beach in the dark saying I’ll remember it instead of taking a picture. She thought about him at her door with his bag, and her mouth not able to make the shape.

“My voice,” she said, slowly. “I think. When I finally use it.”

His father nodded once, as though she’d answered something on an exam correctly.

“Then use it,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Will you tell him?” she said at the door.

His mother looked almost offended. “Absolutely not. I’d never take that from you.”

“Thank you.”

“You’re both terrible at secrets, though,” said his father, from the desk, not looking up. “I’d do it before Easter.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning there were pancakes, and his father reading the paper, and Ren Hao stealing from Song-Zhu’s plate, which she allowed, watching his mother over her coffee with the look of someone turning a piece of advice over and over in her hands.

A moose-shaped biscuit had been put on Wei Long’s plate by somebody.

He looked at it. “What is this?”

“A moose,” said Isla.

“I know it’s a moose. Why is there a moose?”

“Because we’re in Canada.”

“Is the moose associated with Christmas?”

“Not traditionally.”

“Then...”

“Because it’s cute,” said Isla, and he looked at the moose and then broke off one antler and ate it.

She stared at him. “You’ve injured it.”

“It’s a biscuit.”

“It’s a Christmas moose.”

“It’s still a biscuit,” said Wei Long, and Isla took the rest of it out of his hand and ate it herself, to spare it further suffering, and Ren Hao laughed so much he had to put his fork down.

Song-Zhu looked round the table. His father, pretending to read. His mother, watching all of them with her chin on her hand. Isla with moose crumbs on her jumper. Wei Long, on whom something like a smile was slowly happening. And Ren Hao, beside her, wiping his eyes.

Two years ago she’d sat at this table for the first time with his mother’s good napkin on her knee and been asked about the structure of accident investigations. Now she was part of the noise.

His mother met her eyes across the pancakes, and said nothing, and smiled.

✦ ✦ ✦

After breakfast he took Wei Long out into the garden.

Song-Zhu watched from the kitchen window with her coffee. The snow had come down all night, deep and dry, and the garden was the white silent rounded country she remembered, the hedges bulked into walls, the old tree at the end loaded and bowed.

Wei Long stepped off the back step and stopped dead, exactly where she had stopped two years ago.

Ren Hao, beside him, said something she couldn’t hear. Wei Long looked at him. Ren Hao bent down, slowly, and gathered a handful of snow.

Wei Long watched him do it with the expression of a man who had interviewed a great many suspects and recognised the look.

“Oh no,” said Isla, beside her at the window.

The snowball hit Wei Long squarely in the middle of the chest.

He looked down at the white star on his coat. He looked up at Ren Hao. He didn’t move at all for three full seconds. Then he bent, without any hurry, and gathered up a great deal more snow than Ren Hao had, and packed it, and threw it with such precision that it took Ren Hao in the side of the head and knocked him into the hedge.

Isla shrieked with laughter. Song-Zhu put her coffee down.

“That,” said Isla, “is my husband. Nearly.”

“That’s the hedge,” said Song-Zhu. “He did that to me.”

“Did he?”

“I won.”

“Do you have evidence?”

“Your father ruled on it,” said Song-Zhu, and went to get her coat.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night, late, they were across the landing from Isla’s room, in the blue room, which his mother had given them both without discussion this year. He came up behind her at the window where she stood watching the snow come down past the glass in the dark.

“You’ve been quiet,” he said.

“I’ve been thinking.”

“About?”

She looked at him in the window, reflected, behind her own reflection.

“Christmas.”

He put his arms round her waist. “Good Christmas?”

“The best one.”

“Better than the first?”

She thought about the first. The flight suit. The hedge. The board by the wardrobe.

“Different,” she said. “The first one I was a guest.”

He kissed the side of her neck, where the chain was, the silver snowflake she’d worn every day for two years.

“And this one?”

She turned round in his arms. “This one I’m family,” she said.

He looked at her. She almost said it then. She felt it come all the way up, Will you marry me, right there, in the blue room, with the snow behind her. It would have been so easy.

She didn’t. Not because she was afraid. Because she wanted to ask him properly. In her own voice. Somewhere that was theirs. Not as an apology, and not because a window and the snow made it easy. As a question. So she smiled instead.

“Nothing,” she said. “Take me to bed.”

“The board by the wardrobe still creaks,” he said.

“I know,” said Song-Zhu. “I’m not going to be quiet this year.”

And she wasn’t. And the board by the wardrobe creaked all on its own, twice, the way old houses did. And somewhere below them in the dark, a literature professor and a political scientist lay awake in their bed and looked at the ceiling and then at each other, and his mother put her hand over her mouth, and laughed until the bed shook, without making a single sound.

✦ ✦ ✦

On their last morning she walked with his mother along the snowy path at the end of the street. His mother in a long coat and a knitted hat. Song-Zhu in gloves, this time.

“Look at you,” said his mother. “Gloves.”

“I’ve learned.”

“He’ll be relieved.”

“He’ll find something else.”

They walked.

“I haven’t decided when,” said Song-Zhu. “Or where. But I know how, I think. Since your husband asked me.”

“Don’t tell me.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

“Good.”

They walked a little further, with the snow squeaking.

“Are you happy?” said Song-Zhu. “That I’ll ask him? That it’s me, and not him?”

His mother stopped in the middle of the path. She looked at Song-Zhu with such tenderness that Song-Zhu’s eyes stung in the cold.

“My son,” said his mother, “spent his whole life thinking love meant being responsible for everything. That if he made the right decisions, if he got there first and arranged it all, nothing bad would ever happen to anybody he loved. He was a very serious little boy. Even happy, he was worrying about what came next.”

She took Song-Zhu’s gloved hand.

“Then he met you. And he worries still. Of course he does, he’s mine. But he laughs now. He tells stories at the table. He comes home at seven. He lets other people help him.” She squeezed Song-Zhu’s fingers. “You didn’t turn him into somebody else. You showed him he doesn’t have to carry it all on his own.”

“He showed me the same thing.”

“I know he did. I’ve watched you both do it for two years.” His mother smiled. “So, yes. I’m happy. And I’m happiest of all that it’s you who’ll ask. Because he’s spent his life asking everybody else whether they’re all right. Somebody ought to ask him something, for once.”

They walked back towards the house.

“Don’t make it perfect,” said his mother, at the gate. “Just make it yours.”

chapters.title: She Proposes
chapters.desc: She proposes at the flying club fence, in her own voice, out of her father’s recorder. He says yes at volume. A kiss on the apron as a plane taxies past.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m asking the windsock.”
chapters.content:
He’d been told to wear something comfortable. That was the first suspicious thing.

The second was that on Wednesday she’d asked him not to make any plans for Saturday morning, and then added, casually, don’t ask why.

The third was that she was awake before him.

He opened his eyes at eighteen minutes to seven on Saturday the first of April to find her sitting on the end of the bed, fully dressed, looking at her phone with the concentration of a woman defusing something.

“Good morning,” he said.

She jumped. “You’re awake.”

“I am.”

“Go back to sleep.”

“Why?”

“Because it’s early.”

“You’re up.”

“That doesn’t mean you have to be.”

He propped himself on one elbow. “What’s happening today?”

“Nothing.”

He looked at her. She looked at him.

“Then why are you dressed?”

“Because I wanted to be.”

“Why did you tell me not to make plans?”

“Because I want to spend the morning with you.”

“Why did you tell me to wear something comfortable?”

“Because I care about your comfort.”

He considered this. “You’re lying.”

“I’m not.”

“You’re doing something.”

“I’m allowed to do things without reporting them to you.”

“Absolutely.”

She narrowed her eyes. “You’re being very annoying.”

“Good morning,” said Ren Hao.

She leaned over and kissed him, and he caught her hand before she could get away.

“Should I be worried?”

“No.”

“Should I bring a jacket?”

“Yes.”

“Passport?”

“No.”

“Phone?”

“Unfortunately.”

He laughed. She stood up.

“Get dressed. We’re leaving in an hour.”

He lay and looked at the ceiling after she’d gone. Something was happening. He was nearly sure of it. And from the way she’d kissed him, he suspected he was going to like it.

✦ ✦ ✦

She drove. She’d agreed to answer three questions. He spent the first on whether she’d had breakfast. She said yes.

He spent the second on whether they were going anywhere that needed security clearance. She told him to stop watching films.

He spent the third on whether he ought to be nervous.

She looked at him for a long moment at a red light.

“A little,” she said.

He spent the next ten minutes trying to work out whether she was joking.

At twenty past eight she turned off the coast road onto a lane he knew, and he sat up.

He knew the hedge. He knew the windsock. He knew the low brown clubhouse with the corrugated roof and the faded sign, and the field beside it, and the long hangar at the end with its doors rolled half open, and the wire fence round the apron.

The flying club airfield. Where, on the fourteenth of June 2025, a twin turboprop had come down in the field and she’d pulled its recorder out of the tail cone, and he’d turned up at that fence the next afternoon in a suit, with lunch for twelve. He looked at her.

“Song-Zhu.”

“Yes?”

“Why are we here?”

She parked by the fence. Exactly by the fence. In the same spot.

“Come with me,” she said.

He didn’t move.

She looked at him. “Please.”

That did it. He undid his seat belt.

She put her hand on his on the gearstick. “Happy April Fool’s Day, by the way.”

He stared at her. She smiled. “That’s not funny,” he said.

“It’s a little bit funny.”

“You’ve brought me to an airfield on the first of April.”

“Yes.”

“Should I be concerned I’m about to be sold?”

She laughed, and got out.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was a bright, cool morning. The apron was quiet, but not empty. Somebody was pushing a small high-winged aircraft out of the hangar by hand. A man in a club jacket was making tea in the doorway of the clubhouse, the same man, Ren Hao was almost sure, who’d made tea for everybody in a corner three years ago as if it were his sacred duty. At the far end, by the fuel bowser, a little two-seater was running its engine up.

She took him through the gate, and nodded to the man with the tea, who nodded back.

He’d seen her at work for nearly three years. Coming home with an investigation still on her shoulders. Going over briefings at the kitchen counter. Marking twenty-two papers under a wing.

But it was different, being out here with her. This was where she was most herself. The smell of fuel. The low mechanical hum. The open flat concrete and the sky. She walked across it.

“Is this a work surprise?” he said.

“No.”

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

“Am I going to have to sign something?”

“Possibly.”

She stopped beside the hangar, by the wire fence. On the other side of it was the field. The grass had grown back long ago. There was nothing there now, nothing at all, but you could still see it, if you knew where to look: a faint line, a slightly different green, where the turf had been relaid. He knew where to look.

She reached into her coat pocket and took something out, and held it up between them.

It was small and silver, the size of a cigarette lighter, with a speaker grille and a scratch across its face. He went completely still.

“That’s your father’s,” he said.

“Yes.”

“You said you’d never...”

“There’s a new card in it,” said Song-Zhu. “I put it in on Tuesday. His are in the case at home. This one’s mine.” She looked down at the little silver thing. “I wanted you to hear my voice come out of it. Because that’s where I keep the voices that matter most to me.”

She pressed play.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her voice came out of the little speaker, small and clear across the quiet apron.

“Ren Hao.”

He didn’t breathe. It was her voice. Unmistakably. And it was different. Not altered. Recorded. Deliberately, carefully, on her own, at her kitchen table at night, without any of the interruptions and teasing and small changes of face he was used to watching while she talked.

“If you’re hearing this, I’ve managed to get you somewhere without telling you why. Well done me.”

His eyes went from the recorder to her face. She was watching him.

“I thought about a restaurant. But you’d spend the whole evening watching to see if I’d eaten enough. I thought about home. But you’d start the washing-up halfway through. I thought about asking you over dinner, at seven, but you’d immediately start thinking about logistics.”

His mouth moved. Just.

“So I’ve brought you here. To the fence. Where you turned up in a three-piece suit, the day after you met me, with lunch for twelve people you’d never heard of, because I’d said in a voice note that I hadn’t eaten. And where I looked at you over the wire and thought: oh no.”

He laughed, once, under his breath. His eyes had gone bright.

“I know what we’ve been through. I know there were months when loving each other wasn’t easy. I know we had to learn how to make room for each other. How to stop mistaking looking after for managing. How to stay when it was hard, without making the other one feel trapped. I know I couldn’t say it for a year and a half. And that you waited, and didn’t make me.”

A pause on the recording. A breath.

“I’m not asking you because we survived something. It isn’t a prize for what you’ve learned. It isn’t an apology for last year. And it isn’t a promise that nothing hard will ever happen again. Your mother told me not to make it any of those things, and your father told me not to make it a lecture about our history, so I’m going to stop that part now.”

He laughed out loud, and wiped his eyes with the heel of his hand.

“I’m asking because I love the man you are. The one who comes home at seven. The one who remembers everything. The one who can make a room full of people go quiet without raising his voice, and still argues with me about whether oranges go in the fridge. The one who learned he doesn’t have to carry everything. The one who lets me be inconvenient. Who seems to like it best when I am.”

Her voice on the recording softened.

“I want the ordinary days. And the hard ones. I want the evenings when we’re both too tired to talk and the evenings when we can’t stop laughing. I want to travel with you, and argue with you, and come home to you, and keep finding out who we turn into. I don’t need you to promise you’ll never get it wrong. I don’t need you to always know what to do. I just want you to keep choosing me. And I want to keep choosing you. Every day. In my own voice. Out loud.”

A pause.

“So, Ren Hao...”

The recording clicked off. Song-Zhu lowered the little silver recorder. She looked up at him on the apron by the fence. And said the rest herself.

“Will you marry me?”

✦ ✦ ✦

For a moment he didn’t move at all. He looked at her. At the recorder in her hand. At the fence. At the faint line in the grass. Back at her.

She’d imagined this a great many times. In some versions he laughed at once. In some he cried. In one particularly ridiculous version he asked whether she’d checked the weather forecast.

She hadn’t imagined this. His mouth opened. Nothing came out.

She blinked. “Hao?”

He let out a breath that was nearly a laugh. “You’re asking me?”

“No,” said Song-Zhu. “I’m asking the windsock.”

He laughed. Suddenly, helplessly, all the way down. Then he looked at her again, and his eyes were wet, and his whole face broke open into a smile so wide that her own eyes filled.

“YES!”

It went right across the apron. The man with the tea in the clubhouse door turned round. The two people pushing the high-wing stopped pushing. At the far end by the bowser, somebody looked up from the little two-seater. Song-Zhu burst out laughing.

He took one step towards her. “Yes!”

“Hao...”

“YES!”

He reached her and took both her hands, recorder and all. “Yes. Song-Zhu. Of course. Yes. Yes.”

She was laughing and crying at once. “All right.”

“All right?”

“You’re shouting.”

“I’m saying yes.”

“I heard you. The tower heard you. It’s four kilometres away.”

“Good,” said Ren Hao, and pulled her into his arms, and she wrapped herself round him and laughed into his shoulder, and he held her so tight her feet came off the concrete.

He put her down and pulled back far enough to see her face.

“You asked me.”

“I did.”

“You actually asked me.”

“I actually did.”

A tear went down his face. She reached up and wiped it off with her thumb.

“Don’t cry.”

“You’re the one who brought a recording.”

“It was a good recording.”

“It was a perfect recording. In his recorder.”

“I thought you’d notice.”

“I noticed,” he said, and put his forehead against hers, and stood there, and shook.

“Did you make that on your own?”

“Obviously.”

“When?”

“Over several evenings.”

“How many?”

“That’s classified.”

“Song-Zhu.”

“Three. Four if you count the one where I deleted everything and cried and ate a whole tin of your biscuits.”

He laughed. “I wondered where those went.”

“Now you know,” she said, and kissed him.

✦ ✦ ✦

When she drew back he looked alarmed.

“Wait.”

“What?”

“Did I just say yes without a ring?”

She gave him a look. “Hao.”

He breathed out. “Thank goodness.”

She took a small box from her other pocket. Inside it was a plain band, white gold, simple, with nothing on it at all except a fine line round the middle. She’d chosen it in January, in a shop near Tanner’s Row, after Vancouver, and gone back for it three times before she’d let herself buy it.

He stared at it. “You chose this?”

“Yes.”

“When?”

“After Vancouver.”

He understood. The study at the end of the upstairs hall. His mother’s hands. Make it a question.

She held out her hand. “Give me yours.”

He did. She slid the ring onto his finger. It fitted. He looked at it. Then at her.

“Hello, fiancé,” she said.

He made a sound halfway between a laugh and a breath. “Hello. Fiancée.”

“That’s strange.”

“Very strange.”

“You’re my fiancé.”

“You’re my fiancée.”

They stared at each other, and then both of them started laughing, standing on the apron by the fence with the windsock lifting.

He lifted her hand and kissed it. Then he stopped.

“You don’t have one.”

“I didn’t need one. I was the one asking.”

“That’s not...” He looked at her bare hand, and at his, and his face did something determined. “We’ll fix that.”

“Don’t start.”

“I’m not starting. I’m noting.”

“Hao.”

“Tomorrow,” he said, “is Sunday. And I’m noting it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He looked at her a long time.

“You know,” he said, “I’d thought about asking you.”

“Had you?”

“Frequently.”

“That isn’t a number.”

“Very frequently. I had ideas. One involved a booking.”

“Predictable.”

“One involved a trip.”

“More predictable.”

“One involved a very carefully planned evening at home with an agenda.”

“Typed?”

“Laminated.”

She laughed.

He looked down at the ring on his hand. “But I’m glad you asked. You chose where. You chose the words. You chose his recorder. You made it yours. And I got to say yes.”

The little two-seater at the far end of the apron had finished running up. Its engine note changed, and it began to move, and came trundling down the taxiway towards them, past the hangar, past the fence, a small bright plane with two people in it going out to the end of the grass strip to fly on an ordinary Saturday morning.

She heard it first. She smiled against his mouth, because he was kissing her again.

He drew back an inch. “What?”

She tipped her head at the plane. “Your audience.”

He looked round at it. Then back at her.

“I don’t care,” he said.

And he kissed her on the apron with the plane going past, not carefully, not one bit carefully, with relief and laughter and the sudden astonishing knowledge that the person he loved had just asked him to spend the rest of his life with her, out loud, in her own voice, out of her father’s recorder. She held the front of his jacket in her fist. He held her face in both hands. The plane went by, the pilot raised one hand from the cockpit in a cheerful salute, and neither of them saw it, and the engines hummed away across the field towards the end of the strip.

When they finally stopped, he kept his forehead on hers.

“One more thing,” he said.

“What?”

“Can I tell everybody?”

She laughed. “Yes.”

“Now?”

“Yes.”

“My mother?”

“Yes.”

“Isla?”

“Yes.”

“Raymond?”

“Not before your sister.”

He nodded gravely. “You’re right.”

He took his phone out. Then he stopped, and put it back.

“Can we have one minute first?”

Her face went soft. “Of course.”

He took both her hands and looked at the ring on his.

“Fiancée,” he said.

“Fiancé.”

“I love you.”

“I love you,” said Song-Zhu. “I’m going to say it so often now that you’ll get sick of it.”

“I won’t.”

“You might.”

“I’ve waited for it for eighteen months. I’m owed,” said Ren Hao, and then, because he was Ren Hao, he hugged her so hard that she laughed and told him she needed her ribs, and he let go at once.

“Sorry.”

“Don’t be sorry. You’re allowed to be excited.”

He looked at her with his eyes shining. “I am.”

✦ ✦ ✦

His mother answered on the second ring. It was Friday evening in Vancouver.

“Ren Hao? Is everything all right?”

He held up his left hand to the camera.

His mother looked at it. At his face. At his hand.

“Oh,” she said.

“Mum.”

“Oh, my goodness.”

She began to cry. Song-Zhu leaned into the picture.

“Hello, Professor.”

His mother put her hand over her mouth. “Darling.”

“I asked him,” said Song-Zhu.

“And?”

“She asked,” said Ren Hao. “I said yes. Very loudly. The tower heard.”

His mother cried harder. His father’s face appeared over her shoulder.

“What’s happened? Why are you... oh.” He looked at the screen. His face went soft. “Oh. Well. Congratulations.”

“Thank you, Dad.”

“You did it before Easter,” said his father to Song-Zhu.

“I did it on April Fool’s Day.”

“Even better,” said his father. “Nobody will ever believe him.”

His mother took the phone back. “Song-Zhu. Sweetheart.”

“Yes?”

“Thank you.”

“For what?”

“For choosing him. For asking him.” His mother’s voice broke. “Somebody finally asked him.”

Song-Zhu looked at Ren Hao. Then back at the screen.

“I didn’t have to think very hard,” she said.

His mother cried again. His father put his arm round her. “We’ll need more tissues,” he said. “I’ll go.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Isla answered on the move, walking somewhere with the wind in the phone.

“Hello?”

He held up his hand. She stopped walking. She looked at his hand. At Song-Zhu. At his hand. Then she screamed.

“WHAT?”

He laughed. Song-Zhu held the phone a little further from her ear.

“YOU’RE ENGAGED?”

“Yes.”

“SHE ASKED YOU?”

“I asked him,” said Song-Zhu.

Isla made a sound that was almost a sob. “Oh my God. Oh my God. A week. I’ve been married a week, and you’ve...”

“You stole my thunder first,” said Ren Hao.

“I’m allowed, I’m your sister.” Isla was crying now. “Wei Long. Wei Long. Look. Look at his hand.”

Wei Long’s face appeared, close, beside hers. He looked at the screen. Then he looked at Song-Zhu.

“Congratulations,” he said.

“Thank you, Wei Long.”

He looked at her a second longer than he needed to. Something moved at the very corner of his mouth.

“It was a good question,” he said.

Song-Zhu didn’t know why he’d said it like that. She’d think about it for years.

“Did he cry?” said Isla.

“No,” said Ren Hao.

“Yes,” said Song-Zhu.

“HE CRIED!”

“You’re supposed to be on my side,” said Ren Hao to his fiancée.

“I am on your side. I’m on the side of the evidence.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They didn’t leave straight away.

The man with the tea came across from the clubhouse with two cups and put them down on the bonnet of her car without a word, and went back. Song-Zhu put her father’s recorder carefully back into her pocket. Ren Hao tried to take a photograph of her with the hangar behind her and cut off half her face. The second was blurred. The third had his thumb over the lens.

She looked at the screen. “You run a firm.”

“Yes.”

“On three floors.”

“Yes.”

“You cannot take a photograph.”

“I’m emotionally compromised,” said Ren Hao.

She took the phone off him and took one picture: their two hands on the wire of the fence, his ring catching the light, the field behind, blurred, with its faint different line of green.

“That one,” he said.

“Why the field?” he said, later, at the car. “Why here?”

“Because it’s where you first came to my work. Before you understood any of it. You stood at that fence with twelve lunches and you didn’t ask me a single question about what I was doing. You just wanted me to eat.” She looked out at the grass. “And because it was the first time I thought it. Oh no. Right there.”

“And his recorder?”

She was quiet. “Because that’s where I keep the voices I can’t lose,” she said. “And now mine’s on it. Next to his.”

He couldn’t say anything. “Can I have the recording?” he said at last. “Not today. I don’t want it today. I want to listen to it when I’m not standing here trying to understand that I’m engaged.”

“You want to listen to yourself being proposed to?”

“I want to listen to you asking me,” said Ren Hao.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the way home he kept looking at his hand. She caught him turning it to the window at a red light.

“You’re doing it again.”

“I like it.”

“I’m glad.”

He reached across and held her hand on the gearstick until the lights changed.

“We should have dinner with my parents. When they’re over.”

“We will.”

“And Isla and Wei Long.”

“Yes.”

“And perhaps a small celebration.”

She looked at him. “How small?”

He thought about it. “Small.”

“Hao.”

“Reasonably small.”

“Let’s get home first,” said Song-Zhu.

✦ ✦ ✦

At home she made tea. He stood in her kitchen with his sleeves rolled up and his phone buzzing on the counter beside the duck every thirty seconds. Raymond. Ruby. Eliana, in capitals. Dexter, who wanted to know if this meant he finally got a shirt for a party.

She put a cup in front of him. He watched her over it.

“What?”

“I’m working out how to keep this face.”

“You’re staring.”

“I’m looking at my fiancée.”

“You’re going to say that all day.”

“All week.”

“All year?”

He considered. “Possibly.”

She put her cup down and came round the counter and put her arms round his waist and looked up at him.

“Are you happy?”

“Song-Zhu,” he said. “I’m so happy I don’t know what to do with my hands.”

“You said that when Isla got engaged.”

“It was true then. It’s truer now.”

She took his hands and put them round her, where they belonged.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday morning he was gone when she woke.

There was a note on the pillow in his capitals.

GONE OUT. BACK BY TEN. NOTED, NOT STARTED.

At five to ten the front door opened. He came into the bedroom with two coffees and a small box, and sat down on the edge of the mattress, and held it out to her on his palm, and didn’t open it.

“You said you didn’t need one,” he said. “Because you were the one asking. And that’s true. So this isn’t an answer. You’ve had my answer. The tower had my answer. This is just... so that I can look at your hand and know.”

She opened the box. One clear stone. Small. Perfectly plain. The kind of thing you wouldn’t notice across a room, and couldn’t stop looking at from close to.

“I went back to the shop on Tanner’s Row,” he said. “The man remembered you. He said you’d been in three times about a man’s band in January and cried in his shop once. He said he’d been hoping someone would come in for the other one.”

She put it on. It fitted. She looked at it a long time, and then at him.

“You couldn’t wait one day,” she said.

“I waited eighteen months for three words,” said Ren Hao. “I wasn’t waiting a day for this.”

chapters.title: Loud Wedding
chapters.desc: The loudest wedding of the year. Isla’s toast in three languages. The wedding night, quiet, explicit: forty-two buttons, and then every button of the three-piece suit.
chapters.epigraph: “Ask what?”
chapters.content:
By nine o’clock on the morning of Saturday the twenty-first of October 2028, Ren Hao had been told to calm down six times.

The first was Wei Long, his best man, at half past seven, by text, one word: Breathe.

The second was his mother, in person, at eight, in the hotel corridor, holding his face in both hands.

The third was Isla, on the phone at twenty past eight, who rang specifically to say: “If you start managing this wedding, I will have you removed from it. I’m a consular officer. I know people. Wei Long’s got handcuffs.”

The fourth was Raymond, who’d found him in the ballroom at twenty to nine counting chairs.

The fifth was his father, who came into the ballroom behind Raymond, looked at his son over his glasses, and said only, “Son. Sit.” And he sat.
